2982-mark-twain-a-biography-volume-i-par:
Albert Bigelow Paine wrote Mark Twain: A Biography as the personal and literary life of Samuel Langhorne Clemens, dedicating this first part to Clara Clemens Gabrilowitsch. Paine thanks William Dean Howells, Joseph Hopkins Twichell, and Joseph Goodman for six years of help, and admits envying their days going gipsying with Twain long ago. The volume covers 1835 to 1866, from Missouri boyhood to the threshold of fame.

Young Clemens works as a compositor, setting ten thousand ems a day, and subs on the Philadelphia Inquirer after deciding to leave New York. Hudson steamers at twenty-five cents and the phrase about fooling himself into leaving New York show Paine's ear for Twain's voice. The biography remains the authorized life, built from Twain's own papers and friends.
30099-hypochondriasis-a-practical-treati:
John Hill wrote Hypochondriasis, a practical treatise, first published in 1766. It is reprinted here as publication number 135 of the Augustan Reprint Society, from the William Andrews Clark Memorial Library at the University of California, Los Angeles, in 1969. G. S. Rousseau introduces the volume. William E. Conway, George Robert Guffey, and Maximillian E. Novak serve as general editors.

Books on hypochondriasis, the seventeenth-century name for a broad span of nervous diseases, were already old when Sir John Hill published his. Hill was an eccentric English scientist, physician, apothecary, and hack writer, and his treatise had stood for a century and a half of medical writing on nervous disease. The reprint gives modern readers Hill's eighteenth-century account of a condition once filed under melancholy, in the society's plain scholarly format.
30228-officer-666:
Barton W. Currie and Augustin McHugh write a farce of police, millions, and mistaken identity in Officer 666, published by A. L. Burt in New York in 1912. A grapefruit prelude opens, Mr. Hogg enters the lists, and Whitney Barnes comes under fire, telephones to the Ritz, and suffers misadventures in turn. Officer 666 goes on patrol, Travers Gladwin gets a thrill, and a great chest, its lid distinctly rising, draws the hero's gaze in the front picture.

Sadie becomes a conspirator, Helen leaves an important message, and Michael Phelan comes to the rescue, meets his uniform again, and patrols as a millionaire policeman. Travers Gladwin goes in search of himself, meets himself, and comes out of his shell, while old Grim Barnes gets a thrill and auntie takes the trail. The novel promises brisk comic thrills, heroism, love, and something else besides.
3193-mark-twain-s-letters-volume-1-1853-:
Albert Bigelow Paine arranged this first volume of Mark Twain's letters, covering 1853 to 1866. His foreword claims that nowhere is a human being more truly revealed than in his letters. Not literary letters, prepared with care and a thought of print, but letters wrung from the press of circumstance, with no idea of publication in mind.

The young Twain of these pages is a printer, prospector, and river man finding his voice. Jokes, homesickness, ambition, and sharp observation crowd the letters home. Readers meet Samuel Clemens before he fully became Mark Twain, and the collection shows how much of the humorist was already present in the private man.
4163-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-41-jan:
January 1665 to 1666, New Year's Day, calls Pepys up by five, by his order, with Mr. Tooker writing while Pepys dictates his business of the pursers. Without eating or drinking till three in the afternoon, he finishes it to his great content.

Dinner follows with Gibson and Tooker, a plain reward for a hard morning's dictation. The volume opens the year that will bring plague and fire with sheer hard work, pursers' accounts first. Readers see Pepys's method at its most disciplined, turning a holiday into a working day. A holiday turned to dictation sets the tone for a hard year.
4164-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-42-mar:
March 1665 to 1666 sends Pepys to the office all morning, then to dinner at the White Horse in Lombard Street with Lord Bruncker, Batten, and Pen. God forgive them, he writes, for good sport over Captain Cocke's maid, sick of the plague a day or two before.

Plague talk at dinner shows how even fear became table humor among Navy men. The volume moves from office routine to the sickness creeping into households. Readers see the plague arriving not as a headline, but as a maid's illness laughed over at lunch.
4165-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-43-may:
May 1666 keeps Pepys at his Navy desk all morning, then brings his cousin Thomas Pepys at noon to consult about being a justice of the peace. Thomas is much against the office, telling Pepys in confidence that he is not free to punish according to the act.

The volume follows Navy business toward the Dutch war's second summer, with family counsel beside it. Pepys advises kin while running a war's paperwork, a mix that defines the diary. Readers see how public office and private conscience met in one man's noon hour.
4166-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-44-jul:
July 1666, a Sunday, sends Pepys betimes to the office, receiving letters two or three at a time from Sir William Coventry and sending as many back. Business and hurry fill the day, chief among them getting pressed men out of the city down the river to the fleet.

The volume follows the Navy's manpower hunger in wartime, with letters as its engine. Pepys works Sundays as readily as weekdays when the fleet needs men. Readers see war administration at full pressure, in a month when every letter might mean a ship manned or left short.
4167-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-45-aug:
August 1666 finds Pepys betimes settling last month's accounts, blessing God to find them clear and himself worth fifty-seven hundred pounds, the most his book ever yet made out. Prepared to attend the Duke of York, he is stopped by Sir William Pen, just home from Sheerness.

Fire will soon remake the city, but this volume opens in a moment of financial triumph. Pepys counts his worth with open satisfaction, a clerk turned a man of substance. Readers get the last calm weeks before the Great Fire, told by a man who had just learned his fortune.
4168-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-46-oct:
October 1666 keeps Pepys compiling lists at the office all morning, getting the list of all ships and vessels employed since the war, for Parliament's committee. At noon he carries it to Sir William Coventry's chamber and dines there with Coventry, Batten, and Pen.

After dinner they examine the list, a reckoning of a war at sea in ships' names. The volume follows the Navy's accounting after fire, when Parliament wanted answers. Readers get Pepys the record keeper, turning a fleet into a list and a list into a defense. A fleet turned into a list becomes a defense before Parliament.
4169-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-47-nov:
November 1666 brings Burton, one of the smith's wives, presenting Pepys with a very noble cake. He resolves at once that his wife shall carry it with wine today to house-warm Betty Michell, and she readily agrees.

Office sittings fill the morning, but the cake and the house-warming give the day its warmth. The volume follows London rebuilding after fire, with small kindnesses beside great losses. Readers will enjoy Pepys after disaster, still finding room for cake, wine, and friends. After fire, a cake and a house-warming feel like a small victory.
4170-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-48-dec:
December 1666 keeps Pepys sitting with the Board all morning, then home to dinner, then abroad walking to the Old Swan. On the way he sees a cellar in Tower Street in a very fresh fire, the late great winds having blown it up.

Fire still burned in cellars of the ruins, months after the Great Fire, a fact Pepys notes with a walker's eye. The volume follows a city still smoking, with offices working above the ashes. Readers get December after disaster, when even a walk could find a new flame.
4811-the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-comp:
John Lothrop Motley, D.C.L., LL.D., corresponding member of the Institute of France, wrote The Rise of the Dutch Republic, 1555 to 1566, Complete, A History, dated 1855. An editor's note introduces the author: born in Dorchester, Massachusetts, in 1814, died in 1877, author of the novels Morton's Hope and Merry Mount. Motley served as United States minister to Austria from 1861 to 1867, and to England from 1869 to 1870.

This complete volume gathers the history's first span, from Charles's abdication in 1555 and Philip's early reign, through Margaret's administration, Granvelle's ascendancy, and the Compromise and petition of 1566. Where single volumes in this set cover one slice each, this file holds the whole opening arc together, from abdication to the petitioners at Brussels. Readers get Motley's first twelve years of Dutch revolt in one volume, with his introductions, portraits, and narrative unbroken.
a-dog-of-flanders-pg7766: Ouida tells the story of Nello and Patrasche, a boy and a dog of Flanders. Left alone in the world, the two friends share a bond closer than brotherhood. Nello, a little Ardennois, draws likenesses with charcoal, while Patrasche pulls their cart. The tale moves toward the cathedral at Christmas in a story of love and loss.
a-general-history-and-collection-of-voya: Volume eight of Robert Kerr's voyages continues early English voyages to the East Indies. Its sections follow John Eldred by sea to Tripoli and thence by land and river to Baghdad and Basra in 1583. A passage on monsoons explains the winds that carry ships to and from India. Kerr's volume gathers English eastern trade before the exclusive company.
ars-chemica-quod-sit-licita-recte-exerce:
Ars Chemica, printed in 1566, is a Latin volume with a legal argument at its front. The chemical art, it argues, is lawful for those who practice it rightly. The opinions of learned jurists prove the point. In an age when alchemists could be suspected of fraud or sorcery, that defense mattered. Behind the proofs stand the seven golden treatises or chapters of Hermes Trismegistus.

The volume also gives the Emerald Tablet, said to be found in Hermes's tomb, with the commentary of Hortulanus the philosopher. It adds a study of the counsel of the marriage of the mass of the Sun and Moon. Law and hermetic doctrine share one binding here: the art defended in court and expounded from its oldest texts, in two hundred sixty-three pages.
arxiv-2509-00466:
Negar Hashemi leads a team of five authors, with Amjed Tahir, Shawn Rasheed, August Shi, and Rachel Blagojevic, who built JS-TOD. The tool hunts order-dependent flaky tests, tests that pass or fail based on run order, in Jest, a JavaScript testing framework.

JS-TOD pulls tests out, shuffles them, and reruns them, with users able to set how many orders and reruns to try. Its checks found two main causes of order-linked flakiness: shared files and shared mocking state, where fake test data leaks between tests. For software teams, the tool offers a direct way to find tests that look fine alone but break when the order changes.
arxiv-2509-00566:
Marina Ville, writing alone, studies surfaces inside a four-dimensional space. The surfaces form a sequence. They converge to a branched surface. On such a surface, sheets meet along branch points. Ville measures how much curvature gathers near one such point.

She tracks curvature from tangent bundles and from normal bundles. These are families of tangent and upright directions along a surface. Their sums relate to drops in twistor degree. Twistor degree is a count from complex geometry. In some cases she proves a bound linking the two curvature amounts. The cases include few branched disks, area-minimizing limits, and minimal surfaces. She also studies when the bound is met exactly.
arxiv-2509-00666:
Sonya Tiomkin and one co-author, Alexander Gehrke, study hovering membrane wings, thin flexible wings that deform passively as they flap in place. They combine analytical theory for inviscid flow, flow without friction, with water-tank experiments at high angles of attack, the tilt of the wing to the flow.

Their model treats a spanwise section of the wing, assumes small deformation and attached flow, and expresses unsteady lift using the classic Wagner and Theodorsen functions plus membrane response. Experiments show passive deformation suppresses flow separation, the flow detaching from the wing, up to steep angles. Theory predicts lift from deformation well when deformation stays small and flow stays attached, extending unsteady theory beyond its usual low-angle range.
arxiv-2509-00866:
Yizhe Zhang, with two co-authors, Qiang Chen and Tao Zhou, asks whether general-purpose omnimodels can compete with specialists in medical image segmentation, outlining structures in medical scans. They compare the zero-shot performance of a state-of-the-art omnimodel, Gemini, against domain-specific deep learning models on three tasks.

The tasks cover polyp segmentation in endoscopy, retinal vessel segmentation in fundus images, and breast tumor segmentation in ultrasound, with subsets curated as easiest and hardest by specialist accuracy. Specialists excel on easy polyp and breast cases, but the omnimodel is more robust on hard cases where specialists fail badly. For fine-grained retinal vessels, the specialist wins throughout. The authors suggest a complementary role for omnimodels.
arxiv-2509-01466: Maram Almahariq reviews proximal and descriptive topological rings, structures that join ring algebra with notions of nearness between sets. In a proximity space, the open sets form a system that lets one define groups with compatible topology, and the same frame extends to rings. Almahariq revisits basic properties and related results, with special weight on how proximal and descriptive fields are defined, and examines how closed sets behave inside such rings.
arxiv-2509-01766:
Hannah Fox and Sammy Luo study how large a single color linked group must be inside colored random graphs. Color the edges of a full graph with several colors, and linked groups of one color form. A classic build shows some colorings keep all such groups small. A past conjecture claims larger groups can always be forced, and it is proven for some color counts.

Fox and Luo move the question to sparse random graphs and to graphs where each point has many links. They extend key steps from the full graph work to both new settings. Analogues of the known bound hold for all color counts in both settings. The tight case for three colors also carries over to the high link setting.
arxiv-2509-02166:
Enzhi Zhou leads five co-authors in designing beamforming for pinching antenna systems serving users with multiple receive antennas. Pinching antennas radiate from points pinched along a waveguide, regaining line of sight links flexibly. Fluid and movable antennas adapt less freely, with limited range and rigid structures. The multi antenna user case is practical yet little studied.

An analytic link ties received signal strength to pinching positions directly. A two layer strategy first places the central radiation point from large scale channel traits. A compressed placement heuristic then aligns phases across user antennas with a compact active set. Simulations beat conventional single antenna schemes notably. Gains peak at short range with dense pinches and widely spaced user antennas.
arxiv-2509-02266:
Sourabh Dattawad, Agnese Daffara, and Tanise Ceron use media frames to spread news picks on norms based grounds. Click based feeds echo user past and shrink the range of tales a user sees. Side based spread adds mood or class range but skips framing, the slant a tale stresses. Their pipeline treats frame pick as a dial that can be set for spread.

Tests show time with frames a user had not clicked rise by up to half. Same frame on loop can fix bias and shrink how a tale is read, which new frames fight. Frame spread lifts class and mood range as a side gain in the tests. Norms marks of fair share, fit, and spark grade the shift they make. Theirs is the first grade of frame aware feeds by those marks.
arxiv-2509-02366:
Tianwen Zhu and four co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on battery care. They propose a digital twin design. A digital twin is a live virtual copy of a real battery. The authors say current twins stay split into parts. No single design guides a battery through its whole life.

Their framework stacks five tiers. The tiers cover shape models, basic data review, physics-based forecasts, advice on best settings, and self-running control. Tests report very small errors in voltage and heat forecasts. Health estimates also stayed close to measured values, with stated doubt ranges. The authors say the system shifts battery care from reacting to faults toward forecasts and self-running control.
arxiv-2509-02566:
A. Ferrara, D. Manzoni, and E. Ntormousi present a 2025 astrophysics paper challenging the idea of feedback-free star formation, where a dense cloud supposedly turns much of its gas into stars before massive stars explode. The proposed window lasts only a few million years.

The authors show that radiation pressure from Lyman-alpha photons, produced before any supernova, can break those conditions. For steady star formation, their calculations cap the star formation efficiency at low values across a wide range of cloud densities. Higher values need the driven shells to fragment and form stars themselves. Even under generous assumptions, the quoted efficiencies are upper limits. Dust, ionised regions, and turbulence were also considered, and the conclusion held.
arxiv-2509-02666:
Jack Schulte and thirty-two co-authors present a 2025 exoplanet paper from the MEEP survey, which is building a complete brightness-limited sample of hot Jupiters to learn how such giant planets migrate. Data come from NASA's TESS satellite, which watches most of the sky.

This instalment reanalyses one benchmark system and adds four new super-Jupiters, each more than five times Jupiter's mass. One new planet is nearly heavy enough to fuse deuterium and follows an eccentric orbit. Four of the host stars show lithium absorption in their spectra. One subgiant star's lithium signal stands far above a large control sample, making it a compelling candidate for having swallowed a planet. The growing sample will test competing migration pathways.
arxiv-2509-02866:
Kyunghun Han and nine co-authors wrote a 2025 photonics paper. It demonstrates an on-chip optical isolator. The device lets light pass one way. It blocks reflections that destabilise lasers. Past on-chip versions needed magnetic materials or narrow-band resonators. Those needs limited their use.

The new design drives four parallel light channels with periodic radio waves. The travelling drive creates rotating destructive interference. Backward light is cancelled non-stop. Forward light passes untouched. Blocking reached about 30 dB at the test wavelength. It stayed strong across a band of roughly 30 nm. Two lasers at once were also blocked within a narrower window. The band covers key alkali atom lines. That suits laser cooling, locking, and spectroscopy on chips.
arxiv-2509-03266:
Silvia Paparini reviewed phenomenological models for chromonic liquid crystals in a 2025 paper. These materials form when molecules dissolved in a liquid stack into flowing, ordered phases. Because they tolerate living systems well, they attract interest for biological uses, yet their elastic theory is unsettled.

Ordinary nematic liquid crystals rest in a uniform state, but chromonics rest twisted. The classical elastic theory can only explain that twist by violating a basic inequality, which would let the stored energy fall without bound. A newer theory adds a quartic twist term, a higher-power correction, to fix that problem. The review also covers models of droplets where ordered and disordered phases coexist. Those models address defect formation during phase changes and predict an unobserved shape bistability.
arxiv-2509-03366:
Anika Kumar and 9 co-authors charted the neighborhoods of recently quenched massive galaxies in a 2025 astronomy study. Post-starburst galaxies have just shut down a burst of star formation, and their surroundings may reveal why. The team used targeted observations from a survey of such galaxies at a lookback time of several billion years.

Chance detections of carbon monoxide emission revealed gas-rich companion galaxies nearby. About a third of the surveyed galaxies hosted such a buddy, give or take the stated uncertainty. Each buddy held gas in amounts much like its host, but noticeably fewer stars. Their places and speeds fit being bound inside the hosts' dark matter halos. A comparison model says this neighbor count is typical for galaxies of that mass. Post-starbursts, it seems, live in ordinary environments.
arxiv-2509-03466:
In a 2025 research paper, Andrew J. Sargent and seven co-authors examine radio emission near the centres of active galactic nuclei, galaxies with very bright cores. Their sample holds 25 nearby objects chosen through hard X-ray surveys. Observations come from the Very Large Array radio telescope at several gigahertz frequencies.

Earlier sharper images from a continent-wide array had detected only about half the sources, leaving their emission source unclear. The authors argue that coronal emission, from hot gas near the black hole, is unlikely to dominate for the missed sources. Most of the radio glow seems to arise tens of parsecs out. Its strength fits winds driven by the active nucleus, while star formation alone looks too weak to explain it.
arxiv-2509-03566:
In a 2025 mathematics paper, Ruojing Jiang and one co-author compare volumes on finite-volume hyperbolic three-dimensional manifolds. A manifold is a space that looks flat locally but can curve globally, and hyperbolic ones bend negatively everywhere. Different distance rules, called metrics, can be placed on the same space.

Their tool is Ricci-DeTurck flow, a process that smooths a metric over time and here settles exponentially onto the hyperbolic metric. Among metrics whose scalar curvature stays at or above a fixed negative bound, the hyperbolic metric gives the smallest volume. For metrics close to it in a smooth sense, or well-behaved near cusped ends, equality holds only when the metric truly matches the hyperbolic one. The result pins down the hyperbolic metric as a unique volume minimiser.
arxiv-2509-03766:
Achraf Khoudiri and four co-authors' 2025 research paper is about charging a quantum battery with help from coherence, the wave-like alignment of quantum states. Their hybrid system couples a battery and a charger to a small autonomous thermal machine made of two qubits. Each qubit touches a thermal reservoir at a different temperature, so the machine runs by itself on heat flow.

A coherent driving field applied to the charger injects coherence into the whole setup. The thermal machine filters some decoherence, the fading of quantum behaviour caused by the hot and cold baths. It also induces memory effects, where influence flows back from environment to system instead of only outward. Coherence driving raises the battery's ergotropy, the maximum work it can deliver, by roughly forty percent in their results. Charging power also improves, because the charger's internal energy is preserved better during the process.
arxiv-2509-03866:
Samantha J. Alloo and five co-authors' 2025 research paper compares a family of X-ray dark-field imaging approaches on the same samples, for the first time. Dark-field imaging reads how a sample scatters X-rays from structures too small to resolve directly. It complements ordinary attenuation images with information about unresolved microstructure.

Data on two samples were gathered at a synchrotron with three setups: speckle-based, propagation-based, and single-grid imaging. Retrieval algorithms of many kinds then reconstructed dark-field images. Some need one exposure, others several; some analyse pixel by pixel, others globally. The dominant contrast source, diffuse scattering from microstructures too small to resolve, or repeated refraction through larger structures, emerges under every approach. Differences appear for spatially varying structures, though. Each technique carries its own internal ruler: a sensitivity scale set by its design and assumptions. The study guides method choice.
arxiv-2509-04366: Athanasios Beslikas, writing alone, states a sufficient condition in a 2025 mathematics note for when a composition operator between two Bergman spaces is bounded. The two spaces sit on the unit disc in two variables, with different weight settings. The operator comes from non-smooth rational inner functions. The note forms part two of a series on such operators and how they act between function spaces.
arxiv-2509-04466:
Yuxuan Li and three co-authors trace when a language model forms its internal picture of a new task in a 2025 research paper. Models learn tasks in context, from instructions or examples, without any weight changes. Two kinds of internal representation are studied. Transferable ones are vectors that can carry the task into a fresh model instance. Simpler ones merely encode the task category, and those persist steadily through the whole prompt.

Transferable representations behave sporadically by contrast. They condense evidence as examples accumulate, yet they switch on only at certain tokens, showing strong timing locality. Sometimes they also cover just a small subtask scope. Models thus hold tasks both as a constant background awareness and as a just-in-time working sketch.
arxiv-2509-04566:
Rita Megale and seven co-authors build a proper way to measure turbulence inside curved spacetime in a 2025 physics paper. Turbulence near black holes is usually analyzed with flat-space tools, which ignore how gravity bends lengths and volumes. Their formalism computes structure functions and power spectra using true proper distances on any curved manifold. Magnetized accretion disc simulations around a spinning Kerr black hole supply the test data.

Applied near the event horizon, and in the disc, wind, and jet regions, the method recovers the familiar inertial-range cascade. Differences from the flat approach reach forty to eighty percent close to the horizon, shrinking with distance. Strong-gravity turbulence studies need the curved treatment, the team concludes.
arxiv-2509-04766:
Water, plants, and bushfire interact in a three-part model studied by Serena Dipierro and one co-author in a 2025 paper. The reaction-diffusion system describes water stores, plant growth, and fire activity in one ecosystem. The authors ask when uniform states stay stable and when spatial patterns emerge.

Their analysis maps the range of settings where uneven bumps can upset an even state. Spread here calms even states, unlike classic Turing patterns where spread creates instability. Waves that travel in trains arise from the simplified system, with no separate activator and inhibitor roles. The paper also considers plant competition, extending the picture of how water, plants, and fire can self-organise.
arxiv-2509-04966:
Neural networks that solve differential equations often break causality and miss high-frequency detail. Arthur Bizzi, lead author with eleven co-authors, introduce neuro-spectral designs to fix both problems in a 2025 paper. Standard physics-informed networks based on plain multilayer perceptrons can fail to converge on hard initial value problems.

Their design projects the equation onto a spectral basis. That gives a finite-dimensional picture of the dynamics. A neural ordinary differential equation then integrates that picture, preserving causal structure. A starting point based on classical methods puts training near the target solution. Benchmarks on wave equations show faster convergence and better accuracy than other designs.
arxiv-2509-05166:
Car travel across European borders changed sharply during the COVID pandemic. Sujit Kumar Sikder, lead author with three co-authors, study that transition using open road traffic data in a 2025 paper. Luxembourg's sensor-based traffic observatory provides hourly counts by vehicle type at representative points on major roads, with matching context for Germany and neighbouring countries.

The dataset has many missing entries, so the team harmonise it before analysis. They compare daily travel behaviour before the pandemic and during 2020. Traffic volumes fall under lockdowns and remote work, following the global trend, while the spatio-temporal patterns reveal cross-border specifics.
arxiv-2509-05466:
Delays spread over a range of times, rather than fixed at one lag, reshape the behaviour of delayed equations. Isam Al-Darabsah, Sue Ann Campbell, and Bootan Rahman show this in a 2025 applied mathematics paper. Such equations model neural networks and lasers, where signals take time to arrive.

For a uniform spread of delays with a very large mean, they break the eigenvalue spectrum into three parts. Some eigenvalues ignore the delay, some settle to limits set by the instant terms. Infinitely many more crowd toward the imaginary axis, in a pattern with extra horizontal lines from the spread. Examples confirm the analysis. A Wilson-Cowan neural mass model with delayed self-coupling shows the practical stakes.
arxiv-2509-05566:
New nicknames invented on the spot between partners carry over to things never discussed, Anya Ji and four co-authors find in a 2025 cognitive science paper. One view treats such shared labels as arbitrary tags tied only to their original target, like proper names.

The rival view says agreeing on descriptions also aligns each person's broader concepts, so the alignment should generalise. Pairs of participants built shared conventions for abstract tangram shapes through repeated conversation, then described new shapes. Their labels for the undiscussed images aligned more than before the game. The carry-over faded with visual distance in a classic pattern and held across how nameable the images were.
arxiv-2509-05866:
Fast radio bursts could help pin down how galaxy formation stirs the gas between galaxies, argue Kritti Sharma and six co-authors in a 2025 forecast study. These millisecond flashes carry a dispersion measure, a tally of electrons along their path, which traces where ordinary matter actually sits. That gas physics can bias cosmology from galaxy surveys if ignored.

The team builds a three-by-two-point statistic joining burst dispersion correlations with galaxy positions and forecasts its power for ten thousand to one hundred thousand bursts over a third of the sky. Bursts alone constrain cosmology more weakly than galaxy clustering, thanks to shot noise and host-galaxy scatter. Combined, though, the probes break the feedback-cosmology tangle, reaching percent-level limits on feedback strength. Arcminute localizations suffice, which keeps the method realistic for coming surveys.
arxiv-2509-06066:
The superconducting gap of a kagome metal points in some directions more than others, report Yu-qing Zhao and thirteen co-authors in a 2025 paper. Their material is CsV3Sb5, from a family where superconductivity intertwines with an unconventional charge density wave. Whether the gap, the energy cost of breaking a Cooper pair, is uniform was an open question.

Directional point-contact Andreev reflection spectroscopy, which injects current along chosen crystal directions, reveals the answer. Spectra along the plane show a single in-gap conductance peak, while perpendicular spectra show two, and an anisotropic single-gap model fits both. The analysis resolves two gaps from different Fermi surface sheets, one uniform and one varying by roughly seventy percent. The results support unconventional multiband pairing in kagome superconductors.
arxiv-2509-06266:
Robots and cars see the world from several viewpoints at once, and Mohsen Gholami and six co-authors benchmark whether vision-language models can reason about space from such views in a 2025 paper. Their Ego3D-Bench holds over eight thousand human-checked questions on ego-centric, multi-view outdoor scenes. Sixteen leading models are tested against human performance.

A wide gap remains: models trail human spatial understanding badly. The team's remedy, Ego3D-VLM, post-trains a model to build a cognitive map from estimated global three-dimensional coordinates. It lifts multiple-choice accuracy by about twelve percent and distance estimation by over half, on average. The module can attach to existing models, and both tools are offered toward human-level spatial reasoning.
arxiv-2509-06566:
Finding photos that match a rough hand-drawn scene is revisited by Emil Demić and one co-author in a 2025 computer vision paper. Scene-level sketch retrieval must match both the meaning and the layout of a sketch. Earlier work chased better model designs, but the authors argue the real difficulty is that sketches are ambiguous and noisy.

Their response is a training objective built to tolerate sketch variation, combined with suitable pretraining and an encoder design. No extra machinery is added. On the demanding FS-COCO dataset and the widely used SketchyCOCO set, the approach reaches state-of-the-art results. The authors conclude that training design matters more than architectural extras for this task. They also argue that current evaluation setups for scene-level retrieval need improvement, since weak tests can hide real weaknesses.
arxiv-2509-07366:
Altermagnets are a newly recognized class of magnetic materials that could serve future electronics. Sining Zhang and 4 co-authors screen for them among perovskite compounds in a 2025 research paper. Perovskites are a large family of crystals with a shared structure. The team searched a materials database and found many candidate compounds with antiferromagnetic behavior in one crystal symmetry group.

Density functional theory calculations, a standard quantum simulation method, show most candidates settle into altermagnetic ground states. Twenty of them have the perovskite structure. The authors study one example, a sodium cobalt fluoride, in depth. Its favored magnetic order supports unusual effects, including the anomalous Hall effect and strong magneto-optical responses. Such effects make altermagnets attractive for devices that read magnetic states with electricity or light.
arxiv-2509-07466:
G. Tutberidze and 2 co-authors study Cesáro means of Fourier series in a 2025 paper. A Fourier series rebuilds a function from waves in an orthonormal system, a set of building blocks at right angles to each other. Cesáro means average the partial sums. That averaging often tames a series that will not settle on its own. Yet smoothness of a function alone does not ensure its series can be summed for a general system.

The authors ask what extra conditions on the system functions make the Cesáro means stay bounded for all functions of one class. In that class, the derivative of the function lies in the Lipschitz class Lip 1, so it cannot change too fast. They find such conditions and show they are sharp. Sharp means the conditions cannot be weakened. Results like these tell analysts when averaging can rescue a Fourier expansion.
arxiv-2509-07766:
Shivam Sharma and 2 co-authors apply a quantum-ready clustering algorithm to financial assets in a 2025 paper. Clustering assets by return correlations supports portfolio design and statistical arbitrage. Classical methods struggle with signed correlations, where assets can move in opposite ways. They often force lossy transformations, or a fixed cluster count. The method here, GCS-Q, works directly on signed, weighted graphs.

Each partitioning step is written as a QUBO problem. QUBO is a standard format for quantum annealing. It lets the algorithm search huge solution spaces with speed. On synthetic and real financial data, GCS-Q is benchmarked against leading classical methods. Those include SPONGE and k-Medoids. It achieves higher clustering quality on the reported measures. It also decides the number of clusters in a dynamic way, not by guesswork. The authors present the results as evidence of practical near-term quantum utility in finance.
arxiv-2509-07866:
Young planets often settle into resonant chains, where orbital periods form simple ratios, yet most mature systems are not in chains. Mengrui Pan, Andre Izidoro, and Sho Shibata test one chain-breaking mechanism in a 2025 research paper. A young star's magnetic field carves a cavity at the inner edge of its planet-forming disk. As the disk fades, that edge moves outward, a process called magnetospheric rebound.

Using N-body simulations, the team follows compact chains of super-Earths and mini-Neptunes during rebound. The expanding edge spreads the systems outward. That spreading triggers early instabilities and giant impacts, breaking the chains. Even so, the final systems keep the observed patterns of period ratios, similar planet sizes, and the radius valley. Rebound thus explains broken chains without spoiling the statistics astronomers actually measure.
arxiv-2509-08066:
Cosmology's deepest questions may be answered not from Earth but from the surface of the Moon. Joseph Silk sets out that vision in a 2025 research paper written alone. He admits the cost looks daunting, with the Artemis program already expensive and slow. Even so, he argues the Moon is the ideal site for the biggest telescopes anyone can dream of.

Such instruments would span radio, optical, and far-infrared wavelengths. They could image the first stars, galaxies, and supermassive black holes. They might even probe the first fractions of a second after the Big Bang. Sharp images of nearby Earth-like exoplanets are another prize. Silk frames lunar astronomy as humanity's best attempt to learn whether we are alone. The essay is part scientific case, part manifesto for the next several decades.
arxiv-2509-08166:
Hourly electricity prices can herd smart appliances into new congestion, and Phillippe K. Phanivong with 1 co-author design prices to prevent that in a 2025 energy systems paper. Day-ahead hourly retail pricing already exists in several programs. Homes with batteries, electric vehicles, and smart controllers follow prices optimally, but if everyone charges at the same cheap hour, distribution networks overload.

A linear pricing mechanism adds a signal that discourages over-consumption at congested times while keeping the scheme simple enough to publish a day ahead. Distribution operators gain a tool between blunt flat rates and heavy-handed direct control. Price design of this kind decides whether flexible demand helps the grid or merely moves its peaks around.
arxiv-2509-08266:
Vision-language models answer questions about images, but they may lean on training biases instead of looking. Saurav Sengupta and 3 co-authors build a framework to test that suspicion in a 2025 research paper. Their motivating example is a modified American flag with extra stars. Models asked to count the stars often ignore the picture and recite the familiar number.

The framework varies image traits and prompt traits in a controlled, multi-dimensional way. Image size, object counts, background color, and prompt specificity all come under the knob. The team tracks how attention values inside open-source models shift with each change. Even minor edits to an image or prompt caused large swings in answers and performance. The work gives researchers a systematic way to characterize when these models truly see, and when they merely remember.
arxiv-2509-08766:
Gravitational wave detectors must correct their laser beams at megawatt power without adding noise of their own. Tyler Rosauer and 13 co-authors demonstrate a next-generation wavefront actuator in a 2025 research paper. Detectors like LIGO sense spacetime strain over multi-kilometer baselines with extreme precision. Beam control is one of the technologies that sets that sensitivity.

The team bench-tested the full-scale design on a full-size LIGO test mirror. The design delivers higher-order wavefront fixes while adding extremely low displacement noise. Those two traits are exactly what current detectors and the planned Cosmic Explorer need. Cosmic Explorer's much longer arms would push the detection horizon back before the first stars. Better wavefront control thus turns directly into more of the universe's history becoming audible.
arxiv-2509-08866:
Alex Frost and 5 co-authors present uplink pre-compensation for ground to space optical links in a 2025 paper. Correcting a laser beam before it travels up through air is hard, because the uplink path error is rarely measured. The downlink beam, by contrast, is easy to sense.

Repeated downlink measures are used to rebuild a three-dimensional picture of the shared air volume. From that picture, the uplink wavefront error is estimated. Simulations under typical conditions show good performance, especially at large point-ahead angles. Residual error falls by up to about nine times versus using downlink phase directly. The method needs no extra hardware beyond the existing sensor.
arxiv-2509-09666:
Zhiyuan Yan and 12 co-authors recast image understanding and image generation as two halves of one auto-encoder in a 2025 multimodal paper. Reading an image into words and painting an image from words are usually trained apart, wasting their natural link. In the shared view, text is the middle code: the encoder squeezes a picture into language, and the decoder expands language back into a picture.

Their post-training method, Unified-GRPO, rewards faithful reconstruction, so a good code must keep every essential detail for the return trip. Reinforcement learning tunes both halves together toward that goal. The encoder is pushed to extract richer, more accurate meaning, while the decoder is pushed to honour it, raising consistency between an input image and its regenerated twin.
arxiv-2509-09766:
Takayuki Kubo's 2025 theory paper works out how a superconductor's dissipative conductivity changes when the driving field grows strong. His tools come from Keldysh-Usadel theory, which follows both the quasiparticles and the pair potential while the system sits out of equilibrium. Three routes can bend the response: the photon field acting directly, and two detours through a shifting pair potential named the Eliashberg effect and the Higgs mode.

Kubo shows the third-harmonic current, often read as a Higgs fingerprint, actually mixes the direct route with the Higgs route. The first harmonic gathers all three contributions instead. In the dirty limit, its nonlinear correction carries a resonance peak near the superconducting gap energy, offering a cleaner Higgs signature for experiments to chase.
arxiv-2509-09866:
Erdinc Akyildirim and 1 co-author write down a one-line formula in 2025 for a distribution that usually needs long series. Their object is the cumulative distribution of a product of two correlated normal variables, each centred at zero. A compact formula for the matching density was already known, but the cumulative version, the one that answers direct probability questions, had no equally tidy form.

The new expression rests on Humbert's confluent hypergeometric function together with modified Bessel functions. Heavy numerical testing against simulations and rival benchmarks agrees to machine precision. Because products of correlated quantities surface in fading wireless channels, nonlinear signal work, finance, and general probability, a fast exact formula should travel well beyond its derivation.
arxiv-2509-10366:
Averaging down is the theme of Fabien Allemand and three co-authors' 2025 paper on making neural image compression cheaper to run. Learned compressors beat classic codecs, but their networks are too heavy for real-time use on small devices. Knowledge distillation offers a fix: a small student network learns partly from a large teacher's outputs and ends up better than if trained alone.

The team shows distillation works for compression across model sizes and across the trade-off between image quality and bit rate, saving computation and energy in the process. The approach brings new settings to tune, and the authors point to open questions about choosing teachers and loss functions, plus extending the recipe to transformer-based compressors. Their code is publicly available.
arxiv-2509-10466:
Christian Fane's 2025 thesis tackles privacy in mixed reality meetings. Its tool is diminished reality, the digital erasure of real objects. When collaborators share a view of your room through a headset, personal items leak into the meeting. Fane's system lets the host pick sensitive objects. It removes them from what others see, in real time.

The host selects objects precisely, with semantic segmentation guiding the choice. Live inpainting then fills the gaps, from the second viewer's perspective. A mobile depth camera supplies that view. No fixed camera position is needed. No prior 3D scan of the room is needed, either. Detection uses YOLOv11. A modified video inpainting transformer does the filling. At 720p, the pipeline sustains over twenty frames per second. Practical, privacy-preserving erasure during live collaboration is feasible, the thesis shows.
arxiv-2509-10666:
Chongjun Ouyang and four co-authors propose segmented waveguides for pinching-antenna systems in this 2025 wireless communications paper. Pinching antennas radiate from points along a dielectric waveguide, and one long guide suffers a flaw: signals caught by one antenna can re-radiate through the others. Chopping the guide into short segments, each with its own antennas, removes that interference by construction.

On the segmented design they define three operating protocols, selection, aggregation, and multiplexing, and derive placement rules plus closed-form signal-to-noise formulas for both uplink and downlink. Segmentation provably shortens both the antenna-to-user and antenna-to-feed distances, cutting two kinds of loss. Numerically, multiplexing performs best of the three protocols, and every protocol beats the conventional single-guide design, making the segmented architecture a cleaner foundation for this young antenna technology.
arxiv-2509-11166:
V. I. Yukalov and E. P. Yukalova survey dynamical transitions in trapped superfluids in this 2025 physics review. The systems are clouds of Bose-condensed atoms held in traps and shaken by alternating fields, which can push them far from equilibrium.

The review distinguishes resonant shaking, tuned to the trap's own frequencies, from stronger nonresonant driving. Under resonant driving the condensate splits into interacting coherent modes, producing Rabi oscillations, an internal form of the Josephson effect, and even chaotic motion, with sharp transitions that resemble phase changes. Stronger driving instead stirs up vortices, rings, and turbulence of several kinds. The authors explain how quantities like an effective temperature and scaling laws can tell these nonequilibrium states apart.
arxiv-2509-11266:
Konstantin Emming computes a cohomology in algebraic topology in this 2025 mathematics paper. The object is a quotient algebra of the real-motivic dual Steenrod algebra. Its cohomology feeds spectral sequence work aimed at the homotopy groups of spheres.

Emming runs a Bockstein spectral sequence. Its input is the known cohomology of the complex-motivic twin of the same algebra. The payoff lies downstream. The result feeds an Adams spectral sequence for a hoped-for real-motivic modular forms spectrum. That spectrum's homotopy groups would inform the real-motivic sphere spectrum. In time they would inform the classical stable stems. The paper is one careful link in a long chain.
arxiv-2509-11566:
Hua Guo, Yunhong Ji, and Xuan Zhou present a development framework for distributed systems in this 2025 software engineering paper. Distributed systems are hard to build because concurrency and faults behave non-deterministically, so errors can hide until production.

Their framework, Sedeve-Kit, is driven by specifications in three stages. First, the system's specification and invariants are written in TLA+, model-checked for correctness, and used to generate test cases. Second, code is written against the specification to keep the implementation faithful. Third, the finished system is tested rigorously with the cases generated up front. The strong thread from abstract design to concrete code, maintained through continuous verification, is meant to keep quality high in a domain where bugs are expensive.
arxiv-2509-11666:
Amir Mehrnoosh and Gianluca Bianchin optimize systems they cannot model, in this 2025 control theory paper. Feedback optimization steers a running dynamical system toward its best steady state, but most methods need equations for how the plant behaves, which real plants rarely provide.

Their randomized method needs only function evaluations. By probing the system at two points, it estimates the gradient of the objective and updates the control input in real time, borrowing ideas from zeroth-order optimization. The authors prove convergence guarantees: for smooth, possibly nonconvex objectives, the method reaches an approximately stationary point at the same rate known for two-point gradient-free methods in static optimization. Simulations confirm the theory, pointing to model-free tuning of systems that resist modeling.
arxiv-2509-11766:
Andy Zhai and nineteen co-authors push vision-language models into the physical world. This 2025 robotics paper argues that a mismatch blocks embodied AI. Modalities, training data, and objectives all misalign. Space, bodies, and action suffer most. Action grasp and generation form the central bottleneck.

Their model is WALL-OSS. It is an embodied foundation model trained end to end. Large-scale multimodal pretraining feeds it. A tightly coupled architecture joins the parts. A unified chain-of-thought curriculum blends three levels. Instruction reasoning is one. Subgoal planning is another. Fine-grained action synthesis is the third. Long, complex manipulation tasks saw high success. Instruction following was strong. The authors offer a scalable route from passive models to acting ones.
arxiv-2509-12066:
Many weak tests can be fused into one strong verdict, but dependence among the p-values can quietly break the fusion. Parijat Chakraborty and three co-authors settle how heavy-tailed combination tests behave under dependence in 2025, an open problem despite the tests' growing popularity.

Methods like the harmonic mean and Cauchy tests first stretch p-values into heavy-tailed variables, calibrated as if independence held. Borrowing multivariate regular variation from extreme value theory, the authors express the true asymptotic level of any homogeneous combination test through an angular measure describing dependence near zero. One prize result: the harmonic mean test, which matches the Pareto linear combination test, is universally calibrated no matter the tail dependence, and it is the only such test. The Cauchy test stays honest but often turns conservative.
arxiv-2509-12366:
Electrons in quantum electrodynamics can gain mass from their own interactions, even when the bare theory gives them none. Juan D. García-Muñoz and three co-authors revisit that dynamical mass generation in 2025 through the Schwinger-Dyson equation for the electron propagator, in both three and four spacetime dimensions.

With a lean truncation of the equation tower, the gap equation is linearized and recast as a Schrödinger-like problem with a well or barrier potential. The generated mass appears as the zero mode of that problem. It follows the classic Miransky scaling law, which ties the mass to a critical coupling strength.
arxiv-2509-12466:
Satwik Ghanta, Peggy Gregory, and Gul Calikli study sustainability inside one financial services company in a 2025 paper. Sustainable software engineering is becoming an industry need for reputation, profit, and efficiency, but the term has many definitions. That variety makes it hard for organizations to build a shared understanding.

Financial services are highly data-driven, tightly regulated, and handle millions of transactions daily, so generic advice may not fit. The authors ran an exploratory qualitative case study with interviews and a focus group involving senior managers and software engineers of varied experience. They examined how sustainability is perceived in the IT function, how it could be practiced, who owns it, and what blocks it. Their findings address a gap in context-specific research.
arxiv-2509-12666:
Predicting how a drug crosses into the brain needs a physiology-based model with many parameters nobody can measure directly in people. Charuka D. Wickramasinghe and three co-authors fit such a model in 2025 by inverting a physics-informed neural network, for a four-compartment picture of brain drug delivery.

The network respects the model's differential equations while estimating drug and patient parameters from data. An identifiability check first asks whether the data can pin those parameters down at all. Correct convergence demands careful weighting of the data, initial-condition, and equation-residual losses, plus tuned network settings. Accurate parameters yield concentration curves and the metrics clinicians use to design brain therapies.
arxiv-2509-12766:
Dan Haran proves in 2025, with group theory alone, that the smallest embedding cover of a profinite group is unique. The question was listed as an open problem in a key book on field arithmetic, now in its fourth edition.

An embedding cover is a smallest larger group that holds the given group in a set way, and doubt remained whether two such covers could differ. Haran shows they cannot. The proof uses only group tools, with no extra field work. Settling the point cleans up a base fact that later work on large limit groups can rely on without extra checks.
arxiv-2509-12866:
Martin Thissen, Thi Ngoc Diep Tran and six co-authors test in 2025 whether chat models can make useful fake training images for dog joint and muscle checks. Real cases are rare and costly, yet a new chart method marks sore spots as strokes on a dog body map.

They split the map into more than two hundred named zones for muscles and joints. With guided output and few-shot prompts they made a thousand fake charts for a kneecap fault and a thousand more for other faults. A model trained only on fake charts scored high on real charts. The approach may help where real data is scarce.
arxiv-2509-12966:
K. Aditya and Arunima Banerjee investigate how ultra-thin galaxies stay so thin in a 2025 paper. Low surface brightness ultra-thin galaxies have stellar disks whose thickness is only about a tenth of their length scale. How such disks sustain that structure throughout their evolution is the central question.

Using collisionless N-body simulations, the authors evolved model disks inside dark matter halos of steep, shallow, and intermediate concentration. Their models matched the observed properties of the galaxy FGC 2366, including surface brightness, disk scale length, and vertical thinness, while excluding gas to isolate dark matter effects. Bar-driven internal heating, a mechanism that can thicken disks, was suppressed regardless of halo concentration. Disk thinness remained roughly constant, suggesting the low surface brightness nature itself prevents thickening.
arxiv-2509-13066:
The IceCube Collaboration sets out in 2025 what its Upgrade will add to air neutrino swing studies. Seven new dense strings join the DeepCore fill at the South Pole. Each new module holds many light sensors, not one.

Sensor counts more than triple for low-energy hits. That lifts catch rates and rebuild quality in the giga range. Updates to fakes, picks, and rebuilds handle higher rates. Reach covers swing angles, tau births, and mass order. Precision should rival beam tests, with new energies and baselines. Cross checks carry distinct error sources.
arxiv-2509-13466:
Louisa Conwill, Megan Levis Scheirer, and Walter Scheirer ask whether software needs subsidiarity in a 2025 paper. Subsidiarity comes from social thought. It puts decisions at the lowest level that can handle them, guarding human dignity and pushing back against power gathered at the top. A higher authority steps in only when it truly must.

They put data privacy under that lens. Two methods carried the study. The team watched how data actually flows out of common tools, and they interviewed the people who use those tools. From both, they worked out two things: how much control each technology leaves in users' hands today, and how much control users feel they need. Chat platforms came off worst. Slack and Discord, they found, break with subsidiarity more than the other everyday technologies tested. It also shows how the principle can guide designs that help people flourish.
arxiv-2509-13566:
Denis Spasyuk, writing alone in a 2025 paper, presents XASDB, an open web database of X-ray spectra. Labs with synchrotrons around the world now make huge piles of such data, which track how a material takes in X-rays. Shared, well-kept stores of spectra help others check and reuse that work.

The store holds more than one thousand reference spectra, drawn from forty elements and hundreds of compounds, and it is hosted by the Canadian Light Source. A key part is a code library that runs in the browser, so users can clean, scale, and make a first study of a spectrum with no install. A built-in viewer shows spectra on any device. The design aims to take in many file types from many beamlines and labs.
arxiv-2509-14066:
Mirco Tincani and six co-authors build a brain-inspired irrigation controller in a 2025 paper. Precision irrigation saves water by watering only when soil and plants call for it. Continuous monitoring across large fields needs sensors and processors that sip power. They must work without a network link back to the cloud.

Their system runs a biologically realistic spiking neural network on a mixed-signal neuromorphic processor. The chip senses, computes, and decides entirely on site, with no data transmission at all. Fed real soil moisture records from apple and kiwi orchards at several depths, its irrigation commands closely matched conventional methods. Local neuromorphic inference, they conclude, can keep decision accuracy. It enables autonomous, sustainable watering at scale.
arxiv-2509-14166:
Jamie P. McKeown and four co-authors model an invasive moth's advance across Britain in a 2025 ecology paper. Oak processionary moth caterpillars damage oak trees and pose health risks, and the United Kingdom outbreak keeps growing despite management. Predicting where the pest arrives next is the practical prize.

Their framework describes spread with a reaction-diffusion equation over a population density field, solved numerically to extract first arrival times at each location. The expansion rate falls straight out of the model parameters, which they infer in a Bayesian way using Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling against observed spread data. The model captures the outbreak's progress well and shows the expansion has not run at a constant rate, a warning against simple linear forecasts for managers.
arxiv-2509-14466:
Tejas Pagare, Agniv Bandyopadhyay and Sandeep Juneja study learning in matching markets in 2025, where two sides must be paired stably under unknown preferences. Labour platforms must match firms and freelancers quickly from noisy feedback. A stable match leaves no pair wishing to defect.

The goal is pure exploration: find the stable matching with stated confidence using as few samples as possible. Lower bounds on sampling needs are proved for one sided and two sided learning. The authors then propose an efficient algorithm that uses samples adaptively. Markets with a unique stable matching anchor the analysis. Sample efficient learning matters because every exploratory match in a real market costs time and goodwill.
arxiv-2509-14866:
Ali Salar, Qing Liu, and Guoying Zhao propose a face anonymization method based on diffusion inpainting in a 2025 computer vision paper. Portrait images are everywhere in vision datasets, so protecting identity matters. Anonymized faces must still look realistic and stay useful for tasks such as attribute analysis.

Their framework uses a latent diffusion model to repaint the face region with a new identity. An adaptive attribute-guidance module corrects gradients during generation, so the new face keeps the attributes of a chosen synthetic target. Users can also protect only part of the face, leaving selected regions unchanged. Tests on two public high-resolution face datasets beat prior methods, and the approach needs no extra training of the diffusion model itself.
arxiv-2509-15066:
The ATLAS Collaboration reports a precision measurement of top quark pair production in a 2025 particle physics paper. Top-antitop pairs were produced in proton-proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider and recorded over a large accumulated dataset. Events with an electron-muon pair and jets tagged as coming from bottom quarks form the measurement sample.

The production cross-section comes out with a total uncertainty of only about one percent, split among data size, systematic effects, luminosity, and beam energy. Comparing the measured rate with predictions yields the top quark's pole mass, a fundamental parameter of the Standard Model. The same events also provide differential distributions for the leptons, detailed breakdowns of how often each kinematic pattern occurs. Such precision tests the theory of the strong force at the percent level.
arxiv-2509-15166:
Fiaz Ahmed and J. David Neelin explain why rising air over tropical oceans piles up at different heights in a 2025 atmospheric science paper. Over the East Pacific, vertical velocity profiles are bottom-heavy, peaking low. Over the West Pacific they are top-heavy. Differences in sea surface temperature patterns explain part of the contrast, but the physical mechanism stayed incomplete.

Their steady, linear model stacks the atmosphere into layers over a rotating plane, with convection and radiation responding linearly to temperature and moisture changes. The model's free modes, its natural vibration patterns, resemble the observed layered structures of the tropical atmosphere. Each mode carries a characteristic horizontal size. In standard conditions the deepest mode spans a continental scale, while shallower modes sit at smaller scales. The modal view ties basin-scale structure to basic dynamics.
arxiv-2509-15566:
Shaojie Zhang leads a large team that makes screen using agents act more like people. Current agents that click through apps reason in ways unlike human use. The team split the act into three phases named Blink, Think, and Link. Blink spots key screen areas fast, like an eye jump. Think plans at a higher level, and Link turns the plan into commands.

They add two tools to the frame. One builds training data for the Blink phase on its own. The other is a rule based reward that scores both the process and the outcome, a first of its kind for this frame. Their model builds on this setup for human style screen control.
arxiv-2509-15666:
Yongsheng Feng leads a team that pulls apart mixed sounds, such as one voice from a song. Clean, split sounds help both listeners and the training of generative models. In practice, better splitting has meant bigger networks and higher cost. The team wanted growth that can be dialed at training time and at run time.

Their frame, TISDiSS, splits early and trains with many loss points that share weights. At run time, users can repeat the core step more or fewer times to trade speed for quality, with no retraining. Training with more repeats lifts quality at low repeat counts, which suits low delay use. On standard speech tests, the frame tops rivals with fewer parts.
arxiv-2509-15866:
Sebastian De Haro and Enrico Cinti write a book length study of dualities in physics, due out as a Cambridge Element. A duality maps one theory onto a different looking one that makes the same predictions. For over half a century, dualities have sat at the heart of modern physics. They solve problems that resist direct attack.

The book explains what dualities are and gives a spread of cases, from quantum mechanics to gravity. It sorts their main types and the roles they play. Three deep questions get the focus: whether dual theories truly say the same thing, what view of theories dualities suggest, and whether they clash with emergence. The style is an entry point for physics and philosophy readers alike.
arxiv-2509-16266:
When a polymer network is stretched, its molecules shift in ways that change how it vibrates. Julian Konrad and four co-authors show that machine-learned force fields can capture these vibration patterns in epoxy plastics with near quantum accuracy. Their simulations match the shifts in key vibration bands seen in lab tests under load, where a classic model failed.

The shifts track how far molecules stretch and line up, which links them to local stress. A trained model for electric response lets them predict light absorption under strain as well. Vibration marks could thus serve as a safe, touch-free way to read stress in advanced materials.
arxiv-2509-16466:
Patient-level data from drug trials are gold for research, yet privacy rules keep them locked away. Zixuan Zhao and six co-authors generate fake patient data without training a black-box model, using only what a published trial paper shows. Their three steps read survival curves at finer than pixel precision, add at-risk counts, and build patient traits from summary tables.

Two detailed case studies and simulations show the method can mirror real trial data closely. Because no real records are needed to train it, the approach sidesteps the usual access barrier. Faithful synthetic data could widen who can test medical claims.
arxiv-2509-16566:
Omar Eldeeb and Martin Malandro turn to written music in a 2025 paper on finding section breaks. Most tools for music structure work on audio recordings. Written scores, though, state pitch, timing, and instruments in plain form. The pair aim to use that rich form to spot where one barwise section ends and the next begins.

They train a convolutional network on symbolic music for this task. The model beats a matched audio-based method by a clear margin. It also beats an older block-matching approach by more. The team share their data, code, and trained models. Score-based analysis may help tools that sort and search large music libraries.
arxiv-2509-16766:
Seth Gerberding, Jeff Peterson, Jim Ferguson, and Scott Ramsey build test solutions for shock codes in a 2025 paper. The Noh problem is a classic test where gas slams inward and forms a shock. Codes that track fluids are checked against known answers for it. Trouble comes when the gas rule is a black box with no formula.

The team derive a way to build near-exact answers even then. They lay out the theory and the steps of the method. Several derived answers are shown as examples. A classic convergence test runs on one hard case. Verified codes matter for weapons, space, and energy work.
arxiv-2509-16866:
Mohammad Ramezanali, Mo Vazifeh, and Paolo Santi build a tunable test of step-by-step reasoning in a 2025 paper. Their benchmark, seqBench, varies three knobs. One sets how many steps a task needs. One sets how often a solver must backtrack. One sets how much distracting noise surrounds the key facts.

Even top models failed in a systematic way on these tasks. The search needed was small, so the failures point to weak common-sense reasoning. The datasets are shared in public. The knobs can be turned up as models improve. A test that grows with the field gives a cleaner read on true reasoning gains.
arxiv-2509-17066:
Kunrong Li and Kwan Hui Lim recommend a user's next destination with no training in a 2025 paper. Predicting the next point of interest draws on past movements. Classic models need heavy training. Language models can answer with no training, but their picks are often generic or far away. Retrieval grounds the model in the user's own history.

A geographical reranking step then favors nearby, plausible places. Tests on three real check-in datasets show clear accuracy gains. The method beat both classic and language-based rivals. Code is shared in public. Training-free recommendations could serve travel apps that must adapt to new cities fast.
arxiv-2509-18066:
Heejune Kim maps the phase edge for a multi-type spin glass with a centred outside field. His 2025 paper works on the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model, a maths stand-in for a magnet with random links. The Parisi formula gives its free energy, and the ask is where its form changes.

Kim shows that a known surface, the de Almeida-Thouless line in its broad form, marks that edge. On one side, plain symmetric answers hold. On the far side, symmetry breaks and the answer takes a richer form. The terms of the split are field strength and the spread profile of the types.
arxiv-2509-18166:
Xiaoqian Qi, Haoye Chai, and Yong Li build one base model to forecast many kinds of mobile network data. Their 2025 model, MobiGPT, deals with cell traffic, user app use, and channel quality. Past tools were each built for one data type, which adds cost and fuss at scale.

Soft prompts teach the model what each data type is, in a shared frame. A time-mask step guides three tasks: short forecasts, long forecasts, and spread making. On real data sets with a huge sample count, the model forecast all three types with good scores. One frame thus serves many network needs.
arxiv-2509-18266:
Desika Narayanan leads a large team that shows how dust grew so fast in the first galaxies. Their 2025 paper uses cosmic zoom-in sims to match telescope facts: rich dust in far less than a billion years. Star-made dust alone looks too slow for that pace, the team finds.

Stars rule dust output at the start, they show. Past a point, growth on tiny grains takes over and runs fast. A Shapley study ranks local density as the top driver of that growth, with grain size mix next. Shattered grains raise the small share, which lifts growth by adding surface. Blue, bright early galaxies fit the tale.
arxiv-2509-18366:
Factories that print parts for clients hold valuable design files that must stay secret. Aleksandr Dolgavin, Jacob Gatlin, Moti Yung, and Mark Yampolskiy show a new leak: the printer itself. Their 2025 paper demonstrates a side-channel attack on industrial 3D printers. Past attacks of this kind only worked on simple home printers.

The team focused on powder bed fusion, a process used for strong polymer and metal parts. They fitted sensors to the printer's motors and parts to record power use during a print. From power traces alone, they rebuilt the printed model's shape. A trick borrowed from chip attack research sharpened the rebuild by using many traces. On two test models, the rebuild matched the true shape closely, with about ninety percent correct voxels at best. Encrypting files, they warn, cannot stop leaks through power and noise.
arxiv-2509-18466:
Two-legged robots struggle on rough or slippery ground, where foot grip is hard to model. Junnosuke Kamohara, Feiyang Wu, Chinmayee Wamorkar, Seth Hutchinson, and Ye Zhao join two control styles to do better. Their 2025 paper pairs model predictive control, which plans with a physics model, with reinforcement learning, which learns from trial and error. Each style alone has known flaws on hard terrain.

Learning tunes three parts of the planner: the body dynamics model, the swing leg controller, and the step rate. The planner keeps its safety constraints, which pure learning lacks. Tests ran in a detailed simulator across stairs, stepping stones, and low-grip surfaces. The joined method walked with more adaptivity and robustness than either baseline alone. The authors aim it at humanoid robots that must leave flat floors. Real-world trials would be the next step.
arxiv-2509-18666:
A moving robot must dodge obstacles whose future paths are unsure. Kaizer Rahaman, Simran Kumari, and Ashish R. Hota present a planning method that plans for a whole range of possible obstacle futures. Their 2025 paper adds context: the obstacle's path depends on how the robot itself moves. Ignoring that link can make plans either reckless or timid.

The method embeds the conditional spread of obstacle paths in a kernel space, using past data. An ambiguity set then holds all spreads close to that estimate. A robust avoidance rule is built against the whole set, inside a rolling-horizon planner. In simulations of several hard scenarios, the approach dodged more reliably than rivals. The beaten rivals lacked either the context link or the robustness step. The authors frame context as safety-critical information, not a luxury.
arxiv-2509-18766:
Some simple networks hide a strict preference for sparse solutions. Raphaël Berthier studies diagonal linear networks in this 2025 paper. These are networks with linear responses and diagonal weight matrices. Trained from a tiny start, they settle on the predictor with the smallest one-norm among all perfect fits.

Berthier deepens that known picture. He shows the whole training path of such a network tracks the lasso regularization path, a classic curve of sparse regression fits. Time spent training acts like an inverse penalty strength. Under a monotonicity assumption on the lasso path, the match is exact. In general it is approximate, and he proves both versions. Simulations back the theory. The link lets two literatures, deep learning theory and sparse statistics, read each other's results.
arxiv-2509-18966:
Shouryya Ray, writing alone, studies a field theory that may describe phases of matter with no simple known description. The theory is a Wess-Zumino-Witten model whose target space is a Stiefel manifold, a space built from frames of perpendicular vectors. Ray follows how the theory changes as one zooms out to larger scales, a method called renormalization. The key question is whether stable fixed points survive in three dimensions.

In two dimensions Ray finds such a stable point, a cousin of a famous conformal theory. As the dimension rises slightly, that point merges with an unstable one and vanishes. For larger frame counts, though, the merger seems to happen past three dimensions, which hints a stable phase exists there. Ray also compares predicted values with a known related case and gives first predictions for a case with no known dual theory.
arxiv-2509-19166:
Doctors hunting polyps during a colonoscopy can miss some, and a missed polyp can turn into colorectal cancer. Siddharth Gupta and Jitin Singla build an AI pipeline, YOLO-LAN, to flag polyps live during the procedure. It rests on the YOLO family of object detectors, which scan an image in one pass. The team tunes three ingredients: a new loss function, varied data augmentations, and negative examples that mimic real clinical scenes with no polyps.

Trained this way, the pipeline topped prior methods on two polyp datasets, Kvasir-SEG and BKAI-IGH NeoPolyp. Its strictest accuracy score, which rewards exact box placement, rose the most. The authors also check robustness across polyp sizes, since small polyps are the easiest to miss. They argue the precision and speed make the system relevant for AI-assisted screening in real clinics.
arxiv-2509-19466:
Where do the heaviest merging black holes come from, and how has their rate changed over time? Rodrigo Tenorio and four co-authors study that question with the newest gravity-wave catalog, GWTC-4.0. They built a flexible map of how merger counts vary with mass and distance. The map uses a mesh of triangles whose size and shape the data itself chooses, so it needs far fewer settings than past methods.

Past studies of mass alone found a bump near one well-known mass range. This joint study finds no such bump close to Earth. Instead, the rate rises at larger distances around those masses. That shift hints that the heavy pairs formed through more than one route. Dense star clusters and lone pairs of stars may both play a part.
arxiv-2509-19666:
To judge how a black hole feeds, astronomers need its total power across all wavelengths, not just the slice a telescope catches. Mojegan Azadi and four co-authors build a recipe for that bolometric correction at any cosmic epoch. Their accretion disk templates vary with black hole mass, feeding rate, spin, and viewing tilt. Integrating the templates from infrared to X-ray gives the total.

The recipe avoids double-counting reprocessed light and handles wavelength gaps consistently. Corrections depend strongly on mass and feeding rate, weakly on spin and tilt. Hotter, cooler disk trends follow from those dependencies in predictable ways. Feedback studies, which weigh black hole output against galaxy growth, need such totals. A uniform recipe replaces the patchwork of older corrections.
arxiv-2509-19866:
Swiss German is spoken daily by millions yet lacks large corpora of natural speech. Samuel Stucki, Mark Cieliebak, and Jan Deriu present SwissGPC, a corpus drawn from talk shows and podcasts. Roughly fifty-four hundred hours of raw audio were gathered from national radio and video platforms. After automated segmentation and weak labeling, nearly five thousand hours remained.

The speech spans the seven major dialect regions plus Standard German. The corpus supports recognition, synthesis, and dialect identification research. Unlike studio corpora, these recordings hold spontaneous talk with all its mess. That realism is the point: systems trained on clean speech stumble in the wild. Dialect-rich data also serves linguistics. The authors detail their pipeline and counts so others can extend the resource.
arxiv-2509-20166:
Lauren Deason and twenty-two co-authors present a new benchmark suite in this 2025 arXiv paper on cyber defense. Security operations centers face more alerts and threat reports than staff can handle. Large language models could help, but existing tests do not measure the tasks defenders actually do. CyberSOCEval was built to close that gap.

The suite covers two core tasks: malware analysis and threat intelligence reasoning. It forms part of the open CyberSecEval 4 release. Larger and newer models scored better overall, matching the usual scaling pattern. Reasoning models, though, gained less from extra test-time thinking than they do in coding or mathematics. No model came close to topping the tests. The authors offer the suite as an open target for building stronger defensive tools.
arxiv-2509-20466:
Some theories of quantum gravity set a smallest length that can exist. Michael Bishop, Daniel Hooker, and Douglas Singleton compare two ways to build that idea in a 2025 arXiv paper. Most models change the inner product, the rule that gives sizes to states, so that place and momentum operators stay symmetric. That choice warps momentum space itself.

The team shows the same physics comes from a cleaner trade: leave the inner product alone and symmetrize the operators instead. Plain momentum space then stays as it was. States of the changed place operator, even its most localized ones, keep a plain form in space. The paper weighs both routes side by side. The operator route keeps the tools physicists know best close at hand.
arxiv-2509-20566:
Tiny noise, huge consequences: Emanuel Dallas and Paolo Zanardi report a butterfly effect in quantum circuits in a 2025 arXiv paper.
