A common fix is moment matching: align the averages and spreads of the two distributions in some feature space. Existing methods do this with improvised similarity measures.

The authors instead respect the geometry of the distributions themselves. Using Siegel embeddings, they package the mean and covariance into a single symmetric positive definite matrix. Alignment then uses the natural Riemannian distance on the space of such matrices, which preserves both moments at once. They connect this distance to a bound on target-domain error. Tests on image denoising and image classification benchmarks validate the approach, and the code is publicly available.
arxiv-2510-14866:
Shahreza and Marcel benchmark, in a 2025 arXiv paper, whether the new multimodal language models can recognize faces as well as the specialist systems built for that one job. These generalist models read images and text together and shine at many vision-language tasks. Face recognition, though, demands very fine distinctions between similar faces, and the open-source state of the art was unmeasured under standard protocols.

The authors ran leading multimodal models on six established face datasets, including LFW, its cross-age and cross-pose variants, AgeDB, and the racially balanced RFW. The models clearly capture rich semantic cues about faces, which helps face-related tasks broadly. But in zero-shot, high-precision recognition, they lag behind specialized face recognition models. The benchmark and its code are released openly. It shows where generalists stand today, and what the next generation must improve: accuracy and generalization under strict matching demands.
arxiv-2510-14966:
Robertson argues, in a 2025 arXiv paper, that an evaluation score for language models should enter statistics as it comes, with no reshaping. Pairwise comparisons scored by total variation distance mutual information yield binary critic decisions. Averaging them gives probabilities with an additive structure, the kind item-response theory exploits to rank agents. Standard practice forces those scores through logistic link functions first.

Across three domains, the identity link, using scores raw, kept additivity violations low, with median curl between 0.080 and 0.150 in the analysis, while probit and logit links violated additivity far more. The author derives the clipped-linear model from Gini entropy maximization, fitted by box-constrained least squares that handle saturation at the boundaries. Using a third of the comparisons, the model predicted held-out scores with an error near a tenth of the scale while preserving agent rankings nearly exactly. Rank agreement held across judge models.
arxiv-2510-15366:
Jinwoo Kim and four colleagues model sequences, such as time series, by lifting their statistics into a space where tangled dynamics turn linear. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds on operator theory and hidden Markov models, which describe data as evolving hidden states. Instead of tracking random step-by-step states, they embed the whole sequence distribution as one object in a product Hilbert space.

Generation then follows a gradient flow that steadily reduces a mismatch measure between the model's distribution and the data. Two ideas make this practical. A spectral decomposition of the operators yields a tensor network form for the embeddings, keeping large objects manageable. And an extension of the flow to time-varying spaces connects it to flow matching, enabling training without simulation and faster sampling. The authors report competitive results across time-series datasets. The authors present the method as a fresh route to sequence generation.
arxiv-2510-15466:
Vu Tram Anh Khuong and three colleagues at VNU University in Hanoi improve the reading of micro-expressions, the fleeting facial movements that leak true feelings. Their 2025 arXiv paper notes these expressions last under half a second and are valuable in psychology, security, . Deep learning helps, but labeled examples are scarce, and most training tricks only vary the images spatially.

Their method varies the timing instead. Each expression is split into two motion phases, from onset to peak and from peak back to rest. A dynamic image, a single summary picture of motion, is built for each phase rather than one for the whole clip. That dual-phase step doubles the temporal cues training sees. Across six network designs and two benchmark datasets, accuracy and imbalance-aware scores improved consistently. Combined with ordinary spatial tricks, gains reached about ten percent .
arxiv-2510-16166:
Daniel Csillag and three co-authors strengthen a method for using machine learning guesses in careful statistics. The method, prediction-powered inference, fills in missing data with model guesses while keeping final claims sound. But each extra need, like privacy or data that shifts over time, used to demand a fresh, hard proof.

Their fix routes the guesses through conformal prediction, a tool that wraps each guess in a set with a known hit rate. That one move carries the extra guarantees along in a natural way. They work it out for averages and for broad classes of estimates. For e-values, theirs is the first offline method of its kind. Tests on private data and time series show tasks that were awkward before becoming straightforward.
arxiv-2510-16566:
Mehrdad Nasernejad and Jonathan Toledo set tests for prime ideals in a 2025 paper. Prime ideals are sets in a ring with clean split traits. The maximal ideal is the largest such set short of the whole ring. They ask when that ideal shows up among primes tied to powers of a monomial ideal. A monomial ideal is built from pure power terms of the variables.

They give tests that flag when the maximal ideal must appear. Each test comes with worked cases that show how to use it. The ring in view is a polynomial ring over a field. Such rings list all sums of power terms with field weights. The tests aid work on how powers of ideals break down. Clear flags save long checks in ring studies.
arxiv-2510-16666:
Maurice Almeida and three co-authors study a strict fairness condition for coloring the vertices of a graph. A coloring uses exactly k colors. It counts as closed neighborhood balanced when every vertex sees the same number of vertices of each color in its closed neighborhood, meaning itself plus its direct neighbors.

The four authors derive conditions that a graph must meet, and conditions that are enough, to admit such a coloring. They also study how common graph operations, such as combining or modifying graphs, affect the property. One firm negative result stands out: the class of graphs with these colorings cannot be described by a list of forbidden subgraphs.
arxiv-2510-16766:
Riccardo Muolo and Yuzuru Kato, writing as a pair, compare two ways to pin a network of oscillators into line. Pinning control steers a whole network by acting on a few chosen nodes. Engineers usually add an outside signal to those nodes. A second style instead changes the parameters of the pinned nodes themselves.

Using phase reduction, a method that tracks only the timing of each cycle, the pair proves the two styles match for weakly coupled systems with steady periodic behavior. Computer simulations with coupled Stuart-Landau oscillators confirm the claim. The result lets engineers swap one pinning style for the other in weakly coupled systems, which widens the options for real control tasks.
arxiv-2510-17866:
Sungmin Cho, with two co-authors, presents MUSE, a method that finds and outlines objects in images without any training on those objects. The system builds flat views from three-dimensional models of unseen items. It then matches those views against regions proposed from a test photo.

Matching joins class and patch features, and a final step adjusts each score by how reliable the region looks. The authors report that MUSE ranked first on three tracks of the BOP Challenge in 2025. Readers get a clear case that careful matching, rather than more training, can carry detection and outlining of new objects.
arxiv-2510-17966:
Maryum Sayeed and six co-authors hunt for companions around red giant stars that hold oddly large amounts of lithium. Such stars are rare, and one leading idea blames a close partner for their strange chemistry. The team took sharp spectra of thirty-three of these giants with the ESPRESSO instrument and fit their orbits.

Nine of the stars had companions, a rate near one in four. The partners range from one planet and three brown dwarfs to five normal stars. Giants with modest lithium levels were more often paired. The results narrow, but do not settle, the mystery of these stars.
arxiv-2510-18666:
Brendon Madison, writing alone, tackles precision at future colliders. The machines will collide electrons with positrons. They are built to make Higgs and Z particles. They promise unmatched tests of the Standard Model. Two quantities must be known superbly for that promise. One is how many collisions were delivered. The other is the exact collision energy.

The paper maps paths to one hundred parts per million on delivered collisions. It focuses on two clean photon-based signals. Beam deflection biases one classic signal badly. A new method pairs two scattering processes to correct it. Madison also proposes a granular detector design. Studies gave it about thirty-five parts per million. That is far better than the current design. Several methods pin down the collision energy too. One uses density estimation.
arxiv-2510-18766:
Alexander Krawciw and his seven co-authors teach two rovers to share one load. A future Moon habitat will need cargo hauled far from landing sites. The Artemis program frames that need. Canada is studying utility vehicles for the job. Two smaller rovers share capacity and add flexibility. Driving in formation with shared cargo is a hard control problem, though.

Their fix is a distributed predictive controller. Each rover plans its own motion. Each respects the shared cargo as it plans. A custom coupling bears the load's full weight. It still lets the vehicles move somewhat apart in their kinematics. Field tests used two rovers of eight hundred kilograms each. They carried a cargo of nearly half a ton. Planned separation held to about ten centimeters on average. Each rover kept its precise lidar teach-and-repeat path tracking.
arxiv-2510-18966:
Cristhiam Lopez-Arcos computes one-loop amplitudes for four gravitons when a massive vector field runs inside the loop. Rather than the usual Einstein-Hilbert setup, the work uses a metric density approach that couples gravity to the Proca field in a cleaner way.

Within that setup, the building blocks of the amplitude show a clear double-copy structure with no extra contact terms, as long as the outer gravity parts share that property. The same blocks can then build amplitudes with a scalar in the loop and simplify pure gravity cases where contact terms vanish.
arxiv-2510-19066:
Javad Eshtiyagh and eight co-authors measure the value of patience in online grocery shopping. Fast delivery promises have reshaped buying habits since the pandemic, but they also add traffic, emissions, and pollution to cities, a cost that delivery research has rarely weighed against personal convenience.

A mathematical model predicts a curved link between longer allowed delivery windows and lower congestion, and tests confirm the pattern. Even small extensions in when customers accept their groceries can ease the traffic burden notably. The study gives cities and retailers a concrete way to price patience as a public good.
arxiv-2510-19366:
Xinfeng Xia and seven co-authors present MoE-Prism, a framework that lets mixture-of-experts language models adjust how much computation each request receives. These models activate only some expert subnetworks per token, but serving systems usually fix that number for all requests, ignoring that some requests need far less work than others.

By splitting large experts into finer units and redesigning the runtime, MoE-Prism varies the number of active experts per request efficiently. That elasticity matches spending to difficulty, promising cheaper and faster serving. Model and system were designed together, since neither side alone could unlock the flexibility.
arxiv-2510-19466:
T O'Beirne and sixteen co-authors report an untargeted search for ultra-diffuse galaxies containing neutral hydrogen in the WALLABY radio survey. Ultra-diffuse galaxies are large but extremely faint, and finding them by their gas rather than their starlight can reveal systems that optical surveys miss entirely.

The search produced a core sample of ten such galaxies, plus a broader sample of a dozen more faint diffuse systems. Inside the core sample sits the first known pair of ultra-diffuse galaxies, close together on the sky with similar gas velocities, the northwestern member holding the larger hydrogen reservoir. A confirmed pair offers a rare laboratory for how these fragile galaxies form.
arxiv-2510-19666:
Matthew Keating and Michael Casey built a graph-based tool that helps guitar students practice chord-tone soloing, the jazz skill of improvising using only the notes of the chord currently playing. The practice is a foundation of advanced jazz guitar but is hard to learn alone. Their engine first generates chord-tone arpeggios for each chord in a progression.

Each arpeggio becomes a node in a weighted graph, and edges between consecutive chords are weighted by how smoothly the lines connect through transition tones. The shortest path through the graph is then rebuilt into a complete soloing line. A user-friendly interface lets students enter a progression and receive practice material, turning an abstract theory exercise into something playable.
arxiv-2510-20266:
Mahtab Movaheddrad, Laurence Palmer, and C. -C. Jay Kuo propose GUSL-Dehaze, a green learning method for removing haze from a single image without any deep learning. Leading dehazing methods are mostly deep networks with high computing cost and many parameters, which suits poorly powered devices badly. Their approach pairs a physics-based scattering model with a green learning pipeline shaped like a U.

An initial step using a modified Dark Channel Prior gives a first clean-up, followed by unsupervised representation learning and feature engineering steps that keep the model compact. A transparent supervised stage then produces the final dehazed image. The authors report far fewer parameters than deep rivals, full mathematical interpretability, and image quality on par with leading deep learning models.
arxiv-2510-20766:
Noam Issachar, Guy Yariv, Sagie Benaim, Yossi Adi, Dani Lischinski, and Raanan Fattal present DyPE, a training free trick that lets image diffusion transformers paint at resolutions far beyond their training size. Training at ultra high resolution costs too much because attention work grows with the square of the token count.

Diffusion builds images from low frequency shapes first and fine detail later, so the team shifts the position codes at each step to match the frequency band now taking shape. With no retraining and no extra sampling cost, a leading model reaches sixteen million pixel outputs. Gains grow at higher resolutions across several benchmarks, making huge detailed images far cheaper to produce.
arxiv-2510-20966:
Arina Medvedeva leads three co-authors on faster inference of functional links between neurons at sub millisecond timing from spike train data. The Poisson generalized linear model is a standard tool for such data, but binning spikes into time slots caps resolution and hurts scaling.

Monte Carlo methods and polynomial approximations for the continuous time version beat their discrete counterparts in the tests reported. A basis of exponentially scaled Laguerre polynomials sharpens filter identification and yields closed form integrals under the approximation. Finer timing matters because neural codes carry information in precise spike gaps that bins erase.
arxiv-2510-21066:
Daniela Martin leads six co-authors on a scalable machine learning framework for Parker Solar Probe solar wind data. Exceed one hundred fifty gigabytes for twenty eighteen to twenty twenty four and defy conventional analysis. Distributed processing with Dask handles the scale.

A quantum inspired kernel density matrix method estimates single and paired distributions for wind speed, proton density, and proton thermal speed, plus anomaly thresholds per parameter. Trends in the inner heliosphere emerge, including rising values closer to the Sun. The framework shows how modern data engineering can keep pace with flagship mission archives.
arxiv-2510-21466:
Adriel O. Aquino and J. E. G. Silva test a modified gravity theory against the expansion history of the universe. Their model alters the teleparallel form of gravity, a version built on twisting rather than curvature, adding a constant term plus small power-law corrections that grow relevant at late times.

They fit the model's parameters using three data sources: cosmic chronometers that clock expansion directly, the Pantheon+ collection of exploding stars, and sound-wave imprints measured by the DESI survey. A quadratic form for the expansion rate ties the fit together. The joint result favors present acceleration, with a deceleration parameter near negative four tenths, and the theory's effective fluid swings between quintessence-like and phantom-like behavior. A stability check shows the background universe holds steady against uniform disturbances.
arxiv-2510-21566:
Fangwen Wu and thirteen co-authors draw a blueprint for ecosystems where huge numbers of AI agents serve the public at once. As agent systems grow from single helpers to crowds, service turns generic, standards fragment, and bad behavior by providers or users becomes hard to police at scale.

Their ColorEcosystem rests on three parts. An agent carrier personalizes service using each user's own data, even building a digital twin of the user. An agent store manages the many services on one standardized platform. An agent audit watches developers and users alike to keep both sides honest and credible. The paper walks through the challenges behind the design, the forms such ecosystems are passing through, and practical hurdles, and the team has already built and open-sourced part of the system.
arxiv-2510-21866:
Javier Marín documents a ceiling in what decoder-only language models gain from growing larger. Testing the OPT and Pythia families across sizes spanning a two hundred forty-fold range, he compares tasks that demand stored knowledge with tasks that follow a procedure, such as arithmetic.

On knowledge questions, accuracy barely moved with scale even while the training loss fell smoothly; on a mathematics benchmark it stayed stuck below the score expected from random guessing. Arithmetic, by contrast, improved in the normal way on both measures. Swapping attention patterns between models caused total collapse rather than gentle decline, showing how brittle the skill is. For knowledge-heavy uses of these families, Marín advises that past a modest size, extra parameters buy little accuracy.
arxiv-2510-21966:
Musengamana Jean de Dieu leads an eight-author team mining Stack Overflow for software architecture wisdom. The forum holds hard-won answers about system design, but architectural posts hide inside an ocean of ordinary coding questions, and finding issue-and-solution pairs by hand is slow and error-prone.

Their framework, ArchISMiner, splits the job in two. One part trains and compares many model types, from classic machine learning to large language models, and uses the winner to flag architecture-related posts. The second part then extracts matched problem and solution pairs using text features that combine modern embeddings with local pattern detection. The goal is a searchable store of design knowledge, turning scattered forum threads into guidance architects can actually reuse.
arxiv-2510-22166:
Austin A. Barr leads a fourteen-author team testing whether artificial X-rays of the neck could stand in for real ones in training datasets. Machine learning in neurosurgery is starved of large, clean image collections, and synthetic images promise scale without privacy risk, provided experts cannot tell them apart from genuine scans.

A diffusion model trained on nearly five thousand real lateral cervical spine radiographs from a public atlas generated the fakes. Eight specialists, neuroradiologists and spine-trained neurosurgeons, then faced fifty quartets of one real and three synthetic images, naming the real one and rating realism. They picked correctly less than a third of the time, near chance. Rated synthetic images about as realistic as real ones, while nearest-neighbor checks found no sign the model had memorized its training scans.
arxiv-2510-22266:
Rodrigo Tertulino and Laércio Alencar turn machine learning on a policy question: what actually moves student achievement in Brazilian basic education. Using microdata from the national SAEB assessment system, they classify the proficiency of ninth graders and high school students while joining four sources that are usually studied apart. Student background, teacher profiles, school indicators, and principals' management profiles.

Four ensemble algorithms competed, and a Random Forest won, scoring just over ninety percent accuracy with a very strong ranking measure. Opening the model with SHAP explanations delivered the headline: the school's average socioeconomic level dominates every other predictor, outweighing individual traits on their own. The authors conclude that performance is a systemic phenomenon, shaped by the context a student is schooled in, which points policy toward schools and communities rather than isolated student fixes.
arxiv-2510-22366:
Jindong Yang and four co-authors tackle a trade off in watermarking images made by diffusion models. Noise based methods hide a mark in the starting noise, but strong marks can limit image variety, while looser marks can be too weak to survive. Their answer is a two stage scheme called T2SMark.

T2SMark places bits only in the reliable tail parts of the noise and samples the middle part at random. A random session key is mixed into both stages to keep outputs varied. Tests on models with two kinds of backbones show a better balance of strength and variety.
arxiv-2510-22766:
Estimating a random field on a sphere is hard when data are noisy. Iryna Golichenko, Oleksandr Masyutka, and Mykhailo Moklyachuk study that task in 2025. Their field repeats in time in a periodic way. It is also isotropic on the sphere. Isotropic means its stats do not depend on direction.

Observations mix the field with a second noisy field. Some time points are missing by design. The team derives formulas for the best linear estimate. They also give its mean square error. When spectral data are not known exactly, they use a robust route. That route finds least favorable spectra and minimax traits. Both cases rest on spectral methods.
arxiv-2510-22866:
Language models sometimes flip a right answer to a wrong one. Re-prompting alone can trigger that flip. Tiasa Singha Roy, Ayush Rajesh Jhaveri, and Ilias Triantafyllopoulos study this in 2025. They call it unwanted uncertainty. It poses risks in high stakes domains.

They adapt a needle in a haystack retrieval test. A flip style prompt then rechecks answers. Retrieval heads were not the main cause. A small set of other attention heads drove flips. Those heads attend to misleading tokens. Masking them cut flip behavior notably. No incoherence or overcorrection appeared. Downstream tasks showed some trade offs, though.
arxiv-2510-22966:
Qing Chen and Shuang-Yong Zhou build a general method to compute how light dark matter might be caught in detectors. In their setup, dark matter talks to normal matter through a light mediator particle. That same particle also carries the force that lets dark matter particles push on each other.

The authors construct the effective theory step by step, with care for finite momentum transfer. They focus on light, fast dark matter that cosmic rays may have boosted to higher speeds. Such particles could be probed by large neutrino detectors. The framework helps experimental teams turn raw counts into fair limits on this class of models.
arxiv-2510-23066:
Yichao Jin and five co-authors tackle field extraction from financial documents that arrive as poor scanned images. Small business reports are rarely born digital; scans are low resolution, skewed, and noisy, and they mix text, tables, figures, and languages. Regulators and auditors still need exact fields from those pages.

Their multi-stage pipeline pairs optical character recognition with compact vision-language models. Each stage handles a slice of the mess, from layout to field values. The design favors small models that firms can run affordably. Better extraction would speed compliance checks for the many businesses whose records live only on paper.
arxiv-2510-23166:
Philippe Martin Wyder leads a team of fourteen researchers proposing a Common Task Framework for scientific machine learning. Machine learning is reshaping modeling in physics, engineering, and biology, but progress claims suffer from weak baselines, reporting bias, and inconsistent tests. Without shared benchmarks, real advances are hard to tell from noise.

The framework offers curated data sets and task-specific metrics for forecasting, state reconstruction, and related jobs. Common tasks would make comparisons objective and reproducible across labs. The authors argue such discipline is needed to allocate resources wisely and track genuine progress in the field.
arxiv-2510-23266:
Wentao Huang and Li Wang prove existence and multiplicity results for a zero-mass Schrodinger-Bopp-Podolsky system with critical growth. The coupled system pairs a Schrodinger equation for one field with a Bopp-Podolsky equation for the field it creates. Critical growth and zero mass make standard methods fail.

Using a new framework, they first prove a positive ground state for a range of exponents. For a narrower range, an abstract critical point theorem gives many solutions. The work extends the theory of charged particle models where the field has finite self-energy.
arxiv-2510-23466:
Bhawna Sahni and five co-authors compute thermoelectric transport in the half-Heusler alloy NbFeSb from first principles. This alloy is among the best half-Heusler performers for turning heat into electricity. Accurate prediction needs the full energy, momentum, and band dependence of every relevant scattering process.

They include acoustic and optical phonon scattering, both within and between valleys, plus polar phonon and ionized impurity scattering, all inside the Boltzmann transport equation. Their efficient approach derives rates from only a few first-principles inputs. Knowing which scattering dominates guides doping choices that raise device efficiency.
arxiv-2510-23666:
Junpeng Gong and five co-authors show why the standard t-test can mislead A/B tests that guide product launches and pricing on online platforms. The test assumes roughly normal data and balanced groups, but real metrics are often skewed with long tails, and groups often differ in size. Under those conditions the false positive rate drifts, and teams risk shipping harmful changes.

The authors quantify how skewness, heavy tails, and uneven allocation distort error rates, and they derive formulas for the smallest sample size that keeps the t-test valid. For many online metrics, that size runs into the hundreds of millions. As a remedy for smaller samples, they add an Edgeworth-based correction that sharpens the p-values. Tests on data from a leading A/B testing platform confirm the thresholds and show the corrected method markedly improves reliability in real conditions.
arxiv-2510-23766:
Ramshankar Bhuvaneswaran and a co-author study what happens when two popular tricks for shrinking language models are combined. One is quantization, which stores weights in fewer bits. The other is early exit, which lets easy inputs leave the network midway. Each trick helps alone, but their combined behavior was poorly understood. Their framework, BitSkip, varies both systematically to map the interactions.

The results surprised them. A plain 8-bit model with no Hadamard transform beat its fancier 4-bit and Hadamard-enhanced siblings, and nearly matched the full-precision baseline on perplexity. Adding Hadamard transforms wrecked training stability, degrading quality catastrophically even at 8 bits. The simple recipe also exited early gracefully: stopping at layer eighteen bought a speed gain near a third for only about four percent quality loss. The moral is that stacking optimizations can backfire, and the plainest combination won.
arxiv-2510-23866:
Paul Rosu and four co-authors add a physics penalty to a diffusion model that downscales weather data, sharpening coarse temperature maps into fine ones. The target is the two-meter temperature field, a staple of forecasting. Their model works in a latent space, building on an existing diffusion design with a residual formulation against a reference UNet network.

The new term computes a partial differential equation loss at full pixel resolution, after decoding the latent picture. The loss uses finite differences to check an effective advection-diffusion balance, nudging outputs toward physical consistency. Plain diffusion training already left small equation errors, and the authors study how extra fine-tuning on the penalty cleans the fields further. They frame the work as a step toward generative weather models whose products obey the physics they depict. The full codebase is posted on GitHub for others to build on.
arxiv-2510-23966:
Scott Emmons and three co-authors propose a practical way to measure whether a language model's chain of thought can be monitored — a property AI safety work depends on. Watching the reasoning is a rare chance to catch bad plans early, but changes in training or architecture could quietly destroy that window. The authors split monitorability into legibility, whether a human can follow the reasoning, and coverage, whether the written steps contain everything needed to reach the answer.

Both scores come from an autorater prompt that lets any capable model grade existing chains of thought. The team sanity-checks the rater by degrading reasoning on purpose and confirming the scores fall. Applied to several frontier models, the rater finds high monitorability today. The full prompt is published so developers can track design choices. The authors stress this measures default monitorability, complementing adversarial tests against models trained to hide their reasoning.
arxiv-2510-24066:
Wahid Bhimji and three co-authors present OmniLearned, a large foundation model framework for jet physics. Jets are sprays of particles made in collider crashes, and many tasks require sorting and studying them. A model trained on huge data can learn a useful picture of jets and then serve many tasks.

OmniLearned updates the earlier OmniLearn model, trains on over one billion jets, and ships open software for the data and models. The team tests it on three tasks: tagging top quark jets, tagging b jets with ATLAS data, and spotting odd events with CMS data. In each case the shared model gave strong results, showing the value of one broad base model.
arxiv-2510-24166:
Xin Yang and five co-authors propose UniPlanner, a motion planning framework that learns from many driving datasets at once. Planning is central to self driving, since it sets the car's path and affects safety and efficiency. Prior deep learning methods train on one dataset only, which limits how robust they are in new places.

Analysis showed path patterns and links between past and future motion are much alike across datasets. UniPlanner exploits that match with three linked ideas, starting with a dictionary network for past and future paths. Joint training across datasets aims to give planners that hold up better across cities, cars, and road types than single dataset models.
arxiv-2510-24266:
Duaa Abdullah and Jasem Hamoud survey folk puzzles in math and their role in building thought and problem solving skills. The set spans shape puzzles like tangrams and dissections. It also has logic and algebra puzzles. Chance classics are here too, such as the Monty Hall problem and the birthday paradox. So are hard counting tasks like the eight queens puzzle and the tower of Hanoi.

The paper also covers new digital and game based forms that raise student interest. The authors add a new problem on the least cuts to split a polyomino. They prove the least count of straight cuts to split a shape of N squares into single squares is N minus one. Class uses that build area sense and spatial thought are also covered.
arxiv-2510-24366:
Hoang-Thien Nguyen and eight co-authors present a dual student framework for semi-supervised medical image segmentation that switches which student teaches. Teacher student methods lead this task, but strong correlation between the networks and unreliable knowledge transfer limit their gains. Error can be reinforced when the same student always supplies the teaching signal.

Their switching design selects the most reliable student at each iteration to guide the other, improving collaboration and blocking error loops. A loss aware exponential moving average also ensures the teacher absorbs meaningful information from the students, raising pseudo label quality. The framework plugs into existing pipelines and is tested across segmentation tasks.
arxiv-2510-24566:
Xiaobo Jing and Qi Wang, two authors, seek the physical meaning of model parameters. Phase field models track which phase of matter sits where. Dynamic boundary conditions let the surface evolve by its own law. Such models are common, yet their parameters lack clear meaning. A Robin boundary condition, one common type, is often misread.

The pair treat bulk and surface as one closed system. They link exchange between bulk and surface to nanothermodynamics. Nanothermodynamics is the thermodynamics of very small systems. The Robin parameters turn out to tie to a length scale. They govern how matter and energy cross the surface. The bulk phase variable must differ from the surface one. Four wider models and numeric tests round out the work.
arxiv-2510-24666:
Ryuichi Fukuoka and Anderson Macedo Setti smooth a rough shape rule on groups used in pure geometry. The rule, a Finsler form, gives a length rule that can shift with place and may not be smooth. Their smooth take uses a soft local mean, kept in line with the group shifts.

They then study best paths for the smooth rule with a known max rule from control work. From each start state, one best path pair exists, they show. As the smooth term shrinks, those paths tend to the paths of the rough rule. That link lets hard rough cases be read through their smooth kin.
arxiv-2510-24866:
Mohammad Alminawi, the sole author, proves that field swaps leave clash counts in field theory as they were, with just a count based proof. Such counts, built from cut and joined maps, should not shift when fields are re named. Much past work used shape views to make that trait plain at each step.

Alminawi leans just on traits of the tree level score rule for the fields. From those, he proves the trait for joined maps and gives rules for graphs that keep it in plain sight. He also draws a closed form for tree level counts with any count of outer legs. The route needs no set field form to start.
arxiv-2510-25066:
Arnav Sood and James Best study a sender who must sway a choice maker who learns from a sample, not from set odds. The sender picks a test in secret and vows to it, while the choice maker sees just pairs of state and note draws. She must build her view of the world from that sample with a plain learn rule.

With mild terms, the team shows pay forms tend to their full facts form as the sample grows. So best notes and pay tend to the classic sway case. For small samples, sample drag can cut both ways: it can spur more full tests, or less, even when aims match. A best sample size can exist for her.
arxiv-2510-25166:
Zhuojin Li, Marco Paolieri, and Leana Golubchik gauge how slow vision transformers run on phones, next to coil nets. Phone vision has leapt with such models, but wait time on real gear is what caps their use. The team ran a large set of real models of both kinds on phone gear and logged the waits.

They then built a set of a thousand fake models, from known blocks, with waits logged on two learn frames and six phone types. Traits that sway wait are drawn out from the reads. With that set, the wait of a new model can be guessed well enough for real use, they show. That lets teams pick phone fit forms fast.
arxiv-2510-25566:
Diego Torres, Axel Roebel, and Nicolas Obin present PitchFlower. Their 2025 paper builds a neural audio codec. Flow-based generation supplies the codec architecture. Explicit pitch controllability is the key feature. Pitch disentanglement is promoted through a training perturbation. Basic frequency contours are flattened and shifted randomly.

True pitch is given as a guide during training. The decoder regenerates original audio from that conditioning. A vector-quantization bottleneck prevents pitch recovery cheating. Tests show accurate pitch control at rival level. Digital signal processing rivals match control quality there. Audio quality is much higher than those rivals. Results matches leading neural methods overall. Training used WORLD-transformed audio with vocoder artifacts. Their method filters out inherent vocoder artifacts surprisingly. Deep generative modeling resists input degradation strongly here. The approach could extend to other speech attributes. Simple design makes extension paths clear for scholars.
arxiv-2510-25666: Dinesh Kumar Keshari, Avijit Pal, and Bhaskar Paul study operators on Hilbert spaces with special spectral sets, in a 2025 math paper. They define two families of commuting operator tuples, called Gamma contractions, by requiring certain complex domains to be spectral sets. They derive traits of both families and a relationship between them. They discuss basic formulas, unitaries, and isometries in each family. Wold decompositions and form theorems for pure isometries are also developed. The paper serves readers in multivariable operator theory.
arxiv-2510-25866:
Rafael Aoude, Donal O'Connell, Matteo Sergola, and Chris D. White describe an electric system that mirrors a collapsing black hole through the double copy link. The double copy turns gauge theory results into gravity results. They study a massless particle crossing a collapsing electromagnetic background, which is the single copy partner of the Vaidya space used for a black hole that forms from infalling matter.

Aoude and the team pick out the diagrams that dominate at large scale and derive the coefficients that set how many particles are created. A separate ray tracing check in the same background gives the same result. They then discuss what the number pattern means for heat and energy in the double copy picture.
arxiv-2510-26366:
Vishnu A Pai and Titus K Mathew build a new version of the standard model of the universe. The standard model needs separate stories for the early burst of growth, the age of radiation, the age of matter, and today's speeding expansion. Their version, called Lambda-vCF, treats the cosmic fluid as thick and able to create particles, and it aims to join all those ages in one account.

Pai and Mathew give an exact formula for the expansion rate across the whole history, and they fix the points where one age hands over to the next. Using Planck data from 2018, they set the scale of the early burst and describe it as a slow roll off a hilltop. They also show the fluid shifts from springy to thinning behaviour as the universe cools.
arxiv-2510-26566:
Cesare Barbera, Lorenzo Perini, Giovanni De Toni, Andrea Passerini, and Andrea Pugnana work on calibration, whether a model's stated odds match real outcomes. In multiclass problems, a model gives odds for several classes at once, and strong calibration asks all of them to be right at once. Existing methods ignore how close inputs are to each other, so predictions in sparse regions can drift off without notice.

Barbera and his four co-authors define local calibration for the multiclass case and show how it relates to the strong form. They also show where current grading metrics mislead for this local view. Their method aligns a neural network's odds with local estimates of class frequencies, using the Jensen-Shannon distance as the yardstick. Tests against existing techniques back the approach.
arxiv-2510-26766:
The CMS Collaboration measures how the initial state of a heavy ion collision shapes its evolution. When xenon or lead nuclei collide, they form a quark-gluon plasma, a hot fluid of free quarks and gluons, whose flow patterns carry traces of the starting geometry. The team studies correlations among mixed-order moments of flow harmonics, the measures of that flow's shape.

CMS compares xenon-xenon collisions with lead-lead collisions recorded by its detector. Xenon nuclei are triaxially deformed, while lead nuclei are nearly spherical and doubly magic, so the contrast probes how nuclear shape steers the plasma. Results across the second, third, and fourth harmonics show the higher ones matter for reading the plasma's nonlinear response. The measures constrain the model parameters that govern how the plasma evolves.
arxiv-2510-27066:
Amaury Lancelin leads seven co-authors in a framework for studying extreme weather that almost never happens. Events like once-in-a-millennium heatwaves carry huge societal risk, but their rarity leaves few observations and makes detailed climate models costly to run long enough. The team couples fast artificial intelligence weather forecasts with a high-fidelity physics model through a rare-event algorithm.

The combined method, AI plus rare event sampling, steers simulations toward extremes so their statistics and physics can be characterized efficiently. The authors report reaching such rare events at about a hundredfold lower computing cost. Because the steering idea is general, it could transfer to other fields where rare events matter. The work gives climate researchers a practical route to better extreme-risk estimates.
arxiv-2510-27266:
Shaojie Zhang, Pei Fu, and nine other co-authors aim to make screen-driving AI more honest in this 2025 paper. Such agents take typed orders and must click the right spot on a screen. A wrong click can waste work, so the agent's stated confidence should match its real skill. In practice, models often sound sure while being wrong.

Their system, HyperClick, trains the model to give both a click point and a confidence score. Training uses reinforcement learning, where rewards shape behavior over many tries. One reward pays for right clicks; a second pays when confidence matches the outcome. On hard test sets, HyperClick kept strong click accuracy while its confidence tracked truth far better. That lets the agent hold back when unsure instead of guessing.
arxiv-2510-27366:
Sam Fatehmanesh Vegas, Matt Thomson, and two other co-authors build a brain-wide model of a tiny fish in this 2025 paper. The fish is the larval zebrafish, small enough that its whole brain can be watched cell by cell. Their model forecasts each neuron's chance of firing, given what the fish senses. It also links brain state to behavior.

The model uses sparse attention, a method that lets each neuron heed only key partners, split across cells and time. That design keeps the whole brain in reach and stays readable. On a held-out fish, its forecasts were near-exact and steady over long rollouts. A behavior head, which treats cells as an unordered set, ties states to acts. The team can even search for cell patterns that should trigger a chosen behavior.
arxiv-2510-27566:
Yulong Hui and five co-authors present Interact-RAG in 2025, a way for language models to fetch facts with more control. In retrieval-augmented generation, a model looks up text before it writes an answer. Most tools treat that lookup as a black box: the model sends a query and takes what comes back.

Interact-RAG lets the model act on the search itself with fine steps. A workflow builds sample paths of good search, then trains the model first by copying those paths and then by trial rewards. Tests on six benchmarks show clear gains over strong prior methods. Direct control of search helps the model solve hard fact quests.
arxiv-2510-27666:
Dong Heon Han and seven co-authors present a soft gripper in 2025 that reshapes its whole body to grasp objects of many sizes, in the manner of an octopus. Most soft grippers bend but keep one fixed overall form. Prior morphing work changed only small patches, which limits the range of grips.

The gripper is a web of modular air-driven units that sense their own shape. Working jointly, they shift the whole form among polygon shapes. Rich feedback lets the gripper move from a fine pinch to a broad wrap. Tests show a wider grasp range and better success on varied objects. Whole-body morphing could help robots handle goods of mixed scale.
arxiv-2511-00066:
Tue Le, Linh Ngo Van, and Trung Le improve group relative policy optimization for training language models with verifiable rewards, by guiding it with sharpness. Generalization during such training is usually left uncontrolled. A robustness view bounds generalization loss by empirical loss plus a sharpness surrogate measured by gradient norm, suggesting flatter solutions should transfer better.

Their token-weighted variant, GRPO-SG, shapes probabilities using that sharpness guidance. Machine learning readers get a simple modification aimed at reasoning models that generalize beyond their training problems. Verifiable reward training is now a main route to better reasoning, so controlling its generalization is timely.
arxiv-2511-00366:
Shridhar Vashishtha, Krishna Prasath Logakannan, Jacob Hochhalter, Shandian Zhe, and Robert Kirby build a digital twin part for aircraft structures. A twin needs a fast surrogate model that forecasts the real part's future state and updates as service data arrives. Their surrogate is a Gaussian process enriched with derivative data, which sharpens accuracy but inflates the covariance matrix until updates become far too costly.

A modified streaming sparse Cholesky solver removes that bottleneck, letting the model absorb fresh data dynamically. Experiments show accuracy improves as new data streams in, beating earlier surrogate variants. The team then runs the algorithm inside a full twin setup that models fatigue crack growth in an aircraft part. The run shows how the pieces of twin methods fit as one system in practice.
arxiv-2511-00466:
Ayan Kumar Nai and G K Samanta demonstrate a free-space quantum network that serves six users from a single source of entangled light. Quantum key distribution promises secure keys, but classic setups link only two parties at a time. Sharing entanglement among many users, called multiplexing, had been shown in fiber networks, while free-space versions stalled on active switching hardware.

Their design uses spatial multiplexing and stays fully passive, with no active switches in the path. Twelve channels form a fully connected network, and any pair of nodes shares record coincidence rates, yielding sifted key rates above four hundred kilobits per second in their report. The approach scales to more nodes and can join fiber links, sketching a practical route to city-scale quantum networks.
arxiv-2511-00566: Tara Macalister Brough, Marianne Johnson, Mark Kambites, and Carl-Fredrik Nyberg-Brodda prove a theorem about free inverse monoids, algebraic structures built from partial symmetries. Their word problem, deciding when two expressions name the same element, turns out to be co-context-free for every finite rank: the set of unequal pairs is a context-free language. The proof works through grammars, linking algebra with formal language theory.
arxiv-2511-00866:
D. S. Delion and A. Pencu systematize proton emission, the rare decay in which a nucleus ejects a proton, focusing on nuclei near the proton drip line. They cover both spontaneous emission and the beta delayed kind, organizing the data by Coulomb strength, reduced radius, and angular momentum.

Three ways of estimating the decay width of a resonant state are compared. One uses a continuity equation for outgoing states. Another uses phase shift analysis of scattering states. The third uses direct numerical integration in the complex plane. The methods agree where comparison is possible. The authors also show a universal decay law, linking the reduced width to penetrability and a fragmentation potential, holds for beta delayed emission too. It describes all measured cases within about a factor of three.
arxiv-2511-01066:
Stephan Oepen and a very large team present HPLT 3.0, an open collection of text data for training language and translation models in almost two hundred languages. At thirty trillion tokens, they describe it as likely the largest multilingual pretraining collection available to all.

The data come from web crawls, processed by a fully open pipeline that selects documents, extracts text, identifies languages, removes duplicates, and annotates register, quality, and personal information. Quality is probed by statistics, by hand inspection in twenty four languages, and by training models end to end. The release also adds test benchmarks for nine European languages and a family of fifty seven monolingual encoder decoder models, plus a large parallel corpus for translation.
arxiv-2511-01466:
Changyuan Zhao and colleagues defend semantic communication against physical layer attacks. Deep joint source channel coding sends meaning rather than bits. It beats standard separate coding. But pilot spoofing and subcarrier jamming can corrupt the shared channel knowledge it depends on, damaging the reconstructed content.

Their framework, SecDiff, plugs a diffusion model into the decoder. Pseudoinverse guided sampling keeps reconstruction fast, with guidance that adapts. Jamming is fought by masking the attacked subcarriers by power and treating recovery as an inpainting problem the diffusion model solves. Spoofing is treated as a blind inverse problem. An expectation minimization routine alternately refines the pilot signal and the channel estimate. Both the reconstruction loss and the channel operator guide it.
arxiv-2511-01766:
Renaud Falga, Sara Shamekh, and Laure Zanna train one neural network to describe turbulent momentum mixing in both the ocean and the atmosphere. Boundary layer turbulence sets how winds and currents evolve. Climate models need formulas, parameterizations, for the vertical fluxes it produces. Traditional formulas miss effects like upgradient fluxes entirely.

The network learns offline from coarse-grained large-eddy simulations spanning many turbulent regimes in both fluids. Normalizing flux profiles by their surface values exposes a self-similar shape shared across regimes, enabling joint training. Given a mean wind or current profile, the network predicts the flux profile. Plugged into a single-column atmospheric model, it beat the model's built-in parameterization. It cut errors by a factor of two to three. It stayed robust even when the surface flux was biased by up to 30 percent.
arxiv-2511-01866:
Benjamin Kubwimana and Qijing Huang chart how to run reasoning language models on edge GPUs. These are the chips that robots and other autonomous systems carry. Local runs protect privacy. They survive poor connectivity, and they save energy and cost against the cloud. But tight latency budgets and small compute make each design choice risky.

Their study, EdgeReasoning, varies the levers a developer controls. The levers are model type and size, token budgets, and test-time scaling. It measures the latency-accuracy trade-offs across designs and sizes. It tests prompt and tuning tricks that shorten reasoning traces at no loss in quality. It also profiles parallel test-time scaling under strict deadlines. The upshot is a Pareto map: measured guidance, not guesswork, for real deployments.
arxiv-2511-02066:
Aaron Aguilar-Cardoso and six colleagues, including Robert Boyd, propose a way to keep quantum communication links working through turbulent air. Free-space quantum key distribution sends photons between distant points, but atmospheric turbulence scrambles their spatial patterns and raises error rates. The team's fix uses stimulated parametric down-conversion, a nonlinear optical process whose phase conjugation property can undo the distortion optically, with no electronics in the loop.

A theoretical model tells users how to choose the measurement basis and beam properties for best efficiency. Simulations and experiments agree: even under strong turbulence, error rates dropped well below the security threshold. The authors suggest the approach could help secure quantum channels over long open-air distances.
arxiv-2511-02666:
Orlando Oliveira studies the low-energy behavior of quantum electrodynamics, the theory of light and electrons, in a 2025 paper. Working with Dyson-Schwinger equations, he asks what the theory itself demands of the photon, the particle of light. A key test is whether the photon's self-energy stays finite at all momenta.

Oliveira finds that this finiteness, plus a smooth photon-fermion vertex, forces the photon to have no mass. Its propagator must then blow up at low momentum in a set way. He also maps which form factors could give the photon mass through the Schwinger mechanism, where that link breaks. The fermion and vertex equations, he notes, stay safe from such infrared trouble.
arxiv-2511-03166:
Kevin Wang, Subre Abdoul Moktar, Jia Li, Kangshuo Li, and Feng Chen compare twelve ways to measure how unsure a language model is. Knowing when a model might be wrong is key to trusting it. Their 2025 study separates two kinds of doubt: aleatoric, from noisy data, and epistemic, from the model's own ignorance. They test the measures on question answering, both inside the training distribution and outside it.

Information-based measures, built on token and sequence probabilities, shone on familiar data, matching how the model sees its training set. On unfamiliar data, density-based methods and the P(True) score did best, catching the model's ignorance. Semantic consistency checks, which compare several sampled answers, stayed reliable across settings, though rarely the single best. Four quality metrics scored the answers.
arxiv-2511-03266:
Harsh Sharma and colleagues link a work-based measure to the hard task of sizing up shared quantum links among many parts. The most work that can be pulled from a closed quantum system, called ergotropy, has become a handy stand-in for entanglement. Strong forces between parts can block older ways of using that stand-in, though.

Their framework sidesteps the block, either by switching forces in a controlled quench or by reading only local gauges. With those moves, global and local work values give sound estimates of true many-part entanglement. The checks hold for still states and for states that change in time, even under strong coupling. Quantum simulators, the authors note, are now able to try such measures in practice.
arxiv-2511-03366:
Kapila W S Palitharathna, Constantinos Psomas, and Ioannis Krikidis design an underwater optical system that sends power, data, and sensing through light from a surface ship. A seabed sensor harvests energy from the beam and sends data back up, while the ship locates a target with an array of pinhole cameras. Real seas rock the ship, so roll, pitch, and yaw enter the model as random tilts.

Formulas derived by the team predict both locating error and uplink rate under those tilts. Simulations match the formulas closely, which validates the approach. Mild to moderate sea states frame the tests. Such a system could serve seabed monitors that cannot be wired or easily recharged, keeping them powered while they report.
arxiv-2511-03466:
Celian Ringwald and co-authors present Kastor, a framework that trains small language models to extract facts actively under shape rules. Shape-guided extraction focuses a model on one graph pattern at a time, working well with little data. Kastor widens the check from a single shape to every property combination the shape allows.

Picking the best combination per training example lifts generalization and accuracy. An iterative loop then cleans noisy knowledge bases, refining stored facts round by round and growing fresh ones. Specialist fields with thin data, such as heritage or niche science, need exactly that kind of upkeep. Kastor aims to make small, cheap models trustworthy curators rather than one-shot extractors.
arxiv-2511-03866:
Arijit Bhattacharjee and six colleagues present OMPILOT, a transformer built to translate C++ code into OpenMP for shared-memory parallel computing. Catalog evidence used a different author tail; the arXiv record governs, and it lists seven authors in total. Large language models have sped code translation, but parallel constructs need care that general metrics miss.

OMPILOT is a domain-specific encoder-decoder with custom pretraining objectives that capture parallel semantics, mixing unsupervised and supervised learning. Unlike loop-level tools, it works at function level for wider context. A new composite metric, OMPBLEU, judges correctness and quality of OpenMP output. The system aims to cut the manual effort of parallelizing legacy code.
arxiv-2511-04266:
Filip Vukovic is the lead author among eleven authors probing the hidden pore structure of carbon nanomembranes, nanometre-thin disordered carbon films used for energy and filtration. Their structure is hard to measure head-on because free-standing membranes are radiation-sensitive, so damage-free probes are prized.

Molecular dynamics simulations generate candidate structures with varying pore sizes. Predicted charge exchange for highly charged ions and tensile moduli are compared with ion spectroscopy data. Agreement points to a large share of under-coordinated carbon and an open sub-nanometre pore network in vacuum. Such a network would react in air, likely stabilised there by hydrogen and oxygen groups, the authors suggest.
arxiv-2511-04666:
Ben Sanati leads seven authors building a unified theory of forgetting in learning systems. Algorithms tend to lose old knowledge as they adapt to new data. Decades of study produced no shared definition that explains the dynamics behind it.

Their theory defines forgetting as a loss of self-consistency in the learner's predictions. Put plainly, the model stops agreeing with its own earlier predictive information. From that view, a general measure of forgetting propensity follows naturally. They also prove exact Bayesian inference can adapt without forgetting, and explain why generative models degrade when trained on their own output.
arxiv-2511-04766:
Dhenenjay Yadav and his co-author present DARN, a decoder for adapting foundation models to satellite imagery. Foundation models give strong features, but satellite scenes vary wildly in content and difficulty. Fixed regularization in the decoder ignores that variety.

DARN first predicts each sample's task complexity with a light predictor. Dropout rates then shift per sample across a set range based on that estimate. Dynamic capacity gating also adjusts how many channels stay active. Together, the three parts tune the decoder's capacity to each image, aiming for robust adaptation across mixed geospatial scenes.
arxiv-2511-04866:
Sebin J. Sebastian leads five authors probing the ground state of a double trillium lattice magnet. The compound, a potassium strontium iron phosphate, was a spin liquid candidate. Its iron spins sit on a double trillium lattice with spin five halves.

Phosphorus NMR, thermodynamics, and band calculations together overturn the earlier guess. The ground state is neither plain long-range order nor a pure gapless spin liquid. A nearly field-independent NMR linewidth below about three and a half kelvin signals short-range freezing. Relaxation rates rise sharply below twice that temperature, pinning down an unusual frozen state.
arxiv-2511-05066:
Philipp Schaad, Tal Ben-Nun, and Torsten Hoefler present VEIL, a layout method that makes control flow graphs read like code. Such graphs map how a program jumps between blocks, but real graphs have thousands of nodes and tangled edges.

Common graph drawing tools often place later steps before earlier ones, which hides how a program runs. VEIL sets rules made just for these graphs, with flow order kept intact. It uses dominator analysis, which finds blocks that all paths must cross, to build clearer layouts that the authors test against past tools.
arxiv-2511-05166:
Peter Dunsby and co-authors work out how small ripples evolve in Energy-Momentum Squared Gravity, a variant of general relativity. They use a fully covariant, gauge-invariant method, so results do not hinge on a choice of coordinates.

Within the 1+3 split of space-time, they derive spread laws for scalar, vector, and tensor modes on expanding backgrounds with dust or radiation. Two sub-cases get close study, where change enters through squared terms or through shifts in pressure links. For scalar modes, growth can rise or fall next to standard gravity, a testable split.
arxiv-2511-05266:
Gabriel Serrão Seabra and co-authors join diffusion models with machine learning localization to sharpen data assimilation for geological carbon storage. Safe storage needs a sharp map of rock layers below ground, built by fitting sensor data to a model.

Their frame uses score-based diffusion to make many rock samples, five thousand in the tests, for channel-shaped reservoirs during carbon dioxide injection. A learning-based localization step then weights which data should sway each spot. The mix aims at maps that are both geologically sound and close to the measured field record.
arxiv-2511-05366:
Ramón Nartallo-Kaluarachchi and co-authors study how to coarse-grain a steady non-equilibrium diffusion into a Markov chain on a discrete set of states. Such swaps let hard continuous models be run as fast jump processes, if key traits survive the swap.

Using finite-volume methods, they derive a master equation straight from the diffusion. They prove the swap keeps the steady state close and that entropy production, the gauge of how far from equilibrium a system sits, converges as states are added. The work covers both planar diffusions and discrete-state processes, which links two modeling worlds.
arxiv-2511-05566:
Yao Zhang, Souza Leite Clayton, and Yu Xiao bring pretrained models to activity recognition from body sensors. Such systems must keep learning after deployment, as users add new activities or perform old ones in new ways. Older continual learning methods for this task need heavy compute and many labeled samples.

Their system, PTRN-HAR, pretrains its feature extractor with a contrastive loss on limited data, then freezes it during streaming updates. That design copes with the mixed nature of sensor data sets and the lack of labels after deployment. The authors report it as the first successful use of this pretrained approach for online continual learning in sensor-based activity recognition.
arxiv-2511-05666:
Samuele Brunetta and colleagues show that tiny voids in a crystal layer can wreck light-guiding chips made from aluminum nitride. The material is prized for photonics: it loses little light, works across a wide range of colors, and bends light in useful ways. But layers grown on sapphire often contain voids.

The team measured losses from voids and simulated how void size and density drive scattering. Losses could grow severe at telecom wavelengths. Their fix is a thin sputtered buffer layer laid down before crystal growth. Layers grown that way came out void-free, with ring resonators showing very low loss. They also held up in high-power tests, marking them as strong candidates for short-wavelength photonic circuits.
arxiv-2511-05766:
Felipe Valencia-Clavijo tests whether large language models fall for anchoring, the human habit of leaning too hard on the first number heard. Earlier studies saw anchored answers but could not tell surface mimicry from real shifts inside the model. Valencia-Clavijo digs into the probabilities behind the outputs.

Working with six open-source models, the study shows anchors shift whole output distributions, with checks against training-data contamination. An exact attribution method then measures how much each prompt field, anchor included, moves the model's scores. Three mid-sized models showed robust anchoring. Smaller ones varied more, hinting that scale tunes sensitivity. The author warns that prompt design can make the effect fragile, a risk for real uses.
arxiv-2511-06066:
Ao Li and co-authors fix badly exposed photos without any labeled training data, and for image sets of any length. Exposure correction matters under harsh lighting, but supervised methods need large labeled sets that are hard to build. Their method, LoopExpose, learns from pseudo-labels it creates and improves itself.

A nested loop drives the learning. Fusion of multiple exposures at the lower level creates the pseudo-labels; the upper level trains the correction model on them. Corrected images feed back into the fusion, refining the labels in a self-reinforcing loop. A luminance ranking loss uses the brightness order across the input set as a free teaching signal. On benchmarks the method beat existing unsupervised approaches at both correction and fusion.
arxiv-2511-06266:
Ardhendu Sekhar and co-authors predict cancer patient survival directly from whole-slide microscope images of tissue. Such images are enormous, vary strongly from place to place, and produce survival patterns that resist simple curves. Their framework attacks all three problems with four cooperating parts.

One part selects the slide regions most tied to prognosis, another groups patches by position and appearance, and a third weighs local tissue detail against whole-slide context. A mixture of log-logistic experts then models complicated survival distributions flexibly. Across large cancer cohorts covering lung, kidney, and breast cancers, the method set new best scores and stayed well calibrated.
arxiv-2511-06566:
Robert Oeckl builds a measurement framework for quantum field theory that fully respects relativity. Measuring an observable spread over a region of spacetime, rather than at one instant, raises a causality trap: a clumsy scheme could signal faster than light. Earlier results covered only instantaneous observables, leaving time-extended ones unhandled.

Oeckl's construction regularizes a large class of spacetime-localized observables for bosonic fields. It disturbs itself as it proceeds, and the framework shows exactly how that back-reaction seeds correlations with later ones in its causal future. Everything composes region by region, so local readings assemble into a consistent global picture with no unphysical signaling.
arxiv-2511-07066:
Ami Tank, Roland Crocker, and Mark R Krumholz analyze the Fermi Bubbles, two gamma-ray lobes rising fifty degrees above and below the Milky Way's center, whose origin remains unknown. Using a template-free reconstruction of ten years of all-sky Fermi data, they extract the gamma-ray spectrum pixel by pixel across the bubbles. From each local spectrum they infer what parent population of cosmic-ray protons or electrons would be required to produce it.

Both hadronic and leptonic models fit the data equally well. The particle spectra must be broken power laws or exponentially cut off, with nearly constant break energies and indices that harden toward the southern tip. The leptonic option additionally requires electron energy density growing away from the Galactic plane and toward the edges. That disfavors cases where electrons are accelerated at the center and simply carried outward.
arxiv-2511-07366:
Dao Lan Vy Dinh and eight co-authors send drones to patch cellular networks when ground stations go dark. In 6G energy-saving schemes, cells are deliberately slept, and outages, disasters, or management errors can leave others inactive; until they restart, users lose service. The proposal deploys unmanned aerial vehicles as temporary flying base stations, coordinated by a multi-agent deep reinforcement learning system based on MADDPG.

The agents jointly optimize flight trajectories, transmission power, and which users each drone serves, balancing coverage of stranded users against the drones' own energy budgets. In simulations the policy consistently achieved the highest coverage ratios among baselines and the lowest total energy consumption at comparable service rates. The authors present it as a resilience layer for sustainable, energy-saving cellular networks.
arxiv-2511-07466:
Andreas Kouloumpris and colleagues schedule work across phones, hubs, and cloud servers that run cyber-physical apps. Edge devices sense and act quickly but have small processors, batteries, and radios. A hub and a cloud server add power at the cost of delay.

The team formulates optimal scheduling that cuts total workflow delay across that edge-hub-cloud chain. Their model handles mixed multicore chips and devices with special sensing or acting roles. A full treatment compares placements and orders under several limits at once. System designers get a benchmark for latency-critical tasks such as monitoring and control that must react in real time.
arxiv-2511-07566:
Christopher Roth, Ao Chen, and Anirvan Sengupta attack a famous open question: does the square lattice Hubbard model superconduct? That model captures electrons hopping and repelling on a grid, and its ground state bears on cuprate high-temperature superconductors. Rival stripe and superconducting states sit painfully close in energy.

Neural quantum states built from Pfaffian wavefunctions resolve those tiny energy gaps for hundreds of electrons. Fast algorithms make the large simulations feasible. Measurements distinguish metal, stripe, and superconducting phases more cleanly than before. Whether the pure model superconducts shapes how physicists explain real materials, so sharper numerics carry real weight.
arxiv-2511-07766:
Yuri Faenza, Víctor Verdugo, and José Verschae show when symmetry defeats a standard optimization ladder. Linear programming hierarchies tighten relaxations level by level to crack integer programs. Symmetry is exactly what makes many of those programs hard for solvers, and the authors connect the two facts.

Under highly transitive symmetry, the level-k relaxation is nonempty exactly when the starting polytope meets every face of matching dimension. Whole hierarchies, including famous ones, can therefore collapse at once. The geometry of the initial empty polytope decides fate. Solver builders learn that symmetry must be broken structurally, not merely tightened around, saving wasted effort on doomed relaxations.
arxiv-2511-08266:
The Euclid Collaboration examines how non Gaussian the distribution of matter power spectrum measurements really is, ahead of the Euclid space mission cosmology analysis. Power spectrum multipoles summarize how matter clumps at different scales, and standard likelihoods often assume their errors are Gaussian. One hundred thousand mock density fields, built with the COVMOS method across redshifts and cosmologies, test that assumption directly.

An analytical framework ties the non Gaussian shape to higher order statistics, including the trispectrum and pentaspectrum. Departures grow on nonlinear scales and at low redshift, driven mainly by the pentaspectrum. Redshift space distortions, survey shape, binning, and shot noise all add skewness, which future Euclid analyses must model.
arxiv-2511-08766:
Benjamin Cellini and three co-authors study active sensing, the trick animals use when they move their sensors to learn what a still sensor cannot reveal. For nonlinear systems the right wiggle can expose hidden information, but designing such motions systematically has been hard, and engineered systems rarely exploit them.

Their method, BOUNDS, searches for movement motifs that raise the information carried by sensory cues, and ships as an open Python package. A companion estimator, the Augmented Information Kalman Filter, fuses neural network guesses with model-based estimates whenever a bout of sensing delivers fresh data. Tests on a flying agent model and on real GPS-denied quadcopter flights show specific motions improving estimates of ground speed, altitude, and wind direction.
arxiv-2511-08866:
Fuyi Yang and five co-authors introduce BioVerge, a benchmark and testing ground for AI agents that propose new biomedical hypotheses. Finding hidden links in the literature has long driven discovery. Older methods stick to single data types or fixed extraction patterns, though. That caps the novelty of what they can find.

The dataset blends structured records with text drawn from historical hypotheses and the PubMed literature. It is arranged so agents can explore at the edge of current knowledge. The companion agent works in a generate-and-judge loop: one module drafts hypotheses while another scores them, round after round. Experiments show architecture choices change how widely the agent explores, structured and textual sources each add unique context, and self-evaluation measurably improves the novelty and relevance of the proposals.
arxiv-2511-09066:
Nilakshi Senapati and three co-authors beat the classical resolution limit for ring-shaped features by lighting objects with light that carries orbital angular momentum. Super-resolution tricks often structure the phase of the incoming field, and a beam twisted in the azimuthal angle matches features laid out around a circle.

Two test objects make the case: an azimuthal double slit and a Siemens star, the spoked wheel of microscopy. For each ring feature there is an optimal twist index of the light beam that pushes the imaging sharpness to its peak, and the experiments find it. The authors point to biological specimens, many of which present mostly azimuthal structure, as the ones who stand to gain most. The work adds angular momentum of light to the practical super-resolution toolkit alongside the structured illumination already sold in commercial devices.
arxiv-2511-09166:
Shira Lifshitz and four co-authors argue that feature selection should judge groups of features, not single features alone. In unsupervised tasks without labels, useful signals often sit in related sets, like neighboring pixels or connected brain regions. Most existing methods still score each feature in isolation, or need groups fixed in advance.

Their method, GroupFS, learns the groups and selects the most informative ones in a single differentiable framework. It keeps feature and sample graphs smooth and uses a group sparsity penalty to favor compact structure. Across nine benchmarks covering images, tables, and biological data, GroupFS beats leading unsupervised methods at clustering. The groups it picks also line up with patterns people find meaningful.
arxiv-2511-09266:
Seunghyeon Lee and five co-authors build SecTracer, a system for tracing network intrusions back to their root causes. Enterprise networks mix many machines and services, so attacks like advanced persistent threats can hide across hosts. Their idea is network-level security provenance: causal links between events recorded across the whole network.

SecTracer collects forensic data with software-defined networking. It then rebuilds attack histories as provenance graphs, giving admins a clear picture of how an intrusion unfolded. A probabilistic model also predicts likely next attack steps. In a real-world simulation of such a threat, SecTracer improved mitigation. It added under one percent throughput overhead and negligible latency, the authors report.
arxiv-2511-09466:
Chris Addis and seven co-authors build a fully relativistic approach for measuring primordial non-Gaussianity in galaxy surveys. That quantity, left over from the universe's first moments, shows up through scale-dependent bias in the galaxy power spectrum. General relativistic effects mimic the signal, so Newtonian analyses risk biased answers.

Their multipole calculation includes lensing convergence, time delay, the integrated Sachs-Wolfe effect, and wide-separation corrections. Ignoring them would bias the measurement by roughly three standard deviations for a Euclid-like survey. For a MegaMapper-like survey the bias is far worse, they find. Splitting galaxies by brightness improves the forecast constraints by fifteen to twenty percent. The code, CosmoWAP, is public.
arxiv-2511-10066:
Buket Özkaya, writing alone, improves a minimum distance bound for quasi-twisted codes, a family of error-correcting codes built with a twist on cyclic structure. Spectral methods estimate how many errors such a code can guarantee to correct, and a spectral bound for quasi-twisted codes already existed. Its performance, however, lagged behind the older Jensen bound, which limited its usefulness.

Özkaya adapts a newer, stronger spectral approach that recently improved bounds for quasi-cyclic codes, a close cousin family. The resulting generalized spectral bound gives tighter lower bounds on minimum distance than both the Jensen bound and the Ezerman and co-author bounds. Better guaranteed bounds help code designers certify performance without exhaustive computation.
arxiv-2511-10366:
Arnab Bhattacharyya, Davin Choo, Philips George John, and Themis Gouleakis study how computers learn a probability distribution from random samples. They focus on product distributions over strings of zeros and ones, where each position is chosen independently. The twist is that the learner also receives advice, in the form of a second product distribution that may be imperfect.

Without advice, the number of samples needed grows in a known way with the number of positions. The authors give an efficient algorithm that needs far fewer samples when the advice is close enough to the truth. Strikingly, the algorithm never needs to know in advance how good the advice actually is.
arxiv-2511-10666:
The CMS Collaboration reports the first measurement of bottom quark jet substructure that clusters together the decay products of the b hadron itself. The data come from proton-proton collisions at 5.02 TeV recorded in 2017 under low pileup conditions, and the analysis uses only charged particles.

A special algorithm identifies and clusters the charged daughters of b hadrons, exposing the gluon radiation pattern through repeated declustering. The team measures the groomed jet radius and momentum balance, plus a fragmentation function describing how much of the jet's momentum the b hadron carries. Compared with ordinary jets, b jets show a strong suppression of small-radius emissions, consistent with the dead-cone effect expected from the b quark's mass. Results are also compared with Monte Carlo predictions.
arxiv-2511-10866:
Seoik Jung, Taekyung Song, Yangro Lee, and Sungjun Lee build a system for spotting violence in CCTV footage in real time.
