Rather than training on long videos, their Short-Window Sliding Learning framework chops footage into clips of one to two seconds. It uses a large language model to auto-caption them, creating fine-grained labeled data.

Because each short clip uses all of its frames, rapid violent events keep their temporal shape instead of being smeared across a long window. The method reached 95.25 percent accuracy on the RWF-2000 benchmark and 83.25 percent on long videos from UCF-Crime, a substantial improvement there. The authors present the framework as evidence that short-window training generalizes to real surveillance while staying fast enough for live use.
arxiv-2511-11066:
Jiechao Gao, Chang Liu, and Yuangang Li present S2D-Align, a training method for software that writes radiology reports from scan images. Large models that join images and text can draft such reports, but standard training only pairs each scan with its report as a whole. That loose pairing misses the body-part detail that good reports need, so draft quality suffers.

Their method builds alignment in stages, from shallow to deep. It starts with the coarse scan-report pair, adds reference reports for guidance, and ends with key phrases tied to body parts. A memory-based adapter shares features across stages, which grounds the writing in anatomy step by step.
arxiv-2511-11366:
Benjamin Blakely and Daniel Karcz present Grid-STIX, a security ontology for power grids built as an extension of the STIX 2.1 threat intelligence standard. Power grids are cyber-physical systems whose assets and links do not fit traditional IT security models, and general standards lack grid-specific coverage. Grid-STIX keeps full compliance with the base standard while adding the missing domain structure.

Its modular design covers physical assets, operational technology parts, cyber-physical relationships, and security policies, including distributed energy resources, smart metering, and nuclear facilities. Attack patterns, supply chain risks, and cross-domain impacts can be modeled systematically. Modules also address nuclear safeguards and non-proliferation checks, with Zero Trust policy points supported.
arxiv-2511-11666:
Rajit Rajpal, Benedict Leimkuhler, and Yuanhao Jiang improve sampling for Bayesian neural networks, which need to explore a whole distribution over network weights rather than settle on one best setting. Stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics does the exploring, but its accuracy hinges on a stepsize that is painful to tune.

Popular adaptive variants quietly sample the wrong distribution unless an expensive correction is added. Building on the SamAdams framework, the proposed SA-SGLD rescales time so steps shrink in high-curvature regions and grow in flatter ones automatically. Better sampling without hand tuning would make honest uncertainty estimates from neural networks cheaper and more trustworthy.
arxiv-2511-11966:
Steven Cao, Gregory Valiant, and Percy Liang study entropy calibration in language models. The question is whether a model's uncertainty over its own generations matches its true loss on human text. Past work found miscalibration. Entropy creeps up as generations lengthen and errors pile up.

The standard fix truncates the output distribution. That fix sacrifices diversity, which users want to keep. A simplified theoretical setting characterizes how miscalibration scales with dataset size. The real questions follow from it. Does scale fix calibration on its own? If not, can calibration be had without trade-offs? The answers bear on every decoding trick in daily use.
arxiv-2511-12166:
Anders Björn, Jana Björn and David Manolis study whether solutions to nonlinear elliptic equations behave well at a boundary point placed at infinity. The equations are of p-Laplace type, set on unbounded domains, and the relevant range links the exponent to the space dimension. Regularity at infinity is not obvious, since the point lies far from any finite region.

Their approach uses circular inversion, which sends infinity to the origin and turns the equation into a similar weighted one. Known Wiener-type criteria at the origin can then be carried back to infinity. In one range the criterion simplifies greatly, while a counterexample shows the borderline case behaves differently.
arxiv-2511-12366:
Eren Erberk Erkul identifies a counterpart of the Unruh effect inside relativistic fluid dynamics. The classic Unruh effect says an accelerated observer in empty space detects a thermal bath. Erkul asks what a probe moving with a relativistic fluid measures when the fluid is out of equilibrium.

Changes of frame in first-order hydrodynamics are recast as a local, time-dependent hyperbolic rotation in a state space for thermodynamics. The rate of that rotation defines a thermodynamic acceleration, which yields an Unruh-like thermal spectrum. To leading order the resulting temperature does not depend on the frame, and it stays universal across several modern descriptions of relativistic fluids.
arxiv-2511-12566:
Cervane Grimaud and eight co-authors describe how the Virgo gravitational wave detector was calibrated for its fourth observing run, and how bias and uncertainty in the reconstructed strain signal are now computed. Since the first detection in 2015, detector sensitivity has improved so much that precise calibration is essential to trust the strain, the tiny stretch signal from passing waves.

The account covers the photon calibrator used to set mirror motion with sub-percent precision, and the calibration of every mirror actuator. During the run the reconstruction reached a stated precision across the main frequency band. A new frequency-dependent method computes bias and uncertainty, and the strain is corrected online for the bias it finds.
arxiv-2511-12766:
Chaouki Hjaiji, Bassem Ouni, and Mohamed-Slim Alouini map the cybersecurity of high-altitude platform stations, nodes that hover in the stratosphere in future non-terrestrial networks. Such stations link users, control systems, and power systems in one exposed platform, so their attack surface is wide. The authors survey the subsystems and links, sort threats into a stratosphere-aware taxonomy, and match exposures across communication, control, and power subsystems to defenses that fit the platform's tight constraints.

Defenses include encryption and authentication, frequency agility, beam-steered antennas, intrusion detection, secure boot, and supply-chain assurance, each mapped to emerging standards and regulation. A simulation case study in OMNeT++ measures how a distributed denial-of-service attack degrades service and control availability. The study is simulation-based, meant to guide engineering trade-offs rather than validate a flying system.
arxiv-2511-13266:
José J. Gil argues that one algebraic object sits at the root of geometric phase in both light polarization and quantum two-level systems. For an ideal retarder, the antisymmetric block of its Mueller matrix holds a vector that drives motion on the Poincaré sphere. That vector alone fixes the Pancharatnam-Berry phase, while the symmetric block adds no geometric effect.

Gil shows the same generator also controls how pure qubit states move on the Bloch sphere. Because the link is shared, geometric phase can be spotted and steered from lab data in both fields. Mueller matrix readings and qubit process data both fit the same practical test.
arxiv-2511-13366:
Akram Heidari and Mark Podolskij prove a local normality result for the likelihood of watched McKean-Vlasov diffusions. These equations describe particles whose motion depends on the whole group's distribution, a mean-field effect. One shared parameter sits in both drift and diffusion, which makes the statistics harder.

The authors expand the log ratio with Malliavin calculus tools and prove the property under stated conditions. Hidden transition densities are the main obstacle, handled through integration by parts and Gaussian-type bounds. The result extends earlier work on interacting particle systems into the mean-field regime and supports sound inference for nonlinear stochastic models.
arxiv-2511-13566:
Clayton P. Byers and Subrahmanyam Duvvuri use the bispectrum to trace how energy moves between scales in a forced turbulent boundary layer. The bispectrum is a third-order spectrum that keeps phase links between triples of scales, unlike standard spectra. Its normalized form and its phase reveal how much coupled energy sits at each scale and which way it flows.

Summing over matched triples splits the velocity skewness into scale-by-scale parts. Scales smaller than the boundary layer thickness fed a forward cascade on average, while larger scales mixed forward and reverse transfer. Forced scales showed both directions at once, varying by triple and by height, giving a filter-free way to grade outside forcing.
arxiv-2511-13766:
Kaizheng Wang and 3 co-authors compress deep ensembles into a single model that still reports honest uncertainty. Ensembles quantify doubt well and split it into data noise and model ignorance, but running many networks at inference is costly in time and memory. Their credal ensemble distillation trains one network, CREDIT, to carry the ensemble's spread.

Instead of one probability list, CREDIT outputs an interval for each class, and those intervals define a set of plausible distributions for scoring uncertainty. On out-of-distribution detection benchmarks the single model matched or beat several baselines. Inference overhead fell sharply against the full ensemble, making ensemble-grade doubt affordable in deployed classifiers.
arxiv-2511-13966:
Erick Ross studies how the eigenvalues of a Hecke operator spread out over spaces of modular forms. Fixing a prime p, he looks at the normalized p-th Hecke operator acting on the newspace of cusp forms with a given character, called the nebentypus. These operators are central tools in number theory, and their eigenvalue patterns reveal deep structure.

Ross determines the exact distribution those eigenvalues follow as the level and weight grow without bound together. Results of this equidistribution type connect modular forms to random matrix style statistics. The paper pins down the limiting law for this family of newspaces rather than leaving it as a qualitative statement.
arxiv-2511-14266:
Jeet Amrit Pattnaik and S. K. Patra ask whether an exotic kind of neutron star explains a puzzling gravitational-wave event. GW230529 involved a compact object in the mass gap between known neutron stars and black holes. Quarkyonic matter, which blends quark and nuclear descriptions, stiffens sharply at high density and could support unusually heavy neutron stars.

Computing pressure, energy, and mass-radius curves for quarkyonic equations of state, the authors find stable stars beyond two and a half solar masses. The predicted radii stay in a moderate range while the sequences reach into the event's mass window. They conclude the heavier partner in GW230529 could plausibly be a massive quarkyonic neutron star rather than a light black hole.
arxiv-2511-14366:
Hongwei Liu and 35 co-authors introduce ATLAS, a benchmark built to separate frontier language models on hard science. About eight hundred original problems, written or heavily adapted by domain experts with doctorates, span mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology, computer science, earth science, and materials science. The suite was designed against three failures of older tests: narrow scope, trivial answer formats, and contamination from training data.

Answers favor multi-step, open-ended reasoning with formatted mathematics over multiple choice. Cross-disciplinary problems force models to integrate knowledge across fields rather than recall one specialty. The authors present ATLAS as a contamination-resistant yardstick for scientific reasoning at the frontier.
arxiv-2511-14566:
Lucia Makaiova, Martin Fajcik, and Antonin Jarolim examine how to score document level claim extraction in Czech and Slovak. Claim extraction supports fact checking, yet scoring extracted claims is itself unsolved. The authors study ways to align two claim sets from the same document. A good alignment yields a similarity score for model output versus human labels.

The score can also measure agreement between human annotators. Experiments use a new data set drawn from comments under Czech and Slovak news stories. Informal language and strong local context make the task hard. Results expose limits of current scoring methods. The work aims at a more reliable evaluation framework for these languages.
arxiv-2511-14666:
Elkanah Nyabuto, Philipp Otto, and Yarema Okhrin present a way to estimate how effects spread across space and time in panel data. Their model lets each place depend on its own past and on its neighbors, but the strength of the neighbor links is unknown. They use the LASSO method, which shrinks weak links to zero, to learn those links along with the other values.

Tests with simulated data show the method works well, and accuracy grows as more time points are added. The team then applies it to hourly fine particle pollution data as a worked example. The approach helps separate real spatial links from noise in large environmental data sets.
arxiv-2511-14966:
David L. Cole, Jordan Jalving, and two co-authors extend a graph-based modeling language so optimization problems can live across many computers at once. In the Plasmo framework, a problem is drawn as a hypergraph: nodes hold subproblems with their own variables and goals, and edges hold the constraints that link them. Big real problems, though, spill past one machine's memory.

The new RemoteOptiGraph lets those hypergraphs run in distributed memory, with special edges that manage links spanning different workers. Modelers get one unified way to state a huge problem instead of hand-crafting each distributed version. The abstraction also gives algorithm designers a shared target for methods that exploit the distributed structure.
arxiv-2511-15166:
Jie Guo and Quansen Jiu draw a sharp line between blow-up and calm for a one-dimensional fluid model posed on a ring. The generalized Proudman-Johnson equation mimics how fluid particle paths can bunch and steepen. One parameter steers the behavior, and the interesting regime sits right next to the borderline value.

Just above the borderline, smooth flows blow up in finite time, and the blow-up settles into a self-similar shape for a class of starting profiles. Just below it, the very same profiles exist for all time. Rough Holder-continuous data also blow up self-similarly in the inviscid case, and even with viscosity, strong enough settings still break. The paired results map the model's tipping point with unusual precision.
arxiv-2511-15266:
Liangyu Chen, Yichen Xu, and six co-authors build a benchmark and a learning framework for editing charts by instruction. Charts in the wild arrive as images, not as the code that made them, so an editor must work from pixels plus a plain-language request. Earlier benchmarks were small in scope and wrongly assumed the chart code was available.

Their benchmark, ChartEditVista, holds thousands of samples across dozens of chart types and nearly every editable element, built by an automated produce-edit-verify pipeline. Two new fine-grained metrics grade layout, covering element position, size, and color. A reinforcement learning framework trained for the task aims at edits that stay faithful when the code is missing.
arxiv-2511-15366:
Ao Huang, Christian Röver, and Tim Friede rescue meta-analyses that rest on only a handful of studies. Pooling a few trials with random-effects models is routine in medicine, yet the standard math leans on large-sample approximations and wobbles badly with two to four studies. Heterogeneity between studies is then misjudged, and intervals come out far too wide to guide anyone.

Borrowing from work on surrogate outcomes, the authors build the synthesis from subgroup-level data inside each trial rather than one number per study. Two heterogeneity estimators of the classic type are derived on that finer data and plugged into a careful interval method. More data per study should mean steadier answers when studies themselves are scarce.
arxiv-2511-15466:
Henrique Knopki and Iberê Kuntz ask what the correct counting measure should be for the path integral of gravity, a sum over all possible shapes of space-time. No agreed answer exists, yet the choice affects quantum gravity results. They treat the problem with effective field theory, the method of building the most general model that respects the known symmetries at each energy scale.

They expand the metric on the space of shapes in powers of energy and study how its free constants flow. A flat shape space is ruled out by basic consistency. One stable high-energy point appears, and it matches the classic DeWitt metric value, giving that old choice a first-principles reason.
arxiv-2511-16066:
Shreyan Banerjee, Aasifa Rounak, and Vikram Pakrashi introduce Bellman Memory Units. The units form a neuromorphic frame that learns control through synaptic reinforcement learning on a changing network. Neuromorphic edge devices promise low-power control, but gradient-free online learning and hardware scale remain limiting. Their starting point is a synaptic Q-learning method for the classic Cartpole task, with Bellman equations written at the synapse level.

Training evolves the network topology, drawn as a directed graph, alongside the learned values. The units run with a neural engineering frame on Intel Loihi chip. Topology growth plus mixed-signal computation can cut neuron and synapse counts. That supports compact, task-specific chips that adapt on device to unseen control cases.
arxiv-2511-16366:
Gustavo Laranja Thomaello and six co-authors mine patents to enlarge the data available for designing oxide glasses. Patents hold large tables of glass recipes and measured properties that rarely reach the databases machine learning models train on, so the team built scraping tools to extract and clean them.

The haul covers thousands of compositions: about 5,700 with liquidus temperatures, about 4,300 with refractive indexes, and about 1,800 with Abbe numbers. That grows the existing pools by roughly ten, seven, and five percent. More than volume, the patent data add recipes richer in elements such as titanium, zirconium, and niobium oxides, widening the space that predictive glass models can search.
arxiv-2511-17166:
Tim Lakemann and three co-authors turn a nuisance into a tool for drone teams. When several unmanned aerial vehicles fly together, each must know where the others are. Camera-based systems using active markers are often confused by reflections of those markers on water or polished floors. This work instead reads the reflections themselves to localize teammates, needing only a camera, the markers, and a single-beam rangefinder.

The method assumes no prior knowledge of robot size, marker layout, or how reflective the surface is, and it tracks the uncertainty that rippling water introduces. The authors work out how surface tilt biases the estimate and where the level-surface assumption stays safe. Indoor and outdoor flights showed reliable localization across lighting conditions, with better accuracy than rival methods beyond thirty meters.
arxiv-2511-17266:
Leone Costi and Dario Izzo simulate a soft robotic net designed to capture space debris. Dead satellites threaten working spacecraft, and a net thrown or flown around a target is one proposed removal method. Their simulator, built on the open MuJoCo physics engine, models the net's dynamics, its contact with the target and with itself, orbital mechanics. A controller drives thrusters on four small satellites at the net's corners. The test target is Envisat, a large defunct European satellite.

Unlike earlier studies, the capture starts from a nearly static configuration rather than a net already thrown ballistically. More compliant nets performed better at contact, and with a sliding mode controller the soft net captured Envisat in every tested case, wrapping it with more contact points. The work guides design choices for debris removal missions.
arxiv-2511-17366:
Yankai Fu and seven co-authors present METIS, a vision-language-action model aimed at dexterous robot manipulation, tasks where a hand must perceive, reason, and act with fine control. Teaching such skills is bottlenecked by data: teleoperating dexterous hands is slow and costly, so action-labeled examples are scarce. Human video, by contrast, is vast and full of manipulation. The team built EgoAtlas, a dataset merging large-scale human and robot egocentric data from many sources into one consistent action space.

From that data they extract motion-aware dynamics, a compact discretized representation of motion that gives the model efficient, expressive supervision. METIS unifies reasoning and acting in one framework and, deployed on real robots, achieved the highest average success rate across six real-world dexterous tasks. It also generalized better to unfamiliar situations than the alternatives tested.
arxiv-2511-17466:
Zhiyu Dong and Patrick A Lee predict an unusual route to superconductivity in a two-dimensional triangular lattice where electrons repel each other strongly at short range. Repulsion normally breaks the electron pairs that carry a supercurrent, so pairing here sounds unlikely. The key is symmetry: in certain channels with a wave pattern called f-wave, the leading pair-breaking effect cancels out or nearly cancels.

With that term gone, weaker higher-order processes can take over and bind pairs. The authors show this in a standard lattice model with on-site and neighbour repulsion, finding a transition temperature near one percent of the electron bandwidth. For broader screened forces the same idea holds at a rough level, though a fuller calculation is needed to fix the pairing strength.
arxiv-2511-17766:
Mansur Yerzhanuly compares two kinds of neural networks for spotting fake satellite images made by generative models. Satellite pictures guide science and security choices, so synthetic images that pass as real pose a growing risk, yet they differ from fake faces in key ways.

On a set of more than one hundred thousand labeled images, vision transformers beat convolutional networks clearly in accuracy and robustness. Tools that show where each model looks help explain the gap: transformers catch broad structural flaws and repeated textures. Future work will extend the tests to other sensor types and frequency based checks.
arxiv-2511-17866:
Ethan Hartley evaluates large language models as tools for measuring economic policy uncertainty from news text, a widely used index based on word counting rules. Better measurement matters because the index feeds many studies of how uncertainty affects markets and policy.

Modern language model classifiers beat dictionary rules, match human audit judgments more closely, and handle noisy old and multilingual news. Hartley builds a nineteenth century index for the United States from hundreds of millions of newspaper articles, plus exploratory indexes for other countries. The study argues that such models should be treated as explicit measurement tools in economics.
arxiv-2511-18066:
Md Akil Raihan Iftee, Syed Md. Ahnaf Hasan, Mir Sazzat Hossain, and five co-authors adapt models at test time in federated learning. Clients there hold imbalanced classes and face shifting data, yet no labels or raw data may be shared. Prior fixes for imbalance need labels or coordination during training and ignore unsupervised adaptation at inference.

Their tailored framework uses balanced batch normalization during each client's local tuning, treating all classes equally to cut prediction bias. Clients with similar balanced profiles collaborate, and aggregation is class aware, keeping tailoring without sacrificing privacy. Experiments across baselines show stronger robustness and better minority class performance than leading methods.
arxiv-2511-18166:
Daniel Cicala, Yi Jiang, Jane HyoJin Lee, Kristin Kurianski, and Glenn Ledder model how public opinions shift over time, with vaccine denial as the motivating application. Opinions respond to official statements from government and medical authorities and also to influencers whose broadcasts reach large audiences quickly.

Their model treats each person's opinion as drawn toward prominent sources, then lifts that rule into a partial differential equation for the whole opinion landscape. That landscape model has a stable equilibrium, and they illustrate how the equilibrium depends on key parameters using vaccination examples. The framework helps explain when a population settles into a stable split of views.
arxiv-2511-18566:
Di Zhou and H. Jane Bae test if fine scale stress detail matters in simulations of flow over a smooth bump. Wall modeled large eddy simulation resolves big swirls and models the rest, a standard cost saver for turbulent flow. Eddy viscosity models often give bubble size forecasts that jump as the grid refines, a sign of a shaky model.

Models that carry directional, anisotropic fine stress give steadier bubble sizes. To find where the detail counts, the pair switch it on in chosen zones only. The windward side, where flow speeds under a kind pressure slope, proves key for the split zone downstream. Stress transport checks show the fine stress shifts loss and spread there. Grid safe separation forecasts need that detail.
arxiv-2511-18766:
Xintao Chen, Xiaohao Xu, Bozhong Zheng, Yun Liu, and Yingna Wu hunt defects across many views of one object with no labels. View shifts change how a sound part looks, so a single view tool flags false defects when views are treated as lone shots. True flaws must be split from benign view effects.

ViewSense-AD learns view proof features by warping feature zones between near views with a homography, a flat geometry map. That alignment module sits inside a latent diffusion model, so views line up stage by stage as noise clears. A coherent shared code then marks what no view can explain as the defect. False alarms fall when geometry is handled head on. Factory checks from many angles are the target use.
arxiv-2511-18966:
Muhammad Usman Shahid, Chuadhry Mujeeb Ahmed, and Rajiv Ranjan audit the security of C and C++ code written by large language models. Such code is known to ship with flaws and to skip defensive habits. Their study sorts known flaws by the Common Weakness Enumeration and maps them to known exploit records to weigh severity.

Ten models generate code for the test. Static analysis then scans the output for weakness patterns. The count of flaws in the machine written code is, in their word, concerning. The results urge care when developers paste model code into real projects. A clear audit trail of which flaws recur most can steer safer generation and review.
arxiv-2511-19066:
Xiangyu Chang and seven co-authors study federated learning, where many devices train one shared model without pooling their data. In the asynchronous version, the server updates the model as each client reports, so fast clients speak more often. When client data differ, that imbalance bends the shared model toward the fast group, an effect the authors call heterogeneity amplification.

Their analysis links design choices to the errors this effect creates. Two methods follow: ACE, which uses the latest information from all clients in each update, and ACED, which also weighs how stale an update is. Tests across tasks, data splits, and delays show robust gains.
arxiv-2511-19166:
Samantha Dies, Courtney Maynard, Germans Savcisens, and Tina Eliassi-Rad ask whether language models hold their views when a claim is reworded. Small shifts in wording can make a model take back true claims. Their test, called P-StaT, checks that steadiness under matched changes, both in what the model says and in its inner states.

Across twenty-one models and three fields, claims the model has rarely seen prove far less steady than well-known made-up ones. In some tests, models take back more than half of their claims. The dropped cases tend to involve vague wording, hard terms, or obscure ideas. That pattern suggests how well a model knows a topic props up its apparent confidence.
arxiv-2511-19266:
Sina Soltani, Marco Erba, David Schmid, and John H. Selby build a hidden-variable style model for a theory called bilocal classical theory. Such ontological models explain a theory's predictions through underlying states. Building one for a whole theory, not just a few scenarios, is rare, and an earlier conjecture held that no local-realist model existed for this theory.

Their construction refutes that conjecture. The theory also fails local tomography, a property many results assume, yet it still admits a classical explanation. That pairing shows a known structure theorem has a real limit. The authors note the model makes the theory easier to grasp than its original form.
arxiv-2511-19366:
Alan Jia Bao Du and Tarek S. Abdelrahman present HeLEx, a tool that designs layouts for reconfigurable computer chips known as CGRAs. These arrays tile processing elements that can each support many operations, wasting area and power. Given sample data flow graphs and a target array, the tool decides which operations each element really needs.

A branch-and-bound search strips operations from elements while keeping every input graph mappable. Across twelve graphs and nine array sizes, operation counts fall by about two thirds on average. Area drops by nearly seventy percent and power by over half, landing close to the theoretical minimum and ahead of two rival layout tools.
arxiv-2511-19466:
Penghao Rao, Runmin Jiang, and Min Xu estimate how much each training photo sways a vision model's test predictions. Influence scores can flag noisy data, but computing them in deep networks is costly, and scores frozen mid-training go stale as the model changes. Rankings without confidence checks are fragile.

Their framework, SG-OIF, runs online during training and uses algorithmic stability as a live controller. Light anchor computations are maintained with stochastic iterative solvers, while modular curvature backends adjust per-example scores using stability thresholds, anomaly gates, and confidence. The aim is a ranking of key examples that stays reliable while training is still moving.
arxiv-2511-19566:
Dhruva Kashyap and four co-authors find which parts of an open-weight neural network matter most for its predictions, without gradients or the true loss. Modifying such models for pruning or unlearning is hard because training data and loss functions are usually unavailable. Their method needs only distributional access, such as synthetic data.

Theory shows global error is bounded by local reconstruction errors for smooth networks, including well-trained transformers. That motivates a Subset Fidelity score: parts that rebuild local behavior well are judged important. The authors develop selection rules from that score, aiming at safe edits of models whose inner training details stay hidden.
arxiv-2511-19666:
Nikky Avila and five co-authors develop carbon matching, an accounting scheme that assigns grid emissions to every part of an electric system. Companies usually track energy bought and sold, not the emissions caused at the margin. Carbon matching instead uses marginal emission rates, with tons of emitted carbon as the unit of account.

The authors derive the mathematics and prove that distinct emission rates can be assigned to transmission, storage, generation, and consumption so that all grid emissions are fully allocated. Open notebooks compute the rates on simulated electric bus networks. The framework aims to spur stronger, better aimed cuts in system-level emissions.
arxiv-2511-20166:
Schehr and Yılmaz measure how wildly focused light intensity fluctuates through messy media. Their 2025 paper studies wavefront shaping in complex, scattering materials. Shaping an incoming wave can focus it onto target points. The brightness gain is called the enhancement factor. Experiments need that gain reproducible, not random.

Experiments, simulations, and exact theory were combined here. Random matrix theory supplies the analytical backbone. Multi-point focusing distributions were derived in full. The classic Marčenko-Pastur law covers only many-channel limits. Their results predict mean enhancement for finite channels too. Fluctuations are captured when long-range correlations are absent. Weakly scattering media fit that calm regime well. Strong scattering broke the pattern dramatically. Giant fluctuations appeared in experiments and simulations alike. Long-range mesoscopic correlations cause those wild swings. Enhancement statistics thus double as a correlation probe. Biomedical imaging and optical trapping depend on such control.
arxiv-2511-20466:
Boulin and Haufs predict extreme rainfall by deliberately simplifying the problem. Their 2025 statistics paper estimates exceedance chances for environmental extremes. Floods depend on rain accumulated over space and time together. Multivariate extreme value theory is notoriously heavy machinery to use. The authors project such problems onto a single-variable version instead.

Their estimator minimizes the squared distance between data and model curves. It fits a Pareto law to peaks over a threshold. Limit theory for the estimator is derived in the paper. Simulations validated how the estimator behaves. Honest comparison found maximum likelihood slightly better in Monte Carlo tests. The method still shone in the EVA 2025 Data Challenge. Team Bochum's entry used weather ensemble data near Asheville. The grid covered five by five locations in North Carolina. Their submission won the overall preliminary challenge against ten teams. It also took top-three finishes in two of six categories.
arxiv-2511-20666:
Arief Anbiya tackles in 2025 an unstable wave equation, the two-dimensional 'bad' Boussinesq equation, a wave equation from water-wave theory. The nickname comes from its linearised form, which is ill-posed: at high frequencies, tiny changes in the starting state grow explosively, so naive computer solutions blow up. Anbiya asks which wave components can be kept, using Fourier analysis to split the wave into frequency modes.

The analysis yields a bound each kept mode must obey. Anbiya builds it into two solvers: the fourth-order Runge-Kutta method, and Strang operator splitting, which advances the equation in alternating half-steps. Keeping only modes inside the bound gave stable, accurate solutions, checked against an exact soliton wave. Adding even a few modes outside the bound made solutions blow up. Runge-Kutta edged out splitting by a small margin, and a final run showed boundary reflections behaving as expected.
arxiv-2511-20766:
Karen Ullrich and colleagues show in 2025 that AI agents which ace an app can collapse when the app changes its look. Benchmarks freeze one clone of an app, but real apps vary in design and content. Their OpenApps ecosystem ships six configurable apps, messenger, calendar, maps and others, and runs on a single CPU, so thousands of variants can be generated cheaply.

The team ran more than 10,000 independent evaluations across seven multimodal agents, including Claude, OpenAI, and Qwen-VL models. Within one fixed variant, reliability looked stable. Across variants, task success swung by more than 50 percentage points for many agents. Kimi-VL-3B's average success ranged from 63 percent down to just 4 percent depending on the app version. Failure styles shifted too: UI-TARS was five times more likely to hallucinate actions under some configurations than others. The authors argue app variation is a missing axis of reliability.
arxiv-2511-20866:
Alexey Fakhrutdinov and Oleg R. Musin revisit in 2025 the pancake theorem, a classic result in discrete geometry. For any finite set of points in the plane, two perpendicular lines split the set into four equal parts. The authors design an algorithm that finds the two lines in time proportional to the number of points.

That linear running time is provably the best possible, since every point has to be inspected anyway. The result sits beside the older ham-sandwich theorem, which bisects several point sets with one cut and also admits linear-time algorithms in the plane. The authors also treat generalisations, showing that orthogonal hyperplanes, their higher-dimensional analogues, can be found in polynomial time. They note the harder equipartition question behind it all, posed by Grünbaum in 1960: splitting one measure into equal parts with hyperplanes remains open in dimension four.
arxiv-2511-21266:
Lotta Meijerink and eight coauthors clarify a shortcut for judging new medical treatments in a 2025 methodology paper. Trials are the gold standard, but new radiotherapy techniques often enter clinics before trial results exist. The shortcut predicts each patient's outcome under the old standard care with a model built earlier, then compares those predictions with the outcomes actually observed under the new treatment.

Meijerink and her coauthors use the potential outcomes framework to state exactly when this comparison yields a valid average treatment effect. The approach, known in radiotherapy as model-based clinical evaluation, is a form of model-based standardization related to the g-formula. A practical case study in radiotherapy, the setting where the method gauges tools like proton therapy, shows how the conditions bite in practice. The authors close with practices that make such estimates more credible and transparent.
arxiv-2511-21366:
Dmitri Kovalenko builds in 2025 an autonomous robot system that tightens nuts, a manipulation task harder than pick-and-place because it is dominated by contact. Threaded fastening appears everywhere from heavy industry to home repair, yet the robot must seat the nut on the bolt and turn it without crushing anything. Kovalenko's system uses a serial arm with a parallel gripper, guided by a hierarchical planner built from motion primitives.

Its controller switches between position control, for moving through free space, and force control, for the delicate contact phases, as each primitive demands. Extensive simulations show the system tolerates wide variation in initial conditions, so the nut need not start in a perfect pose. Against the baseline controller, the proposed system tightened threaded screws 14 percent faster. It also applied 40 times less contact force to the parts, a margin that protects fragile pieces. The implementation is open-sourced.
arxiv-2511-21466:
William De Deyn, Michael Herty, and Giovanni Samaey train small neural networks by committee vote instead of by gradient, in a 2025 applied mathematics paper. Consensus-Based Optimization lets a swarm of candidate parameter sets drift toward their weighted consensus, a derivative-free training method with an elegant limit theory. When infinitely many particles interact, the swarm's motion lives on a space of distributions stacked on distributions, and its variance shrinks monotonically.

De Deyn and his coauthors couple that limit with the mean-field limit of the network itself, recasting the optimizer in optimal transport language. In experiments, plain consensus training matched Adam's final error on a smooth regression task. A hybrid, consensus plus Adam, proved more robust than Adam on MNIST digit classification and converged faster than consensus alone. For multi-task learning, their reformulation recycles particles across tasks, keeping accuracy high with minimal extra memory.
arxiv-2511-21566:
Ali Amirahmadi and five coauthors predict whether ring-shaped drug candidates can slip through cell membranes, in 2025. Cyclic peptides can reach targets inside cells that ordinary drugs cannot, but only if they cross the membrane, and public permeability data are scarce. Rather than a data-hungry deep network, the team built a chemically informed similarity measure and paired it with Gaussian processes, models that report honest uncertainty with each prediction.

Their monomer-aware decoupled alignment kernel compares peptides residue by residue, using chemical similarity for local matches while decoupling those matches from gap penalties. A variant adds a positional prior and tightens the error bars further. Across extensive experiments the simple kernels beat leading transformer models on every metric, most clearly under the harder split that separates chemical families. Mixing in a fingerprint-based model recovered top accuracy scores as well, showing sequence context and local substructures complement each other.
arxiv-2511-21966:
García Muñoz and colleagues explain a missing signal on warm Neptune-sized exoplanets, where hydrogen absorption is extreme on three planets. So the helium triplet line should also be strong, yet appears on only two, weakly.

The team identifies a chemical culprit: vibrationally excited hydrogen molecules, H2 in an energized state, destroy the helium ions that are the direct precursor of the absorbing helium state. At the temperatures of the atmospheric layers probed, this reaction runs notably fast. Their simulations show the process severely mutes the line on GJ 3470 b and wipes it out entirely on GJ 436 b, explaining the nondetection there in their models. The effect strengthens where the molecule-to-atom transition sits high, set by high-energy radiation received. Weak helium absorption, they warn, does not mean a planet lacks a primordial hydrogen-helium atmosphere.
arxiv-2511-22566:
da Costa-Luis and colleagues report PETRIC, the first organised challenge for PET image reconstruction. Positron emission tomography builds medical images from detected photon pairs. Turning raw data into pictures is an inverse problem whose iterative algorithms are slow, a growing problem as long-scanner designs produce far more data. The challenge gave participants open-source software, an objective function, gold-standard reference images, metrics, and curated phantom datasets from different scanners and tracers, split into training and evaluation sets.

Four teams entered nine algorithms in total, drawing on optimisation tools such as preconditioning and stochastic gradients, plus artificial intelligence. Approaches that looked similar on paper performed quite differently in practice, showing how much implementation matters for reconstruction speed. Because the automated framework is open source, researchers can reuse it to benchmark new or existing methods on new scanners, tracers, and phantoms, and variant editions are already launching.
arxiv-2511-22666:
Bonanno, Haridev, and Narain examine how nonlocal interactions reshape a scalar field theory's long-distance behaviour. Adding an inverse-derivative term makes the field interact across distances, a toy model for nonlocal gravity extensions and condensed matter with long-range forces. Using the functional renormalisation group, tracking the theory at progressively lower energies, they map the infrared fixed points where the flow settles, through approximation schemes of increasing sophistication.

In the simplest local potential approximation, nonlocality shifts fixed points and can induce symmetry breaking. The flow turns singular before the deep infrared when the nonlocal coupling is positive. With derivative corrections, the infrared-stable fixed point is the nonlocal Gaussian one, and critical exponents ignore the nonlocal parameter. Generalising the interaction's power, infrared behaviour is unchanged up to a threshold, then follows Sak's prediction up to the local limit, while the highest-derivative case matches known Lifshitz results.
arxiv-2511-23066:
Matsuoka and colleagues test whether a generative image model can safely clean up medical scans before other AI tools read them. Children's hand X-rays used to estimate bone age often carry non-anatomical markers. And the team asked the foundation model gpt-image-1 to erase those markers by inpainting, filling the spots with plausible-looking tissue, guided only by written prompts.

From 200 original radiographs in the RSNA Bone Age Challenge dataset they generated 600 inpainted versions, then ran established deep learning ensembles on both sets. The cleanup badly hurt performance: bone age error rose from 6.26 months to 30.11 months on average, and gender classification accuracy, measured by AUC, fell from 0.955 to 0.704 in the same runs, with pixel-level shifts showing the model had quietly altered real anatomy, a warning against using such edits in clinical pipelines without task-specific validation.
arxiv-2511-23166:
Amanzhol and Park argue that picking a vision transformer for an edge device by accuracy or operation counts alone is misleading. Real energy use depends on how an architecture interacts with specific hardware. Their two-stage pipeline first screens 13 models with the device-agnostic NetScore metric. It then measures actual time and power on target hardware and ranks the survivors with a Sustainable Accuracy Metric for deployment.

The hybrid LeViT_Conv_192 was benchmarked on ImageNet-1K and CIFAR-10 using a Jetson TX2 edge board and an RTX 3050 mobile GPU. It cut energy use by up to 53 percent on the TX2 against a standard transformer baseline. The distilled TinyViT-11M led on the mobile GPU. Theory alone would have misranked them, since one rival with fewer operations and parameters still ran about 10 percent slower on the TX2 in their head-to-head test in practice.
arxiv-2511-23366:
Syed and colleagues propose an agentic artificial intelligence framework that runs retail inventory replenishment autonomously. Watching stock levels, forecasting demand, choosing suppliers, negotiating orders, and scanning for trending high-margin products to add. Retailers handle thousands of varied products with volatile demand. And the authors note global losses above 1.8 trillion dollars a year from poor demand prediction and inventory mismatch, which fixed reorder rules handle badly in stores.

They build a prototype for a mid-scale mart and test it on three conventional and synthetic datasets against baseline heuristics. Reporting fewer stockouts, lower inventory holding costs, and better product-mix turnover than the baselines. The system combines demand forecasting, supplier-selection optimization, multi-agent negotiation, and continuous learning, and the authors discuss limits honestly. Pointing to scalability to very large catalogs and real-world field deployment as the next steps before wider adoption.
arxiv-2512-00166:
Ultralight dark matter, if it exists, would push gently on ordinary objects with tiny oscillating forces. Louis Hamaide, Hannah Banks, Peter Barker, and Andrew Geraci propose a new sensor to detect those forces in 2025. Their design uses optically levitated objects held in place by light.

Optically trapped sensors are known for high force sensitivity but have been little explored for dark matter searches. The proposed tabletop experiment, called MOLeQuTE, is tunable to different force patterns. A positive signal would be a major discovery, and even a null result narrows the space of allowed dark matter models. Tabletop experiments are far cheaper than collider or space missions, which adds to the appeal.
arxiv-2512-00366:
Forecasting data that moves through space and time, like traffic or weather, usually needs heavy models. Wenshuo Wang, Yaomin Shen, Yingjie Tan, and Yihao Chen present a knowledge distillation method for it in 2025. Distillation trains a small student model to copy a large teacher.

Their method, named in the title with semantic and spectral parts, preserves both meaning and frequency structure. Recent frequency-aware distillation already showed that keeping high-frequency details and low-frequency trends matters. A faithful lightweight student could bring strong spatiotemporal forecasts to devices and services that cannot run the full teacher model. Spectral preservation keeps both the sudden spikes and the slow drifts of the data.
arxiv-2512-00566:
Shape-free regression lets the data choose the curve, but that freedom creates bias that ruins naive confidence ranges. Giuseppe Cavaliere and co-authors improve inference for nonparametric regression in 2025. Such estimators are central to the economist's toolkit, including regression-discontinuity designs.

Large-sample bias throws off the true coverage of standard intervals, so reported confidence is often false confidence. Existing robust bias-corrected intervals help, yet the authors push the theory further. Credible ranges matter wherever policy is judged by estimated effects at a cutoff, from education funding to health eligibility rules. Regression discontinuity is where these intervals are most often used in policy work. Improved inference means narrower honest intervals, not just corrected ones. For folks who judge aid or school rules by a line in the sand, the gain is trust. The spread they quote is the spread the data can back up in full.
arxiv-2512-00666:
L Voigt wrote a 2025 cosmology paper on weak lensing, the slight bending of light from far galaxies by matter in between. Measuring that bend, called shear, helps map dark matter and test models of the universe. New Stage IV surveys will measure shear with great care and detail.

Voigt focuses on a sneaky source of error. Galaxies too faint to be detected still add their light and can bias the shear values. Using a machine learning method built to avoid noise bias, the author measures that effect for a survey like Euclid. The results help planners keep faint galaxies from skewing their maps.
arxiv-2512-01166:
Lily Stelling and five coauthors evaluate the safety frameworks of frontier AI companies in a 2025 paper. After the AI Seoul Summit in 2024, twelve AI companies published frontier safety frameworks. These documents outline how each firm plans to manage catastrophic risks from advanced AI systems.

New laws increasingly treat the frameworks as accountability mechanisms and fold them into reporting duties. The authors ask what the frameworks actually commit each company to do. Comparing promises across firms shows where commitments are concrete and where they are vague. That clarity helps regulators and the public judge whether self-governance is real.
arxiv-2512-02066:
Sorting breast tumor images into benign and malignant is a high-stakes classification task where better feature extraction could help. Ece Yurtseven's 2025 paper builds a hybrid quantum-classical convolutional network for the job, running several quantum circuits in parallel and fusing their features.

The network is tested on BreastMNIST, a standard benchmark of breast tumor images prepared for machine learning. Quantum machine learning promises richer ways to pull signal from high-dimensional medical data, though the hardware remains young. Testing parallel quantum circuits on a real diagnostic benchmark shows where the approach stands and what it might add to classical networks.
arxiv-2512-02366:
Quantum sensors measure temperature, fields, and time with precision bounded by a quantity called the quantum Fisher information. Rui Zhang and three co-authors derive in 2025 a universal upper bound on that quantity for probes in thermal equilibrium with their surroundings.

The work unifies the equilibrium and non-equilibrium frameworks of quantum metrology for many-body systems, under dynamic sensing schemes. A universal bound tells experimentalists the best any thermal probe could ever do, before they build it. Such limits discipline the search for quantum sensors that beat classical instruments in real, warm conditions.
arxiv-2512-02566:
Kun Yuan and nine co-authors train AI models that read medical figures and text together. Biomedical vision language models learn from web scale scientific papers. Most training, though, pairs a whole figure with its caption and drops the fine links between small regions and words.

Clinicians rely on exactly those fine links when they zoom into local structures. The team's zoom in pretraining keeps panel level detail, matching small figure regions with the text that describes them. Models trained this way could support diagnosis and research tools that point to the right spot, not just the right page. Fine links like these are what let a tool point to a spot, not just a page, when it counts.
arxiv-2512-02666:
Ashkan Abedi, Vittorio Giovannetti, and Dario De Santis simulate a classic model of electrons on a square lattice. The two dimensional Hubbard model captures how electrons hop and repel, a core puzzle in condensed matter. Tensor network methods must first flatten the square into a chain.

The team maps the lattice with a Hilbert curve, a space filling path that keeps nearby sites close. That compact mapping yields a smaller matrix product state than the usual snake path. Cheaper simulations let physicists probe larger systems in the search for new phases of matter. Flat maps that keep near sites near are a cheap win, and cheap wins stack up in long runs fast.
arxiv-2512-02766:
Yichao Huang, Jinglin Wang, and Xiaolin Zeng refine a lattice model used to probe disordered quantum systems. The model, known by its H 2|2 label, lives on a hierarchical lattice with a tree like structure. Earlier work by Disertori, Merkl, and Rolles gave an exact coarse graining for its random field.

The authors extend that result to the model's random Schrödinger operator form. They also build fine graining, the reverse move, and prove an exponential martingale property for it. Two way scaling tools help connect small scale randomness with large scale behavior in disordered media. Two way scale moves let a proof climb from the small to the large and back, a round trip few tools can make.
arxiv-2512-02966:
Isha Chaudhary and five co-authors build Lumos, a system for certifying language model systems against stated properties. As these systems spread into more applications, alignment with human ethics grows crucial. Recent works certify properties like fairness, correct answering, and safety, but each method is ad hoc.

Ad hoc certificates are hard to generalize from one property or model to the next. Lumos aims at certification as a reusable system, not a one off proof. Portable certification could give regulators and buyers a common way to check AI claims before deployment. One stamp for many traits beats ten stamps for ten traits. Shops must ship a tool that firms and boards can trust at scale in the field.
arxiv-2512-03166:
Robot soccer is a tough test for teams of AI agents. Aya Taourirte and Md Sohag Mia study learning methods for that test in this 2025 work. Agents must decide in real time, work as a team, and cope with rivals in a virtual field.

Reinforcement learning is a promising route, but it strains under split tasks. Long-term plans and split-second moves need different handling, and many agents add complexity. The authors work on methods that scale better. Progress here could transfer to warehouse robots, rescue teams, and other real multi-agent jobs. Virtual soccer gives a safe, cheap arena to test team tactics before real robots play.
arxiv-2512-03366:
Judging an A/B test method is hard when true effects are unknown. Ryan Kessler, James McQueen, and Miikka Rokkanen offer a way around that in this 2025 work. They split each test's data into two parts to measure method performance.

Their framework shows sample-split estimators are generally biased for full-sample performance. Yet those estimators consistently estimate the sample-split analogues of it. Knowing that gap helps firms judge testing methods honestly. Better method checks lead to better product and policy decisions from experiments. Sample splits are cheap, since they reuse data that testing teams already collect.
arxiv-2512-03466:
Two agents with half the facts each must cooperate to win. Xavier Cadet, Edward Koh, and Peter Chin present AsymPuzl in this 2025 work. Most multi-agent setups use open-ended role-play, which is hard to evaluate in a controlled way.

AsymPuzl is a minimal two-agent puzzle with information asymmetry. Each agent sees a partial, complementary view of a symbolic puzzle. They must exchange messages to solve it together. The setup isolates communication skill, a clean target for testing language model teamwork. Minimal puzzles strip away role-play noise, leaving pure communication skill exposed.
arxiv-2512-03666:
Qi'ao Xu and colleagues build the first benchmark that asks AI to find objects by what they are for, in first-person video. An embodied agent hears a task, not a description, and must locate the tools it implies. Their 2025 ToG-Bench assembles one hundred egocentric clips from ScanNet scenes.

Over two thousand seven hundred instructions demand explicit finds and context-inferred ones alike. A single instruction may also map to several objects the task needs. A semi-automated pipeline drafted annotations with foundation models, then human reviewers refined them. Seven leading multimodal models were benchmarked with task-level metrics, exposing how far task-oriented grounding still has to go.
arxiv-2512-03766:
Step-free stations decide whether many riders can use a transit system at all, yet accessibility is rarely studied as a network property. Katherine Betz examines that question in a 2025 preprint on social and information networks. She builds models of two large systems, London's Underground and the subway network of New York City, keeping only stations with infrastructure such as elevators and step-free access.

In these models, stations are nodes and line connections are edges, letting network tools reveal how the accessible skeleton is shaped. Betz measures clustering, maps where accessible stations sit, and uses centrality scores to find the hubs of the accessible network. She then compares neighbourhood wealth and tourism popularity against the supply of accessible stations. Strong disparities appear in both cities. The work shows how network mathematics can guide fairer upgrades to modern transit infrastructure.
arxiv-2512-03966:
A biological neuron fires only when input crosses a threshold, then rests before firing again. Steven Louis and colleagues build an electronic version in a 2025 applied physics preprint. Their spiking neuron pairs a transistor with a magnetic tunnel junction, adding novel devices to standard chip technology.

Simulated in industry-standard circuit software, the combined unit reproduces the neuron's repertoire: firing past a threshold, resting through a refractory period, integrating synaptic inputs, and accepting inhibition. Those behaviours come from the junction's magnetisation dynamics, so no extra control circuitry is needed. Wired together, the units form an analogue multi-layer network. It updates its weights by a spike-timing rule derived from gradient descent. Training and inference both run in the analogue domain. The network propagated spikes and learned the classic XOR task, a proof of concept for on-chip learning with magnetic devices.
arxiv-2512-04066:
Open quantum systems leak energy into their surroundings, and the mathematics of that leakage can be brutal in infinite dimensions. Pablo Costa Rico, Paul Gondolf, and Tim Möbus study dissipative bosonic systems in a 2025 mathematical physics preprint. For a class of these evolutions, they prove a smoothing property: the dynamics instantly regularises starting states.

The setting is quantum Markov semigroups on bosonic Fock space, with Lindblad operators built as polynomials in the creation and annihilation operators. The team shows such dynamics immediately produce states with finite expectation in every power of the number operator. The headline application is the bosonic cat code, a design for error-resistant quantum computing hardware. There, they obtain trace-norm estimates for convergence speed, sharpening perturbative bounds at short and long times. A generation theorem for multi-mode systems supplies the domain care the arguments need.
arxiv-2512-04266:
Inflation, the early universe's burst of expansion, should have left a three-point fingerprint in how galaxies cluster. Anton Chudaykin, Mikhail M. Ivanov, and Oliver H. E. Philcox search for it in the first data release from the DESI survey, in a 2025 cosmology preprint. The fingerprint's shapes, local, equilateral, and orthogonal, point back to different inflationary physics.

Their analysis models the galaxy power spectrum and bispectrum within effective field theory at one-loop order, keeping scales where that description is trustworthy. The local amplitude comes out consistent with zero, with an uncertainty competitive with the cosmic microwave background's. Adding high-redshift DESI data and BOSS data, plus simulation-based priors on bias parameters, yields the strongest large-scale structure constraints on the non-local shapes. Combined, the local bound tightens by nearly a fifth over the microwave background alone: the strongest limit on multi-field inflation.
arxiv-2512-04366:
Fernando Zampieri explains a family of tests for watching clinical trials as they run, built on betting rather than fixed formulas. Standard trial monitoring leans on assumptions about data shape or on large-sample approximations. Those can mislead when a trial must be checked again and again. His 2025 arXiv paper presents the e-RT approach, which draws its validity from the random assignment of patients itself.

Each test works like a wager. Before each new outcome counts, the method bets on the next random assignment or event label, growing a pool of test wealth. If the treatment does nothing, that wealth cannot grow on average. This gives error control that holds at any stopping point, with no need to state an expected effect size first. Variants cover yes-no outcomes, event timing, and continuous measures. Trial teams can watch results live without spending their error budget.
arxiv-2512-05266:
Loris Di Cairano builds a quantum field theory, for the free-electron laser, that works out of equilibrium — the device turns a relativistic electron beam into coherent light. He starts from a microscopic description of the beam coupled to a single radiation mode. He applies the Keldysh formalism — the standard machinery for systems driven out of equilibrium — and integrates the electrons out of the problem entirely.

What remains is an effective action for the light mode alone. In it, dispersion, gain, and noise all flow from one object: the electronic self-energy built from the beam's current fluctuations. For a steady Gaussian beam he obtains formulas for frequency pulling, gain loss from energy spread, and the noise the field feels. At low frequency the theory shrinks to a Landau-Ginzburg form, and the laser threshold appears as a non-equilibrium phase transition, with the coherent amplitude as its order parameter.
arxiv-2512-05566:
I. Stergakis, Th. Diakonidis, and Ch. Moustakidis use machine learning to read the equation of state of dense matter out of the stars it builds. What matter does at densities beyond nuclear — inside neutron stars and hypothetical quark stars — is a central open problem of nuclear physics. The standard attack is theory checked against collisions and telescope data. The authors instead train machine and deep learning regressors on the mass-radius relations of compact objects, aiming to infer the underlying equation of state from the observable curve.

Their training ground is a library of physically consistent equations of state for neutron stars and quark stars, each satisfying established constraints. Learned models map between the stellar observables and the matter properties in both directions. The results show data-driven methods can refine insight into matter at supranuclear densities and complement classical modelling, relevant as multimessenger astronomy sharpens the observations.
arxiv-2512-05866:
Md Mahbub Hasan Akash, Aria Tasnim Mridula, Sheekar Banerjee, and Ishtiak Al Mamoon restore underwater photographs with a generative network whose eyes are transformers. Water washes colors toward green and blue, fades contrast, and adds haze. Convolutional networks see only small patches at a time, so they struggle to fix a color cast that spans the whole scene. The team's generator arranges Swin Transformer blocks inside a U-Net.

A PatchGAN discriminator judges the output patch by patch, pressing the generator to keep high frequency detail honest rather than smoothing it away. Trained and tested on the EUVP collection of paired underwater images, the system set state of the art scores on the standard quality measures. Visually, colors rebalanced, contrast returned, and haze thinned. An ablation study confirmed the transformer design beats convolutional stand-ins. Clearer pictures mean decisions made on what is actually there.
arxiv-2512-05966:
Waleed Qaisar lifts a classical construction into the world of categories. Isomonodromic deformation slides a flat connection along a path while keeping its monodromy, the data of how solutions wind around singularities, unchanged. The connections here may have logarithmic singularities along a chosen divisor. Qaisar upgrades the slide from an operation on individual connections to a functor between whole categories of them, one functor for each path, and the assignment itself respects how paths compose.

The machinery is the theory of Lie groupoids. Three applications follow. Isomonodromy becomes a map between moduli stacks. Higher information appears, as an action of the fundamental two-groupoid of the base on the connection categories. And the functors themselves are born from something more basic: Morita equivalences, from which the functors can be drawn by passing to representations. It records coherence data the old picture discards.
arxiv-2512-06066:
John Monnier and nineteen co-authors present two decades of watching two massive stars tear each other's winds apart. WR 112 is a binary pairing a carbon rich Wolf-Rayet star with an O star; their supersonic winds collide. Their winds collide in bright shocks, making a dust pinwheel. The team reports first X-ray detections beside twenty seven years of radio monitoring. Seen nearly edge on, the collision zone hides and shows with the twenty year orbit.

Single speed dust models cannot fit the data together. The data demand an accelerating post-shock flow, climbing from near rest to over a thousand kilometers per second within one orbit, which reproduces the spiral and the radio brightening's timing. WR 112 becomes a benchmark for future simulations.
arxiv-2512-06266:
Chen Yang and a large team introduce Nanbeige4-3B, a compact language model built to punch above its size. Small models are cheap to run, yet they usually trail large ones on hard tasks. The team trained their model on a vast set of high grade text, then fine tuned it on tens of millions of varied prompts.

Training came in stages. A warm up plan shifted the data mix step by step, and the fine tuning data was cleaned by a loop that rewrote drafts and rebuilt chains of thought. Later, a top reasoning model taught the small one through a dual preference method, and a final round of reward based training sharpened both reasoning and tone. On many tests the small model beat peers of its size and matched much larger ones. The team released the model weights for public use.
arxiv-2512-06466:
Le Thanh Dung Nguyen and Pawel Parys prove a theorem about logic queries run over strings. The queries are written in the formal languages known as MSO and first order logic. One case shows the idea. Suppose a query over binary strings returns few answers, at most a count tied to the zeros times the ones. Then each answer can be pinned down inside the same logic. Naming a zero position, a one position, and a small piece of fixed data is enough.

The proofs also cover the first order case, tied to aperiodic monoids in algebra. As a payoff, they settle a piece of folklore: that dimension can always be cut down for string to string readings given in first order logic. Theorems of this kind tell language designers exactly how much data a query answer really needs.
arxiv-2512-06666:
Urav Maniar asks whether two fast time series classifiers, teamed well, can rival a champion ensemble that takes weeks to train. Sorting time series into classes, from sensor traces to signals, trades accuracy against computing cost. The champion system is accurate but needed hundreds of hours on a standard benchmark, which bars it from large data. Maniar pairs Hydra, which races convolutional kernels against each other, with Quant, which reads quantile features over nested intervals.

Six ways of joining the pair were tested on ten large data sets. The best pairing nudged average accuracy above either method alone and won on most data sets. Yet prediction level blends captured only a small share of what an oracle join could give, while joining at the feature level beat the oracle by learning new boundaries. The lesson: the hard part is no longer making methods different, but learning how to combine them.
arxiv-2512-07166:
Siyuan Xu and co-authors study the forgotten second half of privacy protection for image-editing models: getting the real content back. Tools that swap private details in a photo for safe surrogates let people use multimodal editors without leaking themselves. But nobody had measured how well the protected content can later be restored, or whether the restored version keeps the edits. That recovery quality is what their work puts under the microscope.

They contribute SPPE, a data set spanning many privacy categories and user instructions, holding protected surrogates beside their edited versions so recovery can be scored directly. Framing recovery as guided generation driven by complementary signals from both versions, their unified method rebuilds the private content while preserving the editor's changes. Tests on SPPE and on a standard editing benchmark show the approach transfers across varied content and tasks.
arxiv-2512-07366:
Alexander Saccani and Paolo Tiso shrink the cost of simulating structures that bend so far their geometry changes the physics. Full finite element runs of such geometrically nonlinear systems are too slow when engineers must sweep many shapes. Their reduced-order framework builds small surrogate models from vibration modes and their modal derivatives. Reading the needed nonlinear pieces straight out of standard simulation outputs, without ever opening the solver's code.

A library of these small models is computed at sampled shapes, and every ingredient, stiffness. The quadratic and cubic coupling pieces, damping values, and the reduction basis itself, is interpolated across shapes with radial basis functions. A two-stage compression yields one global basis, with a reordering step that keeps the interpolation smooth.
arxiv-2512-07466:
A. Karakonstantakis and W. Kluźniak wrote this 2025 astrophysics paper on telling wormholes from black holes. A spinning wormhole might imitate a Kerr black hole in X-ray binaries and galactic centers. Sharper instruments could expose the impostor if a clear difference in accretion exists.

The authors compare how matter orbits and heats up around each object. Using a standard Lagrangian method, they derive the orbital traits of test particles. Thin disk theory then turns those orbits into a disk surface temperature. For circular orbits at the same radius, the two objects match exactly. Speed, energy, angular momentum, and frame-dragging precession are identical. One hard difference remains: a wormhole has no orbits smaller than its throat. Its disk is smaller in area than a black hole's disk. That smaller disk runs visibly cooler when the throat is wide enough. Temperature, they conclude, tests wide-throated wormholes.
arxiv-2512-07766:
Matteo Cipollina, Michail Karatarakis, and Freek Wiedijk wrote this 2025 paper on proving neural network behavior. Networks are everywhere, yet checking what they will do remains hard. The authors formalize two classic network families inside the Lean proof assistant.

Hopfield networks come first in their formal development. These recurrent networks store patterns as stable states they settle into. The team proves the networks converge to those states as claimed. They also prove Hebbian learning correct, the rule that writes patterns in. Boltzmann machines, the stochastic cousins, come second in the work. Their random updates should settle into one unique stationary distribution. Proving that ergodicity needs the Perron-Frobenius theorem about matrices. The authors formalize that theorem fresh along the way. Learning dynamics for the Boltzmann machine are formalized as well. Machine-checked proofs turn folklore about these networks into certainty. The work points toward verified machine learning as a practical craft.
arxiv-2512-07966:
Zhiyi Wu, Xuandong Sun, Songlei Wang, and eight co-authors wrote this 2025 quantum physics paper. Quantum computers must measure qubits mid-calculation to correct errors as they go. Feeding those results back fast enough has limited what experiments can attempt.

Their team built a superconducting processor around that loop. Global mid-circuit checks run with high quantum non-demolition fidelity. Feedback then fires with a decision lag of mere hundreds of nanoseconds. On this platform, two distinct phase changes appear in one adaptive circuit. Single quantum paths show a measurement-induced entanglement transition. The averaged channel shows an absorbing-state shift of its own. Key exponents at the second shift are measured head-on. They match the directed percolation class closely. The two transitions sit at different tuning values. Such circuits thus become a test bed for nonequilibrium quantum matter.
arxiv-2512-08566:
Yorgo Chamoun and Samuel Mimram work in category theory, a branch of math that studies structure in very general terms. They look at relational presheaves, which extend the usual notion by using relations instead of functions and by allowing looser maps. That extra freedom helps model objects with no boundary or with several boundaries at once.

The authors show that these presheaves form models of a cartesian theory, which gives them strong general properties. They then build realization functors that turn abstract presheaves into geometric objects in a suitable setting. A key use is in the study of concurrency, where the method links syntactic and geometric views. It also gives a syntactic form for the blowup operation on directed spaces.
arxiv-2512-08666:
Wang Wei Yu and Bruce Allen combine public data from five pulsar timing arrays to search for a faint background of gravitational waves. Pulsar timing arrays track the arrival times of pulses from many pulsars and look for a shared pattern. The combined set covers more than a hundred pulsars, about four times larger than any single array alone.

For pulsars seen by more than one array, the authors use a new direct method to merge models and data without forcing one best timing model. They estimate the strength and slope of a possible background spectrum. The results fit a nonzero background, but the evidence stays below the standard level for a firm claim. The pattern of correlations across pulsar pairs does match the expected curve for gravitational waves.
arxiv-2512-08766:
Vladimir Parfenyev studies the fastest route for a self propelled agent moving in a two dimensional fluid flow. The classic Zermelo navigation problem asks for the path with the least travel time between two points. Here the agent is carried by the flow, moves at a fixed own speed, and can steer its heading freely.

Flows range from steady rotation and a time dependent sink vortex to a periodic flow and to turbulence. Optimal control theory gives time minimizing paths, but those paths become unstable when the flow is chaotic. The author therefore tests reinforcement learning, comparing a value based method with an actor critic method. Both reach near optimal travel times in regular flows. In turbulent flows the gap grows larger, yet learning still succeeds. Agents trained on coarse grained turbulence also transfer to the full flow, a key point for real ocean and air use.
arxiv-2512-09066:
Simon Sedlacek and coauthors present ORCA, a model based method to judge the correctness of open ended answers from large audio language models. Reliable assessment is essential as audio benchmarks grow more complex and subjective, requiring free form responses rather than fixed choices. Human rating is costly, so a trustworthy automatic judge is needed.

The team builds a three stage annotation pipeline that joins human judgment, structured feedback, and human artificial intelligence correction. That yields thousands of annotations over question answer pairs from many audio models and three benchmarks, with strong inter rater agreement. Training with curriculum learning, their judge matches average human correctness ratings closely on seen benchmarks. It also generalizes well to unseen benchmarks, beating several large model judge baselines. Predicted variance from the judge tracks human disagreement strongly. That signal can flag problematic benchmark items where even humans cannot agree on a single correct answer.
arxiv-2512-09266:
Ryosuke Nagumo and Hironori Fujisawa study density ratio estimation, a statistical task that compares two probability distributions through the ratio of their densities. The task underlies methods for detecting shifts in data. Their focus is robustness: what happens when the data are heavily contaminated with outliers.

They examine weighted density ratio estimation, a method earlier work had shown to be doubly strongly robust in the long-run, asymptotic sense. Nagumo and Fujisawa prove the finite-sample version: even under heavy contamination, the weighted method stays sparse and consistent. Their analysis rests on assuming the weighted ratio is bounded, and on at least one of two conditions holding: contamination is limited, or outliers carry small weights. The paper gives the first non-asymptotic analysis of strong robustness under heavy contamination, a step toward guarantees that hold for real dataset sizes.
arxiv-2512-09866:
Hanyu Cheng, Supriya Pan, and Eleonora Di Valentino test whether today's cosmic data can pin down a dark energy model with four free parameters. Richer models are often dismissed as excessive, since constraining many parameters is hard. But surveys have improved fast, and the authors ask whether combined observations are now up to the task. Their model describes dark energy through its present equation of state, its early value, the time of transition between them, and the steepness of that transition.

They fit the model with cosmic microwave background data from Planck, baryon acoustic oscillation data from DESI, and three separate supernova compilations. The verdict is mixed. The transition time is not constrained by any dataset, the early value and steepness only weakly, while the present value is well measured throughout. For some data combinations the model is mildly preferred over simpler rivals, though not strongly.
arxiv-2512-09966:
Ishan Swamy and Deobrat Singh study a black hole tied to a cosmic string. Rotating black holes with strong magnetic fields launch jets through the Blandford-Znajek mechanism, which extracts spin energy.
