Vision-language models that reason step by step entangle seeing with thinking, so a small perception slip can cascade into a wrong answer. Niccolo Avogaro and 8 co-authors present SPARC, a framework that separates the two stages. The model first searches the image explicitly to localize regions relevant to the question, then reasons only about those regions.

That separation allows each stage to scale its compute on its own. Perception can take more budget when the input distribution shifts. The reasoning stage alone can be tuned when it is the bottleneck. Context can also be compressed by running global search at low resolution and reserving high resolution for the chosen regions. The modular design replaces expensive reinforcement learning with hand-crafted rewards, the authors argue, with a cleaner architecture.
arxiv-2602-06666:
Peter Hochs and Jinmin Wang work on Gromov's band-width conjecture. It sets a precise upper limit on the width of a band of curved space when the band has positive scalar curvature and its cross-section admits none. Versions of the result exist, but they lean on index theory for compact pieces. The paper needs tools that also work when the dividing surface stretches out without end.

The authors build a quantitative version of partitioned manifold index theory that applies to noncompact hypersurfaces. With it, they prove a band-width estimate for Riemannian bands that may themselves be noncompact. The work extends a known circle of ideas in geometry and index theory to settings where the older compactness assumptions fail.
arxiv-2602-06766:
Eleonora Cicciarella, Riccardo Mazzieri, Jacopo Pegoraro, and Michele Rossi make wireless sensing cheaper to run on small, battery-limited devices. Their setting is integrated sensing and communication, where the same radio signals that carry data also reveal what people nearby are doing. Existing recognition algorithms are often too heavy for such devices.

The authors propose a spiking neural network design: a spiking convolutional autoencoder learns sparse spike encodings of the radio channel response, trained jointly with a classifier for human activity recognition. That design removes the need for a separate Doppler preprocessing step. In tests it matched a heavier hybrid method at almost 96 percent F1 score while encoding the signal with over 81 percent sparsity. Pre-encoding the channel data improved both accuracy and efficiency.
arxiv-2602-07066:
Marc Schmitt builds an index that gauges the odds of high stress in the United States equity market one month ahead. Each month, he sums up the cross-section of single stocks into a set of interpretable fragility signals, drawn from CRSP daily data. Those signals feed a logistic regression with an L1 penalty. The model is refit as months roll forward in real time, yielding a forward-looking stress probability.

Out of sample, the index tracks major stress episodes. It beats a lean benchmark built on lagged market return and realized volatility, on both discrimination and accuracy. It gives calibrated probabilities on an economically meaningful scale. Schmitt also shows how the index can serve as a probability tool for measuring, for use in financial econometrics research. The result is a transparent gauge of near-term equity-market stress risk that is easy to update.
arxiv-2602-07266:
Audio description makes video accessible to blind and low vision audiences, yet the tools for writing it are themselves visually driven and hard for blind creators to use.  Franklin Mingzhe Li and three co-authors present ADCanvas, an authoring system built around talk-based control, keyboard playback control, and a plain-text screen-reader-friendly editor.

The system supports live visual question answering, script generation, and editing with a multi-modal language model agent.  A study with twelve blind and low vision creators found them using the agent as an information aide and drafting assistant while keeping control through checking and editing.  Accessibility builders get a system that treats blind creators as authors, not just audiences.
arxiv-2602-07466:
Electrocardiographic imaging reconstructs heart electrical activity from body-surface potentials without surgery, but the inverse problem is severely ill-posed and needs strong regularization.  Manuel Haas and five co-authors present a space-time method that pairs spatial regularization with a learned time prior.

The time prior follows a Fields-of-Experts model that captures complex activation patterns over time, discretized with finite elements on unstructured cardiac surface meshes, with a convergence proof and a scalable optimizer.  Tests on synthetic epicardial data beat handcrafted space-time methods at denoising and reconstruction.  Cardiac imaging teams get a learned, physiologically aware regularization that uses time, not just space.
arxiv-2602-07566:
Smart farms need to recognize individual cows across cameras, but lighting, background, viewpoint, and camera properties shift between monitoring nodes and wreck single-camera models.  Runcheng Wang and four co-authors propose a cross-camera cow identification method based on disentangled representation learning.

Grounded in subspace identifiability theory, the method models how physical data generation separates identity from camera effects, so identity features transfer to new nodes.  Precision livestock farming depends on such non-contact identification at scale, and this work targets the generalization gap that blocks deployment.  Agricultural AI builders get a principled approach to recognizing the same cow from any barn camera.
arxiv-2602-07666:
DARPA's AI Cyber Challenge, running from 2023 to 2025, is the largest contest yet for autonomous cyber reasoning systems that find and fix vulnerabilities in real open-source software. A large team led by Cen Zhang presents the first thorough analysis of the contest.

Drawing on design documents, source code, execution traces, and discussions with organizers and top teams, the paper examines its structure, top-team architectures, and results beyond the scoreboard. It names what truly drove results, what genuine advances teams achieved, and what limitations remain. Cybersecurity teams and teams that run the next one get lessons for self-run vulnerability discovery and for running the next challenge well.
arxiv-2602-07766:
Copper-oxide superconductors hide competing patterns of magnetism, and muon measurements offer a window into which pattern is real. Oleg P. Sushkov re-examines muon spin rotation data for lanthanum barium copper oxide at one-eighth barium doping, a composition famous for its anomalous behavior.

He finds the data do not fit a spin stripe picture, where spins line up in stripes, but do fit a coplanar spin spiral lying in the copper-oxygen plane. The static spin value comes out near 0.37 times one half. The short analysis sharpens the debate over magnetic order in cuprates, favoring spiral order at this key doping level.
arxiv-2602-07966:
Multi-task learning promises knowledge transfer between tasks, but deciding which tasks are similar, and why, remains an open question. Pablo Hidalgo and Daniel Rodriguez propose a similarity measure built from explainable AI: accumulated local effects curves, which show how each feature influences predictions, compared with a distribution-weighted Fréchet distance.

The measure incorporates feature importance, works whether tasks are trained separately or together, and applies across model types, with a scaling factor for differing predictive performance. The authors also offer recommendations for using it in practice. Researchers grouping tasks for transfer learning gain an interpretable, model-agnostic way to justify which tasks should learn together.
arxiv-2602-08066:
Control theory asks whether a system can be steered close to a desired state, even when noise and memory effects tangle the motion. Mamadou Pathe LY and four co-authors study near control for random integrodifferential equations in Hilbert space with far-off initial rules.

Departing from standard assumptions, they drop tightness and Lipschitz rules on the far-off term, relying instead on tightness of the helper tool. Schauder's fixed-point theorem and Grimmer's helper theory prove control of the curved system, and guess arguments extend it to the random case. An example validates the theory. Control theorists gain results under weaker hypotheses than the literature usually demands.
arxiv-2602-08166:
Microservices evolve independently and often across many repositories, so architecture documentation decays almost as fast as it is written. Oscar Manglaras and four co-authors present a method for distributed static architecture reconstruction of polyglot, multi-repository projects.

Technology-specific modules called extractors analyze each service, and the method governs how extractors run, how data passes between them, and how outputs unify into one architecture view. It interoperates with existing static analysis tools, which can be embedded in or invoked from extractors. Software architects gain a way to maintain an up-to-date picture of a sprawling system without forcing every team into one repository or one stack.
arxiv-2602-08866:
HarmonyOS apps are written in ArkTS, a typed cousin of TypeScript, yet the platform has lacked a solid test for automated code repair. Bang Xie and five co-authors fill that gap with ArkEval, a benchmark and evaluation workflow built from a large official Huawei repository holding over 400 ArkTS applications. Careful multi-stage filtering leaves 502 reproducible issues.

Test cases are generated by language models and voted on, including Claude, and problem statements are standardized for fair comparison. Four leading language models are then tested with a retrieval-augmented repair workflow. The scores map both the promise and the limits of today's models in this low-resource language, pointing the way for future repair tools.
arxiv-2602-08966:
Dividing indivisible goods fairly gets harder when each person must receive at least, and at most, a set number of items. Hirota Kinoshita and one co-author study maximin-share fairness under such lower and upper quotas, for both goods and chores. They prove a goods allocation reaching a 2n over 3n minus 1 share of the maximin benchmark always exists and can be found in polynomial time.

A matching chores algorithm reaches the reciprocal-style bound, and the results extend to items split into categories with their own quotas. There, goods reach n over 2n minus 1 and chores the corresponding reciprocal. The work generalizes earlier results that handled only upper quotas, covering staffing and computing allocations where headcounts matter.
arxiv-2602-09066:
Multimodal contrastive learning often collapses embeddings into narrow cones, packing meaning into a few slots while the rest hold noise. Jinjin Guo and seven co-authors propose Spectral Disentanglement and Enhancement, which uses singular value decomposition to split feature axes into strong signals, weak side correlations, and noise. A curriculum plan then amplifies informative components with stability guarantees.

A dual-domain loss tunes alignment in both feature space and spectral space, weaving spectral regularization into training. The result is richer, more robust vectors that transfer better. The work bridges embedding geometry and spectral structure, two views of representation quality that prior methods treated separately.
arxiv-2602-09566:
Deep learning matches experts on auto ECG readings, yet black-box models stall clinic uptake: doctors need to see which body traits drive each call. Vajira Thambawita and four co-authors propose ECG-IMN, a 2026 clear network for high-detail twelve-lead ECG sorting. Standard explain tools guess after the fact, with unstable, costly, and sometimes false credit.

ECG-IMN instead works as a hyper-net: a deep filter backbone makes settings of a strictly linear model fitted to each input sample. Choice logic is thus clear in math, and the made weights serve as exact, high-detail credit maps. A bridge decoder maps latent traits to per-sample weights, spotting diseased evidence such as ST rise and T-wave flip in time and across leads. On the PTB-XL dataset, scores rival black-box rivals while reasons stay faithful and own to each case.
arxiv-2602-09666:
Lorenz Gärtner and five co-authors test invisible particle decays against a Belle II measurement showing an excess over Standard Model prediction. Their 2026 paper examines a two-body decay. A B meson decays to a kaon plus an invisible particle, a natural candidate invoking axionlike particles, Higgs-like scalars, or beyond-Standard-Model gauge bosons. The test uses Belle II's public model-agnostic likelihood.

Posterior distributions for the resonance mass and decay rate are derived, alongside a modified frequentist upper-limit mass scan. Data favor a light resonance of about two giga-electronvolts, with Bayes factors showing very strong preference for the Standard Model plus resonance over the Standard Model alone. A frequentist likelihood-ratio test favors the resonance hypothesis by three sigma. A light invisible resonance plus the Standard Model thus describes the Belle II data compellingly.
arxiv-2602-09766:
Hartosh Singh Bal studies rate moments of split stats arising from Euler products in his 2026 paper. A transform writes moment making functions as a base series times stated divisor-sum series. When the product is modular, often an eta-quotient, the build yields quasi-modular forms whose numbers can be cast to number runs and proven modulo primes by a Sturm bound. A good chain for finding and proving Ramanujan-type matches for rate moments follows.

For plain splits, several matches for odd moments in nonzero residue classes are found and proven. Applied to over-splits, the same chain proves a family of zero-class matches, in sharp contrast: no nonzero residue-class matches appear for over-split moments in the scan range. Sifting the stat through the Glaisher-character key can itself create new Ramanujan-type runs, as a square twist example proven in the paper shows.
arxiv-2602-10166:
Speech provenance is harder than watermark detection, since real audio gets spliced, quoted, trimmed, and transformed across platforms. A 2026 paper by Tatsunori Ono proposes MerkleSpeech, a system for chunk-localized speech provenance verified by public key. It offers two tiers of proof for each short chunk of speech.

A watermark attribution layer survives common distribution transforms and answers whether a known party issued the chunk. A stricter cryptographic layer verifies Merkle inclusion of the chunk's perceptual fingerprint under an issuer signature, using only public information after the payload is pulled out. The result is a splice-aware record showing which regions pass each tier and why others fail.
arxiv-2602-10366:
Spectral methods attack tensor principal component analysis through a linear operator in a space of exponentially high dimension. Quantum methods were previously shown there to save space exponentially and run quartically faster than classical ones. A 2026 paper by Matthew B. Hastings accelerates both algorithms quadratically while keeping the quartic gap, so the quantum version runs at the eighth power faster than the original classical method. A further tweak lifts the quantum edge over the improved classical method to the sixth power.

Speedups are proven only for detection, not recovery, though Hastings offers a strong plausibility case that recovery follows too. A note added after drafting records a catch. A sharper bound on a random operator's spectral norm, pointed out by A. Schmidhuber, removed the provable polynomial speedup. The speedups therefore rest on spectrum properties, including the density of states, holding for the problem at hand.
arxiv-2602-10666:
Riccardo Miccini and four co-authors extract free side information from speech enhancement networks in a 2026 paper. Enhancement on audio devices often pairs with auxiliary modules for voice activity finding, noise estimation, or scene sorting. Running separate models on-device costs runs, while cloud inference adds latency and privacy risk.

Prior work pruned enhancement networks dynamically, disabling channels based on the input. The authors ask whether those pruning masks themselves encode useful signal traits. Simple clear guessers reading the masks reach high scores on voice activity finding and noise sorting, with strong results on pitch estimation. The result is a free lunch of sorts: traits the device needs, recovered from runs it already performs.
arxiv-2602-10866:
Léo Baty and Axel Parmentier tackle random tail assignment at Air France in a 2026 paper. On-time results drives large operational and customer costs, and the tail assignment problem builds flight strings for single airplanes. Wise routing limits delay propagation, but airlines cannot avoid every delay source.

The authors propose a column making approach whose pricing recipe solves a random shortest path problem. Dedicated bounds discard paths during enumeration, and new bounds based on a lattice ordering of piecewise linear convex functions balance quality against machine cost. A diving heuristic recovers integer answers. Number tests on real-world Air France data test the method where it matters: actual airline work under doubt.
arxiv-2602-11166:
Tuning a model cheaply is often assumed to make it more truthful. Xu Hu and six co-authors test that assumption for hallucination finding under setting-fast fine-tuning. They run three open-weight backbones across three fact-seeking question sets, with seven unsupervised detectors spanning consistency, confidence, and entropy methods.

Setting-fast tuning steadily strengthens finding, lifting scores across a wide range of detectors. Probes and form checks suggest the gain comes from reshaping how doubt is encoded and surfaced, not from injecting new facts. The work clarifies a subtle point: tuning can improve a model's ability to flag its own errors even when it adds little new knowledge.
arxiv-2602-11666:
Agents built for fluid dynamics keep tripping over physics. Language models guess setups that sound plausible but break conservation laws or numerical stability. The authors call that failure context poisoning. E Fan and three co-authors answer with PhyNiKCE, a framework that splits neural planning from symbol checks. A knowledge engine treats setup as a constraint problem and rigidly enforces physical rules.

Specialized retrieval covers solvers, turbulence models, and boundary conditions. Tested on practical OpenFOAM tasks with two Gemini models, the framework improves over the best baselines by 96 percent in relative terms. It cuts self-correction loops by 59 percent and trims token use by 17 percent. Replacing trial-and-error with knowledge-driven setup, the authors argue, yields a scalable, auditable pattern for trustworthy AI in factory automation.
arxiv-2602-11966:
Machine learning keeps moving to edge devices, where field-programmable gate arrays win on energy efficiency but demand careful design under tight resource limits. Jiahong Bi and two co-authors propose MING, a framework built on multi-level intermediate representation that abstracts and automates high-level synthesis design for such chips. A streaming architecture with carefully managed buffers handles resource constraints while keeping latency low.

Against recent frameworks, MING runs standard convolutional kernels with up to four layers about 15 times faster on average, and single-layer kernels up to 200 times faster. For larger inputs, it still generates efficient designs within hardware limits where leading frameworks fail to meet constraints. The work shows that edge-focused design, rather than generic synthesis, is what turns convolutional networks into practical low-power hardware.
arxiv-2602-12466:
Cuprous oxide is prized for photovoltaics and emerging quantum devices based on Rydberg excitons, where crystal purity matters greatly. Alistair Brewin led this work with two co-authors, re-evaluating which native point defects cause sub-band-gap photoluminescence lines in Cu2O. Those lines are widely used to diagnose material quality, yet their origins have stayed controversial for decades.

Using density functional theory with supercell-size convergence checks and cross-functional consistency tests, the team evaluates native defects systematically. The widely accepted assignment of the 1.35, 1.5, and 1.7 electronvolt lines to copper and oxygen vacancies is unsupported. Instead, oxygen interstitials, copper interstitials, and one split copper vacancy form are the only native defects that consistently create true in-gap states, giving a revised frame for reading photoluminescence spectra.
arxiv-2602-12666:
Clean numerical simulation can give very accurate time-space paths of Navier-Stokes turbulence over a finite but long enough time span. Shijun Liao led this work with one co-author, Shijie Qin, giving numerical signs that the Navier-Stokes equations admit distinct global solutions from almost the same starts. Their gap is very small, even at the order of 10 to the minus 40 in size.

That finding bears on uniqueness and existence of Navier-Stokes solutions, tied to a Millennium Prize Problem of the Clay Institute. If distinct solutions can arise from nearly identical starts, uniqueness claims need careful qualification. The authors present these examples as insight for the uniqueness question, not as a proof of non-uniqueness, since numerical signs over finite spans cannot settle global maths uniqueness alone.
arxiv-2602-12766:
Most known maximum rank distance codes lean on arithmetic in large extension fields, which gets costly as parameters grow. Zhe Zhai and three co-authors build a new family from circular shifts alone, working entirely over the base field. The size parameter comes from Euler's totient of a chosen number L, coprime to the field size, which keeps encoding efficient and parameter choice simpler.

The authors then relate their codes to Gabidulin codes and twisted Gabidulin codes through linearised polynomials, spelling out where the families differ and where they meet. In many settings with a mismatch parameter, the new codes differ from every Gabidulin code; in the matching case they coincide with one, giving a simpler construction. For binary codes they also count operations, showing a clear saving over the customary build.
arxiv-2602-12866:
When machines, not people, consume images, compression should preserve what the task needs rather than what the eye likes. Andriy Enttsel and Vincent Corlay revisit the fundamental limits of task-oriented source coding through indirect rate-distortion theory. Earlier bounds often assumed tasks were perfectly identifiable and ignored the quirks of the model actually deployed.

The authors spell out when existing bounds can be reached and where they break in realistic settings. They then propose model-aware bounds that account for a task model's flaws and architectural limits. Tests on standard classification benchmarks show current learned schemes operating far from those limits, with transmitter-side complexity as a key bottleneck. The gap points to where future coding designs should focus.
arxiv-2602-12966:
Static benchmarks age fast as language models evolve, and isolated failure examples say little about systematic weakness. Yue Huang and ten co-authors propose ProbeLLM, a benchmark-agnostic framework that turns failure discovery into structured failure modes. Probing becomes hierarchical Monte Carlo tree search, splitting a limited budget between exploring new failure regions and refining recurring error patterns.

Only verifiable test cases are used, with tool-augmented generation and verification grounding discoveries in reliable evidence. Found failures are then grouped into interpretable modes using embeddings tuned to failures and induction that respects mode boundaries. Across benchmarks and models, ProbeLLM reveals broader, cleaner, and finer-grained weakness landscapes than static tests or earlier automated methods, supporting a shift from case counting to principled weakness discovery.
arxiv-2602-13066:
Making image models sometimes duplicate training images in their outputs, a privacy risk that is acute for medical imaging. Yash Deo and seven co-authors propose a calibrated metric, worked out per sample, for spotting memorisation and duplication in making MRI models. The metric draws traits from an MRI foundation model, combines whitened nearest-neighbour similarities across layers, and maps them to bounded overfit-novelty and memorisation scores.

In tests on three MRI datasets with set duplication rates and typical augmentations, the metric robustly detects duplicates and gives more steady values across datasets than alternatives. At the sample level it achieves near-perfect duplicate detection. For hospitals and researchers sharing making models, a calibrated memorisation index offers a concrete check: made images can be screened for training-data leakage before release.
arxiv-2602-13166:
Unmanned aircraft must avoid obstacles while respecting separation rules, but classical optimal control struggles under uncertainty and opaque decisions worry aviation regulators. Hugo Henry and two co-authors build a hybrid architecture pairing clearance-based optimal control with a fuzzy rule system for adaptive constraint handling. A fuzzy layer with three Takagi-Sugeno-Kang stages modulates constraint radii, urgency, and activation from FAA and EASA separation minima and airworthiness guidelines.

Fuzzy-derived clearances enter the optimal control problem as soft constraints. Solved with the FALCON toolbox and IPOPT, the system activates avoidance updates to cut recomputation. A proof-of-concept with a simplified aircraft model generates optimal trajectories in 2 to 3 seconds per iteration in MATLAB, suggesting near-real-time feasibility. But experiments exposed a solver regression: in current FALCON and IPOPT versions, the Lagrangian penalty term stays identically zero, blocking constraint enforcement, a toolbox flaw rather than a modelling one.
arxiv-2602-13266:
Prompts are the raw material of language model apps, yet storing thousands of them in production eats space and slows systems down. LoPace is a compression engine built just for prompts, combining Zstandard compression, token-based packing, and a hybrid of the two. Tested on 386 prompts spanning code, docs, and structured text, it saved an average of 72.2 percent of space with fully lossless rebuilds.

The hybrid path always beat either method alone, reaching mean ratios near 4.89 times with speeds of 3.3 to 10.7 megabytes per second and a tiny memory footprint of 0.35 megabytes. Those numbers make a case for prompt compression as basic plumbing for large prompt stores and real-time apps. Aman Ulla is the sole author.
arxiv-2602-13466:
Language model embeddings are often spoken of as memory, yet how much input they actually retain is poorly characterized. This paper finds that such embeddings typically hold little input information, at any data or compute scale in training, while codes from autoencoders trained to rebuild inputs achieve nearly perfect memory. Swapping memory embeddings for token sequences promises large compute savings, motivating a parallelizable encoder-decoder memory model.

Under causal training alone, the new models form information-poor embeddings that cannot support arbitrary access. Combining causal and memory-keeping objectives teaches them to form and decode information-rich memories, and freezing a strong encoder plus staged training streamlines the process further. Benjamin L. Badger is the sole author.
arxiv-2602-13666:
Clinicians planning high-dose-rate internal radiation for cervical cancer must balance tumor coverage against organ sparing while controlling radiation hot spots, tracking many metrics against ideal aim values and strict limit values. ALMo, an interactive Aim-Limit-defined Multi-Objective system, infers and puts clinician intent to work with a tuning framework that minimizes manual input through auto parameter setup and flexible toxicity control. Clinicians navigate the Pareto surface of dose trade-offs by directly manipulating intuitive aim and limit values.

In a look back at 25 cases, ALMo plans consistently met or exceeded manual planning quality, with 65 percent showing dose improvements. Planning time fell to about 17 minutes on average, against a conventional 30 to 60 minutes, and the framework carries over to other multi-factor clinical decisions. Edward Chen leads the work with six co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13766:
Generative AI tools such as GitHub Copilot and GPT tools are changing software engineering. But most studies are short-term and individual, leaving lasting team-level effects in industrial agile environments largely unmeasured. This multi-case longitudinal study tracked three agile teams at a large technology consulting firm for around 13 months. It compared numeric telemetry from Jira, SonarQube, and Git with survey data from pre-adoption and post-adoption sprints, and measured output through the multi-dimensional SPACE framework.

The key finding is a sharp increase in Performance and felt Efficiency alongside flat developer Activity, suggesting generative AI raises the value density of development work rather than its volume. That pattern supports multi-dimensional frameworks like SPACE, since studies tracking Activity alone would miss the true nuanced impact of generative AI in situ. Rafael Tomaz leads the work with four co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13866:
Jinwoo Park and two co-authors describe a 2026 arXiv paper on planning work for mixed robot teams. Such teams must juggle many tasks over long shifts while traits like battery charge run down. The authors present TRAITS, a time-extended offline planner built for that setting.

Its core is a nonlinear program that sets how fast each robot group supplies traits, weighing feasibility, finish time, and battery use. That rate-aware view gives sharper estimates of task times and total makespan than rival planners, the authors claim. Tests against two state-of-the-art systems showed TRAITS meeting complex trait and battery demands while staying tractable to compute.
arxiv-2602-14166:
Naoyuki Ota and 28 co-authors report a 2026 arXiv in-orbit test of X-ray pulsar navigation. The CubeSat observatory NinjaSat carries two Gas Multiplier Counters, sensitive to 2 to 50 keV, with 16 square centimeters of effective area per module at 6 keV. Timing checks on the Crab Pulsar held stable within 100 microseconds.

For navigation, the team tuned orbital parameters to sharpen the pulsar pulse profile, a method called SEPO. With about 100 kiloseconds of Crab exposure across epochs, they compared the tuned orbit with GPS-derived positions. The line-of-sight position stayed within about 40 km, a concrete step toward GPS-free navigation for small satellites in deep space.
arxiv-2602-14366:
Eden Ketchum and three co-authors prove a 2026 arXiv result toward a conjecture on Sylow 3-subgroups. Navarro, Rizo, Schaeffer Fry, and Vallejo guessed a method to tell from a character table if a finite group has 2-generated Sylow 3-subgroups. The paper proves one direction of that conjecture.

The result also supports the blockwise Galois-McKay conjecture, known as the Alperin-McKay-Navarro conjecture. A key step proves the Isaacs-Navarro Galois conjecture for principal blocks of finite groups with a certain structure. The work thus ties character-table data to subgroup generation, with evidence for a broader blockwise picture.
arxiv-2602-14466:
Lance Calvin Lim Gamboa and two co-authors build a 2026 arXiv bias benchmark for Filipino question-answering models. The Bias Benchmark for Question-Answering form is key for testing stock links shown by generative models, but its scope needed widening to Philippine settings. FilBBQ was built in four phases: template sorting, culture-aware versioning, new template building, and prompt making.

The resulting test holds over 10,000 prompts gauging sexist and homophobic skew apt to the Philippines. Applied to models trained in Filipino, a tough plan averages skew scores across many seeds to account for answer wobble. Results confirm skew scores shift across seeds, showing single-seed skew tests can mislead, and that tough multi-seed plans are needed for trusted skew claims.
arxiv-2602-14666:
Surgery inside body lumens needs tools that bend and see at once. Ruofeng Wei, with nine co-authors, presents a vision platform for flexible robotic endoscopes in early cancer surgery. A single camera must track the tool, judge its angle, and gauge distance to tissue.

New 2D and 3D perception methods are paired with a realistic simulator of flexible tool motion. The simulator supplies large training scenes that real surgery cannot. Tests on a continuum robot prototype cut trajectory-following time by over 70 percent. The platform aims at steadier, safer resections inside the gut and urinary tract.
arxiv-2602-14866:
Wan-Zhe Feng and Zi-Hui Zhang chase gauge-free wave signs from a small dark U(1) patch with sound dark matter picks. Wave seas from first-order phase shifts could bare hid sectors, but gauge wobble in heat laws and tunnel sums clouds hard sums.

Their patch holds a dark Higgs and a dark light bit, with an extra dark fermion at times, tied to known stuff by a Higgs door or a mix link. With the Nielsen identity, a tame slope run, and plain counts, they build a gauge-free heat law in hot and cold ends, so birth rates gain a true, patch-born form. Hid-sector wave signs thus gain sums free of gauge tricks.
arxiv-2602-14966:
Bhaskar and colleagues study Challenge the Champ tournaments, where players enter in a chosen order. The first becomes champion, and each newcomer faces the current holder. Each match is worth the winner's popularity. Earlier work assumed fixed outcomes. Here match winners are probabilistic, and the goal is robust value: the total guaranteed no matter how the uncertain matches fall.

Even in simple binary settings, the best robust value is hard to approximate for non-adaptive seedings. That value is called the value not at risk. The picture brightens with adaptivity, letting later challengers depend on earlier results, or with limits on which matches are uncertain. In those cases the team obtains good approximations.
arxiv-2602-15066:
Ruano and Rajan model bank runs as social contagion among language-model depositors. Digital banking and online chatter have made runs faster and more networked than branch queues. Equilibrium models explain run risk from strategic complementarities, but say little about how beliefs sync and spread. The team builds an agent model that makes information and coordination explicit.

Banks process cash-first withdrawals with discounted fire sales and an endogenous stress index. Depositors differ in risk tolerance and in how much they weigh fundamentals versus social cues. They chat on a heavy-tailed network tuned to Twitter activity in March 2023. Across 4900 setups, within-bank links raise cascade odds and speed. Cross-bank contagion flips sharply near a spillover rate of one tenth, and weak channels combine into strong ones. A scenario tuned to SVB, First Republic, and regional banks reproduces the failure order. It predicts heavier withdrawals by uninsured depositors.
arxiv-2602-15166:
Andrulis and colleagues introduce the Fast and Fusiest Mapper, an optimal fusion-aware mapper for accelerator design. Tensor algebra accelerators must schedule data movement and operations well, and fusion, holding data on-chip between computation steps, cuts energy and latency by avoiding costly off-chip movement. The best fusion choice varies with workload and shape, so a mapper that searches mappings can improve both metrics markedly.

Prior mappers cannot find optimal fused mappings in feasible time, since the count of fused mappings grows exponentially with computation steps. FFM shrinks the search space by pruning partial mappings proven never to belong to optimal mappings, then joins surviving partial mappings into optimal fused mappings. Against TransFusion, a state-of-the-art accelerator with hand-optimized fusion, FFM reduces energy-delay product. It also finds mappings orders of magnitude faster than TileFlow and SET, and at equal runtime reduces energy-delay product further.
arxiv-2602-15566:
Akrami and Reichert study fair division when goods cannot be split and agents value items additively. The field has long split into envy-based fairness, where no one prefers another share, and share-based fairness, centred on the maximin share each agent could guarantee alone. Recent work showed allocations can meet approximate forms of both at once, but ordinal approximations of the maximin share had not been tested against envy notions.

This paper closes that gap with three existence results for ordered and top-n cases. It gives allocations meeting one-out-of-ceiling-three-n-over-two maximin share with EFX for ordered instances, the same share level with EF1 for top-n instances, and one-out-of-four-ceiling-n-over-three share with EF1 for ordered instances. Fair division theorists gain a first map of where ordinal share and envy guarantees can coexist.
arxiv-2602-15666:
Han and Wen prove a rigidity result for Yang-Mills connections on compact manifolds under curvature pinching. They establish pinching conditions under which every weakly stable Yang-Mills connection must be flat, meaning it carries no nontrivial curvature in the relevant sense. The argument turns a geometric squeeze on curvature into a strong conclusion about the connection itself.

As a corollary, they give a dimension-dependent constant delta of n and prove that no non-flat weakly stable Yang-Mills connections exist on delta of n pinched, compact, simply connected Riemannian manifolds. The result draws a clean line: pinch tightly enough, and stable Yang-Mills fields collapse to the trivial case. Geometers will find a sharp link between curvature bounds and the possible shapes of stable gauge fields.
arxiv-2602-15766:
Kumar and colleagues introduce TAC, a timestamped audio captioner for complex acoustic scenes. Large audio language models struggle when events overlap, giving captions that clash in time and inventing sounds that are not there. TAC instead gives audio notes grounded in time, at varying detail and resolution. It learns from a synthetic setup that builds hard, shifting mixes from real-world audio sources.

Across event detection and dense captioning, TAC beats all rival methods, with few invented sounds and accurate time grounding. The team also introduces TAC-V, an audio-visual setup for rich descriptions. Together, TAC and TAC-V serve as a meaning bridge for a text-only thinker. Simple chains into a language model reach state-of-the-art scores on audio tests MMAU-Pro, MMSU, and MMAR, plus audio-visual tests DailyOmni and VideoHolmes.
arxiv-2602-15866:
Goswami and colleagues review 203 peer-reviewed papers on privacy risks when natural language processing meets social media work. Social media content often carries private info, behaviour cues, and meta, raising risks of watching, tracking, and aimed ads. Their NLP-PRISM framework evaluates gaps across six sides: data taking, cleaning, showing, fairness, compute risk, and legal rules.

Transformer models hit F1-scores from 0 point 58 to 0 point 84, but take a 1 percent to 23 percent drop under privacy tuning. Using NLP-PRISM, the team checks privacy reach in six NLP tasks. Counts: sentiment study 16, emotion spotting 14, abusive language tagging 19, mixed-code handling 39, native language tagging 29, dialect spotting 24. Gaps in privacy research stand out. A trade-off in model use of 2 percent to 9 percent is found, with member attack AUC of 0 point 81 and trait attack scores of 0 point 75. The authors urge stronger masking, privacy learning, and fairness training for ethical NLP.
arxiv-2602-16066:
Martin Klissarov leads a team of eight researchers training language models to learn from corrective feedback in conversation, a skill humans use daily but current training largely neglects. Standard training leans on vast static text, which builds knowledge yet skips the feedback loops that let a model adjust its thinking mid-task. The team turns single-turn verifiable tasks into multi-turn teaching exchanges driven by information gaps between teacher and learner.

Flagship models today struggle to absorb corrections on hard reasoning tasks, but models trained with the new method improve sharply at interactive learning. A smaller trained model nearly matches a model ten times larger on multi-turn performance, and training on math transfers to coding, puzzles, and maze navigation. Teaching the model to predict teacher critiques also lets it self-correct without a teacher, pointing toward a unified route to self-improvement.
arxiv-2602-16166:
Jialin Zheng leads a team of four authors finding governing equations for grid-linked inverters from external measurements alone. Unknown inverter dynamics cloud analysis of modern power systems packed with such units. Existing methods struggle to balance spotting of unmodeled nonlinearities against physical rules. Their framework, Physics-Informed Sparse Machine Learning, pairs a sparse symbolic spine with a neural residual arm. The backbone captures main model skeletons. The residual branch makes up for complex nonlinear control logic.

A Jacobian-regularized training design enforces agreement across large and small scales. Symbolic regression on the second arm then maps black-box data to explicit control rules. Tests on a high-fidelity hardware-in-the-loop rig show error cuts of more than three hundred fold versus baselines. Heavy neural networks shrink into compact plain forms. That restores analytical tractability for stability checks and cuts compute sharply.
arxiv-2602-16266:
Guang Lin and coauthors propose tensor network based quantum data encoding, called TNQE, to address a major limiting step in quantum machine learning. Common encodings in wide use are often circuit-inefficient, demanding deep circuits and heavy use of quantum resources. TNQE first represents each classical input via a tensor network decomposition. It then compiles resulting tensor cores into a coding circuit through two complementary strategies. To keep compilation trainable while respecting the unitary nature of quantum operations, a unitary-aware constraint parameterizes tensor cores as learnable block unitaries.

The framework gives explicit control over circuit depth and qubit resources. Across benchmarks, TNQE achieves coding circuits as shallow as four hundredths of the depth of amplitude encoding, while scaling to high-resolution images. The work thus offers a circuit-efficient route to loading classical data into quantum states.
arxiv-2602-16366:
Sandro Coriasco leads a team of three coauthors on global Gevrey hypoellipticity for involutive systems on non-compact manifolds. They investigate first-order differential operators tied to tube-type involutive structures on a product of a non-compact manifold with a torus. The manifold is diffeomorphic to the interior of a compact manifold with boundary, and the work runs in Gevrey classes of Roumieu and Beurling type for orders above one.

A key step builds a scattering metric on the manifold whose coefficients are Gevrey of the same order in every analytic chart. That construction lets the authors use Hodge theory to obtain Gevrey regularity for harmonic forms. Under a natural condition on the defining closed one-forms, they obtain a sharp criterion for global Gevrey hypoellipticity, stated in terms of rationality and exponential Liouville behavior of Roumieu and Beurling type.
arxiv-2602-16666:
Stephan Rabanser and co-authors argue for a science of AI agent reliability beyond single success scores. Agents now run key tasks, and rising benchmark accuracy hints at swift progress, yet many agents still fail in practice. Compressing behavior into one score hides core flaws. It ignores run-to-run steadiness, shock resistance, predictable failure, and bounded error harm.

Grounded in safety-critical engineering, the paper offers twelve concrete scores split across four axes: consistency, robustness, predictability, and safety. Fifteen models are tested on two complementary benchmarks. Recent capability gains yield only small reliability gains. The scores thus complement standard tests, giving builders tools to reason about how agents act, degrade, and fail.
arxiv-2602-16766:
Scott Carlsten and co-authors present first results from ELVES-Field, a survey of dwarf galaxies in the Local Volume within ten megaparsecs, spanning roughly three thousand square degrees. Candidates are found with a semi-automated algorithm tuned for low surface brightness dwarfs. Injection tests show detection is half complete to a stated faint limit.

Candidates are confirmed as true nearby dwarfs through redshift, tip of the red giant branch, and surface brightness fluctuation distances. Isolated field dwarfs are picked by varied environmental rules. Over the footprint, ninety-five Local Volume dwarfs are detected and confirmed, forty-four of them isolated. The inferred field dwarf mass function matches prior redshift surveys and IllustrisTNG predictions at the high-mass end, giving a powerful sample for small-scale structure and environment studies.
arxiv-2602-16866:
Ginevra Larroux, Matthieu Jacobs, and Mario Paolone probe tightness of the second-order cone relaxation of the optimal power flow problem. The focus is meshed networks, with angles recovery and alternating-current feasibility in view. Theory is backed by numerical tests on standard IEEE cases. Implications for power system planning are briefly outlined.

Readers in power systems get a focused letter on when a widely used convex relaxation can be trusted in meshed grids. They also learn when recovered voltage angles fail to yield a feasible alternating-current solution. That tightness question matters because relaxations underpin fast planning and operation tools. A loose relaxation can mislead decisions about real networks.
arxiv-2602-16966:
Sourav Chakraborty and co-authors present a unified frame for locality in scalable multi-agent reinforcement learning. In networked multi-agent reinforcement learning, scalable methods allow planning by each agent from just its nearby agents in the graph. Such local planning is valid only for a value-local system, where a distant agent's long-run value shifts only slightly in response to a disturbance at one agent.

The paper splits the matrix into pieces separately tracking environment sensitivity and policy sensitivity. Decay of the average-reward Poisson solution is then governed by the resulting matrix's spectral radius, whose spectral certificate is, on the same matrix, strictly weaker than the row-sum condition on that matrix.
arxiv-2602-17066:
Sumedh Rasal, writing alone, proposes a cheaper way to speed up language model training: choose each batch by predicted difficulty. Curriculum methods need preset difficulty scores. Hard-example mining tracks every sample's loss at high cost. Predictive Batch Scheduling avoids both: it trains a light linear predictor online from static token features alone.

Four simple features, token frequency, sequence length, vocabulary diversity, and rare token ratio, let the predictor track true loss with a solid correlation that grows as training proceeds. On a 130-million-parameter transformer, the method reached target evaluation loss several percent faster across checkpoints. The finding suggests token frequency patterns carry real signal about sample difficulty, so smart batch choice can come nearly free.
arxiv-2602-17166:
Antonio Franchi led a two-author paper giving fixed-wing flight a coordinate-free inverse dynamics treatment. Force balance for motion is written in the world frame and spin dynamics in the body frame, with drag, lift, and side directions defined by geometry rather than through local attitude angles. Enforcing coordinated flight with no sideslip yields a closed-form map from flight path to inputs.

That map returns attitude, spin rate, and the thrust-angle-of-attack pair, plus aero moment coefficients piece by piece. Applied to tethered flight on spherical parallels, it gives analytic bank angles and a zero-bank locus where tether pull exactly offsets centrifugal effects, separating aero coordination from apparent gravity. Under a simple lift-drag law, the minimal-thrust angle of attack also closes in form, giving path designers a rigorous feasibility tool.
arxiv-2602-17366:
Yiming Zhang led a four-author team improving dense lookup for long-tail question answering. Large language models struggle to acquire and recall less common knowledge, and lookup-augmented generation helps by adding external lookup, yet dense lookup models also falter on rare or niche knowledge. The paper introduces RPDR, a data augmentation system that selects high-quality, easy-to-learn training data to strengthen dense lookup models.

Three parts drive the approach: synthetic data creation, data choice with Round-Trip prediction to spot easy-to-learn cases, and lookup model training on those cases. Tests on two long-tail lookup benchmarks show substantial gains over existing lookup models, especially on extremely long-tail groups. Detailed human analysis maps RPDR's strengths and limits, and a dynamic routing plan is proposed to send queries to specialized lookup modules for further gains.
arxiv-2602-17666:
Gabriel Malavé and team uncover an anisotropic marginal Fermi liquid in generalized Weyl semimetals in three dimensions. Power-law anisotropy in quasiparticle dispersion boosts the density of states, so long-range Coulomb effects grow strong. The semimetals carry integer monopole charge at their Weyl nodes, and the charge value shapes the physics.

With a Wilsonian renormalization group method, the team finds an interaction-led scaling regime for charge above one. It shows anisotropic dynamic screening, a finite fermionic anomalous dimension, and power-law suppression of quasiparticle residue. The effective fine structure constant flows slowly to zero, so the marginal liquid appears as a broad crossover. Charge-one systems instead keep an isotropic marginal Weyl-liquid character, testable in heat, optics and photoemission.
arxiv-2602-18266:
Stefan Wahl and four co-authors recast machine-led model discovery as probability, not craft. Their 2026 paper notes that agent-style workflows propose and revise simulator models by imitating human scientists, but existing language-model versions rely on hand-built heuristics with no explicit probability frame. The team instead treats discovery as sampling from an unknown spread of mechanisms that could explain the data.

That single frame unifies proposing, refining, and choosing models. Its concrete form, ModelSMC, runs sequential Monte Carlo sampling: candidate models act as particles, repeatedly proposed and refined by a language model and weighted by fit. On real scientific systems the method finds readable mechanisms and improves posterior predictive checks. The paper offers a principled lens for building and judging language-model discovery tools.
arxiv-2602-18766:
Pathology slides are gigapixels wide, so a model must learn from a handful of labelled slides without wasting that scarce signal on a bad start. Pablo Meseguer, with two co-authors, shows in 2026 that how a classifier is initialised matters greatly for few-shot adaptation of vision-language models to histopathology, and proposes a fix called ZS-MIL.

Standard random initialisation can underperform even zero-shot prediction in multiple-instance learning, where patch features are pooled into one slide-level decision. ZS-MIL instead starts the classification layer from the text encoder's class embeddings, so each slide's bag-level probabilities begin from knowledge the model already has. Experiments on subtype prediction show stronger and steadier performance than well-known initialisation techniques.
arxiv-2602-18966:
Speech recognition still struggles with domain-specific speech, even for strong systems like Whisper. Yonathan Ron, with two co-authors, introduces Whisper: Courtside Edition in 2026. It is a multi-agent LLM pipeline that improves Whisper transcripts without retraining.

The pipeline intercepts Whisper's first transcript. Specialised agents identify domain context, recognise named entities, and detect jargon. Compact prompts from those agents then guide Whisper's decoder. Evaluation on hundreds of NBA commentary segments, dense with proper nouns and technical terms, shows a statistically significant relative reduction in word error rate of about one-sixth. Improvements appear in about forty percent of segments, with degradation in only about seven percent. Prompt-based augmentation thus offers scalable domain adaptation without costly fine-tuning.
arxiv-2602-19166:
Accent normalisation often sounds unnatural or distorts content. Qibing Bai, with five co-authors, fixes both flaws in 2026 with CosyAccent. Poor training data and rigid duration modelling cause the trouble. Their source-synthesis method generates source second-language speech and uses authentic native speech as target. No real second-language data is needed for training, and text-to-speech artefacts are avoided.

CosyAccent itself is non-autoregressive. It models rhythm implicitly for flexibility, yet controls total output duration explicitly. That resolves the naturalness-versus-control tradeoff. Despite training without real second-language speech, it preserves content better and sounds more natural than strong baselines trained on real-world data. Accent normalisation thus gains a data-efficient path.
arxiv-2602-19566:
Why small collision systems show collectivity-like signatures is a major open question in high-energy nuclear physics. Subhadeep Roy and Sadhana Dash study two-particle counts and sideways-push link functions in proton-proton crashes at 13 teraelectronvolts, run with PYTHIA 8. Events get sorted by their sideways activity, testing how background-event activity shapes links in the soft-QCD regime.

A long-range near-side signal shows up in the charge-blind counter only for the busiest class, with sideways activity between 2.5 and 5.0. No twin signal shows up at lower activity, hinting background-event activity drives the effect. The work gives a keen test of how soft-QCD forces make such patterns.
arxiv-2602-19766:
Building an explorable three-dimensional scene from a single photo is hard, because views far from the original often collapse into distortion and noise. A 2026 arXiv paper by Pengfei Wang and five co-authors introduces One2Scene, a framework that splits the problem into three manageable steps.

First a panorama generator creates anchor views from the input image. Then a feed-forward Gaussian splatting network lifts those anchors into an explicit geometric scaffold, recast as multi-view stereo matching with a fusion module that enforces cross-view consistency. Finally that scaffold guides a novel-view generator to render photorealistic, geometrically sound views at arbitrary cameras. Tests show large gains over prior methods in panorama depth, full-circle reconstruction, and explorable scene generation.
arxiv-2602-19866:
A doubly charged Higgs boson would be a striking sign of physics beyond the Standard Model, and future electron-positron colliders could hunt for it. A 2026 arXiv paper by Brahim Ait-Ouazghour and six co-authors studies its discovery prospects in a two-Higgs-doublet model with type-II seesaw.

The team scans parameter space under theoretical and current experimental constraints. It focuses on three-body production channels. Over wide regions, especially above key decay thresholds, these channels can outrun conventional pair production, reaching large cross sections at collider energies in the hundreds to low thousands of giga-electronvolts. A detector-level study of a four-lepton plus missing-energy signature shows discovery sensitivity is achievable at the highest energies. That holds with realistic systematics, even against multiboson and top-quark backgrounds.
arxiv-2602-19966:
People recovering from surgery for strabismus, a misalignment of the eyes, lack accessible tools for tracking their own eye alignment day to day. A 2026 arXiv paper by Joydeep Chandra and two co-authors presents GazeFlow, a browser-based system for passive self-monitoring through ambient sound.

A personalized temporal autoencoder detects eye drift patterns from webcam gaze tracking, and the system morphs musical parameters in proportion to drift severity, staying in peripheral awareness rather than sounding alarms. That calm-computing design suits self-awareness better than alert-based tools. New techniques handle differences between people and the gap between research-grade and webcam tracking rates. Tests on a gaze data set show strong drift detection, and a small user study finds participants more aware of their eye behaviour and preferring ambient feedback over alerts.
arxiv-2602-20166:
Agents flood users with alerts, mostly false. Users grow numb and miss the critical ones. That numbness is called alert fatigue. A 2026 arXiv paper by Yongda Yu and eleven co-authors proposes ConceptRM, a way to build clean training data for a reflection model that catches false alerts.

Reflection models normally learn as filters from user verification feedback. That feedback data is noisy because it comes from production use, and cleaning it by hand costs too much. ConceptRM starts from a small set of expert labels used as anchors. It builds noisy variants of the data at several noise levels. Several distinct models then learn together through co-teaching. Their agreement reveals which examples are clean. Those examples form the corpus for training the reflection model.
arxiv-2602-20766:
Sean Dewar and two co-authors tackle a basic question in discrete geometry: how many ways can a rigid graph be built from a fixed set of edge lengths? They give two new tools that work in any dimension. One links subgraph inclusion to divisibility of these counts. The other sets lower bounds under common graph operations.

With these tools they prove a lower bound for triangulated spheres. With n vertices, at least 2 to the power n minus 4 placements exist in three dimensions. That extends a two-dimensional result of Jackson and Owen. Their tools also settle a family of conjectures by Grasegger on how three local moves change realisation numbers.
arxiv-2602-20866:
Recomputing everything from scratch wastes effort when only part of an input changes. Timon Bohler, Tobias Reinhard, David Richter, and Mira Mezini present DeCo in this 2026 arXiv paper, a core calculus for incremental functional programming that supports user-defined data types. Unlike generic methods that treat domain operations as black boxes, DeCo incrementalizes those operations statically and at fine grain.

The authors mechanized DeCo in Lean and offer that mechanization as proof that incremental runs match full reevaluation. An executable implementation covers case studies from linear and relational algebra to dictionaries, trees, and conflict-free replicated data types, with a brief performance evaluation. Programmers get a principled route to faster recomputation without giving up genericity.
arxiv-2602-20966:
Do language models grasp grammar, or only patterns that look grammatical? Paola Merlo, Chunyang Jiang, Giuseppe Samo, and Vivi Nastase probe that question in this 2026 arXiv paper using Blackbird Language Matrices. These multiple-choice problems, inspired by intelligence tests, are structured within sentences, across sequences, and within candidate answers.

The curated yet naturalistic datasets ask whether models detect linguistic objects and their properties, use systematic patterns across sentences, and lean toward linguistic or reasoning errors. Simple baselines solve the tasks at good levels in more than one language, and tailored models do better, by spotting systematic patterns. The paper argues such structured datasets support deeper, explainable study of why models behave as they do.
arxiv-2602-21066:
Knowledge graphs promise rich information, but newcomers face a basic problem: they do not know what to ask or where to begin. Claire McNamara, Lucy Hederman, and Declan O'Sullivan name that problem in this 2026 arXiv paper: the Initial Exploration Problem. Drawing on information behavior and human-computer interaction theories, they characterize it through three interdependent barriers.

Scope uncertainty, ontology opacity, and query incapacity converge at first contact, setting this problem apart from related ideas that assume a starting point or goal. Analyzing exploration interfaces at the level of interaction primitives, the authors find many systems assume knowledge newcomers lack. The paper argues the design space is missing primitives for scope revelation, and offers a lens for building entry-point scaffolding.
arxiv-2602-21566:
Yunhao Mao and six co-authors introduce Minerva, a control design for geo-replicated databases. Geo-distribution is vital for service trust and high uptime in modern online apps. But strictly ordered jobs in geo-copied databases stay hard, due to excess joint work in atomic commit, side-by-side work, and fault-tolerance copies at high latency.

Minerva uses an epoch-based non-blocking copy protocol splitting data spread from commits, for non-stop copies. Any copy can run jobs side by side and commit with no sync. Instead of aborting on clashes, Minerva settles them with fixed re-runs, keeping order with no speed loss. A clash graph plus a max-weight free-set method picks the commit subset, cutting re-runs. Tests show Minerva beating copied databases, with over 3 times higher speed in scale tests and nearly 3 times higher speed at high latency on TPC-C.
arxiv-2602-21966:
When shoppers search an online store, the ads they see are sold in auctions, and one seller can win several slots at once for different products. Paul Dütting and four co-authors study these sponsored shopping auctions, where the prize is a bundle of slots rather than a single link. They focus on autobidding, in which software places one shared bid across a seller's whole catalog while trying to earn the most value within a set return on spending.

The authors test two common auction rules, called generalized second-price and Vickrey-Clarke-Groves, and prove that a stable bidding outcome always exists under both. They also show that the loss from selfish bidding is capped at a factor of two, and that this cap cannot be improved. The result gives marketplace designers a firm limit on how much efficiency such auctions can lose.
arxiv-2602-22266:
State-space models promise efficient long-range sequence modeling, but most projection-based versions lean on polynomial bases spread across all time. Ruben Solozabal and five co-authors argue that global support mismatches signals with local, transient structure. They introduce WaveSSM, a family of state-space models built over wavelet frames, whose localized time support suits precise localization tasks.

On equal footing, WaveSSM beats orthogonal rivals like S4 on real-world transient data, from physiological signals to raw speech commands. The wavelet construction keeps the HiPPO-style stability and memory efficiency while fitting signals that flare and fade. For sequence modelers, it offers a basis matched to the bursts and blips of real data.
arxiv-2602-22366:
Planetary nebulae bathe their surroundings in harsh ultraviolet light, an environment thought hostile to fragile ices. Charmi Bhatt and twenty-two co-authors report JWST observations that defy that expectation. Carbon dioxide ice was detected in the dusty torus of the planetary nebula NGC 6302, alongside cold gas-phase carbon dioxide along the same sightlines.

The ice absorption shows a double-peak profile characteristic of pure, crystalline carbon dioxide ice. Its gas-to-ice ratio runs more than ten times higher than in young stellar objects, pointing to distinct formation or processing in evolved stars. The dusty torus evidently shields ice chemistry well enough to sustain it, and chemical models of planetary nebulae must now include ice-mediated surface reactions.
arxiv-2602-22766:
You Li and six co-authors challenge latent visual reasoning, the idea that hidden states can silently imagine like humans do. Using causal mediation analysis, they model input as treatment, latent tokens as mediator, and final answer as outcome, then perturb each link to test whether it truly matters.

Two disconnections emerge. Input changes barely move latent tokens, suggesting those tokens ignore the input sequence. Latent-token changes barely move the final answer, suggesting weak causal force on outcomes. Probing also finds latent tokens carry little visual detail and look highly similar. The team therefore questions latent reasoning and offers CapImagine, which teaches models to imagine explicitly in text, beating complex latent baselines on vision benchmarks.
arxiv-2602-22966:
JinHoo Ahn and one co-author give criteria for a first-order theory to be NCTP or NBTP, using tree-indiscernibility. In model theory, first-order theories describe structures with a formal language, and tree-indiscernibility means sequences that stay indistinguishable when arranged in tree-shaped patterns. The criteria turn that symmetry idea into a test for the two properties.

As an application, the authors show that Mekler's construction preserves both NCTP and NBTP. Mekler's construction builds new structures from graphs, so the result says these two tree-related properties survive the passage from graph to structure, a stability fact for classification theory.
arxiv-2602-23066:
Zach Walsh presents a new construction of matroids from gain graphs over quotient groups, generalizing several existing constructions at once. The construction takes a gain graph over a Frobenius group and outputs an elementary lift of the frame matroid of the underlying gain graph over the quotient group.

While requiring a Frobenius group may seem unusual, Walsh proves it is in some sense necessary. Suppose any finite group with a nontrivial proper normal subgroup admits such a construction, with a cycle a circuit exactly when it is balanced. Then that group must be a Frobenius group with that subgroup as its Frobenius kernel.
arxiv-2602-23166:
Zhaochen Su and twelve co-authors introduce AgentVista, a benchmark for generalist multimodal agents that must carry out realistic, multi-step work grounded in what they see. Real tasks, such as fixing a device from a wiring photo plus a schematic, need long chains of tool use across images, text, and code. Existing benchmarks mostly test single-turn visual reasoning or narrow tool skills instead.

AgentVista spans 25 sub-domains in seven groups. It pairs detail-rich visual scenes with hybrid tool use, including web and image search, page navigation, and code for image work and general programming. Tests of leading models reveal wide gaps. Even the best system, Gemini-3-Pro with tools, scores only 27.3 percent overall, and hard cases can demand more than 25 tool calls. The benchmark is meant to push agents toward more reliable long-horizon work.
arxiv-2602-23266:
Siyuan Liu and eight co-authors present DDTSR, a low-latency framework for spoken dialogue systems that can listen while thinking and speak while thinking. Standard pipelines chain speech recognition, language modeling, and speech synthesis in strict sequence, waiting for full transcription and full reasoning before synthesis starts. That sequence creates the high response latency that keeps synthetic voices from feeling human.

DDTSR rests on three mechanisms. A small auxiliary model drafts minimal-committal discourse connectives while a large model reasons in parallel. Streaming overlap across recognition, inference, and synthesis moves the earliest speakable moment forward. Curriculum learning keeps early responses coherent with later reasoning. On two spoken dialogue benchmarks, latency falls by 19 to 51 percent with discourse quality preserved, and the module works as a plug-and-play add-on across language-model backbones and utterance lengths.
arxiv-2602-23466:
Adam Moss presents nanoCMB, a short, readable Python code for computing the unlensed CMB temperature and polarisation power spectra of flat Lambda-CDM cosmologies. In about 1400 lines, it implements the full line-of-sight method, including RECFAST recombination, coupled Einstein-Boltzmann equations, Bessel function tables, and tailored grids in wavenumber and conformal time.

Despite its brevity, nanoCMB matches CAMB to sub-percent accuracy across multipoles from 2 to 2500, running in about 10 seconds on a modern laptop. The whole calculation lives in one easily modified script, with every approximation and numerical choice made explicit. Designed as a bridge between textbook treatments and research-level solvers, it pairs detailed physics exposition with code snippets at each stage.
arxiv-2602-23566:
Asiri Wijesinghe and three co-authors present Flowette, a flow matching method for graph making with graphette priors. The work models graphs with repeat subgraph motifs, using a graph neural network-based transformer to learn a speed field over graph forms with node and edge traits.

The model aids shape-aware matching through optimal transport-based coupling and builds global shape unity through smoothing. Grapettes, a new chance-based family of graph form models, extend graphons via set shape edits for motifs such as rings, stars, and trees. The authors analyze coupling, sameness, and shape traits in theory, test on mock and atom-scale benchmarks, and isolate each part's share through set cut-out tests. Flowette gets strong scores overall, with state-of-the-art results on several metrics across multiple benchmarks.
arxiv-2602-23666:
R. I. El-Kholy and one co-author apply pool-based active learning to livable-world sorting under extreme class skew. Growing, mixed exo-world lists make full livable-world checks challenging, above all given the rarity of possibly livable worlds and shifting labels.

The team builds a unified data set from the Habitable World Catalog and NASA Exoplanet Archive, framing livability as binary sorting. A guided starting point using gradient-boosted choice trees is tuned for recall to favor rare possibly livable worlds. That model is placed in an active learning method, testing doubt-based margin sampling against random tagging across multiple runs and tagging budgets. Active learning a lot reduces tagged cases needed to approach guided scores, showing clear gains in tagging speed. Calls from alone-trained active-learning models are pooled into an ensemble, whose mean odds and doubts rank worlds first tagged non-livable.
arxiv-2602-23766:
Zheng Dou and four co-authors present UniFAR, a single system for finding scientific papers in two common ways: from a seed paper, and from a plain question. The 2026 paper notes that past systems handle those two tasks apart, which wastes what each could teach the other.

UniFAR encodes short questions and long papers in one shared space, using several levels of detail and learnable anchors that mark the parts of a paper a question may target. Training joins both tasks, mixing paper-to-paper contrast with question-to-paper contrast and facet-level matching. Tests on three benchmarks, across both tasks and several base models, show steady gains over strong rivals and good transfer across models. The design suits research tools that must serve both browsing and question answering.
arxiv-2602-23866:
Ibragim Badertdinov and three co-authors introduce SWE-rebench V2, a language-agnostic pipeline for harvesting real software engineering tasks to train coding agents. The 2026 paper addresses a bottleneck. Reinforcement learning for such agents needs many tasks with reproducible setups and trustworthy tests, which existing collections supply only in limited scale and language range.

The pipeline builds repository-specific install and test steps with an interactive setup agent, then filters unsound tasks with an ensemble of language-model judges checked against human-verified annotations. It yields tens of thousands of tasks across many languages and thousands of repositories, with prebuilt images for repeatable runs, plus a larger set with install steps, fail-to-pass tests, and metadata. A diagnostic study across languages and models validates the collection and flags confounders such as overly strict tests.
arxiv-2602-24266:
Amir Asiaee introduces causal mechanism reduction, a framework asking, for a neural network, which internal mechanisms can be replaced while the computation it performs is preserved. The 2026 solo paper joins two questions: structured pruning, which seeks smaller deployable networks, and causal abstraction.

The framework replaces selected internal variables in a trained network treated as a deterministic structural causal model. By bias and weight folding, those replacements compile exactly into smaller dense networks. A unified second-order replacement-risk objective recovers mean replacement, variance-based pruning, logit-distortion scoring, and affine neuron merging as special cases. The framework also exposes an invariance requirement: identical rectified networks should induce the same reduction. Empirical tests show competitive pruning performance with clearer separation on invariance and interchange tests.
arxiv-2603-00066: Aijaz sets out a 5E plan for judging the morals of artificial moral agents, machines said to reason about right and wrong on their own. It judges such machines on five grounds: ethical, explainable, empirical, evaluative and epistemological. It also maps zones of ethical sway from the single person through the local and societal to the global level. A draft time plan shows builders where disputes may crop up, or where they might dispute their own work to keep it in line with good values.
arxiv-2603-00166: Li and colleagues spot a Paradox of Simplicity: models that render complex scenes often fail at trivial tasks like making a uniform pure-colour image. They blame an aesthetic bias, where strong priors for beauty and complexity override deterministic simplicity as models scale, blocking the shift to intellectual abstraction. The authors formalise AI Obedience, a five-level framework grading the move from probabilistic approximation to pixel-level determinism. Their Violin benchmark tests Level 4 obedience via colour purity, masking and shape generation, finding closed-source models ahead on deterministic precision.
arxiv-2603-00466: Tan and nine colleagues give video generators a fuller world model instead of surface plausibility alone. Past systems add only one kind of world knowledge or align it rigidly, missing the joint mix of physical sense, three dimensional shape, and time consistency. DreamWorld predicts video pixels and foundation model features together, then steadies training with gradual constraint tightening and enforces learned priors at inference. Tests show stronger world consistency, beating Wan2.1 by 2.26 points on VBench.
arxiv-2603-00566: Du and four colleagues extend rock paper scissors ecology with higher order interactions where local resources tune intraspecific competition. Stronger higher order effects shrink spatial wavelength and pack species into tighter domains, sharpening local patterns. The same change also heightens mobility sensitivity and lowers the extinction threshold. That resource rule thus both builds local structure and weakens resilience to dispersal, a dual lesson for saving species.
arxiv-2603-00666: Yan and eleven colleagues make open federated learning payoffs practical with FWeb3, a Web3 enabled system for participation. Past plans stress code design while neglecting coordination, secure update handling, and ease of use. FWeb3 separates learning functions from Web3 support services, decoupling off chain training from on chain settlement while keeping payoff execution verifiable. Pluggable aggregation and contribution scoring plus a browser native app lower the barrier to joining. Tests show end to end payoff aware training with modest overheads and setup in under three minutes.
arxiv-2603-00966: Hoang and six co-authors extend band-unfold tools to full Bloch states in solids where flaws break the neat crystal pattern and hide states tied to wave motion. Their method unfolds both band shapes and the wave states beneath them, going beyond band-only tools. On flawed graphene it captures wave-level effects, like flaw-driven shifts in Berry curvature, for a sharper account of what can be seen.
arxiv-2603-01566:
Liang Zhang studies how a nucleon interacts with a rare triple-charm particle in this 2026 physics work. Both are hadrons, particles bound by the strong force, and their pull on each other cannot be read from lone traits. The study runs at the physical point, where model masses match real-world values.

Using lattice QCD, a grid-based way to compute strong-force behavior, Zhang applies a time-based HAL QCD method. Both spin channels show an overall attractive pull between the pair. Measured scatter values suggest the pull is too weak to bind the pair into a stable two-particle state. Splitting the force shows a main spin-free pull plus a small spin-linked part that flips sign by channel. Links to kindred systems help pin down what drives the force.
arxiv-2603-02366:
Esen Tütüncü, Qian Zhou, Frederik Brudy, and colleagues build a mixed-reality storytelling system in this 2026 paper. Text prompts fit poorly with stories that grow from moving and playing with objects. Their system, PlayWrite, lets users stage scenes with virtual characters and props. Actions are read by a multi-agent AI pipeline as they happen.

Each action becomes an Intent Frame, a story beat shown as a marble on a timeline. Users rearrange marbles to shape the plot before a language model writes the tale. Thirteen writers from varied fields tested the system. They worked in a playful, improvisational way and treated the AI as a partner. Its surprises sparked ideas and broke creative blocks, participants reported.
arxiv-2603-02566:
Roberto Vila, Felipe Quintino, and Marcelo Bourguignon model doubly bounded data with linked parts in this 2026 paper. Many measures on the unit interval arise as a ratio of two positive quantities. Existing models assume those two parts vary on their own. Real uses break that assumption, since shared drivers link the parts.

Their model joins two gamma parts with a copula, a tool that links distributions. Positive and negative links between parts are both allowed. Depending on settings, the model can look symmetric or skewed, with one peak or two. Simulations show the likelihood estimator performs well across parameter choices. The authors discuss where likelihood computation stays efficient. Economic data sets demonstrate the model's fit in practice.
arxiv-2603-02766:
