Physics-informed nets, neural operators, and diffusion solvers each help in part but stall on stiff, long, or template-bound cases. Flow learners instead learn transport fields and grow trajectories by integration, echoing the smooth dynamics of PDEs. This match aids continuous-time prediction, built-in uncertainty, and new solver designs, and the paper lays out the research path ahead.
arxiv-2604-07566: St-Pierre and three colleagues propose MR-Quantile, a Mendelian randomization method using weighted quantile regression. It holds up to correlated and uncorrelated pleiotropy, where variants affect many traits and threaten key rules. Uncorrelated pleiotropy means genes affect the outcome directly, not via the trait. Correlated cases mean genes affect trait and outcome via shared causes. The authors pick the best quantile of ratios through a chance-based form with the skewed Laplace curve. Monte Carlo tests show strong results, especially with many invalid tools with weak side effects.
arxiv-2604-07666: Plesner and two colleagues study how reward noise affects reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards in code generation. In Qwen3 8B tests on MBPP, mean reward stays within 1 point of the clean baseline at noise rates through 20 percent, and within about 2 points at 30 percent. They also examine full-program pass@k, four noise structures, two model-based verifiers, plus policy models from three families. Advantage distributions for symmetric and asymmetric grouped noise show why clipping limits gradient-scaling arguments. Overall, imperfect verification can support effective RLVR here.
arxiv-2604-07866: Chen, Wang, and Zhou study maximal hypersurfaces with multiple light-like cones in Lorentz-Minkowski space. They approach the problem through weak solutions of the mean curvature equation with multiple Dirac masses. Such solutions are built by approximation, using smooth-source regular solutions that converge weakly to the Dirac measures. The construction handles several light cones at once rather than a single cone. The paper establishes the existence of these weak solutions and the approximation route that produces them.
arxiv-2604-07966: Cai and six colleagues present LiVER, a diffusion system for video making with direct scene control. Current models entangle layout, lighting, and camera paths or model them weakly, curbing use in film work and virtual production. LiVER bases video building on 3D scene factors, backed by a large dataset with dense labels for layout, lighting, and camera settings. Drawing control signals from one unified 3D model splits those factors apart. A lightweight control module plus staged training then yields videos that obey chosen scene settings.
arxiv-2604-08166: Perera-Lago, Torras-Casas, and Gonzalez-Diaz offer L-fuzzy simplicial homology for L-fuzzy parts. It is an old tool giving module chains to simplicial shapes, giving markers for studying topological properties. Here, every simplex carries a lattice value from a fully distributive lattice L. The paper gives its definition and main traits plus methods to compute its structure. It also reads poset filtrations and chromatic datasets in this setting, opening further applications in data analysis.
arxiv-2604-08366: Tolga Dimlioglu and four colleagues tackle training data choice for end to end driving systems, where one data mix must serve many scoring rules at once. Their MOSAIC method splits data into domains, fits scaling laws from each domain to each score, and grows the mix by adding data where scores gain most. On a driving planner score it beat varied rivals while using up to 80 percent less data.
arxiv-2604-08666: Bretscher and sixteen colleagues review how tuned fluctuations in cavity quantum materials steer correlated quantum matter. Shaping fluctuation frequency, space, and mode patterns can shift phase edges and stabilize or suppress orders, surveyed here through a design toolbox and recent milestones. The review notes light based observables and maps steady and driven control across superconducting, magnetic, moiré, and topological platforms, flagging theory experiment gaps in real multimode regimes.
arxiv-2604-08766: Diana Romero and five colleagues present the first backdoor attacks on scanpath models, where models forecast fixation sequences during visual search. A fixed path backdoor clusters tainted samples and proves easy to spot. They tune hostile training on each scene instead: spatial tricks send search to a foe chosen object, while time stretch lengthens search with extra gazes. Time stretch reaches up to 93.5 percent success from just 540 tainted samples, and no tested defense removes the backdoors without breaking output quality.
arxiv-2604-08966: Jin and four colleagues study how video language models should output time when locating a moment inside a video, a task known as temporal grounding. Past methods tangle the output format with different backbones, datasets, and training recipes, so the format's own effect stays unclear. Edge deployment adds a cost question. Comparing paradigms on equal footing, they find the output choice shifts both accuracy and cost regardless of model size. A continuous distribution format gives the best balance of precise localization and low latency.
arxiv-2604-09166: Werner and six colleagues model batch distillation to build a hybrid dataset for deep anomaly detection. Deep anomaly detection needs large, varied, well-annotated data rarely found at plants. The team already released a fully tagged test dataset for batch distillation under normal and faulty states. This study adds matching model data, creating a hybrid dataset released openly. The work shows large test campaigns can be simulated by machine in a steady way. The hybrid data supports moving from models to tests, pseudo-experimental data, and future deep anomaly research.
arxiv-2604-09266: Allu and Kumar compute the second and third Hankel determinants for a starlike MA-Minda subclass tied to quadratic polynomials. The class covers analytic functions with f of zero equal to zero and derivative at zero equal to one in the unit disk. It is defined through a subordination involving one plus z plus a ratio times z squared, with twice the numerator at most the denominator. The authors show the bounds are sharp by determining the extremal functions for the determinants.
arxiv-2604-09666: Fan and three colleagues ask whether agentic search can replace costly GraphRAG pipelines with plain dense retrieval. Most systems serve a fixed document set in one pass, while agentic search retrieves dynamically across rounds. Their RAGSearch benchmark standardizes backbones, budgets, and protocols for training-free and training-based agentic inference on several question sets. Agentic search substantially lifts dense RAG and narrows the gap to GraphRAG, especially in reinforcement-learning settings. GraphRAG still wins on complex multi-hop reasoning, with steadier behavior once its offline cost is amortized.
arxiv-2604-09866: Geng and five co-authors develop language models automating frame analysis across platforms. Structural engineers rely on finite element tools, such as ETABS, SAP2000, and OpenSees. The models use a two-stage architecture: first, agents interpret user input and infer geometric, material, boundary, and load information, then output JSON. Second, agents convert the JSON into scripts across platforms, each prompted with its software's syntax and workflows. The models face 20 frame problems across ETABS, SAP2000, and OpenSees. Ten trials show reliable performance, with accuracy exceeding 90 percent across all cases.
arxiv-2604-09966: Standish argues splitting acts as a variety ratchet in nature. A broken landscape weakens links between species, leaving higher variety than a linked landscape would allow. Joining a split landscape triggers a die-off event, culling the most highly linked species first. Back-to-back splitting and merging cycles drive variety ever higher, ratchet-like, beyond what an always-linked landscape would hold.
arxiv-2604-10866: Hu and colleagues offer OccuBench, a test of 100 real job tasks across 10 fields and 65 domains, run with language simulators that fake work settings. A pipeline auto-makes test cases that are solvable, graded in difficulty, and varied in texts. OccuBench scores task success and toughness under planted faults. Testing 15 top models from 8 families, they find no one model tops all fields, and hidden faults prove harder than plain errors. Bigger models and more reasoning effort raise scores. Strong agents are not always strong simulators, so simulator quality is key.
arxiv-2604-11166: Botero, Küronya, and Vital show that the long-run behavior of rank functions for linear series on tropical curves is governed by asymptotic invariants. In plain terms, growth rates of ranks settle into stable patterns as powers grow. This parallels volume theory in algebraic geometry. They define tropical volumes for divisors and tropical modules, prove optimal asymptotic results for each, and show tropical volume agrees with tropicalization of curves.
arxiv-2604-11266: Darnas and fourteen colleagues demonstrate multiplexed cryo-CMOS control of an isolated silicon double quantum dot at 0.5 kelvin. Sample-and-hold multiplexing programs several gate voltages through few input lines, cutting wiring and heat load. The circuit deterministically loads and isolates four electrons, reaches all five charge states from (4,0) to (0,4), and pulses rapidly across a transition, resolving single-electron tunneling events and stochastic switching.
arxiv-2604-11366: Zhao and five colleagues estimate the Turán number of Bt, the Cartesian product of a t-edge star and an edge. Bt is t four-cycles sharing one edge. They give two-sided estimates in both settings for t at least two, using random C4 constructions for lower bounds. The limit lies between 1/(2√2) and 1/2, and between 1/4 and 1/(2√2) bipartite. For B2 the bounds sharpen to between about fifty-two and sixty hundredths times n to the three-halves. The bipartite bounds run between about thirty-nine and forty-seven hundredths.
arxiv-2604-11566: Agadagba and ten colleagues interview users in Nigeria, Tanzania, and Zimbabwe about choosing among digital payment categories, from mobile money and transfer apps to cryptocurrencies, stablecoins, and central bank digital currencies. Many trust government issuers to guard against scams but not to build reliable products or prioritize customers. Most users hold accounts on several systems and pick platforms per payment type, weighing money, security, privacy, and trust. The authors urge regulators and researchers to design systems balancing trust and utility needs.
arxiv-2604-11766: Farooqui works on Lorentzian spaces built without smooth geometry, and links two notions of curvature. He sets out a strong timelike Brunn-Minkowski rule for exponents between zero and one. In the timelike essentially non-branching case, he proves the curvature-dimension rule is the same as the Brunn-Minkowski rule, while its entropic form is the same as a reduced strong rule. The work extends to rough spaces an earlier result that tied Ricci curvature to the Brunn-Minkowski inequality on smooth spacetimes.
arxiv-2604-11866: Gogoi, Bora, and Övgün study equatorial periodic orbits around an Euler-Heisenberg black hole wrapped in perfect-fluid dark matter. With an effective metric and potential analysis, they set conditions for barely bound and innermost stable circular orbits and sort paths, finding a rich range of zoom-whirl motions in strong fields. Gravitational-wave signals from the kludge method show burst-like features during whirl phases. Dark matter shifts stability thresholds and damps waveform amplitude, while quantum corrections boost high-frequency parts near the horizon.
arxiv-2604-11966: Bezrukavnikov and three colleagues find a new geometric form for the principal block of module categories for a root-of-unity quantum group. They realize it inside microsheaves on an affine Springer fiber. They also prove a Langlands-type equivalence with wild ramification, matching that category to the dual group's Springer resolution sheaves. The result also reads as a version of homological mirror symmetry in this setting.
arxiv-2604-12166: Lara and Ramos refine Karush-Kuhn-Tucker and Fritz-John optimality conditions for nonsmooth, nonconvex programming problems, with special care for strongly quasiconvex constraint functions. After analyzing the strong subdifferential, they express, in these terms, the normal cone of the supremum function and apply the result to the programming problem. Examples close the work by illustrating the refined conditions.
arxiv-2604-12266: Saiprudhvi and three colleagues jointly plan paths and resources for a dual-aerial reconfigurable surface network linking ground and satellite users for sixth-generation wireless. A ground station and a satellite serve their users together with UAV- and HAP-mounted active surfaces, sharing the channel by power-domain non-orthogonal access. Block coordinate descent tunes beamforming, surface coefficients, and 3D paths to a stationary point. Tests show about 8.44 percent higher average sum-rate than passive surfaces.
arxiv-2604-12566: Yu Xia and 12 colleagues demonstrate a compact 3D silicon nitride photonic interposer. The prototype routes light across two layers for chip-to-chip links. Its fully connected 12-node network cuts intralayer crossings from 495 to 150. That beats the planar lower bound of 153 crossings. Average loss per waveguide falls by about 46 percent in experiments. The design is symmetric and scales to more nodes, layers, and wavelengths. Denser, lower-loss interposers for high-performance computing should follow.
arxiv-2604-12966: Sophia Sirko-Galouchenko and four colleagues sharpen visual perception in multimodal models with grounded tasks. Vision tasks fail not from weak vision but from underuse during tuning. Language priors alone solve many tasks, sidelining visual evidence. Classical self-supervised pretext tasks become image instruction response triplets. Rotation, color matching, and cross view correspondence force reliance on visual evidence. A small share, 3 to 10 percent, of such instructions lifts vision scores. No human labels, architecture changes, or extra stages needed.
arxiv-2604-13166: Dravins, Ludwig, Steffen, Allende Prieto, and Koesterke model how magnetic active-region granulation shapes solar lines, a key noise source in hunting low-mass exoplanets. Using 3D fluid models, they compare non-magnetic areas with strongly magnetic granulation at 240 mT. Fields inhibit rising gas motion, even out lines, and erase the usual blueshift. Oddly, magnetic granulation shows rising-gas redshifts, traced to hot bright downflows created when rising gas is forced into channeled sinking streams.
arxiv-2604-13366: Moroncelli and four colleagues compare plain and generative sequence models for predicting robot motion in context. They take a Transformer meta-model as a plain baseline and add two diffusion options: inpainting diffusion, which learns the joint input-observation distribution, and conditioned diffusion, which makes future observations from control inputs. Large random simulations show diffusion models hold up far better when the test data shifts from training data, with inpainting diffusion best overall. Warm-started sampling also lets them run within real-time control limits.
arxiv-2604-13466: Peiris tests two rival readings of emotion vectors in the Claude Mythos Preview system card, which studies model internals during misaligned behaviour. One reading says emotion vectors track functional emotions that drive behaviour. The other says they project context structure onto human emotional axes. Emotion probes on concealment episodes, studied only with autoencoder features, can separate the two. Which reading is right decides whether emotion monitoring will catch dangerous behaviour or miss it.
arxiv-2604-14266: Taylor and five colleagues interview fifteen queer artists on how generative AI has unsettled their art worlds. Art-making serves these artists as political resistance, identity work, queer memory, and community, yet GenAI development and use feel anti-relational against that fabric. Participants refuse and resist GenAI in varied ways, seeing only narrow room for it, such as the queer aesthetic promise of surreal image models. Using queer theory as a lens, the authors urge researchers to refuse dominant AI imaginaries and back queer world-building.
arxiv-2604-14466: Haghighat, Dehghanian, and Smith verify a flat guided-wave terahertz filter built from a spoof surface plasmon polariton waveguide on a coplanar stripline with grooves and periodic gaps. The design pairs the low-pass edge of the polariton band with the high-pass action of gaps acting as series capacitors, so cutoff frequencies follow from unit-cell geometry. A demo device centers near 1 terahertz with a bandwidth of 0.25 terahertz, and measurements show the passband plus cutoffs in line with simulation. The work confirms the filter concept in hardware.
arxiv-2604-14566: Liu presents a physics-informed machine-learning framework for steady-state temperature profiles of pouch cells under indirect liquid cooling. Heat-transfer equations enter the network's loss function directly, giving high-fidelity predictions that converge far faster than purely data-driven methods. Tests across varying cooling-channel geometries show faster convergence and markedly higher accuracy, cutting mean squared error by about half against the data-driven model. Independent test cases confirm the edge, especially in regions away from cooling channels.
arxiv-2604-15266: Frenkel and three colleagues simplify safety proofs by splitting one hard inductive invariant into a chain of easier steps. Their system mixes forward reasoning, backward reasoning on a time-reversed system, and prophecy steps that supply witnesses for existential claims. Each rule is proved sound and strictly adds proving power, and a Paxos and Raft case study shows the steps stripping away tangled Boolean structure and quantifiers.
arxiv-2604-15666: Wang and four colleagues build the first clear-box quantum fit tool, where the quantum state holds the old-style data grid and tune knobs map straight onto fit weights. The held shape cuts gate cost for the fit map, and plain pre-work builds bent traits for deep nets. Read-out slips and sample needs are worked out for one-hot and tight codes, with tight codes cutting qubit needs at an exponential rate.
arxiv-2604-15866: Kim and Yoon introduce DiZiNER, a framework that improves zero-shot named entity recognition, picking out names and terms in text without task-specific training, by mimicking pilot annotation. Several varied language models annotate shared texts as annotators, while a supervisor model studies their disagreements to refine task instructions. Across 18 benchmarks, it tops prior results on 14 sets, lifting the best score by 8.0 F1 and narrowing the gap to supervised systems by over 11 points. It even beats its own supervisor, GPT-5 mini, showing the gains come from disagreement-driven refinement.
arxiv-2604-16166: Wyper and 21 colleagues review proposed origins of magnetic switchbacks. Switchbacks are sharp deflections of the magnetic field in the solar wind, which Parker Solar Probe found dominating near-Sun wind. They sort mechanisms by whether they act mainly in the low solar atmosphere or out in the wind itself. The focus is mechanisms able to reverse field direction. Their consensus: low-atmosphere processes alone do not make full reversals, but supply seeds that in-wind processes turn into switchbacks.
arxiv-2604-16466: Do, Aldridge and Nguyen develop a quantum approach to near Nash equilibria in two-player zero-sum games. Mixed strategies become Born distributions of parameterized quantum circuits, turning the game into a smooth minmax problem. A dominated embedding maps games of any size to qubit-friendly power-of-two dimensions, preserving equilibrium structure. A projected extragradient method using shot-based estimates comes with variance bounds and near-stationarity convergence. Judged by Nash gap, it solved structured 32 by 32 games with high precision, though unstructured games stayed hard.
arxiv-2604-16566: Arya and colleagues propose AUSS, a multi-agent system for education. It joins custom help for students, teacher tools and school-wide insight in one design. Existing systems stay split, while agentic AI moves from waiting to acting ahead on its own. It mixes language models, reward-based learning, forecast data work and set rules. Tests reported recommendation accuracy of about 92 percent, grading efficiency of about 94 percent, and dropout prediction near 90 percent.
arxiv-2604-16666: McLeod and colleagues determine the evolving ultraviolet luminosity function over redshift twelve point five to eighteen point five. Search covers zero point six square degrees. They find an accelerated decline in ultraviolet luminosity and star-formation density across about 100 million years between redshift eleven and thirteen point five. A lack of candidates beyond redshift fourteen point five signals more rapid descent. Star-formation density at redshift fifteen point five falls below early JWST extrapolations. A piecewise relation fits with decline beyond redshift twelve about 4 times steeper than below it.
arxiv-2604-17066: Byun, Ryu, and Song propose the Reference-state System Reliability method for judging coherent systems such as infrastructure networks and supply chains, where decomposition methods scale poorly. Instead of splitting state space into disjoint hypercubes, RSR classifies Monte Carlo samples against reference states with batched matrix operations. It evaluates a 119-node, 295-edge graph within 10 seconds and scales to hundreds of thousands of reference states, though convergence slows when boundary states grow very large.
arxiv-2604-17366: Ajjour, Quensel, Lipka, and Wachsmuth create ArgBench, the first unified benchmark for computational argumentation in language models. It gathers 33 earlier datasets into one form and tests five model families across 46 tasks, from mining arguments and judging quality to reasoning about arguments and generating them. A systematic analysis then weighs the roles of model size, training skills, reasoning steps, and few-shot examples. The benchmark aims to make argumentation ability comparable across models instead of scattered across incompatible tests.
arxiv-2604-17566: El Messaoudi and two colleagues revisit how diffusion models should be trained for nonlinear system identification with spatial outputs. Old methods fail in turbulent flow, where dynamics are many-sided and sensitive to growing rollout errors. Many diffusion models borrow target choices from image generation, usually noise or velocity prediction. Using a patch-based transformer on fields with turbulent flow as testbed, the authors find clean-state prediction lifts rollout stability. It cuts long-horizon error versus noise- and velocity-based targets, with the edge growing with per-token size.
arxiv-2604-17766: Enomoto and two colleagues propose clock noise cutting for heterodyne links between cavities in gravitational-wave telescopes below 10 Hz. Heterodyne links relax arm-length control but invite clock jitter, and back-linked Fabry-Perot devices need clocks far steadier than current ones. Their scheme uses two signals with flipped beat-note rates from inbound and outgoing beams, without added clock tweaks. A weighted mix with time-varying weights removes jitter, keeping signal data. B-DECIGO tests show the signal regains reach and lifts shot-noise ratio by root 2.
arxiv-2604-17966: Zheng and two colleagues build TPS-CalcBench, a first diagnostic benchmark for closed-form calculations in hypersonic thermal protection engineering, where wrong heat-flux answers can break design margins. Current benchmarks test abstract math, score only final answers, and miss physically invalid reasoning. Their benchmark uses a domain taxonomy with four difficulty levels and eight categories. It scores results and reasoning quality on dual tracks, and offers 420 high-confidence items plus 810 pre-gating items drawn from 4,560 raw items. Tests on thirteen models show wide performance gaps, with scores from 12.6 to 87.9.
arxiv-2604-18366: Chua studies two-body charmed anti-charmed baryonic B decays with the topological amplitude approach. Decomposing amplitudes topologically, he models SU(3) breaking effects tied to the strange-quark line position. In low-lying decays, the exchange diagram proves sizable and largely cancels the internal W-tree amplitude, with SU(3) breaking at 35 percent working differently across amplitudes. Predicted rates carry large uncertainties, so measuring them would sharpen understanding of SU(3) breaking.
arxiv-2604-18566: Leitch evaluates model families, both cloud APIs and local open-source models, on two benchmarks for System Dynamics AI assistance: causal loop diagram extraction and model discussion. On extraction, cloud models achieve 77 to 89 percent pass rates, while the best local model reaches 77 percent. On discussion, the best local models reach 50 to 100 percent on model building, but only 0 to 50 percent on error fixing, where long prompts expose memory limits. The central analysis compares reasoning versus instruction-tuned architectures, backends, and quantization levels, finding backend choice matters more than quantization.
arxiv-2604-18766: Coniglio and Ongaratto introduce a hierarchy of logics, inspired by da Costa's systems. The logics cover degrees of paraconsistent stance, from skepticism to dogmatism. One way, they grow more paraconsistent as the consistency operator is allowed to misbehave up to a fixed number of steps. In another way, negation is strengthened step by step. The hierarchy comes with swap-structure semantics and proofs of soundness and completeness, and well-known logics appear as special cases. An extension, a five-valued logic called LFI3, is given a set of axioms.
arxiv-2604-18966: Long and four colleagues study reward guided post training for tabular language models. Such models train once and serve as synthesizers, while likelihood misses the qualities used to judge synthetic data. Their generate score align protocol samples rows, ranks them by task reward, and updates the model against a reference. They propose TabGRAA, comparing high and low reward groups with averaged ratios instead of pairwise preferences. Across five benchmarks, TabGRAA beats supervised tuning and tops DPO, KTO, and NPO baselines on fidelity and utility, with privacy near baseline.
arxiv-2604-19066: Shan asks whether activity's link to frequent distress, defined as 14 or more days a month, varies by age. Ten U.S. survey waves covering more than 3 million adults show a clear age gradient in weighted logistic regression. The adjusted odds ratio is 0.89 for young adults 18 to 24 and strengthens steadily with age. Over the decade, the young adult effect eroded to null in 2018 and 2024. Causal Forest names age as the top driver of treatment effect heterogeneity. Sensitivity checks confirm this, suggesting the exercise link may not generalize to youngest adults.
arxiv-2604-19166: Ahn studies the optical conductivity of a layered van der Waals niobium-silicon-tellurium family, noted for its tunable electronic structure with a quasi-1D nodal state. At zero temperature, the Drude weight is anisotropic: finite along the nodal line at charge neutrality, but vanishing quadratically with Fermi energy across it. Interband conductivity shows the same linear frequency trend in both directions, with only a varying slope at low frequency. Thermal corrections leave these results valid up to lab temperatures.
arxiv-2604-19266: Bulatov, Gong, Khoussainov, and Wang study constraint problems whose rules come from finite automata. Their automatic constraint satisfaction problems capture infinite sets of relations with finite descriptions, giving compact forms for hard constraints. They show that testing an operation for the polymorphism property in such a language takes polynomial time. Building on that, they prove sorting results, including an extension of Schaefer's dichotomy theorem to this setting.
arxiv-2604-19466: Bu, Zeng, and Zhang introduce an adjacency tensor for hypergraphs and a general eigenvector centrality. A hypergraph is uniform when every hyperedge holds the same number of vertices, and many real systems, like email and co-authorship networks, yield non-uniform cases. Uniform cases match their adjacency tensors one-to-one, and Benson proposed this centrality in 2019. The new measure reduces to Benson's for uniform cases, and to ordinary graph centrality when each edge holds exactly two vertices.
arxiv-2604-19566: Remy presents Diagnosable ColBERT, a method for debugging late-interaction retrieval models. Reliable biomedical and clinical retrieval needs more than strong ranking. Practitioners need a practical way to find systematic failures and curate training evidence. ColBERT exposes interpretable token-level scores between document and query tokens. Yet those scores explain one pairwise score only, without showing whether a clinical concept was learned in a stable, reusable way.
arxiv-2604-20766: Muir, Duru, Hudson, and Hole present a robust and exact numerical method for the anisotropic diffusion equation in curvilinear coordinates. The method uses sums by parts with joint approximation terms for finding the diffusion perpendicular to field lines. To extend the method to complex geometry they use a multi-block approach with patched smooth ordered meshes. In other words, the domain breaks into sub-grids whose nearby edges couple weakly using weights. They prove the semi-discrete stability for the curvilinear version by drawing discrete energy bounds.
arxiv-2604-20966: Dayal compares two stories for massive black holes the James Webb Space Telescope finds in the first billion years. Many are overweight for their hosts and poor in metals. One story grows light or heavy astrophysical seeds through mergers and accretion, in the DELPHI model. The other grows primordial black holes by accretion alone in the PHANES model. Only Eddington-limited growth on light seeds is ruled out. Primordial holes and Eddington-limited heavy seeds both match the masses and tiny metallicities seen.
arxiv-2604-21266: Ankit Kulshrestha and Sarvagya Upadhyay hunt for good starting parameters for parameterized quantum circuits, a choice that shapes training success. Rather than picking a distribution, their evolutionary search tunes the distribution's hyperparameters for each circuit and task. Tests show the tuned starts converge faster and perform better, without worsening the barren-plateau problem, the fading of gradient signals that plagues large circuits.
arxiv-2604-21466: Hector Iga-Buitron, Tom Mackay, and Akhlesh Lakhtakia set out theory for scattering of a Gaussian-pulse plane wave by a coated chiral sphere. The spherical core and shell use two homogeneous isotropic chiral materials, with the core vacuous and the shell's parameters found in tests. They compute extinction, total scattering, and absorption efficiencies. All three depend on the shell's relative thickness and the carrier wave's circular polarization state.
arxiv-2604-21766: Kabir and five colleagues introduce AUDITA, a benchmark that tests genuine audio reasoning rather than shortcut cues in audio question answering. It offers human-authored trivia questions grounded in real-world audio, with hard distractors and long-range temporal dependencies that cannot be answered from isolated text or sound alone. Humans average 32.13 percent accuracy, while state-of-the-art models average under 9 percent. Item Response Theory analysis then exposes systematic model and data weaknesses.
arxiv-2604-21866: Winter, Guedes, and Müller present SCALA, a non-hierarchical cellular automaton decoder for quantum repetition and toric codes. Local decoders avoid global decoding bottlenecks, offering fast real-time decoding. SCALA, short for Signaling CA with Local Attraction, is compared with Harrington's hierarchical one. It achieves a capacity threshold of about 7.5 percent and sub-threshold scaling as p_L to the power d over 4 on the toric code. Local resources stay the same whatever the system size, and SCALA proves robust to readout errors and decoder noise.
arxiv-2604-22066: Gümüş builds a small-space formulation of the classical double copy for stretched Lifshitz spaces in any dimension. With fixed symmetries in the action, the gravitational system shrinks to a one-way radial problem with one shape. All theory details sit in one potential. Here, he finds a radial operator matching Maxwell's operator for the time part of the single-copy field. It comes straight from the reduced pull, with no equations used.
arxiv-2604-22166: Kumon and Yanaka ask whether language models share neural workings across sentence patterns, testing filler-gap dependencies and negative polarity licensing with causal methods. Using activation patching, they pin down the roles of attention heads and MLP blocks. They find a local, shared mechanism for filler-gap links in early to middle layers, while negative polarity handling shows no single mechanism. Patching-found mechanisms carry over out of distribution, while distributed alignment search fails on narrow cases. Finally, tweaking the found components improves acceptability judgment scores.
arxiv-2604-22266: Datta and five colleagues study when Qwen3-4B's final answer is actually fixed during long chain-of-thought reasoning. Using forced answer completion to read off intermediate predictions, they find predicted answers change in only 32 percent of queries. Once the final answer switch occurs, the model still generates an average of 760 extra reasoning tokens per query. Simple early-stopping rules, including probe-based stopping, cut token use by 500 per query at a cost of only 2 percent accuracy. Much chain-of-thought output is thus redundant, the authors argue.
arxiv-2604-22366: Cazelles, Pauwels and Portales introduce an estimator for Monge transport maps in Euclidean space. For sources with densities, the map is uniquely the gradient of a convex function, by Brenier's theorem. Without densities, maps become couplings on the subdifferential of a convex function, called a Brenier potential. That potential grounds their method for sample-only data, and they construct an optimal potential for the empirical problem from dual answers. It picks from the subdifferential, able to extend to higher dimensions, with convergence rates.
arxiv-2604-22566: Webb, Li, and McDevitt use a physics-informed neural network to describe the plasma sheath, the boundary layer where plasma meets a surface. The sheath's rich physics has blocked a general description. Unlike ordinary deep learning, physics-informed networks constrain predictions with governing equations, needing no experimental or simulation data to train. The team uses the network to find parametric solutions for fluid sheath models of varied fidelity. Offline training often takes longer than a traditional solver, but once trained the network predicts sheath profiles across a broad parameter range.
arxiv-2604-22966: Lovén argues that the AI revolution has flipped the scarcity story: good-looking judgment is now cheap at scale, while real signals, legitimacy, true provenance, and integration grow scarce. Since judgment is the substance of institutions, courts, journals, and legislatures now vie with the technology for that role. The piece traces that pattern across science, licensing, property rights, democracy, and model concentration. It closes with a three-part agenda: remake institutions, build provenance and verification as commons, and build tools for joining institutions under strategic agents.
arxiv-2604-23066: Mukherjee and seven colleagues present Urban Flood Observations, a global hand-labeled data set of post-flood inundation in urban settings. It holds 215 image chips from 14 flood events between 2017 and 2021, derived from 3-meter PlanetScope imagery, each labeled inundated or non-inundated. A segmentation model trained with leave-one-event-out cross-validation reaches a mean Intersection over Union of 77.3 overall. That beats two widely used surface water products, supporting the data set for developing and validating urban inundation mapping.
arxiv-2604-23266: Pugatsov, Ileri, and Decouchant tackle validator profit versus fair ordering in execution. Parallel systems sequence blocks to maximise parallelism and fees, but defer transactions without keeping fairness, while fair ordering forces sequential runs. Their model runs sequencing and execution at once, returning its best result when time runs out. A genetic search using gas prices, object sets, and times lifts profit by 15 percent and speeds relief by up to 58 percent on Sui and Ethereum. Strict fair rules can cut profit by 50 to 60 percent when congested.
arxiv-2604-23466: In an independent evaluation, Yadav, Zhao, and Kumar test NVIDIA's tile-based Python GPU programming tool across Hopper and Blackwell hardware. On a datacenter Blackwell chip, its fused attention beats a leading rival by two and a half times in little code. Yet the same kernel reaches only about half the rival's speed on a workstation Blackwell card. Triton, by contrast, stays portable across all tested platforms, the authors find.
arxiv-2604-23566: Como and colleagues study how productivity shocks spread through production networks when firms face rigid information and borrow from outside lenders. Rigidity breaks the classic result that leverage does not matter, and can trigger default even in equilibrium. They prove a unique rigid equilibrium exists, show welfare falls short of the ideal exactly when leverage and rigidity combine, and give conditions for default cascades.
arxiv-2604-23666: Saber and six colleagues add a check to protection relays in inverter-based microgrids. These relays read digital current data, which attackers can fake to trigger false trips. Their scheme reads short windows of synced current data and judges if the waveform is physically plausible. It uses a recurrent net trained only on relay data. It needs no extra sensors or network map, and hardware tests confirm it meets protection timing.
arxiv-2604-23766: Ghosh proves a Hales-Jewett theorem in abstract form, for semigroups with a finite family of retractions. The Hales-Jewett theorem is a Ramsey-type result guaranteeing monochromatic patterns in coloured words, and this version extends it to a broad algebraic setting. Retractions and tensor products of ultrafilters drive the proof.
arxiv-2604-23966: The DUNE Collaboration describes the charge readout electronics for the horizontal drift far detector of the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment. Its far detectors will be the largest liquid argon chambers of their kind, built to work in extreme cold. The custom front-end system was tested on ProtoDUNE-HD, a 770 ton prototype chamber run at CERN in 2024, and the paper reports its performance.
arxiv-2604-24166: Langlois-Rémillard and Stroiński build a category with diagrams whose strict functors capture lax monoidal functors. For a strict monoidal category, 2-monad theory promises such a classifier category, but the paper builds it directly with diagrams. Variants cover oplax and Frobenius lax functors, with diagrams modeled on McCurdy's treatment of lax monoidal functors.
arxiv-2604-24266: Li and colleagues survey VT data processing and burst IDs using X-band data. VT follows up bursts in two channels at once, by self-guided slewing or fast follow-up observations, hunting counterparts, glows, and high-redshift targets. The paper covers the ground chain for X-band data, with prep, astrometric calibration, and photometry. Through December 2025, VT tracked 111 bursts from SVOM or external missions. It found matches about 75 percent of the time overall, 77 percent for ECLAIRs bursts seen within 30 minutes, and 81 percent for outside triggers with rapid follow-up.
arxiv-2604-24466: Marquart and Lavail present a reprocessed CRIRES+ L and M band archive from September 2021 to March 2025, totaling 11,131 raw frames. CRIRES+ covers Y through M bands, but calibration sources work only to K band. L and M thus lack calibration and slit-tilt measurement. The team fits atmospheric features with the telluric tool viper. Slit tilt comes from A and B frame solutions, and updated inputs feed standard recipes. New wavelength scales come from telluric fits. The archive holds 5,649 calibrated spectra across 156 targets from 68 programmes.
arxiv-2604-24566: Durech and colleagues reconstruct the spin state of asteroid Apophis from brightness observations gathered during its 2012-2013 and 2020-2021 apparitions, using light-curve inversion for a tumbling body. Several period combinations fit the data almost equally well, yet all acceptable models give nearly the same orientation just before the April 2029 close approach. Earth's gravity will widen later uncertainty, though the short-axis spin mode will very likely survive.
arxiv-2604-25066: Cedeño-Pérez and López-Velázquez build a measure on fixed-energy level sets of Hamiltonian systems. The measure stays unchanged under the flow, which opens a probabilistic way to study systems at fixed energy. They show it yields the microcanonical partition function of physics and turns into the canonical partition function in an asymptotic limit. In this way the work reproduces classical statistical physics and offers a new answer to Simon's second problem.
arxiv-2604-25166: Xu and three colleagues show that a small transformer can learn to execute programs in MicroPy, a simple universal programming language. Given a procedure plus an expression to evaluate, it predicts each small step with PENCIL scaffolding. Trained only on random, meaningless MicroPy programs, it handles human-written programs for bit copying, binary addition and SAT solving. Since MicroPy can express any computation, this suggests ordinary transformers could serve as general-purpose computers.
arxiv-2604-25266: Janno takes on finding a source that shifts in space and time, plus a start state, in a fractional diffusion equation. The only clue is one late check of the slope at part of the edge. He proves the pair is fixed for sure when the order of the fractional rate is irrational. The same proof spreads to a linked set of fractional diffusion equations. There, all sources and start states are unknown, and only the first part of the state is checked at the edge.
arxiv-2604-25666: Liu and five colleagues present GIC-Reg, a coupled registration frame for pose-free pairwise registration in single-photon multi-view sensing. Single-photon point clouds are sparse and corrupted by outliers and depth distortions, making registration hard when poses are poorly known. The frame joins intensity-guided preprocessing, grid aggregation, global matching, and local disambiguation to estimate rigid transformations. On a synthetic benchmark it posts the lowest rotation, translation, and root mean square errors. Under the most degraded dropout it cuts rotation error from about 13 degrees to about 8 degrees.
arxiv-2604-25866: Shu, Singh, and ElSherief ask why language models handle some emotions well and others poorly, using sparse autoencoders. Recognition is uneven, yet the mechanisms behind the gaps were little understood. The authors find causal sparse features driving emotion inference and map their layout within and across feelings. Surprise and fear rest on concentrated sets. Disgust spreads across weaker signals that co-activate with other emotions and are overshadowed by anger. Steering those signals mitigates failures and lifts overall recognition.
arxiv-2604-26066: Gupta and five colleagues examine where Green Pea and Blueberry galaxies live. Both kinds are small, compact galaxies forming stars at extreme rates. Counting neighbours within five megaparsecs, they compare 339 Green Peas and 56 Blueberries with a large control sample. Both kinds sit at the isolated end of the range, with the lowest neighbour counts of any group studied. That isolation argues against mergers triggering their starbursts. It points instead to internal processes or fresh gas inflow, and strengthens their role as nearby analogues of early-universe galaxies.
arxiv-2604-26566: Orfanoudakis and six colleagues built a learning-based router for electric trucks under battery, charging, and traffic uncertainty. Truck routing couples logistics with energy: limited range, slow charging, and shared chargers defeat heuristics at scale. Their reinforcement-learning formulation uses an event-driven semi-Markov decision model with shared charging, stochastic travel and energy needs, and realistic nonlinear fast charging. A graph state representation plus a rule-based action mask keeps policies admissible. Tests across fleet sizes beat baselines and neared optimization benchmarks while holding high success rates under congestion.
arxiv-2604-26766: Aljohani, Ho, McKinley, Ren, and Wang test whether open small language models can serve as sound, private decision support for ER triage. Assigning Emergency Severity Index levels from free-text triage notes remains error-prone, driving mistakes and workflow waste. Across prompting setups, they find clinical vignettes, concise summaries of triage notes, give the most exact calls, with Qwen2.5-7B balancing hit rate, steady results, and speed best. Domain tuning on expert and silver-standard pediatric triage data cuts disagreements and serious errors, beating rivals and closed large models.
arxiv-2604-26866: Dimakopoulos, Cohen and Konstas trace how fine-tuning on new facts makes language models hallucinate, inventing answers instead of retrieving stored knowledge. They fine-tune Llama 3.1 8B, Gemma 2 9B, and Mistral 7B on controlled mixtures of one question-answer dataset, varying the share of new knowledge and training length. More new knowledge means more hallucination, especially with longer training. Using sparse autoencoders, they introduce MoRFI, which isolates features that respond monotonically to new-knowledge mixtures, and single-feature interventions partly restore lost knowledge.
arxiv-2604-26966: Jahannia, Amirany and Dalir present a scalable photonic accelerator built from 4 by 4 tensor-core units, tackling the memory wall, where data movement dominates energy use. Their analysis folds in insertion loss, fanout penalties, and laser power caps, which block monolithic scaling. Tested on GoogleNet, ResNet-18, MobileNet, and AlphaGo Zero with up to 1024 elements, they find a layout bottleneck, the Utilization Wall, where grid layout rather than hardware size governs performance. Symmetric grids lift use up to 6 times and cut memory access by over 40 percent versus linear layouts.
arxiv-2604-27466: In this note, de Brecht defines computable étale spaces over a topological space within the TTE framework. He shows they are equivalent to computable functions from the space to ODS, the effective category of overt-discrete spaces. For a computable category or groupoid, he establishes an equivalence between functors to ODS and étale spaces equipped with an action by that category. The note links étale spaces, which arise in topos theory through the sheaf-space equivalence, to computable functions and functors.
arxiv-2604-27966: Bilò and colleagues simplify the construction of replacement path coverings, families of subgraphs that preserve short routes after some edges fail. Their derandomisation by conditional expectations is far simpler than earlier algebraic methods and cuts both the number of subgraphs and the query time. They also give a new randomised construction and tighten a known lower bound, showing one case is essentially optimal.
arxiv-2605-00066:
Yiru Wang and six co-authors ask whether open-loop scores can predict closed-loop driving success. Open-loop tests are fast and reproducible, but older displacement metrics showed no reliable link to closed-loop driving scores. The team tests whether the newer safety-aware metrics of the NAVSIM benchmark do better, by pairing published results for state-of-the-art methods across NAVSIM and the closed-loop Bench2Drive.

Eight methods have complete paired data. The aggregate score correlates strongly but not monotonically with closed-loop success, with clear ranking inversions. Among single metrics, ego progress predicts best, beating the collision metric. Methods that trade progress for safety shine in open loop but lose in closed loop to timeouts and slow driving. A simple three-metric formula matches the full score's predictive power on their sample.
arxiv-2605-00166:
Ankur Dhar, Mohamed A. K. Othman, and Valery A. Dolgashev describe a compact device that squeezes radio-frequency pulses into much stronger, shorter bursts. Such bursts power high-gradient photoinjectors, which fire electron beams in accelerators and free electron lasers. Their design uses two spherical cavities joined by a waveguide hybrid.

The cavities support modes that keep electric fields low on the metal surfaces, which should help the device survive high power. Built and tested at SLAC, it turned a moderate input pulse into a peak of 317 megawatts. That is the highest the authors know of for a single-stage compact device of its type at X-band. They argue the design opens a route to shorter, stronger pulses for future machines.
arxiv-2605-00266:
Harald Grobner examines a recent claim about the consistency of arithmetic. Artemov had argued a subtle point. Gödel's second theorem bars a strong theory from proving its own consistency as one sentence, yet a uniform selector method can still verify each proof attempt in turn. Grobner asks how far that phenomenon reaches.

In this note he argues that it extends to all sufficiently strong, uniformly reflexive theories of a certain form, including set theory. A fixed mechanical selector takes any derivation, picks out the finite set of axioms it uses, and builds a proof that it does not end in a contradiction. The note also analyzes why this step-by-step verification does not collapse into the single forbidden sentence, and places selector proofs within the wider theory of provability and reflection.
arxiv-2605-00866:
Suraj Prasad and Raghunath Sahoo study symmetry-plane correlations driven by nuclear geometry in oxygen-oxygen and neon-neon collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. These correlations are sensitive to how the medium transports momentum, and they originate in correlations among participant planes in the overlap region. Simulations use nuclear shapes from lattice effective field theory and generator coordinate methods, followed by a multi-phase transport model.

Neon-neon collisions show larger values for one main correlation, while oxygen-oxygen shows larger values for another. The pattern points to a strongly deformed neon-20 nucleus and a tetrahedral structure for oxygen-16. Checks using tip-tip and body-body collision orientations support the same reading of the two nuclei's shapes.
arxiv-2605-00966:
Christoph Mathys and four co-authors fix a failure in volatility updates for Hierarchical Gaussian Filtering, a method agents use to update beliefs about hidden states. In such networks, parent nodes can target a child's mean or its variance. The original variance update can produce negative posterior precision in parts of parameter space, a logical impossibility that stops the algorithm with an error.

Their fix uses a modified quadratic approximation that interpolates between expansions at the prior prediction and at a second mode found in closed form with the Lambert W function. The new updates stay robust across the whole parameter space and track the variational posterior well even for large prediction errors.
arxiv-2605-01166:
Hongyu Wu and Raul Rodriguez develop a mission-centric cyber-resilience benchmark for electrified ground platforms operating in silent-watch mode, when the engine is off and mission loads run from stored energy. Supervisory energy management becomes critical in that mode. Their benchmark connects battery state-of-charge spoofing to mission outcomes, rather than judging an attack only by detector response or control error.

Components include a reduced-order DC-bus model, residual-based detection, fallback load shedding, and five mission-facing metrics covering endurance, critical-load service, loss-of-load cost, unsafe-voltage exposure, and detection delay. Spoofing shows a structured stealth-versus-impact pattern: small biases matter little, intermediate biases create a predictable endurance deficit, and large biases disable the guard. Defense value depends on fallback depth, not detection alone.
arxiv-2605-01266:
Suraj Pai and five co-authors explore how prompt wording aligns with clinical factors in zero-shot segmentation models for lung cancer tumors. Promptable vision-language models offer an alternative to task-specific training for delineating gross tumor volume in non-small-cell lung cancer, but which prompt dimensions govern spatial behavior is poorly understood. The team splits prompts into diagnosis, demographic, staging, anatomical, generic, and irrelevant parts on a held-out dataset.

Anatomical location emerges as the dominant driver of spatial attention. Most location perturbations cause catastrophic performance drops, while histology and stage substitutions matter little. Irrelevant prompts correctly yield nothing. Swapped prompts confirm per-patient conditioning. The zero-shot model studied is statistically indistinguishable from strong fine-tuned baselines on overlap score, while beating other zero-shot models.
arxiv-2605-01466:
Zhaoyang Li, Zhichao You, and Tianrui Li fill in missing parts of 3D point clouds by leaning on a matching photo. Blending the two data types should help, but the usual step of projecting the sparse cloud onto the image plane leaves a near-empty sketch, so visual clues cannot flow across.

The authors name this failure cross-modal entropy collapse and fix it with soft splatting. Each point is painted as a soft Gaussian blob, giving a dense, smooth image the network can learn from. Attention layers then tie the views together. On standard shape sets the method sets new best scores. A stress test on real street scans from KITTI is sharper. Rival methods quietly ignore the photo when it is removed, while this one truly depends on it, which proves the cross-modal link is real.
arxiv-2605-01566:
Florian Valentin Wunderlich and four co-authors compare ways to spend extra computing time at inference so a language model answers better without retraining. The field often chases raw scores; this study prices every gain, since real deployments run on fixed budgets.

Four strategies face off: self-consistency, which samples many answers and votes; self-refinement, which revises; multi-agent debate; and mixture-of-agents, which merges. Across two hard reasoning benchmarks and many model sizes, the authors draw the Pareto front of best accuracy per unit of compute. They sweep dozens of settings for sample counts, agent counts, and debate rounds. At equal budgets, debate and mixture beat self-consistency by clear margins, and their gains keep growing on harder tasks where voting saturates early. One design rule emerges: mixture works best when parallel drafts outnumber the merging steps.
arxiv-2605-01766:
Itai Allouche and Joseph Keshet catch multimodal models in the act of ignoring their eyes and ears. Such models answer questions about images and sounds, yet sometimes reply from language habit alone, producing hallucinations that clash with the input in front of them.

Using layer-wise relevance propagation, which credits each input token for a prediction, the pair first confirm the mechanism. Hallucinations bloom when perceptual tokens carry little relevance, and shifting that reliance moves the answers. Their fix, LIME, needs no training. During decoding it adjusts the model's key-value memory to steer relevance toward the perceptual tokens, with no map of where to look supplied. Relevance nonetheless gathers on the regions the question names. Across vision and audio benchmarks, hallucinations fall and grounding improves while text quality holds, a rare fix that costs nothing but inference-time arithmetic.
arxiv-2605-01866:
Tang and six colleagues design a brain-inspired neuron that speaks in more than binary spikes. Spiking neural networks suit low-power edge devices because they compute only when events arrive, but standard leaky integrate-and-fire neurons send just yes-or-no spikes, which limits what they can express. Earlier multi-level neurons widened the vocabulary, yet often used uniform steps that mismatch how membrane voltages actually distribute, or added costly multiplications. ShiftLIF maps membrane voltages onto logarithmically spaced powers of two.

That spacing gives fine detail where voltages cluster near small values, and lets synapses compute with cheap bit shifts instead of multiplications. Across ten datasets covering wireless, sound, movement, and vision sensing, ShiftLIF matched or beat existing multi-level neurons while keeping energy use close to plain binary spiking. The design offers edge sensing a better trade between accuracy and power, without giving up hardware-friendly computation.
arxiv-2605-01966:
Ichiro Oda addresses a problem in quadratic gravity: a massive ghost particle that would break unitarity, the rule that probabilities stay consistent. He works in the covariant canonical form of the theory. He asks whether the ghost can be confined and removed from physical states, rather than appearing as a free particle.

Oda shows a bound state can form between the massive ghost and the Faddeev-Popov ghost. That pair can then be confined into zero-norm states through the BRST quartet mechanism. Unitarity is restored in that way. In a superfield form, the ghost's far field must act as a dipole, while the bound state follows a massive Klein-Gordon equation. He notes a likeness to colour confinement in QCD.
arxiv-2605-02266:
Danish Ali, Li Xiaojian, Sundas Iqbal, and Farrukh Zaidi test the reliability of language models for orthopedic diagnosis from free-text notes in three languages. Such models are proposed for clinical support in low-resource settings, but reliability, calibration, and safety for structured, high-risk tasks remain unclear. Notes are written in English, Hindi, and Punjabi in this study.

The authors compare multilingual transformer encoders, a fine-tuned DistilBERT baseline, and a domain-adapted model built for orthopedic text, against zero-shot instruction-tuned large models. Large models spoke fluently but showed unstable calibration and weaker reliability under structured multilingual conditions, notably in low-resource languages. The paper also gives a conceptual validation framework for judging such systems before clinical use.
arxiv-2605-02566:
Lauri Lovén argues that AI has changed what is scarce in science, in an essay on the institutions that certify research. AI can now produce reviews, rankings, and checks that look like expert judgment at almost no cost. A common view says prediction gets cheap while human judgment stays scarce; Lovén says what got cheap is a counterfeit of judgment itself.

That matters because journals, universities, funders, and learned societies exist to manufacture trusted judgment, and now compete with a cheap look-alike. Four things become scarce instead: verified signal, legitimacy, authentic provenance, and the capacity to absorb AI-delegated judgment without losing trust. The last, Lovén argues, binds most and cannot be bought with better tools. The fix proposed is redesign of certifying systems, not faster science.
arxiv-2605-02766:
William Misener and three co-authors simulate how young, small exoplanets lose their atmospheres, to separate two escape mechanisms that are usually studied apart. Ultraviolet light can drive photoevaporation, while heat from the planet's interior can power a slower wind. Each alone can match observed planet statistics, yet both likely act together on real planets.

Using a radiation-hydrodynamics code coupled to a planet evolution model, the team follows a typical sub-Neptune as it contracts. Young, puffy planets drive a core-powered wind, because ultraviolet light cannot reach the key point. A mixed regime follows, and as the radius shrinks, escape nears the pure photoevaporation limit. Scaling rules for the switch are derived: it happens at smaller radii for lighter and more strongly irradiated planets.
arxiv-2605-02966:
Soumyadip Sarkar analyzes QBalance, a Python workflow library for choosing quantum compilation and error control strategies across a dataset of circuits. Near-term quantum work is shaped by coupled choices: qubit layout, routing, basis changes, gate suppression, measurement fixes, shot counts, and keeping artifacts reproducible. Picking a strategy per circuit and machine is a many-goal selection problem, and ad hoc choices hide what worked.

QBalance formalizes that selection with a weighted goal, a non-dominated choice rule, an error proxy built from survival products, and a Bayesian ranking surrogate for ordering candidates. Its place among known compilation and mitigation tools is mapped in detail. The analysis also states a limit plainly: the ranking step orders candidates but does not itself cut how many circuits must run.
arxiv-2605-03366:
Omar Mustafa and Abdullah Guvendi study a PT-symmetric KG oscillator in a wormhole that breaks Lorentz symmetry. The wormhole has a smooth throat and no horizons. It joins two far regions. Lorentz breaking rescales the radial geometry and the oscillator strength.

A special imaginary coupling yields a regular confining well. The radial equation maps to the confluent Heun equation. Truncation gives an exactly solvable sector. In that sector, frequency, throat size, breaking strength, spin, and quantum number must satisfy linked constraints. Bound energies come out real and discrete, with exact particle-antiparticle symmetry.
arxiv-2605-03566:
Nick Brown and Gabriel Rodriguez-Canal lift scientific loops into tensors to compile them for AMD AI Engines, specialized cores now integrated into CPUs. These engines promise energy and performance gains, especially at the edge, but porting codes demands rare expertise and extensive rewriting.

Their pipeline needs only an OpenMP-annotated loop; tensor semantics capture the loop's intent and map richly onto the engine. On six AI and scientific kernels, the neural processing unit matched the multicore CPU on float precision at lower energy. Running two kernels across CPU and accelerator together improved performance and cut energy further.
arxiv-2605-03866:
Ryan King, Gang Li, Bobak Mortazavi, and Tianbao Yang propose a memory-efficient way to keep CLIP models learning new tasks without forgetting old ones. CLIP links images and text well, but adapting it usually requires a memory buffer of past-task examples, and its contrastive loss degrades when that buffer is small. Their method works with minimal memory.

The approach is distributionally robust: it dynamically reweights losses per class during training, so classes at risk of being forgotten get more attention. Tests cover class-incremental settings on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-1K and a domain-incremental setting on DomainNet. The adapted models picked up new tasks quickly while minimizing catastrophic forgetting, even under tight memory budgets.
arxiv-2605-04066:
Yiming Huang and five co-authors propose Adaptive Power-Mean Policy Optimization to improve language model reasoning under reinforcement learning with rewards that can be checked. Existing methods rely on static schemes. They misalign with the model's evolving reasoning capability. Their proposal adapts both the objective and the clipping rule to live training signals.

The power-mean objective lets the model move between two behaviors. One is the signal-amplifying behavior of the arithmetic mean. The other is the consistency-enforcing behavior of the geometric mean. Feedback-adaptive clipping adjusts clipping bounds from real-time reward statistics, beating static limits. Across nine datasets and three reasoning tasks, the method beat state-of-the-art baselines; on math reasoning benchmarks it raised average Pass@1 by several points over GRPO with a three-billion-parameter instruction model.
arxiv-2605-04266:
Etienne Gauthier, Francis Bach, and Michael I. Jordan examine a feedback loop in training language models from human feedback. Once a model is deployed, it creates the data on which its own reward model is retrained, so the two shape each other over time.

They split the model's true training signal into a normal part and a steering part that captures its effect on future reward models. Standard training drops the steering part, and the authors show this leads to collapse, with the model exploiting blind spots. Their fix restores an approximation of that term and prevents collapse in tests.
arxiv-2605-04966:
David Ruiz-Guirola and eight co-authors study uplink reporting for ambient Internet of Things devices, tiny battery-free gadgets that harvest energy from their surroundings. Such devices face patchy energy and frequent collisions when many try to report at once. The work builds on the cellular standard framework for these networks, using paging-triggered random access.

The authors add an energy-aware control in which the reader broadcasts an access probability with its paging message, limiting how many devices attempt access. In dense deployments their method kept collisions nearly flat, improved access efficiency, and cut the paging rounds needed for successful reporting. Light reader-side control, they argue, is key to reliable reporting.
arxiv-2605-05466:
Rydberg atoms can sense radio-frequency fields, and their spectra split into sidebands when driven. Noah Schlossberger and five co-authors explain extra spectral lines that simpler theories miss. The missing piece is polarization: an elliptical field couples many magnetic sublevels at once, so each sublevel cannot be treated alone.

The team built a Hamiltonian covering all coupled sublevels and predicted two, three, or four peaks depending on polarization. In a shielded lab setup they resolved the dressed states fully for the first time. Theory matched the measurements closely, a result that matters for Rydberg-based electric field sensing.
arxiv-2605-05666:
Risk calculators tell doctors the chance of heart disease among people observed at a given blood pressure. Suchibrata Patra argues that is the wrong number for deciding treatment. What treatment needs is the interventional probability: the risk if pressure were actually set to that value. Confounding can make the observational figure overstate the benefit of lowering pressure.

Patra applies Pearl's do-calculus to the Framingham Heart Study offspring cohort, with over four thousand participants and 574 coronary events in ten years. A corrected causal graph of the variables supports the analysis. The study separates genuine treatment effect from statistical association.
arxiv-2605-05866:
A powder diffraction pattern from a mixed material stacks the marks of every phase inside, and untangling them usually needs a candidate list. Hanyu Gao and four co-authors present XDecomposer, which needs no such list. It jointly splits a mixed pattern and names the phases without templates or prior knowledge of how many phases exist.

The method treats the task as a set prediction problem. Earlier retrieval and generation methods had assumed single-phase inputs and broke on mixtures. Prior-free splitting opens routine identification for the messy mixtures that real synthesis actually produces.
arxiv-2605-05966:
Jennifer Paige, Denis Patterson, and Alan Hastings review the science of multiple stable states in ecosystems. Under the same conditions, a lake, forest, or reef can settle into two or more distinct states. The field has rich case studies but no shared framework that links real mechanisms to dynamical models.

The review gathers empirical and theoretical work on stability, tipping points, hysteresis, and transient dynamics into one mathematical frame. Well known ecosystem models serve as running examples throughout. Positive feedback loops stand out as a central and needed feature in such systems. The authors close with open questions, including how new data tools could sharpen tests of these ideas in the field.
arxiv-2605-06066:
Cristiano da Costa Cunha and three co-authors build a benchmark for causal reinforcement learning out of a complex card game. Magic: The Gathering mixes sequential choices, hidden information, and huge masked action spaces, all with clear causal structure. Few existing benchmarks combine those traits, which limits tests of causal credit assignment and policy audits.

Their Gymnasium benchmark exposes a 3,077 part observation, 478 masked actions, and five competitive deck archetypes. A hand specified causal model over strategic variables ships with it, plus predicted effects of interventions for each episode. Reference agents include random, heuristic, and masked policy methods, plus a proposed causal variant. Paired statistics show where scalar win rates hide diagnostic detail that per factor measures reveal.
arxiv-2605-06166:
Xinrui Chen, Liu Yang, and Ou Wu unify parameter selection and data selection in language model fine tuning. Both choices cut fine tuning cost, yet separate scoring rules drive them, which wastes effort and blocks coordinated selection. When a parameter mask and a data subset jointly shape a restricted run, the split becomes a real obstacle.

The authors cast both choices as bilevel selection problems under one validation objective. A shared scoring rule then yields parameter importance and data utility as two views of a single gradient interaction matrix. Their one shot algorithm, DualSFT, extracts a mask and a subset from the same gradient statistics. On models of three to nine billion parameters, it gave a better joint trade off than sequential hybrid baselines at matched budgets.
arxiv-2605-06366:
Alexander Conzelmann, Albert Catalan-Tatjer, and Shiwei Liu uncover a layer collapse pattern inside diffusion language models. These models rival autoregressive ones, yet their internal activation dynamics were poorly understood until now. In the LLaDA model studied, a few early layers show nearly identical activation patterns. One huge outlier dominates them and persists across long stretches of tokens. The structure looks redundant at first glance.

Removing that outlier wrecks the output, collapsing it into repetitive random token loops, so the apparent redundancy is load bearing. The authors trace the pattern to overtraining rather than undertraining, the reverse of what drives redundancy in autoregressive models. Practical tests follow: the diffusion model survived hard low bit quantization nearly unscathed while a rival autoregressive model collapsed.
arxiv-2605-06666:
Songtao Huang and seven co-authors establish an exact link between quantum thermalization and short-time response measurements. Interacting quantum systems relax toward thermal equilibrium over long times, yet experiments mostly probe brief transitions, interpreted through Kubo's linear response theory. The two views seemed fundamentally disconnected until this work connected them directly.

Their Kubo-thermalization correspondence ties long-time thermalized magnetization under weak driving to short-time response spectra for a spin in a thermal bath, even when the end state differs greatly from the start. Ultracold fermions in a Fermi sea confirm it experimentally. The result lets researchers infer thermalization behavior from equilibrium response, regardless of coupling details.
arxiv-2605-06766:
M. Glowacki and eleven co-authors describe PINK, a set of updates to the CELEBI pipeline that processes fast radio burst data from the Australian SKA Pathfinder. Well-localized bursts inform studies of cosmology and the gas between galaxies, and fine polarization data test ideas about their sources. CELEBI turns raw antenna signals into finds localized to under an arcsecond with tiny time steps.

The updates improve position correction, add time and band gating that boosts faint signals, and redo how polarization is calibrated, for truer fractions and spin measures. New tools refine spread estimates, package the software for other setups, and speed the pipeline. One case is a burst with no known host galaxy.
arxiv-2605-06866:
Ege C. Kaya and Abolfazl Hashemi give a sharp mathematical theory for a family of reinforcement learning methods. The methods learn a full distribution of future returns, not just an average, and they update in an asynchronous, categorical way. Earlier work lacked precise guarantees for how many steps they need to become accurate.

Kaya and Hashemi prove high-probability bounds for both random sampling and sampling along a continuing Markov path. They cover single-value and multi-value versions, plus discounted and fixed-length settings. Matching lower bounds show their leading rates cannot be improved, making the analysis the first complete rate picture for the multivariate version.
arxiv-2605-07066:
Paul Whitten, Li-Jen Chen, and Sharath Baddam help language models build block structures from spoken or written instructions. Models make systematic coordinate errors when placing blocks in three dimensions. Their pipeline lets the model plan only the flat, horizontal layout, while a fixed executor computes all vertical placements from column heights.

On a building benchmark, a modest model with the pipeline reached high structural accuracy, beating a stronger model working alone. Removing the vertical dimension proved to be the main source of the gain. The same pipeline ran on edge hardware with even slightly better accuracy, and prompt changes cut response time sharply while keeping quality high.
arxiv-2605-07166:
Nikhilesh Prabhakar and four co-authors combine neural and symbolic learning so imitation can use extra training-only information. Pure neural copying handles rich data but needs many examples and overfits easily. Pure symbolic methods generalize well yet struggle with high-dimensional input like images.

Their hybrid approach uses extra information only during training, here human gaze data, to guide learning. Neural perception handles the raw input, while rule structure supports spread to new cases. Evaluations reported by the authors show gains in impact, speed, and spread, making the approach attractive where expert demonstrations are scarce but extra training signals exist.
arxiv-2605-07366:
Yash Ganpat Sawant reports a blunt negative result: adaptive sizing of LoRA adapters, guided by gradient importance, fails under reinforcement learning fine-tuning. The same approach works well in supervised fine-tuning, where a few layers carry most gradient signal. Under the GRPO method tested here, the gradient landscape was far flatter across layers.

Giving more room to favored layers lowered the score versus uniform sizing at the same budget. Worse, uneven sizing fed on itself, as high-rank layers took still more gradient. A random-allocation control showed rank itself drives measured weight. Sawant presents the single-task finding as early evidence against importing supervised-era rules of thumb into alignment training.
arxiv-2605-07466:
Ioan-Tudor-Alexandru Anghel and seven co-authors build a pipeline for spotting fatty pancreas in ultrasound images. The condition is often missed yet linked to metabolic syndrome, insulin resistance, and pancreatic cancer risk, while diagnosis usually rests on a doctor's own reading. Their framework first segments the pancreas and a nearby vein with a hybrid network.

Guided by the anatomy, the system extracts patches and compares tissue patterns, much as doctors judge brightness gaps. On a hospital dataset, a support vector machine scored strongly under cross-checks, and even an unlabeled rival did well. The authors claim the first end-to-end system of its kind.
arxiv-2605-07766:
Yingfeng Wang and two co-authors define a new vision task, head similarity, for uses that need identity consistency when a face is turned away, covered, or missing. Ordinary face recognition erases, by design, appearance differences like hairstyle, squeezing each person into one representation. That sameness is exactly what look-sensitive uses cannot afford.

Their setup models the look of the whole head. It keeps the gaps between one person's looks at different times, and ranks likeness in layers across identity and look. They built a large benchmark from long videos with weakly labeled look states, spanning varied poses, blocked views, and changes over time. A first framework joining identity checks with look-sensitive likeness showed the task is feasible, where standard face models failed to capture it.
arxiv-2605-07966:
Anunay Prasanna and three co-authors film what happens inside a droplet blasted by ultrasound. Acoustic droplet vaporization turns micron-scale droplets into vapor bubbles, and when those bubbles collapse unevenly they can fire high-speed liquid microjets. Using ultra-high-speed imaging at the microscale, the team observed acoustically driven jetting and jets from interacting bubble pairs inside the vaporizing droplet.

Complex pressure fields from the continuing sound wave and multiple nucleated bubbles make the dynamics rich, and the tiny jets behave self-similarly to millimetric bubbles under comparable conditions. Evaporative instabilities during bubble growth can impede jet formation, and the paper examines when jets pierce the droplet surface into the surrounding fluid. Such microjets could permeabilize cells for targeted drug delivery and cancer treatment.
arxiv-2605-08066:
Tianrui Tan, Evan Anderson, Michael Bullock, and Boulat Bash study covert signaling. A sender must hide the very fact that a signal was sent. Square-root laws cap the mean energy per channel use. Two plans meet the cap. One spreads weak energy over all uses. The other sends normal signals rarely, and stays silent the rest of the time.

The sparse plan suits modern digital senders. The team tests it on the lossy thermal-noise bosonic channel. That channel is a quantum model for optical, microwave, and radio links. They pin down how well it works for both messaging and active sensing. The results push covertness theory toward systems that can be built.
arxiv-2605-08366:
Mohit Raghavendra, Soham Dan, Miguel Romero Calvo, Yannis Yiming He, and coauthors broaden how coding agents are graded. Most benchmarks reward fixing a reported issue, while professional work also means answering questions about a codebase, writing tests, and refactoring. SWE Atlas covers those three workflows with two hundred eighty-four tasks in total.

Its tasks are deliberately under-specified, the way real requests arrive, and scoring mixes programmatic checks with rubric judgments of completeness, maintainability, reusable abstraction, and codebase hygiene. Frontier closed models led the field in the authors' runs, while the best open-weight models scored poorly, exposing how much agent evaluation has been missing.
arxiv-2605-08466:
