Kaushik Bhattacharya introduces neural operators as a tool for multiscale materials modeling. A material's behavior emerges from processes at several scales at once. Passing the right information from fine scales to coarse ones has resisted decades of effort. Neural operators generalize neural networks to maps between functions. They work independently of any grid.

The article explains the operator idea in accessible terms. It walks through three selected examples. In each one, learned operators carry information across scales in materials problems. Bhattacharya presents the method as a practical bridge. Fine-scale physics can be computed once and learned. It can then be reused inside coarse-scale predictions, with no rerun of the expensive detail.
arxiv-2605-08566:
Yongkang Li and seven coauthors present MicroDiffuse3D, a pretrained model that restores three dimensional chemical microscope images. Chemical imaging shows cell chemistry without labels, but slow capture limits its use for surgery guidance and drug studies. Their model rebuilds sharp volumes from sparse or noisy low grade scans taken much faster.

Across three hard tests, including sixteen fold sparse sampling and heavy noise, the model beat strong baselines with cleaner depth continuity and fewer artifacts. Cell splitting quality and profile matching both rose by clear margins. Fast, trustworthy volume repair could bring chemical imaging to larger samples and quicker clinical or lab workflows.
arxiv-2605-08966:
Nabil Mlaiki gives word models a memory that fades the way speech does. Stock focus lets far words fade at an exp rate. Real speech holds long links that fade by power laws. The new build gives each word a learned part order. That order sets a power law keep curve. The curve is near matched by a sum of exp parts. Each part steps in one plain loop step, so cost stays in hand.

Four proof claims back the build. They span the near match, a code size bound, an energy case on lost reach, and the pace of a shape rule. Two made tests back the edge. One is a skewed fetch task. One is a tag copy task with flat lags.
arxiv-2605-09166: Yves Aubry and José Felipe Voloch improve an earlier bound, due to Voloch, on how many rational points a smooth surface in three-dimensional projective space can have over a finite field. Rational points are solutions whose coordinates lie in that finite field. The pair also study families of surfaces that reach the bound, or come close. For those families they compute the exact number of rational points. These counts may be of interest in their own right, apart from the improved bound.
arxiv-2605-09266:
Xiang and seventeen colleagues test whether multimodal models keep the same reasoning when information moves from text to image. Their benchmark, SeePhys Pro, gives four aligned variants per problem with progressively more visual elements, unlike single form benchmarks. Frontier models fall far short of representation invariant reasoning: scores drop as information moves from language to diagrams.

Grounding visual variables emerges as the most critical bottleneck in that transfer. The team also builds large training corpora for multimodal RLVR and uses blind training, masking all images, as a diagnostic control. Remarkably, RL with all images masked still improves performance on unmasked validation sets. Deletion, masking, and format controls suggest those gains come from residual textual and distributional cues, not valid visual evidence. The results argue for judging multimodal reasoning on robustness under modality transfer and on diagnostics of whether gains rest on task critical visual evidence, not accuracy alone.
arxiv-2605-09366:
Han and six colleagues build NEXUS, an autonomous multi-agent system for neuroimaging analysis that aims at a virtual neuroscientist. It turns brain scans into clinic-ready markers without today's manual trial-and-error. Standard workflows such as fMRIPrep are fixed in setup and cannot reason about downstream goals or weigh other strategies. They cannot close the loop between mid-run evidence and later decisions as a human researcher would.

Unlike flat tool-calling agents, NEXUS uses a code-first style in which specialist agents jointly build and tune working programs from composable domain-specific primitives. That gives robust long-horizon workflows that adapt as they run. A layered checking system pairs cohort-level metric screening with agent visual checks to drive evidence-grounded fixes. Experiments on ADHD-200 and ADNI show NEXUS beating standard workflow baselines in predictive performance while showing strategy search and adaptive refinement.
arxiv-2605-09466:
Kang and Riordan study random graph processes where each step offers two candidate edges and only one is kept. This power of two choices scheme, proposed by Achlioptas, includes the Bohman Frieze process. Such processes are harder to analyze than the classic random graph process of Erdős and Rényi, because edge choices at different stages depend on each other. Most prior analysis is dynamic, built on differential equations. The authors instead revive a static counting approach.

Applied to the Bohman Frieze process, the method yields an expected count of tree components of each size that grows linearly with the number of vertices. A complicated formula for the growth constant is then replaced using known dynamic results. The payoff is a set of new results near criticality, including extremely sharp bounds on the largest non giant component and the limiting distribution of its fluctuations.
arxiv-2605-09766:
Starčič, working alone, gives a recursive algorithm for computing the centralizers of the complex orthogonal and symplectic groups, two families of matrices that preserve geometric structure. A centralizer is the set of matrices that commute with every member of a group. It also yields the isotropy groups for the action of these groups on skew-symmetric and Hamiltonian matrices. The paper treats similarity, the change-of-basis action, throughout.

The groups that emerge match, up to conjugation, groups of nonsingular block matrices built from rectangular block Toeplitz pieces, arrays constant along their diagonals. Recursion means each step reduces the problem to smaller pieces of the same shape, so the full centralizer can be built up piece by piece. The result is a precise description, not an approximation, aimed at readers in algebra and geometry.
arxiv-2605-10266:
Karim K. Alaa El-Din and three colleagues make a deliberately narrow bet in quantum chemistry. Density functional theory estimates molecular behavior from electron density, and its exchange-correlation term, which captures complex many-body effects, is always approximated. Their 2026 paper trains a neural-network version of the simplest approximation, the local density approximation, tuned specifically for water.

Trained with a differentiable Kohn-Sham solver on as few as eight configurations, the specialist model reached 1 kcal per mol errors against gold-standard coupled-cluster energies. It also improved spectral lines, electron density, and equilibrium geometry. Transfer learning then matched higher-rung PBE and B3LYP functionals on the WATER27 test set, even from a single two-molecule binding energy. The lesson is that cheap specialist functionals may beat general ones on one system.
arxiv-2605-10566:
A 2026 paper introduces affine tracing, a new paradigm for probabilistic linear solvers. Probabilistic linear solvers return distributions sizing doubt from limited computation for linear systems. The literature has split them into Bayesian solvers and probabilistic iterative methods, or PIMs. Bayesian solvers update a prior on system projections, while PIMs lift iterative solvers to probability space. This paper shows that split to be false: Bayesian solvers are a special case of shifting affine PIMs.

The authors also prove that any realistic affine PIM is well-tuned. Affine tracing builds a PIM from an affine iterative method by passing symbol tracers through the computation to build an affine graph. The graph can be reshaped to compute posterior covariances, and equality saturation simplifies algebra under prior choices. The framework is demonstrated by generating a multi-grid solver, tested on Gaussian process fitting.
arxiv-2605-10766:
Sergii Favorov and Özkan Değer extend results of Fourier quasicrystal theory on the real line to a horizontal strip of finite width. For measures in a strip they use a natural generalisation of the usual Fourier transform on the line. They consider positive or translation-bounded measures whose Fourier transform is a pure point measure. The paper proves that the measure formed by squared magnitudes of the Fourier coefficients has exponential growth.

Moreover, suppose that for some positive interval length, the points of the spectrum in every interval of that length are linearly independent over the integers. Then the Fourier transform itself also has exponential growth. The work builds on the theory of crystalline measures and Fourier quasicrystals, forms of Poisson formulas used by Radchenko and Viazovska. It extends line results including analogues of Olevskii and Ulanovskii's connection between Fourier quasicrystals and zeros of real-rooted exponential polynomials.
arxiv-2605-10966:
Chiyeong Heo and six colleagues present MMTB, a benchmark for terminal agents that must work with audio and video files, not just text and code. Real workflows constantly demand media handling, yet terminal-agent tests have stayed grounded in text, code, and structured files.

The benchmark holds 105 tasks across five categories where agents operate directly on media files, alongside Terminus-MM, a harness adding audio and video perception to terminal agents. Controlled studies show how different forms of media access shape outcomes and which evidence agents lean on when building terminal workflows. Agent builders get a media-realistic testbed for a blind spot in terminal automation.
arxiv-2605-11066:
Shubhanshu Karoliya, Ekta, and Gargee Sharma show that uneven strain can control and swap low-energy states in disordered superconductor-semiconductor hybrids. Telling true Majorana states apart from trivial look-alikes, especially partly split Andreev states, has blocked clear calls.

Simulations of nanowires and graphene ribbons, with superconductivity, spin-orbit coupling, magnetic fields, and disorder, show small strain reshaping the low-energy spectrum by shifting band traits and redistributing wave weight. In nanowires strain tunes Majorana overlap and shifts the topological boundary, enabling controlled moves among trivial, Andreev, and Majorana states. In ribbons strain curbs subband mixing and steadies edge modes. Device physicists get strain as a knob for Majorana calls.
arxiv-2605-11166:
Elena Sirotkina develops the Perspectivist Visual Political Sentiment classifier, or PVPS, to show that political images do not mean the same thing to everyone. Political and social identities shape how people judge political information, yet computational tools often output single scores that treat a text, image, or video as if it speaks identically to all viewers.

PVPS learns from about 82,000 evaluations by 5,575 U.S. adults and forecasts how audiences grouped by political and social identity will judge the same image. Unlike tools that average systematic disagreement away, it returns an evaluative profile noting agreement, divergence, and the identity lines along which they split. Applied to prior studies of visual sentiment, it shows perceived violence in protest imagery and the emotional drivers of protest image engagement both shift once audience identity counts. Political scientists get a tool that treats audience identity as part of the measurement.
arxiv-2605-11666: Ye and five others present EvoTD, evolutionary task discovery for advancing reasoning frontiers via skill mixes and hardness scaling. Post-training like reward-based learning remains constrained by training data variety and hardness, while random mutation methods suffer sameness collapse. EvoTD treats data making as directed search over skills and hardness levels. Crossover mixes novel skills for variety, and parametric mutation scales size and depth limits for transfer. A dynamic learnable-zone filter keeps tasks within the model's learnable region.
arxiv-2605-11966: Sri Devaki Meduri and Shantanu Desai search for high-energy muon neutrinos from the galaxy cluster Abell 119. They use ten years of IceCube muon track data. A tentative Fermi-LAT gamma-ray detection hinted at a hadronic origin. They apply an unbinned maximum likelihood method and find no significant excess. Their 90 percent upper limit sits about ten times above the flux expected under the hadronic model. That model thus survives, awaiting IceCube-Gen2 and TRIDENT.
arxiv-2605-12066: Zeguan Wu and eight colleagues benchmark Augmented-Lagrangian Quantum Hamiltonian Descent, a hybrid that embeds quantum descent within an augmented Lagrangian scheme to solve limited bumpy problems through open subtasks. Tests on standard bumpy functions plus repeated passes raised scores at fixed qubit cost. A gate-based resource analysis on Texas7k-derived power-system subtasks found steep scaling: about 44.6 million linking gates in a NISQ model and 942 million T gates in a fault-safe model at about 530 active knobs, implying real use needs large fault-safe hardware.
arxiv-2605-12266: Matteo Ballegeer and eight colleagues enrich graph-based learning for sheet metal bending estimation with recognized CAD features. Pure shape data lacks process meaning: surface roles and bend intent hide in geometry that models infer poorly. Their hybrid method adds rule-recognized manufacturing features, like bend traits, flange lengths, and surface roles, as node attributes on boundary graphs, focusing learning on process patterns. Tests on a large synthetic benchmark and a real industrial dataset with measured bending times show domain knowledge plus graph learning beats geometry-only models.
arxiv-2605-12366: Martin and Roger warn that safety monitors for coding agents fade as transcripts grow. Earlier tests rarely passed one hundred thousand tokens, yet real transcripts often exceed five hundred thousand. On a task hiding a dangerous action inside long benign logs, leading models miss it far more often late in the transcript than alone. In one case the miss rate rises dozens of times. Periodic reminders help somewhat, but tests that ignore length likely overstate monitor reliability.
arxiv-2605-12466: Fein-Ashley and Rashidinejad replace fixed-depth looping in transformers with Attractor Models that solve for a fixed point. A backbone first drafts output embeddings, then an attractor module sharpens them until they converge, with gradients from implicit differentiation. Training memory therefore stays constant in effective depth, and iteration counts adapt to convergence rather than being preset. The models beat standard transformers and stable looped rivals in large-scale pretraining and tiny-model reasoning, improving perplexity by up to about half and downstream accuracy by about a fifth.
arxiv-2605-12966: Liao and four co-authors argue that agentic AI, not just scaling one model, is a foreseeable path to artificial general intelligence. They contrast the optimisation limits of monolithic learners with the efficiency of agentic systems, moving from simple routing to general directed acyclic graph topologies. Their derivations claim exponentially better generalisation and sample efficiency for agentic systems. They reinterpret mixture-of-experts models and multi-agent instability and call for more research focus on agentic AI.
arxiv-2605-13166: Pulcu, Koltai, Kormányos and Burkard use first-principles theory to study hexagonal germanium-tin alloys in the dilute tin regime. Unlike cubic germanium-tin, lonsdaleite germanium is intrinsically direct-gap. Their 48-atom quasirandom cells show the alloys keep a direct bandgap at Gamma, with gap shrinkage shifting absorption toward the mid-infrared. As the gap nears zero its value grows touchy about atomic arrangement and cell size. Pristine polarisation anisotropy persists under dilute alloying, favouring light polarised perpendicular to the c axis.
arxiv-2605-13566: Solomiia Kurchaba and Angela Meyer combine geostationary and polar satellite readings to provide urban land surface heat at high spatial and temporal resolution. Their fields reach 1 km spatial detail at 15-minute intervals, shown for intraday forecasting. A U-Net model maps SEVIRI/MSG fields at 3 km to Terra/Aqua MODIS fields at 1 km. Trained on large cities in Europe with over one million people, the model reaches an RMSE of 1.92 degrees Celsius and near-zero bias on hold-out data.
arxiv-2605-13766: Tejaswin Parthasarathy and three colleagues introduce Elastica++, an open-source fast build of the Cosserat model for large-scale slender-body motion tests. Elastica++ mixes fast kernels with shared-memory teamwork to sustain huge throughput despite complex meshing zones and real links. The frame links with outside number solvers, aiding lean multi-field flows. Case studies span passive nest-like meta-matter, group active-matter motion, cilia carpets, soft magnet tiny bots, and schooling swimmers.
arxiv-2605-13866: Wang, Shen and Thaler test hiring bias in 29 language models across 177 jobs that cover near half of jobs in the United States. They find the models favor female and Black job seekers, yet penalize disabled ones. The gaps match the effect of six months to a year of added schooling. Post-training alignment, which tunes models to human norms, makes the gaps far worse. It lifts the female and Black edge about fourfold, and deepens the penalty for disabled job seekers.
arxiv-2605-14166: Carraro and four co-authors offer a lightweight U-Net for face super-resolution guided by YOLO-World landmark heatmaps. Recovering high-resolution faces from badly degraded inputs is hard, since extreme upscaling erases fine facial detail. Existing methods lean on heavy networks, adversarial training or separate alignment networks, raising complexity and cost. The proposed network rebuilds 128 by 128 face images from severely degraded 16 by 16 inputs, an eightfold magnification. Heatmaps from YOLO-World, an open-vocabulary detector, pinpoint eyes, nose and mouth to steer reconstruction.
arxiv-2605-14366: Su and colleagues tackle the alignment tax paid when a language model learns a low-resource language at the cost of its general skills. They replace rigid supervised fine-tuning, which forces token-by-token copying, with reinforcement learning guided by semantic rewards, meaning-based scores from embeddings. On Tibetan-Chinese translation and Tibetan headline writing, the method gains the new language while preserving general competence better than fine-tuning. Open-ended writing also gains semantic quality. Few-shot transfer improves too.
arxiv-2605-14666: Gianola, Montali and Winkler develop early-warning monitoring for linear-time properties plus an SMT theory over finite traces. Monitoring here is hard. The state depends on both the trace seen so far and every possible finite continuation. Under mild assumptions on the background theory, they prove a framework correct. It pairs automata methods for the temporal side with machine reasoning for the first-order side. Decidable cases are also found, covering linear arithmetic with uninterpreted functions.
arxiv-2605-14766: Parcollet, Zhang, Zheng and van Dalen propose a language-model architecture for live streaming speech-to-text translation. Existing SpeechLLM systems wait for a full utterance or emit tokens at fixed intervals, which suits real use poorly. Their model learns not only to output tokens but also to judge whether it has heard enough audio to do so. Training uses automatic alignments of speech and text. Across language pairs, translation quality is claimed to sit close to a non-streaming baseline at only one to two seconds of latency.
arxiv-2605-14966: Wei Ding and six others propose MHSA, a light fix for hallucinations in large vision-language models, which sometimes describe things absent from the image. A small three-layer network learns corrected cross-modal attention, guided by a hallucination detector and the model itself. At run time the corrected attention simply replaces the original, with no changes to model weights. Tests show it curbs both kinds of hallucination, in sorting tasks and in free generation, across datasets and models.
arxiv-2605-15666: Haozhe Si, Yuxuan Wan, Yuqing Wang, Minh Do, and Han Zhao build ChronoEarth-492K, a hyperspectral data set for long-range Earth study. Past sets stay shallow in time, which blocks models of change over years. Their set rests on NASA's EO-1 Hyperion archive, the longest unbroken hyperspectral record, from 2001 to 2017. It holds 492,354 tuned patches at 185,398 sites over 17 years. A linked benchmark spans static, short-range, and long-range tasks from six open geospatial products.
arxiv-2605-15866: Huyen Pham and Bilhanan Silverajan test spiking neural network jobs run under Kubernetes in a virtual edge setup. Trials on a one-node K3d cluster tracked speed, load, accuracy, overhead and conduct under joint load. Capping CPU at 0.5 cores raised median wait 47.6 times and cut load 49 times. The tightest setup failed for lack of memory, though accuracy held steady. Default round-robin routing also added long tail waits under replica growth, a poor fit for long-running inference jobs.
arxiv-2605-15966: Masahiro Tanaka offers a quasi-Bayesian way to estimate local projection instrumental-variable models, which trace how a shock ripples through an economy over time. He builds a moment-based quasi-posterior from a generalized method of moments objective and smooths impulse responses with a roughness-penalty prior. Simulations show the smoothing cuts error versus standard GMM, mainly at medium and longer horizons, and a Danish electricity market example shows it working in practice.
arxiv-2605-16766: Majumder and colleagues study a 170-kilosecond XRISM Resolve look at Cygnus A's core, focusing on its iron K-alpha line complex. They resolve two Keplerian components: a broad one near 3,400 kilometers per second in dispersion, and a narrow one near 440. At inclinations of 50 to 85 degrees, the broad component arises 0.1 to 0.17 parsecs out, matching the broad line region, while the narrow one comes from 6 to 10 parsecs, matching the torus. A possible iron XVII line and a redshifted iron K edge suggest inflow or torus motion.
arxiv-2605-16866: Frederiksen, Matsui and Pedersen study predictive-accuracy tests when errors have heavy tails. With infinite-variance differentials, the Diebold-Mariano statistic converges to a nonstandard non-Gaussian stable limit, so standard critical values distort inference. A nominal 5 percent test may reject true nulls 70 percent of the time. The authors prove a new stable limit theorem for strongly mixing infinite-variance series, then build sub-sampling inference for any tail weight, needing neither variance nor tail estimates. Emerging-market exchange-rate risk figures show heavy-tail corrections change conclusions substantially.
arxiv-2605-16966: Tan's team surveys AI methods for inverse partial differential equation problems, where hidden causes, designs, or physical states must be inferred from observed effects. The review covers basics, key challenges, and traditional numerical foundations, then groups work into inverse problems, inverse design, and control problems, with sample methods for each. It also covers uses across medical imaging, earth science, materials, flight, and full-wave inversion. It closes with open challenges such as physics-informed designs, scarce real data, uncertainty measures, and inverse base models.
arxiv-2605-17066: Nayak's team shows field-tunable Josephson diodes reaching 17 percent efficiency above liquid helium via supercurrent spin Hall effect. Standard Josephson diodes use Rashba coupling plus an outside magnetic field to break inversion and time-flip, but field-tunable output stayed below 10 percent, often below 100 mK. Their niobium-platinum-niobium pillars realise spin split in the barrier: the induced spin moment follows the bias current, so a field makes phases add oppositely for opposite currents, giving nonreciprocal supercurrent. The result beats prior field-tunable diodes while working far warmer.
arxiv-2605-17866: Masahiro Suzuki and three colleagues propose DAD4TS, a diffusion-based augmentation method for forecasting on small datasets. Augmentation helps small-data forecasting, but generating good samples is hard. DAD4TS trains a data generator alongside a forecasting model, steered by reinforcement learning toward samples that lift forecasts. Instead of VAEs, it trains the diffusion model by projecting data into geometric space. Tests against seven rivals on six real sets and eight forecasting models validate DAD4TS on five sets. The method suits settings where data are scarce.
arxiv-2605-17966: Yue Wu studies a failure in Extended Dynamic Mode Decomposition with control, trained on behavior data. Such data can predict behavior well while failing to reveal how new inputs change the lifted state. Wu frames this as control-channel informativity, introducing a conditional intervention check: residual input covariance after projecting inputs away from the lifted feature span. He proves its strict positivity is the condition for finite-sample identifiability of the lifted control block. When it vanishes, lifted models agree on all collected transitions yet disagree under new inputs.
arxiv-2605-18366: A 2026 paper by Mi-Ryang Kim and thirteen colleagues tracks day-scale brightness changes in young stellar objects in Orion A using two nights of 7-Dimensional Telescope medium-band imaging. After filtering satellite trails, they measure variability in 769 candidates and flag 110 variables, about fourteen percent. Comparing five templates, they find spot-like patterns dominate, with cold spots leading, followed by extinction-like and gray changes.
arxiv-2605-18566: Lekan Molu and two co-authors present HJ-Gauss, a 2026 Monte-Carlo Hamilton-Jacobi reachability scheme free of grids and discretization. A Cole-Hopf-type transformation reduces the HJ equation to linear heat equations, whose values return via Gaussian heat-kernel expectations. Memory scales as N times n for N samples in n dimensions, with polynomial sampling cost and conditional linear convergence. Tests include a 45-dimensional multi-rocket pursuit-evasion game and safety certification for 100,000 starlings in murmurations.
arxiv-2605-18766: Taehee Kim and three co-authors propose, in a 2026 paper, an adaptive table retrieval method that varies the number of tables per query. Fixed top-k retrieval either misses needed evidence or pulls in irrelevant tables, since required table counts differ across queries. Their method uses adaptive thresholding to select tables per query need, plus a sliding-window reranking algorithm to process large table corpora efficiently. Experiments on Spider, BIRD, and Spider 2.0 show the method beats fixed top-k retrieval in retrieval and downstream task performance.
arxiv-2605-18866: Huaxi Huang and five colleagues reconstruct continuous flow fields from a handful of surface sensors for aerodynamic design and digital twins. Inspired by 3D Gaussian splatting, their FLUIDSPLAT model predicts anisotropic Gaussian blobs that form an interpretable scaffold for the flow. Theory shows how many blobs to use as sensor counts and noise change, and a residual decoder handles what the scaffold misses. Across four two- and three-dimensional benchmarks the method cuts error by roughly eleven to twenty-eight percent against strong baselines.
arxiv-2605-18966: Charlie Nation and six colleagues find symmetries of quantum many-body models with an algorithm built on the classically efficient Clifford group. Symmetries are a critical first step toward solving a model, yet finding them usually depends on human insight. Their method represents Hamiltonians as graphs and extracts symmetries for arbitrary many-body systems, demonstrated on random and physical Hamiltonians with up to one thousand qubits. The approach not only automates a hard search but can deepen understanding of the models it analyzes.
arxiv-2605-19066: Vukosi Marivate surveys ten years of low resource tongue tests, naming the Annotation Scarcity Paradox. Fast growth from cross tongue transfer and huge multi tongue models hides a thin, lopsided tongue skill base. He tracks three stages, from early hope through scale dreams to now, when made text tests choke. He faults take first pipes, weak paid ghost work and data flaring, and urges town built tests with shared rule and own.
arxiv-2605-19166: Fausto Mauricio Lagos Suarez and three colleagues present a method for tunable reinforcement-learning quadrotor control through reward design and termination rules. Their reward uses dual bandwidth exponentials for a critically damped baseline in setpoint tracking with low steady-state error, reached in six million steps with proximal policy optimisation. Simple rules adjust reward weights and coefficients for faster or slower settling, keeping the damped response and about two percent steady-state error. Three policies tested over one hundred trials show tunable position and yaw tracking from random starts.
arxiv-2605-19266: Wanyi Ning and colleagues build FormalASR, a compact system that turns spoken Chinese straight into formal written text. Ordinary transcription keeps fillers and spoken habits that suit writing poorly, while a two-stage fix with a large model adds delay and memory cost. Their end-to-end models, at two sizes, learn from two large spoken-to-formal datasets built by rewriting and filtering. They cut character error by up to 37.4 percent against verbatim baselines while also improving overlap scores, with no extra model needed at run time.
arxiv-2605-19466: Odahara and Haze report spectroscopy of ionic-core transitions in alkaline-earth Rydberg atoms, a region not previously explored at high resolution. They measure isotope shifts and hyperfine splitting of dipole lines in ionic cores. A key gain comes from active control of the Rydberg electron orbit, cutting linewidth by more than a hundredfold and sharply improving resolution. To pin down shifts without doubt, they compare the core-ion spectrum directly against a single trapped ion as a best frequency reference.
arxiv-2605-19866: El Hachem and colleagues fix a two hop bottleneck in document parsing by vision language models. Before a decoder can extract content, it must classify and localise the enclosing layout entity; failure there collapses extraction into omissions or repetition. Their method runs a light RT-DETR detector outside the decoder, serialises detections in DocTags, and injects them beside the full page image. On a ten thousand page unseen layout benchmark, markdown F1 rises sharply, Chinese table scores jump, and loop failures fall, at small cost.
arxiv-2605-19966: Mohammed Alshaalan and Miguel Rodrigues treat fluent jailbreak suffixes as a change in a language model's token-by-token surprise stream. Their training-free detector standardises each token's entropy against a baseline from the system prompt and applies a one-sided CUSUM test to spot the onset. Across six open-weight chat models it beats windowed perplexity baselines, and as a gate for Llama Guard it cuts guard calls sharply while keeping detection quality.
arxiv-2605-20066: Jann Pfeifer, Debayan Banerjee and Ricardo Usbeck test whether outcome-based reinforcement learning can train a small language model to write SPARQL queries from questions. Using group-relative policy optimisation on Qwen3-1.7B over DBLP-QuAD, they reward execution, structure and answer accuracy, with one variant adding gold-query shaping. The trained model far exceeds the zero-shot baseline and generalises competitively, though supervised DoRA fine-tuning scores higher overall. Ablations show execution rewards drive most gains, with extra shaping adding little.
arxiv-2605-20266: Kaiwen Luo and thirty-four co-workers survey large audio language models. The survey studies how they work, detailing design ideas and alignment methods. It builds a trustworthiness taxonomy covering break-ins across modes, latent acoustic backdoors, and biometric privacy leakage. It reviews leading models through six pillars: hallucination, robustness, safety, privacy, fairness, and login checks. The imbalance between a mature offensive landscape and weak defenses highlights gaps and wide risks. It offers a roadmap with layered defenses, causal auditory world models, and intrinsic engineering.
arxiv-2605-20366: Sandron and four co-workers test new Solar Fusion III reaction rates against Sun models. Solar rates shape stellar lifetimes and energy output, and the Sun offers sharp checks through Sun-quake waves and neutrinos. The new rates slightly improve agreement with helioseismic data but lower predicted beryllium, boron and CNO neutrino fluxes. Rate shifts within their stated errors fall far short of closing the model gap, hinting other processes are at play.
arxiv-2605-20666: Jovan Menezes and Mark Campbell propose a semantic, occlusion-aware birth model for a Gaussian-mixture tracking filter. Earlier filters often assume new objects appear uniformly or under simple rules, which hurts tracking in dense driving scenes. Their model uses deep-learning semantic cues and explicit occlusion regions to say where new objects are likely to appear. Tests on simulations and the KITTI driving set show faster track initiation and lower cardinality error.
arxiv-2605-20866: Yassine Maziane and three colleagues propose LOSCAR-SGD, local SGD with communication-computation overlap and delay-corrected sparse model averaging. Communication is a big bottleneck in distributed learning, especially at large scale and in federated settings with slow links. Three standard cost cutters are communication compression, local learning, and communication-computation overlap. Methods combining all three work in practice but lack theory, and LOSCAR-SGD studies a heterogeneous-compute setting where workers take different numbers of local steps.
arxiv-2605-21566: Michael Eniolade evaluates calibration and deployment fit in kidney disease risk prediction. Models for CKD risk often post strong separation scores on internal test sets, but tuning and uncertainty measures receive far less attention. He trains five models on the UCI CKD dataset of four hundred patients and tests each on tuning quality, conformal coverage, and eight deployment tests.
arxiv-2605-21866: Jean Godard and Lucas Reis study graphs from quadratic forms over finite fields, defined by values in a proper subspace. They determine all forms with undirected graphs for every subspace. Besides Reis's earlier XY, they are X squared plus or minus Y squared and X squared plus bXY plus Y squared with nonzero b. X-squared-plus-or-minus-Y-squared graphs are disconnected, clique number up to subspace size, while Q-b graphs are connected, diameter two for large subspaces, with clique number negligible against subspace size.
arxiv-2605-22066: Yanan Liu and co-authors present Echo4DIR, a framework for 4D heart reconstruction from 2D echo videos. Rebuilding 4D cardiac geometry, meaning 3D shape over time, from sparse 2D echo views is challenged by geometric ambiguity and time gaps. The method learns 3D shape priors from shape models via a conditional signed distance function and an epipolar mask encoder. A radial alignment strategy then locks shape evolution to the velocity field, ending mesh drift. Tests on synthetic and clinical data reach up to 98.35 percent Dice and 96.75 percent IoU overlap.
arxiv-2605-22166: Tianshi Xu and co-authors present Life-Harness, a lifecycle-aware runtime harness for frozen LLM agents that leaves model weights untouched. Failures in rule-governed domains often come from interface mismatches, not the model itself. Life-Harness turns recurring training failures into reusable fixes for contracts, skills, action realization, and trajectory control, then stays fixed for unseen tasks. With Qwen3-4B-Instruct it beats Meta-Harness and AHE by 28.7 and 7.5 points while using far fewer optimization tokens. It also lifts frontier models by 3.5 points on average.
arxiv-2605-22266: Pérez-Corral and colleagues propose a light geometric check for federated learning, where many clients train together on unlike data. Rather than comparing parameters or gradients, their signal measures how each client's local training reshapes the way the shared model splits input space, judged on a common probe set. The metric separates stable but unlike clients from truly divergent ones, supporting safer aggregation.
arxiv-2605-22666: Szegedy compares three ways of calling a Boolean function simple. The first is sampling recovery from few coordinates. The second is closeness to a low degree polynomial in few linear forms. The third is nearness to a neural net output. He names the sampling trait holography and proves the three views equivalent up to shifts in parameters. The step from sampling to the second view leans on a form of hypergraph regularity. The result ties a sampling intuition, a shape account and a computational model of complexity into one equivalence.
arxiv-2605-23066: Gaffney and fifteen coauthors present Orbax, a modular JAX-native checkpointing library for distributed machine learning. JAX's modular design leaves it without a standard checkpointing solution, so Orbax abstracts distributed accelerator complexity while keeping checkpoint handling flexible across the model lifecycle. It beats comparable PyTorch rivals by up to 3.5 times on saving and 2 times on loading. The library is openly available, giving JAX users a shared, user-friendly checkpointing standard.
arxiv-2605-23466: Alecci and colleagues show that henselian valuations that can be defined with arithmetic stay definable under the tilting correspondence, a bridge between mixed and equal characteristic worlds. If a perfectoid valuation is definable this way, no extra parameters are needed. They also ask whether one set of rules can work uniformly across cases, and discuss how complex the quantifiers in those rules must be.
arxiv-2605-23566: Saxena and Singh present MT-SeCom, a trust-driven secure communication framework for cloud-based digital twins, live virtual copies of real systems. Mixed clients, resource contention, and evolving attacks make trusted links hard. MT-SeCom runs four phases: trust monitoring, trust evaluation, client classification to spot malicious nodes, and traffic management that reroutes and isolates compromised clients. Tests show threat detection scores up 18.7 percent and anomaly counts down 24.3 percent.
arxiv-2605-23666: Fioravanti proves optimal a priori regularity estimates for the ratio of two solutions to the same elliptic equation with Lipschitz coefficients. The result assumes the zero set of one lies inside the zero set of the other. He addresses the case where the zero set is a product of zero sets of two-dimensional functions. This extends regularity estimates earlier proved in dimension two by Logunov and Malinnikova in 2016 and by Terracini, Tortone, and Vita in 2026.
arxiv-2605-23866: Victor Reis proves a sharp bound for balancing vectors inside a zonotope, a stretched image of a cube in higher dimensions. He shows that plus-or-minus signs can always be chosen so the signed sum stays inside a fixed multiple of the shape. That multiple grows only with the square root of the dimension. The result settles a question posed by Schechtman in 2002 and extends Spencer's six-standard-deviations theorem to this wider setting.
arxiv-2605-24166: Agyemang and three co-authors build a geometry-aware frame for quantum differential privacy from the Quantum Fisher Information, which governs both sensing sharpness and how easily two quantum states can be told apart. Instead of uniform scrambling noise, they align direction-dependent noise with the Fisher eigenstructure. Six results follow: minimax-optimal noise placement, privacy gains from dephasing, a tight privacy-utility link, and saturating composition. Tests on model runs and IBM hardware reach equal utility at a far tighter budget than older methods.
arxiv-2605-24466: B. Li and colleagues model how spin arises in nuclear fission, tracking the spontaneous splitting of californium-252 with time-dependent density functional theory. On symmetric paths, fragments must twist against each other along the split axis, with bending motions equally likely across it. Breaking that symmetry widens the spread of fragment spins and permits tilting rotations that symmetric paths forbid. The study also finds that symmetry breaking weakens spin correlations along the axis while sideways correlations hold up better.
arxiv-2605-24666: Hyukpyo Hong and others find Koopman subspaces with personalized PageRank. Picking a finite observable dictionary whose span stays fixed is central to Koopman approximation. Any sub-dictionary induces an exact zero block in EDMD matrices, even for finite data. Such blocks surface by applying ranking to a row-normalized matrix from a large set. Theory extends to approximate spans, with stronger guarantees when seeds sit inside the target block. Tests on Duffing, Van der Pol, Lorenz, and Ramachandran systems find compact dictionaries with accurate predictions.
arxiv-2605-25066: Esra Yeniaras exposes a channel-substitution attack on quantum machine learning pipelines. A malicious provider can substitute the channel with one that passes every test and check, yet differs at the channel level. QML-PipeGuard detects the attack at runtime from statistics collected. Its guarantee: any substitution shifting a single-qubit marginal by delta forces a deviation of at least delta over root three. On an IBM Heron, the verifier halts a substituted quantum-kernel intrusion-detection pipeline that evades the weak contract.
arxiv-2605-25566: Xiaoyang Fan and colleagues make language-model diagnosis auditable by pairing it with formal logic. Patient stories and guidelines enter a neural base, where the model extracts entities, time relations, and fuzzy symptom patterns that decode into symbolic fuzzy logic and declarative rules. Two-stage reasoning then generalizes patterns inductively and checks each diagnosis with a logic engine, so every path can be traced, explained, and corrected by a clinician. Tested on public benchmarks, accuracy matches strong language models while adding verifiable step-by-step chains.
arxiv-2605-25666: Lin and Xing characterize the fixed points of a convex operator behind the Lutwak-Yang-Zhang claim. They prove a convex body meets the fixed-point formula when it is an origin-centred ellipsoid, settling it here. The proof uses variational analysis along linear shadow systems. The tool, the Lp-Projection Rolodex, reduces the projection-body volume to weighted sectional functionals. A change of variables plus Ball's harmonic inequality forces the volume constant, and Steiner symmetrization closes the rigidity claim.
arxiv-2605-25866: Solà-Garcia, Solé and Ruiz-Hidalgo present UNATE, a framework learning atomic representations from unlabeled crystal structures. Crystal property prediction suffers from scarce labeled data and costly calculations. UNATE pairs a denoising autoencoder without supervision with contrastive learning that supervises itself, to build robust atomic features. Swapping atomic numbers for UNATE node embeddings beats the full-data baseline. Gains grow when labeled data is scarce, reaching about 10 percent with only a quarter of the labeled data.
arxiv-2605-25966: Thomassen asks whether the best learning-rate schedule for quantisation-aware training changes with bit-width. That training anticipates low-precision arithmetic in small decoder models. A 720-run grid finds one answer everywhere: a 33 percent final slowdown wins at every bit-width and size. Follow-up runs totalling 625 more trials leave that null result intact. The result holds across optimiser, schedule shape, training length and size range. The six-bit penalty follows a log-linear law that predicts five held-out sizes well.
arxiv-2605-26066: San, Rasheed, Bozdemir and Deng trace how digital twins grow from reactive mirrors into agentic systems. A digital twin links a live model, its data and human users. The authors argue that realising self-learning, autonomous twins hinges on three things: systems that interoperate, shared standards, and joined-up artificial intelligence with advanced reasoning across sectors. The paper surveys that shift from tools that merely reflect a physical system toward systems that learn and act on their own. It frames the twin as an evolving partner, not a static copy.
arxiv-2605-26366: Xinpeng Wang and three colleagues study why hallucination signals live more strongly in middle layers than at the final layer of large language models. They test several hypotheses and selection criteria across architectures, scales, and tasks, covering question answering and summarization, but none performs well. Their new criterion, First Effective Peak of Intrinsic Dimension, finds optimal or near-optimal layers and beats existing baselines. It needs no training and adds negligible compute, and a simple truncation strategy further strengthens these signals, in this paper.
arxiv-2605-26666: Victor Rodriguez-Mendez and four others compare clustering tools on daily sea-surface maps of the western Mediterranean. They test K-means, Self-Organizing Maps, and InfoMap on temperature and kinetic-energy snapshots to find steady regional patterns. K-means and Self-Organizing Maps agree on four seasonal temperature clusters that persist after removing the yearly cycle. For energy, the pair of partition methods catch broad regimes, while InfoMap adds fine jets, eddies, and extreme-event flags.
arxiv-2605-26766: Panda and Parida model charm-quark motion in lopsided copper-gold collisions at top RHIC energy. The uneven starting energy profile creates a dipolar flow pattern, and charm quarks pick up a directed flow about ten times larger than that of charged hadrons. That flow reacts sharply to the quarks' starting layout and to the medium's drag, so precise measures of it could pin down how heavy quarks are slowed in hot nuclear matter.
arxiv-2605-27166: Jiang and co-authors map the zero-heat phases of a one-dimensional Rydberg spin chain with competing local drive and dipole exchange. Using exact diagonalization, density-matrix methods, and matrix-product states, they find three phases: a Luttinger liquid, an ordered antiferromagnetic phase, and a polarized paramagnet. Order dies in two ways: a sharp Ising shift under strong drive, and a smooth melt into the liquid under weak drive. Inside the ordered phase they also find an exact factorization line with zero entanglement.
arxiv-2605-27266: Sebastian Reyes-Carocca and Yazmin Rivera Nene classify compact Riemann surfaces with a triangular group action whose order is twice the square of an odd prime. They show every such surface matches a curve defined over the rational numbers. The same work also classifies the matching orientably regular hypermaps with that group order.
arxiv-2605-27366: Huawei Lin and colleagues build agents whose skills evolve through a full lifecycle of creation, memory, management, evaluation, and refinement. Their MUSE-Autoskill system builds skills when needed, keeps them across tasks, and reuses them through a catalog. Self-created skills beat human-authored ones on the covered subset and transfer to other agents better than rival-created skills.
arxiv-2605-27466: Nicole Koenigstein presents AgensFlow, a setup treating multi-agent coordination as online policy learning with partial views. Coordination choices become seen and learnable from past runs instead of fixed pipeline design. Learned routing beats a fixed pipeline on coordination-heavy tasks, and warm-started graphs cut search cost while holding plateau quality.
arxiv-2605-27566: Shijie Cao, Yuan Yuan, and Jing Liu build a tuned benchmark for dynamic job shop scheduling. Their event-space calibrator scores schedule stress to sort cases by difficulty, beating evolution-based baselines on speed while hitting target metrics reliably. In this tuned setting they find an observability paradox: giving scheduling agents full structural detail can hurt performance versus concise detail.
arxiv-2605-27666: Niharika Mathur and Smit Desai argue that AI explanations should be studied as dialogues, not static artifacts. The conversational layer around an explanation, shaped by timing, tone, persona, and history, drives how well it works. Drawing on three cases, they invite research into interactive conversational exchanges and present a vision for human-centered conversational explainable AI.
arxiv-2605-27766: Aman Priyanshu, Supriti Vijay, and Esha Pahwa test privacy in multi-agent systems with a Moltbook-style simulation of thousands of agents over a simulated month. Moving from one-round to many-round social tests lifts privacy violations from about 20 percent to about 45 percent across OpenAI models. Leakage spreads from peer to peer, with agents 8 times likelier to reveal secrets after seeing a peer do so, and safeguards leave leakage above about 38 percent.
arxiv-2605-27966: Jaime Ripoll argues that AI's power in mathematics reveals a longer story, not a sudden break. Modern mathematics, he writes, steadily built formal systems that run on their own, growing stable and navigable apart from concrete experience. The essay asks whether AI threatens mathematics itself or instead the image of the mathematician as its privileged interpreter.
arxiv-2605-28066: Tsai and colleagues make text embeddings portable across language-model backbones without retraining from scratch. PromptEmbedder splits the job between a prompting model that writes soft prompts and a frozen embedding model that uses them, so new backbones need only a small alignment matrix retrained. It matched LoRA fine-tuning on a standard suite while using far less memory and training faster.
arxiv-2605-28266: Boris Shapiro and Guillaume Tahar open a new topic in the geometry of rational vector fields: their inflection curves over the Riemann sphere. They derive an explicit defining equation, degree bounds, local forms near poles, and asymptotic directions, plus a maximum-principle barrier to compact pole-free components. The curves prove to be real dessins of exact rational differentials, classified through degree two.
arxiv-2605-28366: Bridgette Amoako, Ihechukwu Chinyere, and Bernard Bainson take up a question about which groups given by special presentations are large. For each whole number from 3 upward, they build a one-relator group with n generators. Its star graph is the complete bipartite graph, and the group is large and hyperbolic. They also sort concise special presentations with star graph K3,3, finding exactly twelve torsion-free cases up to equivalence, with torsion cases as powers of those relators.
arxiv-2605-28966: Pouya Sadeghi, Anamaria Crisan, and Jimmy Lin interview eight computing researchers on their real use of large language model leaderboards. They find a near-universal paradox of pragmatic skepticism: researchers deeply distrust the rankings yet still use them as rough aids. Peer networks, not leaderboards, drive model choice, and human-voted arena boards beat static boards. Needs differ by subfield, but cost transparency tops the wish list, named by seven of eight, and the authors offer fixes such as task score splits and voter disclosure.
arxiv-2605-29066: Suhas Vijaykumar derives a scale-free bound on the density of the peak of a centered Gaussian vector. The basic bound is uneven, grows only with the log of the dimension, and allows any covariance matrix. When the largest marginal variance stays away from zero, the peak density stays controlled at all quantiles above two-thirds. That covers many testing uses, yields valid Gaussian and bootstrap approximations for peaks of high-dimensional sums below one-third, and bounds the peak absolute value density.
arxiv-2605-29366: Kyuil Sim presents a solver free, sampling method for integer linear programming. It models many combinatorial problems, solved by exact solvers or rules of thumb. Learning methods work but carry over poorly to new cases and depend on solvers. It searches discrete feasible regions without training or solvers, using a locally balanced Proposal for a jump kernel. Parallel tempering handles bumpy energy terrain, with penalty shifts tuning constraint barriers while keeping the goal over feasible points. It beats SCIP on four benchmarks and matches Gurobi on two tasks.
arxiv-2605-29466: Gabriel McCoy presents pandemonium, an R package for analysis in linked spaces. A challenge in data analysis is finding links between inputs and outputs. It joins cluster analysis with linked views. Grouping is performed on one value set to find regions with similar patterns in that space. These clusters are shown in both spaces using linked views. The package is shown through two cases: input values mapped to latent signals in a neural network model, and a complex model from physics.
arxiv-2605-29666: Bruno Ćurjurić and six colleagues measure carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen in giants across open clusters, to sharpen clocks for age dating. Spectra were analyzed differentially, deriving carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen from band and line features. They give abundances for 88 giants in 28 clusters and two Theia stars, for carbon-nitrogen relations with age. Precise dating needs separate calibrations for first-ascent and red clump giants, accounting for bump changes. Giants with larger turn-off masses show higher ratios than models predict, and the two Theia stars are probably field stars.
arxiv-2605-29966: Yiming Liu and eight colleagues free marine lead records from burying papers, where hand reading cannot scale and plain models invent facts. Their Compass agent follows a Knowledge Tree built with marine scientists, splitting extraction jobs into checkable steps. Run over an open-access corpus, it pulls thousands of never-joined lead records, forming the largest merged lead base to date. Expert checks put accuracy in the low nineties, with new coverage in East Asian and far-southern waters. An open visual platform lets anyone explore the joined data.
arxiv-2605-31366: Kong and Chen propose an integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) open uplink based on artificial path delay shifting. A user device sends uplink information by shifting the delay of a set artificial path from the downlink waveform. Unlike layered schemes, uplink and downlink coexist in delay sensing. One weak artificial path inside the cyclic prefix lets the access point decode uplink symbols from channel wobbles, barely harming the planned user. Even 15 dB weaker than the downlink signal, the user beats the planned user on bit error at 16-QAM.
arxiv-2605-31466: Ngo, Gan, and Kalogerakis present VolFill, a generative tool that rebuilds a full 3D scene from a single photo. It covers parts hidden from view, not just what the camera sees. A hybrid 3D autoencoder compresses sparse distance grids into a compact latent code. Then a diffusion transformer denoises that code into the whole scene, guided by geometry models. Unlike methods tied to single rays or loose point clouds, it allows direct surface extraction and occupancy queries, and it beats current baselines on two test sets.
arxiv-2605-31566: Della Casa and team hunt for the shortest variability hidden in gamma-ray burst light curves, with special focus on bursts with measured redshift. Burst profiles range from a single pulse lasting a few seconds to many superimposed pulses spanning tens or hundreds of seconds. Such variability may reflect activity in the central engine, as well as magnetic reconnection at larger distances. The team links this variability to traits of the central engine and to spectral parameters such as isotropic energy and peak energy.
arxiv-2606-00266:
Szczech and co-authors let software agents learn how to share a wireless channel with care. Fair, swift access to a shared channel is a long-run design snag. Fixed rules rule most nets in use. The team asks if lone agents can find good rules on their own, with no chief and no chat between them.

Each agent learns online through a deep Q tool with a Bayes twist. The channel runs in slots, and no pre-training is used. Learned play adapts to shifts in load and crowd size. It nears the best known marks for speed while it keeps shares fair. Close reads show play much like slotted ALOHA. The twist is a send chance that tunes itself as the net shifts.
arxiv-2606-00566:
Syed and Yasaei gauge how trust in a bad note shifts with the path it takes to a model. Tool-using models read feeds, call tools, and act on third-party text. That widens their risk face past what a user types. No set test had weighed path-based trust till now.

Their score, SAS, pairs the same bad text in split paths. Paths span user text, tool facts, and tool out text. Ten live models face three attack lines in the test. Plain models shrug off tool-fact notes next to user text. Agent-born models shrug far less at the same notes. In tool space, the lean flips in their tests. Facts read as rules, while outs read as mere data.
arxiv-2606-00666:
Schaufelberger and Jorner build a tool for chemistry in this 2026 paper. Transition metal complexes sit at the heart of catalysts, drugs, and new materials. What they do depends a lot on their three-dimensional shape. Yet their odd bonds and wide range of electron states make shapes hard to generate well.

Their model, TMCgen, grows shapes with a diffusion process set on a curved space. It works on the angles between the metal and its ligands, plus twists and turns of the ligands. That focus keeps the search on the traits that matter most. The authors report that TMCgen makes sound coordination shapes for a broad set of real complexes. It needs few steps, so it runs fast. The work points toward design of new complexes tuned for a chosen trait.
arxiv-2606-00866:
Xia and co-authors manage memory for AI agent workloads in this 2026 systems paper. Agent sessions call models dozens of times, with tool calls in between. Each step reuses a KV cache, which speeds the next call. Total cache size soon tops GPU memory, so caches spill to CPU memory. Moving them back and forth is costly.

Tool calls vary wildly in length, and agent work falls into busy and idle phases. Flat rules like least-recently-used miss that shape. Their system, MORI, treats idleness as a spectrum, not a switch. It ranks all live programs by idleness. The busiest sit in GPU memory and the idlest in CPU memory. The split line slides to match the true hardware ratio. Admission control guards each tier. On real coding-agent traces from Claude Code, the authors report, MORI uses both tiers well and cuts wasteful evictions.
arxiv-2606-01066:
Ray fuzzes the graders that train AI with checkable rewards in this 2026 paper. In RLVR, executable checkers replace human taste: math answer tests, JSON validators, code unit tests. The reward is thus partly a software artifact. If the checker is wrong, training can learn the bug itself. The failure grows quietly, since scores still rise.

His framework is light by design. It crafts adversarial completions meant to slip past a weak checker. Each output faces both the suspect verifier and a stricter reference one. Paired verdicts are logged for every case. The report then counts false positives, false negatives, and splits between the two graders. Exploit and uncertainty rates round out the scorecard. The point is timing: catch verifier bugs before the model learns to love them. The paper serves teams who build reward code for reasoning training. A buggy grader, left alone, becomes the lesson the model studies hardest.
arxiv-2606-01166:
Feng and co-authors train guard models from fresh threat signals in this 2026 paper. Computer use agents act on files, terminals, browsers, and tools over long runs. Harm can grow from steps that each look benign alone. Static safety benchmarks age fast against that open world risk. Their framework, BraveGuard, keeps the guard's training diet current by design.

The loop starts by mining recent research for new risks and attack patterns. Those are built into executable computer use tasks. Agent rollouts on the tasks yield trajectory level supervision for guard training. As new threats and validation failures show up, the loop repeats. Guards are trained on several backbones, including Qwen and Llama guard variants. On trajectory level safety benchmarks, detection improves across the board, they report. On AgentHazard, accuracy rises from 38.79 percent to 82.38 percent under the averaged guard in their tests.
arxiv-2606-01366:
Wang, Wei, and Ling test what keeps learned plasma rollouts stable. Learned surrogates can match short-term states yet fail over long rollouts. Charge accounting and density limits are often not enforced. Field reconstruction may also clash with the Poisson equation. Their test bed is a 1D drift diffusion Poisson benchmark. Walls have fixed potential and zero species flux. The benchmark checks conservation, not full sheath physics.

A conservative finite volume core alone nearly nails the rollout. Its error sits near roundoff level in their headline test. It beats direct learned regressors by many orders of magnitude. Across 64 settings, it wins rollout error in 60 cases. Yet it wins one-step error in just 19 cases. Local conservative structure matters more than one-step accuracy.
arxiv-2606-01466:
Basualdo Bonatto and Robertson build a higher-genus Grothendieck-Teichmüller group. They construct a modular operad of mapping class groupoids. It models the higher-genus Teichmüller tower. Compositions and contractions encode how surfaces glue together. A presentation theorem describes maps out of this operad. Genus-zero and genus-one generators and relations suffice for it. Work by Nakamura and Schneps then applies to the structure.

A faithful action of their subgroup follows from that work. Hence a faithful Galois action arises as well. The genus-zero truncation matches parenthesized ribbon braids. Its automorphism group is the classic GT group. Completed classifying spaces form a modular infinity-operad. Their values are étale homotopy types of moduli stacks. The action agrees with the étale model in low genus.
arxiv-2606-01566:
Barnard builds RobustModelMaker, a framework for sound scientific machine learning. Small scientific datasets strain learning pipelines in two ways. Feature picks shift a lot under small data changes. Using the same data to select, tune, and evaluate inflates scores. These two failure modes interact in practice, she argues. Unstable picks raise the variance of an already optimistic score. Her framework couples bootstrap stability selection with nested cross-validation. All preprocessing and selection happen inside each fold.

It outputs a stability-tested feature subset plus a leakage-safe score. Nine algorithms span classification and regression tasks. A deterministic test suite checks unit, performance, and reproducibility behavior. Three real datasets compare it with three other selectors. It matches the best score on each dataset. Its joint score-stability position is unmatched across task types.
arxiv-2606-01666:
Bamba and co-authors convert dense models into sparse experts via optimal transport. MoE designs decouple model size from inference cost. Training them from scratch is unstable and compute-heavy, though. Converting a pre-trained dense model is an attractive alternative. Past conversion uses heuristic neuron clustering or random splitting. Those partition the feed-forward network into experts crudely. DOT-MoE formulates the split as a differentiable optimal transport problem. Neuron assignment becomes a balanced transport task in that view.

Sinkhorn-Knopp iterations enforce strict expert capacity limits. Straight-through estimators learn assignments and routing jointly, end to end. Tests span multiple architectures and benchmarks. DOT-MoE beats pruning, clustering, and random-split baselines clearly. It retains 90 percent of dense performance while halving active parameters.
arxiv-2606-01766:
Doshi and Shah ask when hospital AI jobs should run on graphics chips. Their 2026 study uses a computer simulation, not real patients. Grid power shifts in carbon cost through the day. The team tests 13 rules for scheduling jobs. Jobs stand in for patient-style tasks with urgency tiers.

One simple rule runs low-urgency jobs at night. A richer rule mixes urgency and carbon cost. The authors report the night rule closes most of the carbon gap. It also misses fewer urgent deadlines than the rich rule. They stress that all numbers are queue results. The results do not speak to patient care or health.
arxiv-2606-01966:
Procter and co-authors reinterpret an ATLAS search for triple Higgs production. The search targets a final state with six b-jets. A deep neural network selects the signal events. A statistical model in HS3 format supports the analysis. The team rebuild the search in CheckMATE and Rivet.

Rich validation material from ATLAS aids the rebuild. Neural network input features get a thorough check. Exclusion limits are validated in the Standard Model. A two-singlet extension, the TRSM, is also tested. Projected limits cover several TRSM benchmark models. Those go beyond the cases ATLAS considered. High Luminosity LHC prospects are discussed as well. Systematic uncertainty scenarios shape those forecasts.
arxiv-2606-02166:
Hariharan and co-authors build a transformer based system that forecasts the onset of epileptic seizures from EEG data. Epilepsy is one of the most common neurological disorders in the world, marked by recurring seizures that strongly affect quality of life. The unpredictability of seizures is a core risk for patients, so an accurate forecast of onset can reduce harm. Their EEG-FuseFormer framework fuses features from two different network branches to make that forecast.

One branch pairs convolutional layers with LSTM layers and reads spatial and temporal features straight from the raw signal. The other branch uses ResNet-18 on a short time Fourier transform representation of the same signal. Fusing the intermediate features of both branches is the core design choice. The aim is a richer signal view than either branch gives alone.
arxiv-2606-02666:
Verma and co-authors test exponential f(R) gravity against a stack of cosmic datasets. Modified gravity rivals the standard model as an account of late-time acceleration. In f(R) models, the Ricci scalar in the action is replaced by a function. The exponential form is the case here. Extra scalar degrees of freedom shape expansion and structure growth.

PPS, BBN, cosmic chronometer, DESI-DR2, and CMB data are combined. A detailed statistical analysis fits the free parameter b with standard cosmological parameters. The Hubble constant comes out slightly lower than in the standard model. The H0 tension is not significantly relaxed. S8 values run systematically higher, though. Late-time datasets ease the S8 tension by up to about 1.2 sigma. The model does not resolve all tensions at once. It does improve the account of large-scale structure formation.
arxiv-2606-02866:
Parmar and co-authors test when multi-agent debate helps or harms data cleaning. They ran three benchmarks across four model families. The study covers more than 6,000 task and condition pairs. The headline result is that debate cuts both ways.

Debate made text generation worse for all four model families, by 1.6 to 15.5 points. The cause was feedback from a critic role that the generator accepted without checking. Some of that feedback was hallucinated. Yet debate improved error detection sharply, by 27.4 points in F1 score. The authors derive a condition that predicts which way debate will go. It weighs the odds of fixing a wrong output against the odds of spoiling a right one. A setup with a separate critic, code execution, and evidence gates beat a single agent on a generative task. The condition matched all nine task types they checked.
arxiv-2606-02966:
Ofengeim, Shternin, and Piran examine how mass and radius measurements shape our picture of neutron-star matter. The equation of state links pressure to density inside these stars. The team updates earlier results with recent observations, plus theory from chiral effective field theory and perturbative quantum chromodynamics. The new constraints agree with past work but are tighter.

Theory plus the requirement that the maximum neutron-star mass exceed two solar masses dominates the inference over most densities. Radius measurements mainly sharpen the low-density regime, below about twice nuclear saturation density. Masses well above two solar masses improve constraints over a wider density range. Looking ahead, the biggest gain would come from pinning down the maximum mass, for instance by finding an extremely massive neutron star. But observations far outside the allowed region would point to new physics in neutron-star cores.
arxiv-2606-03066:
Shen and co-authors build CORE, a way to spot faked news that mixes text and images. Generative AI has made such fakes look real and spread fast. Past detectors lean on models tuned to one fake type and on big labeled sets. The team says the core of a fake is conflict: parts that clash with each other or with how the world works.

CORE trains large multimodal models to catch those clashes head-on. A new corpus, built for this work, tags each conflict by kind and source. Training on it sharpens the models' clash sense and clash reasoning. The result spots fakes of kinds not seen in training, with few or no samples of the new kind. Wide tests show CORE ahead of the best past models. The work reframes fake checks around clash, not around the marks one generator leaves behind.
arxiv-2606-03466:
Sobien and Trzebinski report on tagging charged fragments in the ATLAS detector during a special 2025 run. That summer the LHC collided protons with oxygen, oxygen with oxygen, and neon with neon. ATLAS recorded the runs with its Forward Proton detectors in place. The detectors sat on both the proton side and the ion side. They can catch scattered fragments that fly far forward.

Catching those fragments opens many studies of the collisions. The authors present a few analysis ideas for this data. Early studies then show what the forward detectors might actually see. The note is a short conference-style report, written on behalf of the ATLAS Collaboration. It maps the chances this oxygen campaign gives for fragment tagging work. Readers in collider physics get a first look at a fresh dataset. Later analyses can build on the ideas sketched here.
arxiv-2606-03666:
Cui and co-authors rebuild images from compressed sensing data with more than one candidate at a time. Deep unfolding networks blend classic iterative steps with learned parts. Most such methods search in a single solution space. The sensing task is ill-posed, though, so many images can fit the same data. Their network, MHC-DUN, tracks a set of candidate solutions jointly.

The design tracks proximal gradient descent. An AlphaNet sets step sizes that vary across space for all candidates at once. A proximal module then refines them, using links within and across candidates. A mixed loss weighs fidelity to the data, spread among candidates, and final accuracy. Tests show the method beats prior sensing networks. The multi-candidate view turns the ill-posed flaw into extra signal. Imaging teams gain a stronger base for reconstruction work.
arxiv-2606-03766:
Siukaev finds invariant densities for multi-dimensional continued fraction algorithms with a graph method. Such algorithms extend the classic continued fraction to higher dimensions. Their invariant densities are hard to find head-on. Rauzy induction inspires the new approach. The simplicial systems of Fougeron supply the base language.

A win-lose induction runs on a graph linked to the original algorithm. A dual graph then builds the natural extension in full. The whole dynamics are rebuilt in the process. The invariant domain splits into pieces that map onto each other. Ergodic traits are studied in the same frame. The Modified Triangle algorithm, in any dimension, admits a unique ergodic measure. That measure matches Lebesgue measure. Dynamicists get an explicit route to densities that were out of reach.
arxiv-2606-03966:
Mdhluli presents the flagship work of the IAU Office of Astronomy for Development. The office uses astronomy to meet social needs and aid lasting development. Over a decade of funded projects gave it a tested base. Its flagship projects span jobs, diplomacy, skills, equity, and tech transfer. They are built to scale beyond single sites.

A new Flagship Ecosystem backs their growth and long life. It rests on four pillars: resources, training, community, and implementation. It offers open resources, skill building, and groups of practice. Funding paths and evidence work sit inside it as well. Its values stress inclusion, openness, and proof-led practice. The aim is wider global reach through cross-sector teamwork.
arxiv-2606-04366:
Yanshun Zhao and co-authors propose MeshTok in 2026, a tokenization scheme that lets transformer models spend their attention where a partial differential equation actually gets interesting. Standard patching cuts the domain into uniform tiles, wasting equal effort on calm regions and on sharp fronts.

Borrowing from adaptive mesh refinement, MeshTok refines tiles that show steep gradients, transient features, or multiscale structure, producing a mixed set of coarse and fine tokens over one fixed grid. A single transformer sequence then holds global context and local detail together, with no specialized architecture. The token count grows only moderately. Across several equation families and benchmarks, the efficiency-versus-accuracy trade-off consistently beat uniform-grid baselines, which the authors offer as a general design principle for neural equation solvers.
arxiv-2606-04566:
AF_Cache is a software pipeline, meaning a linked chain of computing steps, for predicting how proteins interact. Sarah Narrowe and her coauthors presented it in 2026 on arXiv, a public research site. Proteins are the working molecules inside cells, and knowing which ones bind together explains many cell processes. Tools called AlphaFold, which predict protein shapes, can test such pairs but run very slowly at scale.

The team tackled two slow steps: building alignments, which line up similar sequences, and restarting the model for new lengths. They cached finished alignment work for reuse and grouped protein pairs into buckets of similar length. On 5,050 human mitochondrial pairs, the full AlphaFold2 run took about half the usual time. The alignment step ran up to thirteen times faster, making large screening studies far more practical. The pipeline runs on both AlphaFold versions in the study.
arxiv-2606-04666:
Xie and Xu construct a new kind of coupling between light and qubits, in a 2026 arXiv physics paper. They show it can sharpen quantum measurements. It is widely used for quantum information readout. Prior work concentrated on reciprocal coupling, which behaves the same in both directions. The authors build the nonreciprocal version. They apply it to quantum sensing, where tiny signals must be measured as precisely as possible.

For measuring photon number in a cavity, nonreciprocal dispersive coupling delivers higher precision than its reciprocal counterpart. The advantage grows as photon number increases. For directly measuring a single-photon driving strength, it shows no superiority. But the authors convert driving-strength information into cavity photon numbers. After that conversion, the nonreciprocal scheme wins again. The advantage grows at larger driving strengths. They present the method as a novel route to boost quantum sensing and enable ultra-precise quantum sensors.
arxiv-2606-04866:
Hennig and colleagues prove that good prior knowledge provably reduces the cost of tuning machine learning models, in a 2026 arXiv paper on hyperparameter optimization. Automated machine learning burns substantial compute searching hyperparameters, and practitioners use prior information heuristically to accelerate the search. The authors provide the first distribution-dependent sample complexity bounds for multi-fidelity optimization with priors, by casting the problem as fixed-budget best-arm identification.

Their error bounds relate prior quality to the evaluation budget: informative priors yield provable reductions in required evaluations, and with uninformative or misleading priors the baseline performance is recovered without degradation. Proof-of-concept experiments on a synthetic benchmark and on LCBench confirm the theory, achieving up to 80 percent budget reduction while retaining solution quality.
arxiv-2606-04966:
Chen and Lai simulate a star on an eccentric orbit around a black hole to find where gentle stripping becomes total destruction, in a 2026 arXiv astrophysics paper. Stars can transfer mass while keeping eccentric orbits, and stellar-mass black holes strip such stars in micro tidal disruption events. Prior simulations focused on compact systems near disruption. Using smoothed-particle hydrodynamics, they model a Sun-like star with a ten-solar-mass black hole across initial eccentricities and pericenter distances.

Two pathways emerge, set by competition between mass-transfer-driven stellar expansion and orbital widening. Closer in, mass loss at pericenter inflates the envelope, with debris forming a thick, hyper-Eddington accretion flow that could power fast X-ray transients. Farther out, the binary settles into stable mass transfer lasting at least 150 orbits. The results bridge two literatures that had treated these regimes separately.
arxiv-2606-05266:
Anda Skeja, Daniel Gutiérrez Espinoza, Fiona Skerman, and Alexander Wein establish the first sharp thresholds for low-degree polynomial tests in planted-versus-planted settings in this 2026 arXiv paper. The task is hypothesis testing with a twist: the data were certainly generated by one of two structured planted mechanisms, and the tester must decide which one. Low-degree polynomials are the standard test class for probing computational limits in such problems.

The authors prove matching low-degree upper and lower bounds for counting communities in the planted submatrix and planted dense subgraph models. The resulting testing threshold coincides, down to the sharp constant, with the known low-degree recovery threshold. Telling the two plants apart is exactly as hard as recovering the structure. Weak testing, which only asks to beat random guessing, behaves differently: it has no sharp threshold but a smooth transition.
arxiv-2606-05366:
Haoyu Wang and Guangxu Yang prove an exponential quantum space advantage for approximating Max-kSAT in the streaming setting in this 2026 arXiv paper. Max-kSAT asks for an assignment satisfying as many clauses as possible, each clause joining at most k literals. The question is how well it can be approximated from one pass over the clauses.
