Here they are unknown functions of an underlying economic distance. They are estimated nonparametrically in the outcome, lagged outcome, and disturbance channels alike.

Matrix function operators carry those unknown weight functions through the system. Autoregressive and matrix exponential spatial specifications are unified. Allowing unknown heteroskedasticity, sieve GMM estimators are built from stacked linear and quadratic moment conditions. As regions and periods both grow, the parametric component converges at the classical rate with asymptotic normality. Feasible optimal and best versions result. The 2026 framework lets the data, through distances, draw the map of economic interaction.
arxiv-2606-25066:
Farahnaz Wick asks whether vision language models search a scene the way humans do. Human search time scales with the number of items: flat for pop out features, climbing for conjunctions that demand attention. Wick adapts four paradigms, including feature versus conjunction search, a T versus L configuration task, counting, and a tilt asymmetry test. Since a model call has no reaction time, the reasoning tokens spent per trial serve as the effort measure, benchmarked against humans.

Several signatures reproduce. Feature search effort stays flat, while conjunction search effort climbs with set size. Frontier models stay accurate where mid tier models fall to chance, and a resolution control confirms the conjunction cost is search. The divergences instruct too. Effort slopes for finding a target exceed those for reporting its absence, reversing the human order. Counting stays accurate where humans lose track. One reasoning model declines to deliberate on detection tasks.
arxiv-2606-25266:
A point particle in general relativity follows the straightest possible path, but real bodies spin, and spin bends the path. Finnian Gray, Sebastian Murk, and Daniel Terno sort out the variational maths behind such motion in 2026. Models of spinning bodies, and of light rays whose polarisation slightly deflects them, define their key quantities only along one representative path. Varying that path carelessly mixes up quantities living at different points of spacetime, so the authors define careful covariant variations for each variable type.

Following an older construction by DeWitt, the framework makes parallel transport's role explicit whenever path variables couple to tensor fields. Applied to the classic equations for spinning bodies, the treatment becomes simpler than textbook versions. It also yields a clean Lagrangian for the model where light travels as a spinning massless particle beyond the basic ray approximation.
arxiv-2606-25466:
Cryptocurrencies trade around the clock and push each other's prices around in ways that shift over time. Shubhangam Shukla, Mahesh Peyyala, and Abhijit Chakraborty map that influence as a directed network in 2026, built from high frequency returns across twenty twenty to twenty twenty five. Links appear where one coin's past returns significantly predict another's, a Granger causality test, and link weights record the strength. Ranking coins by outgoing influence exposes a moving hierarchy at the market's core.

Returns showed the heavy tails typical of financial markets, and influence concentrated in a small subset of assets. Ethereum held the top influence rank consistently across the whole window. Bitcoin, by contrast, slid gradually down the order while other coins rotated through top spots. The authors describe an ecosystem that stays competitive and unstable in its leadership.
arxiv-2606-25966:
Jinze Ge, Jingcheng Sun, and Chengxu Zhou ask whether the sole of a prosthetic foot can feel as well as carry weight. Their prototype hides magnetic pressure sensors inside a 3D-printed lattice footplate, the springy load-bearing part of a semi-active prosthetic foot built at low cost. A servo-driven hydraulic damper, whose settings map to measured damping levels, adds adjustable resistance at the ankle.

Compression tests confirm the lattice stiffness can be tuned as designed. Under repeated loading, the buried sensor tracks the test machine's reference force closely, showing ground pressure can be estimated without a separate insole. Standing trials at roughly body weight separate front-foot and rear-foot loading cleanly across four set postures. A feedforward damping schedule follows a reference ankle motion through early and mid stance, though a purely damping device cannot supply push-off power.
arxiv-2606-26266:
Daniele Nello, Giuseppe Patera, and Lorenzo Columbo map squeezed light inside a semiconductor laser. Squeezed light beats ordinary laser noise in one quadrature, a property prized for sensing and secure communication. Chip-scale sources would carry that advantage into integrated devices. Their study treats a quantum well laser with a fully quantum Langevin approach, tracking noise dynamics rather than assuming them. A frequency-resolved squeezing map is the main product.

Structure fills the map. Optimal squeezing curves trace where the effect runs strongest across frequencies. Two features surface for the first time in such a device: squeezing that varies with frequency, and complex, hidden squeezing that naive measurements miss. The linewidth enhancement factor, a semiconductor quirk that couples amplitude and phase, shapes both features. Semiconductor lasers emerge as a genuine platform for non-classical light. Quantum communication and sensing are the named destinations for the effect.
arxiv-2606-26566:
Abrar Alotaibi and Moataz Ahmed survey adversarial attacks and defences built on diffusion models. Diffusion models generate content by gradually removing noise. Attackers in four separate research communities now use them. One track attacks text models, another image classifiers, a third jailbreaks vision-language models. A fourth uses diffusion to purify inputs and strip attacks away. Each track grew its own vocabulary and benchmarks.

The survey fuses the four tracks into one framework. It catalogues fifty published papers across the areas, plus baseline studies for comparison. A six-class taxonomy sorts the roles diffusion plays in attack pipelines. A threat-model axis records attacker knowledge, query budget, and target access. Five scoring dimensions are then applied uniformly across all areas. The result is a shared map and a research agenda, with emphasis on the language model side.
arxiv-2606-26666:
Muhammad Ahmed presents PersistentKV, a scheduling study for serving large language models on modest graphics hardware. When a model generates text, it reuses a key-value cache of past context. Moving that cache, not arithmetic, now limits speed. Long contexts make the problem worse, and mixed request lengths create awkward batching choices.

PersistentKV is a decode engine that works directly over paged cache tables. It schedules only work units that are actually non-empty. A compact work queue organises tasks by row, cache head, and sequence split. Tests ran on a consumer RTX 3060 card. A calibrated policy picked the best engine for each regime. Small batches favoured an existing optimised kernel. Long single requests favoured sequence splitting, and grouped long requests favoured the new work queue. Held-out traces improved under the policy.
arxiv-2606-26766:
Jayanta Pari, Pratibha Bhandari, and Soumyendu Raha find communities in networks using electrical resistance as a ruler. A community is a group of nodes linked more tightly inside than outside. Effective resistance measures how hard current flows between two nodes. Close nodes in a community have low resistance. The authors turn those values into similarity scores between all node pairs.

A weighted graph is built from the scores. Its minimum spanning tree, the cheapest set of links joining all nodes, anchors a sparser graph. Weak extra links are cut by a threshold rule. A classic modularity method then finds the communities in the sparse graph. Tests on synthetic and real networks followed. The method recovered community structure accurately while staying fast to compute.
arxiv-2606-27066:
Couto studies a pursuit game played on hypergraphs, which generalise ordinary graphs by letting each link join many points at once. In Cops and Robbers, a team of cops chases a single robber across the network, moving turn by turn. The cop number counts the fewest cops that still guarantee capture. Meyniel's famous conjecture caps that number near the square root of the network size for connected graphs. In 2026, a hypergraph version, proposed by Erde and colleagues, scales the cap down by the link size.

Expanding hypergraphs, which spread connections widely, satisfy the conjectured cap in Couto's proof. Random hypergraphs also obey it with high probability under stated conditions. Those conditions ask link size to grow at least like a cubed logarithm of the network size. Average degree must also outgrow that same cubed-log scale.
arxiv-2606-27566:
Thakur, Vrba, and Saska design a visual marker that spacecraft can track through every phase of docking. Fiducial markers give visiting robots a reference for rendezvous and proximity operations, but existing markers are single-scale and leave the camera's view at close range, exactly when tracking matters most. AstraTag builds its template from a square Spidron pattern with a recursive, self-similar structure that stays detectable across many scales. In 2026, a forty-eight-bit signature, derived from triangular sub-regions and protected by a generalised Reed-Solomon code, identifies each marker.

The detection pipeline locates the marker's four-sided outline, normalises perspective, and matches the code against a dictionary. A thin-plate spline re-warping step recovers markers stuck on curved hulls. Benchmarked on flat and curved spacecraft mockups against two leading marker families, AstraTag achieves the higher detection rate on curved surfaces in the reported tests.
arxiv-2606-27666:
Large language models are starting to enter hardware design work. Most studies there still use text-only tasks. Multimodal schematic generation has had no proper benchmark. Dhruv Kulkarni and Sai Manoj Pudukotai Dinkarrao introduce MultModLM in 2026 to fill that gap. The task is to draw hardware schematics from RTL descriptions. RTL is the register-transfer level used to describe circuits.

The dataset holds ninety-nine diverse RTL modules. They span arithmetic, control, and state-based designs. Schematics have no single correct form, so scoring is multi-stage. Rubric scoring, self-evaluation, cross-model checks, blind review, and human validation are combined. State-of-the-art models were tested. They produced schematics that look interpretable. Functional correctness remained limited, though. One finding stands out. Language-model evaluators showed near-zero agreement with human raters. Judging by language models is unreliable in structurally precise domains, the authors conclude.
arxiv-2606-27766:
Offline reinforcement learning trains policies from fixed data. That suits safety-critical work where live trial and error is costly. Diffusion planners model rich trajectory patterns and perform strongly offline. Most are risk-neutral, though. They can overlook rare but catastrophic outcomes. Shiqiang Gong proposes RS-Diffuser in 2026 to make diffusion planning risk-sensitive.

Three parts work together. A diffusion planner generates state paths. An inverse dynamics model decodes actions from them. A critic estimates the return distribution of candidate plans by quantile regression. At sampling time, a risk signal guides the denoising. Gradients come from tail-aware measures such as Conditional Value at Risk. One trained model can then act cautiously, neutrally, or boldly. Only the inference-time risk parameter changes. Tests on risk-sensitive D4RL tasks and robot navigation followed. RS-Diffuser reached state-of-the-art results, with better worst-case robustness and fewer safety violations.
arxiv-2606-28066:
Verifying message-passing concurrent programs is hard. Takashi Nagatomi and four colleagues reduce the problem to constrained Horn clause solving in 2026. Their trick, inspired by RustHorn, is prophecy. Each sender channel is represented by the list of values it will send in the future. Sender and receiver threads then encode as clauses, module by module. Time stamps on each message capture causal links between channels.

The reduction is proved sound and complete. A program is free of assertion failures exactly when the clause system is satisfiable. A prototype verifier for Rust-like programs was implemented. Experiments confirm the approach's effectiveness. Prophecy variables let the encoding reason backwards from future behaviour. That is what makes modular treatment of senders and receivers possible. The work brings a Rust verification technique to message-passing concurrency generally.
arxiv-2606-28166:
Difan Jiao, Raghav Singhal, Robert West, and Ashton Anderson tackle a side effect of training language models with rewards for correct answers. Models trained this way can drift into reasoning styles that weaker models, and people, find hard to follow. Their 2026 work brings an idea called tandem training into that reward-based setting.

Under their method, a stronger model being trained writes each solution together with a weaker, frozen partner, and the pair is rewarded as a team. Training on competition mathematics, Jiao and colleagues match the solo reasoning skill of standard training. Three gains appear together: smoother handoffs to the weaker partner, less drift away from its style, and chains of thought it can read more easily.
arxiv-2606-28266:
Yelin Wang and eight colleagues, including Zitong Yu, teach large vision-language models to describe what changed between two satellite images of the same place taken at different times. Earlier change-captioning systems used conventional networks whose limited capacity capped quality, while simply retraining a large model stumbles on scarce data.

Wang's team built RSICCLLM, a post-training framework with a difference-aware fine-tuning stage that forces the model to extract change features before describing them. A preference stage then trains against two kinds of deliberately wrong captions, sharpening fine-grained accuracy. They also released an instruction dataset and a benchmark for the task. With a modest seven-billion-parameter model, their system surpassed far larger models on change captioning tests.
arxiv-2606-28366:
Branko Sretenović, in a solo preprint, claims a solution to a centuries-old eclipse puzzle. Shadow bands are rippling stripes of light and dark that sweep the ground in the moments around totality, and their physical origin has stayed unresolved despite reports going back hundreds of years.

Sretenović models the Sun's extended face as producing a celestial analogue of Young's double-slit experiment, the classic demonstration of wave interference. The geometry yields an interference-like pattern on the ground, modulated by the atmosphere, with predictions in numbers for fringe width and spacing. The model, he argues, reproduces the main observed features of shadow bands and explains why they are so elusive and sensitive to conditions. A fuller, more pedagogical version appears in his 2025 book of the same name.
arxiv-2606-28666:
Liam Kearns, writing alone, rebuilds a medical report-writing agent with security as the blueprint rather than the paint. Language-model agents often hold access rights beyond ordinary users, and bolting security on afterward invites data exposure and regulatory breaches. Kearns applies the AI TRiSM framework, covering trust, risk, and security management, to redesign the workflow.

Across five language models, two report types, hundreds of generations, and five hundred attack scenarios, the guided workflow cut attack success sharply. Poisoning of the retrieval store succeeded about a third as often, and data-field injection dropped from over two fifths to a quarter. The network injection route vanished entirely once prompts were built server-side. Accuracy rose at the same time, by fourteen points. Least privilege and defense in depth, the study concludes, buy reliability as well as safety.
arxiv-2606-28866:
Dasgupta, Mukherjee, Verma, Sajja, Singh, Phan and Kalagnanam test variational quantum algorithms on the Maximum Independent Set problem, choosing the largest set of graph nodes with no edges between them. They ran two algorithms, VQE and QAOA, on benchmark graphs with 64, 99 and 180 vertices, under two classical optimisers and several circuit depths. A preprocessing pipeline reordered each graph using spectral information and thinned connections to cut circuit depth while keeping solution quality.

Classical post-processing, guided by run history, then repaired candidate answers and recovered the exact optimum on every instance. One variant sampled many distinct optima per run on the smaller graphs. The 180-node case needed a new trick: extra qubits prepared a superposition over classically found near-optimal answers, letting the search improve several seeds at once and find the exact optimum. On real IBM hardware, VQE kept about half its simulator performance. QAOA found no valid sets.
arxiv-2606-29166:
Durbha, Tmar, Wu, Katsavounidis and Bovik propose a self-supervised way to cluster videos by how hard they are to compress. Adaptive streaming delivers video over the internet at varying quality, and choosing the best encoding settings per video matters for cost and quality. Those settings depend on content, so knowing a video's encoding complexity in advance helps plan the bitrate ladder.

Their framework, Compression Echo Contrastive Learning, uses a video's response to compression itself as the teaching signal. This compression echo reveals underlying encoding traits during pretraining, with no manual labels needed. The learned representations are then used for the downstream task of grouping videos by encoding complexity. Extensive experiments show the method improves on leading general visual encoders at this task. Against a fixed bitrate ladder, the approach also delivered strong bitrate and quality savings, which the authors present as the practical payoff for streaming platforms.
arxiv-2606-29466:
Rejmund and Lemasson present a way for lab tools to calibrate themselves, without expert tuning or labelled data. Calibration, the step that aligns a tool's readings with known values, usually needs set procedures and hand labels. Their method is self-supervised and guided by physics. It learns hidden calibration values and task predictions together from raw readings. Known physical rules create pseudo-labels, rough stand-in labels, in repeated rounds.

They test the method on the VAMOS++ spectrometer, which sorts ions by charge. The model learns the settings of a segmented ion chamber while inferring ionic charge states at the same time. Starting from a weak guess about the mean charge, the rounds steadily sharpen the predictions. The learned values also track gain drift, pressure changes, and detector aging. The authors frame this as a step toward tools that can monitor and correct themselves during use.
arxiv-2606-29866:
Gorshkov and Vasil'ev prove a characterisation in finite group theory. A group is the set of symmetries of an object together with the rule for combining them. The alternating and symmetric groups are the fundamental examples built from permutations.

The authors show that any finite group matching an alternating or symmetric group in both order and conjugacy class sizes must actually be that group. Order means the number of elements. Conjugacy classes group elements that are mirror images of each other inside the group. So this coarse fingerprint is enough to identify these groups completely. Combined with earlier results, the same identification now holds for every finite simple group.
arxiv-2606-29966:
Ma and thirteen colleagues present RiverONE, a lightweight vision-language model for understanding quantum calibration plots, the diagnostic charts used to tune quantum hardware. Their twist is using simulated quantum computation while constructing the model, since real quantum hardware cannot yet run such models.

RiverONE pairs a specialised visual encoder with an InternVL-based language backbone. Quantum-generated parameters, produced by the simulated quantum process and stored as ordinary classical tensors after training, compensate for information lost in compression, so the model runs entirely on classical graphics processors. At about 1.9 billion parameters it reaches at least 95 percent of the performance of NVIDIA's Ising Calibration 1 system while using under a tenth of its parameter count.
arxiv-2606-30566:
Jun Wen Leong hunts in his 2026 paper for a telltale sign that an AI agent's long-term memory has been poisoned. In the setup he studies, agents fetch stored facts through visible memory-tool calls before acting. A successful data-stealing attack must first recall a fact from memory and only then send an email, a step order honest sessions rarely show.

Leong shows this ordering follows from what the attack needs, not chance, and that blocking it breaks the attack. A simple rule using the ordering alone separated attacks from normal sessions with strong accuracy. A random forest, an ensemble of decision trees, using nineteen trajectory features did better still. Removing every recall-related feature left accuracy unchanged, so the attack marks behaviour across many channels. Tests on nine held-out models confirmed the pattern, and the signature appeared in two frontier models without retraining.
arxiv-2606-30766:
Marcel Franz predicts exotic superconductivity in a family of layered materials built from vanadium-oxygen planes. A recent discovery motivates the work: a sodium vanadium oxychalcogenide in this family superconducts at about sixteen kelvin. The family's single layers are thought to be altermagnets, a newly recognised kind of magnetic order. In bulk form, though, two members likely act as ordinary antiferromagnets, with altermagnetism only at their surfaces.

Franz analyses pairing across the family. The magnetic and sublattice structure, he finds, blocks standard spin-singlet pairing, where electrons pair with opposite spins. The dominant instability is instead equal-spin triplet pairing, where the paired spins align. The predicted phases are topologically special, a trait tied to protected surface states. They could also support spin-polarised persistent currents, which flow without resistance while carrying spin. Franz presents these traits as potentially useful for future technologies.
arxiv-2606-30866:
Daniel Jerison proves a data-dependent version of the Dvoretzky-Kiefer-Wolfowitz inequality for Markov chains that regenerate. The classical inequality bounds how far an empirical distribution can sit from the true one, giving confidence bands for distribution and quantile functions. Markov chain samples are dependent, though, and Jerison's setting assumes the chain periodically restarts in distribution, which lets the sample path be cut into independent tours.

His band holds uniformly at a stated confidence level, is fully explicit, and is nearly optimal. Its leading width term is computed straight from the observed path, with no prior knowledge of how fast the chain converges; the convergence bound enters only a smaller correction term. Such empirical bounds suit chains that mix far faster in practice than theory can prove.
arxiv-2606-30966:
Arshia Rafieioskouei, Tzu-Han Hsu, Matthew Lucas and Borzoo Bonakdarpour let formal logic steer teams of learning agents. In multi-agent reinforcement learning, agents must cooperate under partial observation, each seeing only part of the world. Reward shaping struggles to express relational goals, statements about how agents' behaviours should relate over time. Their framework, HyPOLE, instead guides learning with hyperproperties written in HyperLTL. That temporal logic can compare multiple execution traces at once. It can express goals that hold only for some pairings of behaviours, not all.

HyPOLE plugs into centralised training with decentralised execution, the standard pattern where agents learn together but act alone. On the SMAC, MessySMAC and WildFire benchmarks, the guided approach showed clear advantages over baselines. The authors argue formal specification brings rigour, expressiveness and tactical guidance that shaped rewards cannot.
arxiv-2606-31866:
Ciardelli introduces inquisitive action logic, a multi-agent modal logic for reasoning about action and determination. Standard agency logics ask what outcomes an agent can force. They say less about which aspects of an outcome an agent determines, such as one sibling shaping a clay animal while another chooses its color.

Determination claims are analyzed as claims about questions: an agent determines a question when fixing the agent's action settles its answer. Built as a multi-agent extension of inquisitive neighborhood logic over concurrent game structures, InqAL matches the individual-agent fragment of socially friendly coalition logic in expressive power. Ciardelli supplies an axiomatization, proves completeness and decidability through the finite model property, and characterizes which neighborhood frames come from games.
arxiv-2608-00166:
Assi and co-authors study the flavour structure of an SU(15) composite theory. Standard Model quarks, leptons, and the Higgs emerge as bound states there. Two scalar fields supply flavour-breaking spurions. Their representations are the conjugate antisymmetric and conjugate symmetric ones. Those spurions generate Yukawa couplings and flavour-changing processes alike.

Up and down Yukawa matrices are tightly correlated by a symmetry. It predicts a trivial CKM matrix without spontaneous breaking. Lepton Yukawas correlate with quark ones through the shared spurions. A judicious texture fit reproduces all quark and charged lepton masses plus the CKM matrix. The electron EDM and kaon mixing give the strongest reach, near ten thousand TeV. Other flavour probes add complementary reach at lower scales.
baring-gould-curious-myths-1866:
Sabine Baring-Gould, an English clergyman and folklorist, published Curious Myths of the Middle Ages in 1866. Baring-Gould collected strange tales that medieval people told and believed. Each chapter takes one myth and traces where it came from and how it changed.

Stories include the Wandering Jew, Prester John, the Seven Sleepers, and other saints' tales and wonders. Baring-Gould compared versions across lands and languages to find the root of each tale. He wrote as both a believer in old lore and a careful scholar of it. The book helped start the modern study of folklore and shows how myths travel and grow.
baring-gould-curious-myths-first-series-:
Sabine Baring-Gould was a priest and scribe of vast range in Devon. His Curious Myths of the Middle Ages, First Series, came out in 1866. The book digs up the odd tales the mid ages loved most. A Second Series came after to round out the set.

The Wandering Jew, William Tell, and the man in the moon all get a look. Baring-Gould traces each tale to its root and weighs how it grew. His tone is warm, keen, and full of lore from old books. The book is still a joy for fans of the myths of the folk.
bunyan-grace-abounding-1666:
John Bunyan was a tinker and lay preacher in Bedford. In 1666 he wrote Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners, as he faced prison for preaching without a license. The book tells, in plain and searching prose, how he came to settled faith. It is the classic Puritan conversion narrative.

Bunyan recounts years of despair, in which Bible verses struck him by turns as promise and as threat. He describes his fears of having sinned beyond pardon and the slow peace that followed. Later readers, from Wesley onward, treated the book as a map of the troubled conscience.
cavendish-blazing-world-1666:
Margaret Cavendish wrote The Blazing World in 1666. Cavendish was Duchess of Newcastle and a bold mind of her age. The work tells of a lady stole by sea thieves and swept by storm to the north pole. A door at the pole leads her to a new world.

Beast men of all kinds serve her as she weds the lord of that world. She talks with spirits on God, stuff, and the soul at great length. She then leads a fleet back to aid her own land in war. The work is one of the first tales of its kind in English.
chelmsford-witches-examination-confessio:
Printed in 1566, The Examination and Confession of Certaine Wytches at Chelmsford holds a first in English print. No earlier English pamphlet on a witch trial is known to survive. The Essex assizes town of Chelmsford gives the case its name.

The pamphlet sets out the questioning of the accused women and the confessions said to follow. Its plain question-and-answer shape set the pattern for scores of trial pamphlets after it. Readers see the charges grow out of sick beasts, spoiled goods, and neighborly spite. The small book opens two centuries of English witchcraft in print.
cia-0000008866:
Mainland Southeast Asia's outlook fills a CIA survey dated February 1961, weeks into the Kennedy administration. Laos was sliding toward crisis, South Vietnam faced a growing insurgency, and Cambodia and Thailand watched their neighbors nervously. The paper treats the mainland as one connected problem.

Regional surveys weighed how trouble in one country might spill into the next. That domino logic shaped much of Washington's thinking in these years. Readers can see it stated in the analysts' own frame, before massive American involvement. The file helps explain why the region drew such intense attention so early in the decade.
cia-0000009766:
Bodies of two American soldiers were sighted in Son Ha district, Quang Ngai province, a March 1973 report states. Son Ha is the same district where three living prisoners were reported the year before. War's end did not end the flow of such news.

Reports of bodies served the recovery side of the accounting: graves found could mean remains returned. Each claim needed checking against loss records for that district. Many claims dissolved under checking, and some held. This file records one claim as it arrived, weeks after the ceasefire, in a province that kept producing them.
cia-0000009866:
American pilots were imprisoned in a cave in Houa Phan province, an April 1968 report states. Houa Phan, in Laos's northeast, is limestone country cut by rivers and caves. The Pathet Lao made their wartime capital in its cave systems at Vieng Xay.

Cave prisons were secure, hidden, and wretched: damp, dark, and cut off from news. Men held there could vanish from every list for years. A report placing pilots in a Houa Phan cave therefore carried special weight. It pointed later searchers toward the single province where the enemy's whole leadership also sheltered underground.
cia-0000012266:
A letter written in Russian about Penkovsky survives in the files from June 1960. Oleg Penkovsky was a colonel in Soviet military intelligence who would soon offer the West a stream of secrets. Letters in his own language sit in the case file alongside the translations and reports his work produced.

The sheet preserves the spy's world in the tongue he lived in. It belongs to the buildup of a case whose product later helped Washington read Soviet missile strength during the Cuban crisis. For readers, the letter is a small, human piece of the paperwork behind a famous operation.
cia-0000013866: Do Luong District in Nghe An Province is where an American pilot was captured, in a CIA note dated July 3, 1967. Nghe An lay along key supply routes in North Vietnam. Pilots downed there were far from any rescue force. The note records his capture at the district level, the finest grain these reports often reached.
cia-0000014766: Saving the Rosenbergs was the campaign of Trieste's pro-Cominform party, in a CIA file dated February 3, 1953. The file places the drive in the free territory's tangled politics. With the execution four months off, the campaign ran at full pitch. Files like this map the worldwide mercy drive city by city.
cia-0000015266: Reports of unidentified flying objects are gathered in a CIA file dated January 5, 1956. The plural title hints at a bundle rather than one sighting. Roundup files let analysts hunt for shared shapes, speeds, and paths. This early 1956 bundle belongs to the years when the saucer question sat on many desks.
cia-0000015366: Office responsibilities for non-conventional types of air vehicles fill a CIA file dated May 1, 1954. The title's stiff phrase covers what others called saucers. Three files on duty charts share this one date in the set. Together they show a whole morning of 1954 given to who owned the strange sky desk.
cia-0000015466: Unidentified flying objects over Morocco and French West Africa fill a CIA record dated in 1952. France still ruled much of West Africa then, and reports moved through colonial channels. Officers, settlers, and local witnesses all fed such accounts in that era, though none is named here. The entry extends the 1952 wave to land most American readers never saw covered.
cia-0000022366: Defense counsel met the Powers family, and an American lawyer praised Soviet judicial ways, a CIA record dated in 1960 reports. The heading's praise line was gold for Soviet writers covering the trial. Powers' parents had traveled to Moscow for the proceedings that August. Meetings between counsel and family were part legal work, part public theater, in that watched courtroom.
cia-0000022666: A United States helicopter was reportedly shot down on January 8, 1973, and four pilots captured, a CIA record dated in 1973 reports. The title breaks off at the word pilots, in the catalog's clipped style. The date fell in the war's last weeks, just before the Paris peace was signed. Late losses like this were felt with special bitterness by all sides.
cia-0000037166:
A CIA record dated January 2, 1983 gives the purported location and identification of an American officer's remains. The words purported and alleged run through files of this kind for good reason. Nothing in the postwar accounting could be taken as settled until it was proven.

Inside, a place and a name are joined, which is what every recovery lead aimed at. If the claim held up, a family would gain the answer it had waited years to hear. If it failed, the file still showed the lead had been chased. The record preserves that moment of hope, held carefully between rumor and proof.
cia-0000042766:
Church reports told of worsening human rights abuses, in a CIA record dated November 3, 1989. The title ties the reports to the Farabundo Marti National Liberation Front. Church workers often saw abuses that no one else dared record.

Inside, the church's account of the worsening record is preserved. Parishes and missions kept lists of the dead and the detained. Their reports reached foreign capitals with unusual force. The file shows why. The church in El Salvador had paid for its witness with its own martyrs. Its word on abuses was hard for any government to wave away.
cia-0000045166:
A statement on the Zona Rosa killings was clarified, in a CIA record dated August 4, 1985. Clarifications follow statements that landed badly or caused confusion. The killings had taken place in San Salvador's Zona Rosa district.

Inside, the corrected official wording on the attack is preserved. Governments clarify when the first version costs them too much. Each new version invites readers to compare it, line by line, with the old one it replaced in the public record. The file holds the second draft of the official story, and with it a small lesson in how states manage the news of a massacre.
cia-0000049066: Captain Carlos Alfonso Morales Figueroa was detained in El Salvador in 1983. A CIA item from that year preserves the record, kept with the Truth Commission files. The title gives the fact without the charge, which the document's pages would carry. Detentions of officers thread through these records as the war's slow grind toward accountability.
cia-0000049166: House intelligence committee members were briefed in 1990 in connection with Congressman Moakley's delegation, in a partly blacked-out CIA item. Moakley led the House task force on the Jesuit murders, and his delegations went to San Salvador to press the case. The briefing prepared the members for what the agency would say, and would not.
cia-0000049266: A Senate intelligence committee staffer was briefed in 1990 on El Salvador and Honduras, and a CIA item preserves the session. Honduras was the war's back yard: American bases, Salvadoran refugees, and the contra war next door. Briefing the two together showed how the committee's map joined them, country to country.
cia-0000049366: Dated November 2, 1983, declassified CIA document 0000049366 is a Central American threat assessment marked for the Truth Commission. The paper weighs threats across the region rather than in one country. It survives as a short declassified assessment whose title states its purpose. It belongs to the agency's regular regional reporting. Its job was to sum up dangers in Central America for its readers.
cia-0000075166: Briefing of a redacted person to load drop for a redacted recipient is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000075166, dated April 3, 1961. Both key names appear as blanks in the catalog heading. The file is a brief declassified briefing record whose redactions are its defining feature, showing the limits of what the released record actually reveals.
cia-0000096666: Sixth Report to the President by the President's Board of Consultants on Foreign Intelligence Activities is declassified CIA document 0000096666, dated January 1, 1961. The heading is cut short in the catalog. The brief file is a later board report in the same series as the third reports, showing the board still reporting at a new decade's start.
cia-0000100166: Soviet Union Urals town contaminated by radioactive waste, to be evacuated, is declassified CIA document 0000100166, dated January 2, 1991. The heading joins the pollution to a planned evacuation. Readers find a short declassified contamination record from the Soviet Union's final year, its title carrying both the problem and the intended response in one line.
cia-0000102966: Alleged use of forced labor on the Siberian pipeline is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000102966, dated July 5, 1982. The word alleged is part of the heading, so the record presents a claim, not a settled finding. The brief file ties prison labor to a major Soviet gas project. It was filed while that pipeline drew wide outside attention.
cia-0000109066: Status of Cuban-soviet Trade Relations; Soviet Gift of Atomic Reactor to Cuba is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000109066, dated November 2, 1967. The title pairs a trade status report with a striking gift: an atomic reactor for Cuba. A semicolon joins the two items in one heading. The brief record is a trade and reactor item from 1967.
cia-0000119766: As of 9 a.m. on November 1, 1956, this CIA report gives the situation in Hungary on the morning after Nagy declared the country neutral. Hope stood at its highest that day, and the Soviet answer was still two days off. The paper captures the peak of that optimism. Neutrality, declared November 1, was the revolution's boldest act, and a morning report from that date catches the country holding its breath in hope.
cia-0000126866: A March 1964 CIA document reports Babu's agreement to a union with Tanganyika. Abdulrahman Babu, a leading figure in Zanzibar, was helping broker the joining of island and mainland that formed Tanzania. The paper records the agreement as the agency understood it. The union took effect in April 1964, creating Tanzania, and this March paper catches the deal in its final stage of bargaining between island and mainland.
cia-0000126966: A September 1968 CIA situation report covers Panama a month before the National Guard's October coup. That takeover would bring Omar Torrijos to power for years. The paper captures the country on the edge of the change, as the agency reported it. The October coup that followed made this September paper the last of the old order's file, a baseline against which the Torrijos years would later be measured.
cia-0000132266: Situation report 573, from January 1991, covers political developments and reaction to an Iraqi act the heading leaves unfinished. By that number, the daily crisis watch was running at full tempo. The report collects the responses as they came in. Reaction items near a series' end tend to gather the world's second thoughts. This one's cut-off heading leaves the provoking act to be found in the text.
cia-0000132566: Arms aid planned by the Castro regime for Guatemalan leftists fills item 5 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated October 5, 1960. Guatemala had been the agency's own success story in 1954, when a coup it backed took power. Now Havana was treating the country as a target for exported revolution. The short item tracks the aid plans.
cia-0000132666: Cuba getting ready to mark the anniversary of Castro's victory fills a CIA paper dated November 5, 1960. The date ahead was January 1, 1961, two years since Batista fled the island. The second anniversary was planned as a showcase of the revolution's gains. The short paper covers the plans for parades, speeches, and displays that winter.
cia-0000132766:
Seizures of American property drive this CIA briefing on Cuba, dated June 4, 1960. Castro's government was taking over U.S. firms on the island. Washington watched with growing alarm as the revolution turned hard left.

Property fights mattered because they turned ideology into losses that businesses and newspapers could count. Each takeover pushed the two governments further apart that summer. The briefing, one of two Cuba papers dated June 4, tracks the early-summer radicalization that made a break hard to avoid. It survives through the CIA Reading Room, mirrored online by the Internet Archive.
cia-0000134266: Trade missions between China and Cuba being set up fill item 1 of a CIA general series dated February 2, 1960. Trade missions were the plumbing of the new bond between the two states. Beijing and Havana were building the machinery for regular commerce that winter. The short item reports the arrangement and the first visits planned under it.
cia-0000135866: From 4 August 1952 comes a CIA document, since declassified, on links between Calligeris and General Trujillo of Santo Domingo, a tie with a fellow strongman. The paper sits inside the CIA drive against President Arbenz, run under the code name PBSUCCESS and crowned by the June 1954 coup. Later books on the coup rest on stacks of paper exactly like this, dated, coded, and only partly opened.
cia-0000136166: From the CIA files comes a cable dated 5 April 1954, long since declassified, on an urgent message from SEMANTIC for passage onward. The name Lincoln marks the forward station of PBSUCCESS, the CIA campaign that brought down President Arbenz in June 1954. A reader gets the unpolished version here, complete with code names, short titles, and gaps left by the censors.
cia-0000136266: The CIA cable of 1 May 1954 is about a request that authorization for bombings come from Lincoln, and it survives in declassified form. Lincoln was where PBSUCCESS staff worked the Guatemala operation day to day, under code names, in 1953 and 1954. The file rewards slow reading, since its short heading is often the only summary the agency ever gave it.
cia-0000136566: This Spanish text, dated 5 November 1960, belongs to the 2506 Brigade papers in the CIA's declassified release. The brigade was then a secret exile unit in training. The catalog record states no subject for the document. It joins the cluster of brigade items from the first week of November 1960, all in Spanish. Dated and placed, it is left to speak for itself in the full text held here.
cia-0000136766: An estimated 1961 date, given only as the year, heads this Spanish text from the 2506 Brigade collection. The brigade was the CIA-trained exile force whose story peaked at the Bay of Pigs that April. The catalog record flags the date as estimated and names no subject for the item. It survives in Spanish in the declassified release, a loosely dated piece of the brigade's final-year paperwork.
cia-0000136866: Tone down the propaganda, headquarters tells LINCOLN in this March 1954 cable. It went to Dunbar and Notting from Whiting. All agree an abortive coup has propaganda value. But bigger points come first. For now, efforts should focus on intelligence work. The event must be fully documented. Evidence tying Guatemala in matters most of all. A strong record could support charges before the OAS. Sloppy claims could be disproved. That would waste the incident's impact.
cia-0000136966: Propaganda for the SHERWOOD broadcast is drawn from a Guatemala City cable. The cable is dated 19 June 1954. A propaganda chief sent a warning telegram. He worked for the National Agrarian Department. He warned Arbenz and the armed forces chief. He warned the police chief and labor leaders too. One hundred Hondurans were in Champona, he said. Five thousand local men backed them. Little word had come from that area since. The item could encourage internal resistance. It could also hurt enemy morale. False sourcing would need care.
cia-0000138966: Islamic fundamentalism is the newest and most dynamic force on the Lebanese political scene, this May 1987 CIA assessment opens, but an Islamic republic is only a distant possibility. Major opposition comes from key militias including moderate Shias and Sunnis, Christians, and Druze, and from Lebanon's neighbors Syria and Israel. Barring a full-scale Syrian move, the excerpt begins, before the text cuts off. Dated during Lebanon's civil war, the report weighs Hezbollah-era fundamentalism against the country's fractured militia politics.
cia-0000139366: Terms of reference for National Intelligence Estimate 11-3-61, Sino-Soviet Air Defense Capabilities Through Mid-1966, are forwarded in this 30 December 1960 memorandum from Deputy Assistant Director Chester Cooper. Representatives are asked to meet on 6 January in the Administration Building to discuss the draft terms, which state the problem the estimate will answer. The sample contains the framing paperwork only, not the air defense judgments. It documents how the community scoped its forecast of Soviet and Chinese air defenses at the U-2 era's end.
cia-0000139466: Document 0000139466, dated 1988, is one of the SUN STREAK files: the remote viewing program in which the United States paid people to try to see far-off targets with the mind alone. Sessions under the program produced typed reports, sketches, and scores, and files like this one held them. The catalog gives no hint that this item differs from its neighbors. It survives as evidence of a real, funded program that later reviews judged to have produced no usable intelligence.
cia-0000141166:
CIA historian Jack Pfeiffer sat down with James A. Cunningham on 11 October 1977 and taped his account of the Bay of Pigs air war. Cunningham had run office work for the Development Projects Division, the unit behind the U-2 and the Cuba air effort. The excerpt kept here centers on a dry but sharp dispute: what time did the bombers really take off?

Cunningham walks through rival mission logs. One shows pilot Herrera leaving alone at 0700Z. A later fix by Gar Thorsrud moves Doug Price's takeoff beside Connie Seigrist's. A book on the landing had stirred the fight, and the Taylor Committee had used one version. The talk shows how hard the basic facts were to pin down.
cia-06701366: DETENTION OF ARGENTINE SOCIALIST LEADER CAUSING SECURITY AND HUMAN RIGHTS PROB, a CIA document. The detained leader. This file preserves that declassified paper. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
cia-06862566: MOZAMBIQUE-SOUTH AFRICA: NEW IMPETUS TO CAHORA BASSA TALKS, a CIA document. The dam negotiations. This file preserves that declassified paper. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Scholars prize such firsthand sources from long ago.
davis-death-after-life-1866:
Death and the After-Life, from 1866, gathers three discourses by Andrew Jackson Davis. Davis, the Poughkeepsie Seer, taught that death is a birth into a higher sphere. His name for the spirit world was the Summer Land. The discourses give his core statement of the spiritualist afterlife.

He describes the process of dying as his clairvoyant sight reported it. The spirit leaves the body by stages, then wakes among scenes of the after life. Friends and guides greet the new arrival in his telling. Comfort for mourners runs through every page. The small book carried his teaching to a wide audience. It stays a key spiritualist text.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-41-january-:
Work opens the year in Volume 41 of Pepys's Diary, January and February 1666. On New Year's Day he is called at five in the morning. He dictates his great business of the pursers to Mr. Tooker until three in the afternoon, without eating or drinking, and finishes it to his great content. The pursers, the shipboard stewards who fed the crews and robbed them, are Pepys's chosen quarry. His report is a reformer's brief, written before breakfast on the year's first day.

Winter business follows the same pattern: tickets unpaid, seamen's wives begging at the office, and the fleet to fit for a second war summer. At home his wife is returned from the plague exile. Music and good dinners resume in Seething Lane. Readers get Pepys the administrator at full stretch in this volume, attacking corruption with a full stomach and an empty one by turns.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-42-march-ap:
A dinner joke opens Volume 42 of Pepys's Diary, March and April 1666. At the White Horse in Lombard Street, Pepys dines with Lord Bruncker, Batten, and Penn. Their sport is Captain Cocke, whose maid sickened of the plague and lies in the pest house. Cocke will say only that she is well. God forgive us, writes Pepys, laughing in a city that buried its thousands and still fears the next bill. The plague is dying, not dead, and humor is how these men handle the ashes.

Spring turns the office to the fleet again. A second war summer is fitting out, with money shorter than the last. Pepys audits, argues, and keeps his household merry against the news. Readers get the Diary between catastrophes here. The plague is behind, the Fire five months ahead, and between them a working spring of dinners and dread.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-43-may-june:
A cousin's conscience opens Volume 43 of Pepys's Diary, May and June 1666. Thomas Pepys consults the diarist about becoming a justice of the peace. He is much against it, he confides. He cannot in conscience punish Quakers and others for religion under the Act. Nor does he know Latin enough for the bench. Pepys records the scruple without mockery. The family's private hesitations sit oddly beside the month's public thunder, for June brings the Four Days' Battle with the Dutch.

News of the great sea fight arrives in broken pieces: victory claimed, then losses counted, then both at once. Pepys at the Office works through rumor, lists, and wounded men landed at the ports. Readers get war reporting from the desk that paid for the fleet. The volume's two sounds, a cousin whispering about Quakers and guns audible in the Channel, are the whole of Pepys's England in one month.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-44-july-166:
Letters open Volume 44 of Pepys's Diary, July 1666, arriving two and three at a time from Sir William Coventry. Pepys answers as fast, full of variety of business and hurry. The chiefest business is men: pressed sailors must be got out of the City and down the river to the fleet. The summer's campaign hangs on such hauling. Sir William Penn comes unexpectedly to town. The diarist's table fills with colleagues, cousins, and dispatches, and the shorthand struggles to hold them all.

Late in the month the fleet fights the St. James's Day battle, a hard draw within sight of the coast. Pepys counts ships and men while London counts rumors. Readers get war administration at its sweatiest in this volume. July 1666 is the Fire's eve and nobody knows it: a hot month of press gangs and paperwork, written by the clerk at the center of the web.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-45-august-s:
His own worth opens Volume 45 of Pepys's Diary, August and September 1666. Settling the month's accounts, he blesses God to find himself worth fifty-seven hundred pounds, the most his book ever made out. Then, on the night of September 2nd, his maid Jane wakes him: the City is burning. Pepys's fire entries are the most famous pages in the Diary. He watches from the Tower, rows to Whitehall, and tells the King to pull down houses ahead of the flames. He buries his wine and his Parmesan cheese in a garden pit.

For five days the shorthand runs on smoke, carts, and churches falling. Pepys saves his house, his papers, and his office's records by inches. Readers get the Great Fire from its best witness. The volume begins with a man counting his money in peace and ends with the same man walking the ashes, already planning the navy's winter.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-46-october-:
A list opens Volume 46 of Pepys's Diary, October 1666: every ship and vessel employed since the war began. Parliament's committee wants it. Pepys spends the morning compiling, then dines at Coventry's chamber with Batten and Penn to examine the figures. The numbers will do them much right, he finds. The navy's spending, attacked in the ashes of London, can be answered with arithmetic. This is Pepys's native weapon, and all month he sharpens it: lists of men, ships, and money, each one a small fortification.

Around the defense runs the ruined city. Rebuilding acts are debated; cellars still smolder; the office answers creditors with ledgers instead of cash. Readers get the Fire's paperwork in this volume. October 1666 belongs to the clerks, who fought the catastrophe's second battle, for the navy's reputation, one honest column at a time.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-47-november:
A cake opens Volume 47 of Pepys's Diary, November 1666. Burton, a smith's wife, presents a very noble cake. Pepys resolves at once that his wife shall carry it, with wine, to housewarm Betty Michell in her new rooms. The gesture is pure post-Fire London: neighbors rehoused among ashes, celebrating with cake. Then he walks to the office and finds the day's real business. The day's work is answering creditors. The navy is broke, and great disquiet fills the Office.

The month runs on that contrast. London argues over rebuilding in brick while unpaid seamen's wives beg in Seething Lane. Pepys gives what help he can and records the shame of having no more to give. Readers get the Fire's long tail in this volume: not flames, but invoices, petitions, and a great city trying to restart on empty coffers.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-48-december:
A burning cellar opens Volume 48 of Pepys's Diary, December 1666. Walking in Tower Street, Pepys sees a cellar freshly ablaze, fanned up by the recent high winds. The editor's note explains: fires burned in the ruins' cellars for four months after the Great Fire, through ten days of October rain. London's ground itself is still alight at Christmas. Pepys notes the fact between an office sitting and his dinner, and walks on through the city he is helping to restart.

December mixes the year's ends: accounts, gifts, his wife's fine dressing, and the navy's unpaid thousands. He closes 1666 as its most durable servant, tired and necessary. Readers get the strangest Christmas in the Diary here. The city gives its clerk smoldering cellars for a yule log, and he responds in character, by writing it down and going home to a good fire of his own.
drake-witchcraft-delusion-vol1-1866:
Samuel Gardner Drake, a Boston antiquarian and bookseller, built his Witchcraft Delusion in New England around two famous Salem-era books. Volume one, issued in 1866, reprints Cotton Mather's Wonders of the Invisible World in full. Mather first published that defense of the trials in 1693, while the Salem hangings were still fresh.

Mather, a leading Boston minister, wrote to prove the trials were just and the threat was real. Drake adds his own preface, opening essay, and notes to set the scene. Readers get the case for the prosecution in its own strong words. The volume pairs a key source with a guide to its world.
drake-witchcraft-delusion-vol2-1866:
Volume two of Drake's Witchcraft Delusion in New England answers volume one. Where the first volume gave Cotton Mather's case for the Salem trials, this 1866 volume reprints the reply. Its author was Robert Calef, a Boston merchant with no love for the Mathers.

Calef's More Wonders of the Invisible World, first printed in 1700, charges that ministers and judges fed the Salem panic. He retells cases, prints letters, and questions the proof used to hang men and women. Drake's notes frame the feud for later readers. The book stands as the first close, on-the-spot attack on the trials.
drake-witchcraft-delusion-vol3-1866:
Volume three closes Samuel Drake's three-volume Witchcraft Delusion in New England, printed in 1866. The set reprints the great books of the Salem era with Drake's prefaces and notes. This last volume carries the story past Mather's defense and into the long argument that followed.

Its pages hold further tracts and records from the New England witchcraft years. Read with the first two volumes, it fills in names, cases, and charges the famous books leave out. Drake meant the set to serve as a working archive, not a tale retold. Together the three volumes give the trials and their fallout in full.
duncan-masonic-ritual-1866:
Malcolm C. Duncan put out his Masonic Ritual and Monitor in 1866. The book prints the rites of the craft lodge in full. It runs from the first grade, Entered Apprentice, up to Royal Arch. Duncan wrote for Masons and for the keen man in the street.

Signs, grips, oaths, and floor work stand in plain print, grade by grade. Cuts show the lodge room, the tools, and the dress of each rank. Past books had hid the rites; Duncan sold them to all. The work is still the stock guide to the craft rites of its age.
espositione-di-giovanbattista-agnello-ve: Espositione di Giovanbattista Agnello Venetiano, 1566. The Venetian exposition. This book preserves that work. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc10957466:
Marin and a large team tested a ready-made cell therapy for blood cancers in this 2024 trial report. Natural killer cells are immune cells that kill infected or cancerous cells. The team fitted such cells, taken from donated cord blood, with a sensor that targets a marker called CD19 on B cell tumours. The cells also carried a growth signal called interleukin-15. Thirty-seven patients with B cell cancers took part.

No severe side effects such as cytokine release syndrome or graft-versus-host disease appeared, the team reports. Half the patients, 48.6 percent, had responded by day 30, and the rate held at day 100. One year after treatment, 68 percent were alive. Responses were strongest when the cord blood had few red cell precursors and was frozen within 24 hours of collection. Those best units yielded cells rich in attack genes.
europmc-pmc10958066:
Deng and colleagues give a full account of one key growth signal in health and disease in this 2024 review. TGF-beta is a signal protein made by nearly every tissue and cell type. Its signals guide embryo growth, wound healing, and the day-to-day balance of tissues and the immune system. When the signal goes wrong, it can drive disease instead.

The review retraces the field's history and explains how the protein is made, switched on, and passed into cells. It then details what the signal does in healthy states and in illness. Therapies that target the signal are highlighted, since they have brought new options for linked diseases. The authors aim to give readers one systematic map of the whole topic. They also flag where fresh work is most needed.
europmc-pmc11405266:
Argentieri and a large team build a blood protein clock that estimates biological age in this 2024 study. Plasma proteins can potentially measure how fast a person is ageing, beyond years lived. The team developed the clock in the UK Biobank with 45,441 people, using a platform that measures 2,897 plasma proteins. They then tested its use for predicting disease and death in diverse populations.

A set of 204 proteins predicted chronological age with a correlation of 0.94, they report. Faster proteomic ageing tracked with 18 major chronic diseases, including heart, liver, kidney, and lung diseases, diabetes, brain degeneration, and cancer. It also tracked with having several diseases at once and with all-cause mortality. Links appeared with telomere length, frailty, and reaction time. Top clock proteins act in matrix structure, immunity, inflammation, and hormone pathways.
europmc-pmc11880366:
Xiao and co-authors surveyed peptide drugs in a 2025 review. Peptides are short chains of amino acids, the building blocks of proteins. They can act as precise drugs for many diseases. Weak points include fast breakdown in the body.

New design methods and smart delivery systems now ease those faults. Peptides treat diabetes, weight gain, cancer, and rare diseases. They also serve as vaccine parts and as guided carriers. Xiao tracks market growth and trials in progress. Artificial intelligence now speeds the search for useful peptides. It appeared in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy.
europmc-pmc1247566:
Bornehag and colleagues linked house dust phthalates to child allergy symptoms in 2004. Allergy and asthma rates in children had climbed for three decades. Dust was sampled in homes of 198 symptomatic children. A matched set of 202 symptom-free children served as controls.

One phthalate, BBzP, ran higher in case homes, at 0.15 versus 0.12 milligrams per gram. BBzP tied to runny nose and eczema symptoms. Another, DEHP, tied to asthma instead. Each child got clinical and home technical checks. Bornehag shows indoor chemical dust may track with lasting allergy. Cases and controls came from a wider cohort of 10,852 children in Sweden.
europmc-pmc1253666:
Nash and colleagues exposed zebrafish to a potent hormone drug across generations in 2004. Ethynylestradiol is a birth control drug found in waterways. It acts at very low concentrations in fish. Breeding groups were kept on realistic water levels for life.

Lifelong exposure at 5 nanograms per liter cut egg output by 56 percent. That generation then failed fully, with no fertilization at all. Males lacked working testes and showed disturbed sex development. By contrast, 40 days of exposure in adult parents caused no harm. Nash proves life-stage timing decides the damage. The harm thus skipped the first group and struck the next generation in full.
europmc-pmc1318466:
Akins, Tolson, and Cole tested expert panel stability with bootstrap methods in 2005. Delphi surveys poll experts in rounds to reach consensus. No rule fixed how many experts a panel needs. The test case was a first-round survey of 23 health quality experts.

Responses covered 54 survey items on hospital excellence criteria. Bootstrap sampling expanded the data to two larger fake panels. Means, trimmed means, spread, and confidence ranges were compared. First-round data were chosen for their widest diversity. Akins checks whether small panel results hold up when virtually enlarged. In the end, the small panel's answers stayed stable under both larger fake panels.
europmc-pmc1564166:
When SARS struck in 2002, doctors had no tested treatments. Stockman, Bellamy, and Garner reviewed all treatment studies in 2006 for the World Health Organization. They covered ribavirin, steroids, two HIV drugs, interferon, antibodies, and patient plasma.

In lab dishes, ribavirin, lopinavir, and interferon slowed the virus. In patients, proof was far weaker. Of 26 ribavirin studies, all were inconclusive or flagged possible harm. Of 29 steroid studies, four suggested harm. Plasma and antibody studies were also inconclusive. Stockman concludes no treatment had proven benefit, a stark brief for future outbreaks. Strong trial proof was missing throughout.
europmc-pmc2000966:
Conenello and colleagues pinpointed in 2007 a single change that makes influenza A far more deadly. The viral protein PB1-F2 helps trigger cell death and worsens disease in mice. Comparing H5N1 viruses from the 1997 Hong Kong outbreak revealed one amino acid difference linked to harm. That same change appears in the 1918 pandemic virus.

Swapping in the serine form at position 66 raised virus growth in mouse lungs 100-fold. Infected mice lost more weight and died more often. Reversing the change in the rebuilt 1918 virus weakened it greatly. Its lethal dose rose about 1,000-fold, and lung virus levels fell. Both harmful forms also raised inflammatory signals called cytokines in the lungs.
europmc-pmc2022666:
Cohn and colleagues asked in 2007 whether DDT exposure early in life predicts later breast cancer. Earlier studies measured exposure late, after DDT had faded from the body and been banned. This team used stored blood from young women in Oakland, California, taken in 1959 to 1967 just after childbirth. Cases were 129 women who developed breast cancer before age 50.

Controls were 129 women matched on birth year, and follow-up averaged 17 years. High blood levels of p,p'-DDT, the active ingredient, predicted a five-fold higher cancer risk. That link appeared only in women exposed before age 14, as DDT use peaked. Women first exposed later showed no association. The authors warn many heavily exposed girls had not yet reached the age of highest risk.
europmc-pmc2124966: A medical paper on the relation of the spleen to blood destruction and regeneration. The spleen's work. This article preserves that hematology. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2125966: A medical paper with further studies on pure vaccine virus cultivated in vivo. The vaccine, grown. This article preserves that virology. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
europmc-pmc2126266: A medical paper on experimental trypanosomiasis applied in chemotherapeutic investigation. The sleeping sickness model. This article preserves that pharmacology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2128466: A medical paper on a reaction product in Trypanosoma lewisi infections which inhibits reproduction. The parasite blocker. This article preserves that parasitology. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2131266: A medical paper with studies on pathogenic B. coli from bovine sources, the pathogenic action. The cattle E. coli's harm. This article preserves that veterinary bacteriology. Later readers can locate it. It retains its place in time.
europmc-pmc2140366: A biology paper on influence of a slight modification of the collodion membrane on the sign of charge. The membrane's charge. This article preserves that biophysics. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2140566: A biology paper on the adhesiveness of leucocytes to solid surfaces. The sticky white cells. This article preserves that cell biology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2248166:
Sidney and colleagues derived binding motifs in 2008 for 19 MHC class I molecules from humans and mice. These molecules display protein fragments to T cells, and each variant prefers particular fragment patterns. Knowing those motifs helps find vaccine targets. The team used positional scanning combinatorial peptide libraries, mixtures where each position is varied systematically, to measure binding preferences quantitatively and without bias.

All 19 alleles, fifteen human and four mouse, yielded distinct binding patterns under one uniform approach. The team introduced a method to convert the data into classical anchor positions, the key slots in the fragment, with their preferred building blocks. The matrices successfully identified candidate binding peptides and T-cell epitopes in vaccinia and influenza viruses. Motifs are provided for several alleles lacking detailed descriptions before, including HLA A*3001 and B*1501.
europmc-pmc2361666:
Illing and colleagues reported early Western trials of focused ultrasound for liver and kidney tumors in 2005. The method, HIFU, beams high-intensity sound from outside the body to cook a small zone of tumor, with no cut at all. The device used was a Chinese system already in use in Asia since 1997.

Thirty patients had one treatment session under general anaesthesia, then scans 12 days later. Among 27 patients who could be assessed, 25 showed a clear killed zone in the tumor. Liver tumors responded every time, while kidney tumors succeeded in 67% of cases, a gap the authors reported plainly. Side effects compared well with more invasive methods. Some patients later had tumors removed, letting doctors confirm the scan findings in real tissue.
europmc-pmc2375266:
Pérez-Tenorio and Stål, working with the Southeast Sweden Breast Cancer Group, tested a survival protein in breast cancer in 2002. The protein, Akt, helps cancer cells stay alive and keep growing, and it sits below the erbB-2 growth receptor in the cell's signal chain. All 93 patients were under 50 and received hormone-based treatment.

The team measured both the protein and its switched-on form, called pAkt, in tumors. Patients whose tumors showed pAkt were far more prone to the cancer spreading to distant sites. That link held after accounting for growth rate and lymph node spread, with a significance value of 0.004 in the adjusted analysis. The on-form also came with a lower share of cells in the copying phase. The authors said Akt activation may flag patients whose hormone treatment will fail.
europmc-pmc2519166:
Deco, Jirsa, Robinson, Breakspear, and Friston reviewed in 2008 how computer models capture the living brain's activity at every scale. The cortex, the brain's outer layer, supports perception, language, and thought. Its moment-to-moment dynamics are far less mapped than its wiring. The authors set out to unify modelling work from single neurons up to the whole brain.

They show how models at each level answer different questions, from how single neurons exchange signals to how large regions interact. Mean-field models, which track average activity across cell groups, link the levels and can be fitted directly to brain recordings such as EEG and fMRI scans. The authors argue that such principled models are a prerequisite for grounding brain data in real theory.
europmc-pmc2568866:
Fullerton, Bruce, and Gordon reviewed in 2008 the health toll of indoor smoke from biomass fuels such as wood, dung, and charcoal. About a third of the world's people burn such fuels for cooking, heating, and lighting, mostly in the developing world. The smoke fills homes with high levels of pollutants, and the authors summarised what is known about the damage.

Biomass smoke is linked to more respiratory infections, including pneumonia and tuberculosis, and to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. It is also associated with low birthweight, cataracts, cardiovascular events, and higher death rates for adults and for children. Why these links arise is not fully understood. The review highlights where the evidence is solid and where knowledge gaps remain.
europmc-pmc2627866:
Knowlton and colleagues assessed the health impact of the 2006 California heat wave in 2009, focusing on illness rather than deaths. Heat waves are projected to grow more frequent and severe, yet few studies had measured the hospital burden. The team counted hospitalisations and emergency department visits across six California regions during the 18-day event and compared them with a reference period.

The heat wave produced 16,166 excess emergency visits and 1,182 excess hospitalisations statewide. Visits for heat-related causes rose 6.30-fold, and hospitalisations for heat illness rose 10.15-fold on the rate ratio measure. Kidney failure, electrolyte imbalance, diabetes, and cardiovascular problems also climbed significantly. Children under five and adults over 65 were at greatest risk. Even modest-temperature regions like the Central Coast suffered. Acclimatisation seems to shape vulnerability.
europmc-pmc2658866:
van Dam and colleagues followed 77,782 American nurses for 24 years to measure how five daily habits, combined, shape the risk of death. The study, published in 2008, scored smoking, body weight, exercise, alcohol use, and diet quality. The women were 34 to 59 years old and free of heart disease and cancer at the start in 1980.

Over the follow-up, 8,882 women died. Each habit on its own predicted death, and the effects stacked. Women with all five risk habits faced over four times the death risk of women with none. For heart deaths the gap was eight-fold. The team estimates smoking alone accounted for 28 percent of all deaths. Smoking, excess weight, inactivity, and poor diet together accounted for over half, a share alcohol barely changed.
europmc-pmc2683166:
Kelly and co-authors tackled in 2009 a measurement problem in synthetic biology: gene switches called promoters have no shared unit of strength. Labs building with standard DNA parts, called BioBricks, reported promoter strength in raw instrument numbers. Those numbers shift with growth conditions and machines, so one lab's strong promoter was another's weak one.

The team chose one promoter as a living reference standard, measured in the same sample beside every test promoter. Reporting strengths relative to that standard cut the scatter from differing conditions and instruments by about half. They named the ratio the Relative Promoter Unit and built a kit so any lab could adopt it. Sending test promoters to several labs confirmed the fix: relative values agreed far better than raw ones. Shared units, they argue, turn scattered part descriptions into engineering data.
europmc-pmc2698066:
Jensen and colleagues found in 2009 a marker, Lrig1, that picks out a distinct reservoir of stem cells in mouse skin. Skin renews itself from several stem cell pools whose borders were fuzzy. In humans, Lrig1 already marked one quiet stem cell type, and it helps keep those cells resting rather than dividing.

europmc-pmc2745766:
Dick and co-authors used genome sequence signatures in 2009 to sort DNA fragments from an acid biofilm microbial community without growing the microbes first. Metagenomic data, DNA taken straight from an environment, mixes many species, including rare ones that are hard to assign. Composition patterns in a genome, such as letter frequencies, are fairly constant within a species and can act as a fingerprint.

Applying signature clustering to the acid mine community, they identified and grouped fragments de novo, recovering information about low-abundance members that standard methods miss. The approach helps trace fragment origins and reveals population diversity and gene exchange inside a community. It offers a culture-free window on microbes that drive chemical cycles in extreme environments.
europmc-pmc2762766:
Eysenbach framed in 2009 infodemiology and infoveillance, public health methods that analyze how health information spreads and is sought on the Internet. Search queries can predict flu outbreaks, social media posts can support syndromic surveillance, and web content can reveal gaps in health information or the reach of anti-vaccination sites. Seven years after coining the concept, he revisits and expands the framework.

The framework separates supply-based work, studying what is published online, from demand-based work, studying search and navigation behavior, and passive from active surveillance. New metrics include information prevalence, concept occurrence ratios, and information incidence, all measurable in near real time. Such measures can follow or even predict health events, and need standardization for public health use.
europmc-pmc2814866:
Ortega and colleagues profiled tiny gene regulators called microRNAs in human fat tissue and fat cells in 2010. MicroRNAs are short RNA pieces that fine-tune gene activity, and they had been tied to body weight in mice but never mapped across human fat cell growth. The team screened more than seven hundred microRNAs in belly fat from lean and obese women, some with type 2 diabetes.

Fifty microRNAs showed different levels in fat cells taken from lean versus obese donors. Seventy swung up or down as young fat cells matured, showing a near mirror-image pattern between the two states. Eleven differed in fat from obese women, and most of those also shifted during cell growth. The authors flag them as candidate markers and drug targets for obesity.
europmc-pmc2815666:
Kabsch laid out the working principles in 2010 behind key steps of his XDS program for processing crystal diffraction data. The four steps covered are modeling where spots should fall, adding up spot strengths, correcting and scaling the data, and assigning the crystal's symmetry group, called its space group.

Much of the theory dates back about thirty years to film methods, later extended for fast electronic detectors at synchrotron beamlines, machines that make intense X-ray beams. The article explains the methods as XDS applies them.
europmc-pmc2831066:
Soscia, Kirby, Washicosky, and a large team reported in 2010 that the amyloid beta protein, long blamed as mere waste in Alzheimer disease, actually kills germs. The protein builds the plaques found in Alzheimer brains and was thought to have no normal job. Its traits, though, mirror a family of natural antibiotics called antimicrobial peptides.

In lab tests the protein fought eight common disease germs as strongly as, and sometimes more strongly than, a benchmark human defense peptide called LL-37. Brain tissue from Alzheimer patients killed germs better than tissue from matched healthy donors, and the strength rose with amyloid levels. Stripping the protein out with antibodies erased the extra killing, tying the effect to amyloid itself.
europmc-pmc2851566:
Cunnington, Santibanez Koref, Mayosi, Burn, and Keavney asked in 2010 how one stretch of chromosome 9 gained links to heart disease, diabetes, stroke, and several cancers. The risk variants there sit outside genes, so the team suspected they tune the output of nearby genes instead.
