The team treated it with cold plasma, a gas rich in reactive oxygen and nitrogen species, then mapped the chemical changes in fine detail.

Fifty-nine distinct changes were listed, and the pattern shifted with how the plasma was run. In transgenic mice carrying Ag85B-specific T cells, the oxidized antigen set off stronger T cell action and more interferon-gamma release. Plasma rich in hydroxyl radicals leaned the response toward a Th17 profile. Antibody levels stayed the same, a sign that cell-based defense rose without weakening the antibody side.
pmc-13233666:
Eduard Feireisl, Ansgar Jüngel, and Mária Lukáčová-Medviďová published a 2026 mathematical analysis of the Euler equations, the classic system describing a compressible gas with no friction. These equations are notorious for forming singularities and for admitting too many weak solutions, which leaves physicists without a rule for picking the right one. A proposed selection rule, Dafermos' criterion, favors the solution that dissipates the most.

pmc-13234266:

pmc-13235366:

pmc-13237466:

pmc-13238966:

pmc-13239266:

pmc-13240966:

pmc-13241766:

pmc-13241866:

pmc-13242766:

pmc-13242866:

pmc-13243066:

pmc-13243166:

pmc-13243266:

pmc-13243866:

pmc-13245466:

pmc-13245766:

pmc-13246466:

pmc-13249066:

pmc-13249966:

pmc-13253666:

pmc-13254866:

pmc-13255066:

pmc-13255766:

pmc-13256466:

pmc-13257066:

pmc-13259166:

pmc-13260066:

pmc-13260266:

pmc-13260566:

pmc-13263466:

pmc-13263566:

pmc-13263766:

pmc-13263866:

pmc-13264366:

pmc-13264566:

pmc-13264866:

pmc-13265166:

pmc-13266766:

pmc-13267566:

pmc-13267766:

pmc-13268166:

pmc-13268766:

pmc-13269066:
Marina Weiler, Marieta Pehlivanova, and Philip J Cozzolino argue in 2026 that laboratory tests of out-of-body experiences are designed in ways that may hide the very phenomenon they chase. pmc-13269166:

pmc-13269266:

pmc-13269966:

pmc-13270566:

pmc-13270866:

pmc-13271466:

pmc-13271566:

pmc-13272166:

pmc-13272466:

pmc-13278766:

pmc-13280466:

pmc-13280566:

pmc-13281766:

pmc-13281866:

pmc-13282166:

pmc-13282866:

pmc-13283166:

pmc-13285266:

pmc-13286366:

pmc-13286866:

pmc-13287266:

It also changes when fallen leaves return nutrients to the soil.
pmc-13287666:

pmc-13287766:

pmc-13288566:

pmc-13288866:

pmc-13288966:

pmc-13289066:

pmc-13289166:

Clinical care came next with 31. Mind programs numbered 13 and social ones 10. Social outcomes went unreported in the set. The map shows where new work is needed.
pmc-13289266:

pmc-13289566:

pmc-13289766:

pmc-13290166:

pmc-13290866:

pmc-13291066:

pmc-13291266:

pmc-13293766:

pmc-13293866:

pmc-13294366:

pmc-13294466:

pmc-13294766:

pmc-13294966:

pmc-13295066:

pmc-13295866:

pmc-13296466:

pmc-13296566:

pmc-13296766:

pmc-13297266:

pmc-13297766:

pmc-13298066:

pmc-13298366:

pmc-13298466:
Eryk Andreas and Justin C. St John ask whether moving a nucleus between eggs itself disturbs gene balance, separate from mitochondrial carryover, in a 2026 study. Nuclear transfer could help patients with high mitochondrial mutation loads or repeated fertilisation failure. A small amount of mitochondrial DNA travels with the nucleus, complicating interpretation.

The team compared hatching blastocysts made by spindle transfer with embryos receiving mitochondrial supplementation, both using the patient's own material. Gene expression differed across metabolic, cell cycle, immune, inflammatory, and epigenetic networks. Developmental delay did not explain the pattern. The authors warn such shifts could matter for offspring health.
pmc-13298566:
Dental care leaves a large mark on the earth, and Thomas Gerhard Wolf and his team ask what can shrink it in a 2026 review. They searched five data banks with no bar on tongue. From more than two thousand hits, 51 studies made the cut.

The work spans life-cycle checks of dental goods, greener ways to run a clinic, and ways to teach the theme. Reused safety gear and water-saving tools showed clear scope to cut waste and harm. Dentists and patients, for the most part, backed greener care. Cost and thin know-how held change back. The team urge schools to teach the theme and funds and rules that make green picks pay.
pmc-13298966:
Ildefonso Serrano-Belmonte and co-authors compare colour staying power between standard and graphene-reinforced dental PMMA, in a 2026 lab study. Temporary crowns can discolour in the mouth, hurting appearance. Eighty discs were split across set-ups combining saliva-like acidity changes, coffee exposure, and simulated chewing movements, with colour measured before and after.

Both materials changed colour measurably. The graphene version changed less in the coffee and combined conditions, where the gap reached statistical significance. Plain PMMA exposed to coffee passed the clinical acceptability threshold for colour change. Neither material stayed fully stable, so the authors present graphene reinforcement as an improvement, not a cure.
pmc-13300666:
E Von Felten and co-authors compare complication rates between atrial leadless pacemakers and conventional lead-based dual-chamber devices in sick sinus syndrome, in a 2026 retrospective study. Guidelines still favor the lead-based route, yet leads drive many complications and revisions. The single-center series covered fifty-two consecutive patients implanted between July 2024 and May 2025, seventeen receiving the new leadless atrial device and thirty-five the conventional system.

Procedures were far quicker with the leadless device, averaging twenty-seven minutes against seventy-two. Within ninety days, one leadless patient, about six percent, had a complication, against five lead-based patients at about fourteen percent. No leadless patient needed revision, while three lead-based patients did. None of these gaps reached statistical significance in so small a sample. The authors call the trend encouraging and ask for larger studies with longer follow-up to settle the comparison.
pmc-13300766:
A helpful fungus that fights root-knot nematodes finally has a genetic toolkit, Ning Luo and colleagues announce in a 2026 study of Trichoderma longibrachiatum strain 40418. Without a way to insert genes, the biocontrol strain's inner workings stayed obscure. The team tuned protoplast production with response-surface methods, then used PEG transfer to add a glowing GFP marker.

The optimized recipe yielded about 2.05 × 10^7 protoplasts per gram. Tomato plants treated with the labeled strain suffered 47.6 percent less root galling from Meloidogyne incognita. Defense enzymes climbed, and the resistance gene PR2 rose nearly thirty-fold over controls. The platform now lets researchers probe which fungal genes drive the protection.
pmc-13300866:
Chun-Gon Park and co-authors describe an endoscopic technique for removing a cervical osteochondroma while sparing the opposite side of the spine, in a 2026 technical note. Their patient was a twenty-five-year-old man with multiple hereditary exostosis. A small bony growth pressed into his spinal canal at the third neck vertebra, causing pain, numbness, and an electric shock sensation on bending his neck. Wide open removal risked destabilizing the neck, so the team worked through a partial one sided opening with two endoscope portals.

The growth came out in one piece with clear margins, and pathology confirmed the benign diagnosis. Symptoms resolved, the patient left hospital on day three, and scores for pain, function, and myelopathy all improved markedly by eighteen months, with no recurrence on imaging and neck curvature preserved. The authors offer the approach for selected benign lesions, pending larger comparative studies.
pmc-13301966:
T Kanda and co-authors examine, in a 2026 multicentre study, a frequency-based mapping method for pinpointing the extra electrical pathways ablated in a racing-heart condition. These accessory pathways let signals shortcut the heart's normal route, and standard timing maps can blur their exact location. Omnipolar near-field analysis isolates sharp local signals from background interference.

Thirty-three patients had high-density mapping during ablation, and every procedure succeeded. Successful burn sites showed high peak frequencies, yet in every case a nearby spot registered a distinctly higher frequency. That hottest spot sat a few millimetres away on average, often shifted along the valve ring. The authors propose the offset fits the slanted course of these pathways and can serve as a practical landmark.
pmc-13303066:
Five percent tantalum hits the sweet spot in a magnetic alloy that must also bear load, Shizhan Zhang and colleagues report in a 2026 study. Iron-cobalt-nickel multi-principal alloys with three, five, or seven percent tantalum plus aluminum were cast and probed for structure, strength, and magnetism. Tantalum coaxed out a Ta-rich Laves phase and shrank the grains of the face-centered matrix.

The middle composition yielded near 992 megapascals while keeping ten percent elongation. Its saturation magnetization reached 94.16 emu per gram with a coercivity of only 6.69 oersteds. Heavier tantalum dosing bought little more. The balance suits high-efficiency motors that need strength without magnetic sluggishness.
pmc-13304866:
Johannes Gröne and co-authors test whether tea compounds that form as green tea's main polyphenol breaks down carry its cell effects in a 2026 study. The parent compound, EGCG, falls apart quickly in mildly basic lab fluids.

Liver cancer cells were exposed to the parent and to three stable breakdown products. Gene patterns for cell death differed by compound, and killer enzyme activity shifted unevenly. In extracted cell nuclei the breakdown products cut a gene-silencing enzyme's activity, though whole-cell tests did not mirror that result. Protein scans flagged ribosome parts as further targets.
pmc-13305366:
Banhi Biswas leads a 2026 study of a remdesivir parent compound against a virus tool that strips a host defense tag. Coronaviruses use this macrodomain part to dodge immune attack, making it a tempting drug target.

The compound, GS-441524, blocked the SARS-CoV-2 version of the tool while sparing a similar human protein, and it engaged the target inside living cells. A related MERS virus version was not engaged. Its two-phosphate breakdown form proved the strongest blocker of all. Selective, cell-active blocking supports this drug family as a lead against coronavirus immune evasion.
pmc-13305666:
Adam D. Walsh ran a 2026 prospective study asking whether bedside oxygen measures could guide clot removal for pulmonary embolism. Twenty-seven patients having large-bore mechanical thrombectomy for intermediate-high risk disease gave blood samples just before and just after the procedure.

The gap between alveolar and arterial oxygen narrowed after treatment, reaching clear significance once implausible outliers were removed from analysis. Mixed venous oxygen fell slightly in most patients, alongside a small drop in estimated cardiac output, while breathlessness scores mostly improved. The authors suggest these mixed signals reflect changed oxygen extraction and may complement existing procedural endpoints.
pmc-13305766:
Sachika Paththamperuma and co-authors describe a 2026 case of cholera bacteria reaching the bloodstream of a traveller who had returned from Tanzania. The patient, a fifty-four-year-old woman with hypertension, arrived with watery diarrhoea, vomiting, and fever ten days after her trip. She had eaten street food while staying in hotels abroad.

Blood cultures grew Vibrio cholerae, identified quickly by mass spectrometry, even though her stool culture stayed negative. Clinicians first gave intravenous ceftriaxone, then switched to a three-day course of azithromycin alongside fluids and electrolyte replacement. She recovered and went home. The case stresses travel history, blood cultures, and early treatment when returning travellers show signs of whole-body infection.
pmc-13305866:
Aleksander Szpakiewicz-Szatan reported in 2026 on glass-ceramic composites holding a fast ion-moving phase of bismuth oxide. Grains of the delta-like phase sit inside an aluminosilicate glass after heat treatment and pressing above 750 MPa.

Total oxygen conductivity reached 4.5 × 10−4 S/cm at 600 °C in the reported tests, while conductivity inside grains alone was higher still. Two energy barriers appeared across temperature, likely tied to ordering changes among moving oxygen ions. The authors present the material as promising for electrochemical devices that run in a middle heat range of roughly 300 to 600 °C.
pmc-13306266:
Rongbing Xu and colleagues test in 2026 whether cheap wearable sensors can flag workload and stress in pilots during real flight training. Thirty-five pilots flew four segments in a Cessna 172 while wearing devices that tracked sweat response, heart signals, and wrist temperature. Ratings after each segment were converted into personal deviation scores.

Models were checked by leaving each pilot out in turn, a strict test of use on new people. Combined signals classified stress modestly above chance, and sweat response alone did similar work for workload. Scores looked far better when models were tuned within each pilot, but that approach proved unstable. The authors suggest debriefing after flights as the realistic near-term use. Uncalibrated prediction across pilots, they conclude, is not yet strong enough for live monitoring.
pmc-13306566:
Yusuke Ishii used the inner gaps of layered oxysulfide crystals as reaction sites for making hydrogen in a 2026 study. New solid-state cooking gave submicrometer particles of five lanthanoid variants, small enough for inner layers to take part.

Nickel swapped into the gaps in place of sodium ions lifted hydrogen output well above surface-loaded versions in reported tests. Electrons made by light were used more fully inside each particle in the authors' account. The result offers a fresh design route for visible-light water splitting with layered materials. Such inner space use may lift yield in sun driven fuel making as a whole.
pmc-13307066:
Antonio J. Santos coated glass with niobium-doped vanadium dioxide for smart windows in a 2026 study. Films at 3, 4.5 and 6 percent niobium were laid on soda-lime and borosilicate glass, then rapidly heated to set their heat-switching behaviour.

Both glasses held the wanted VO2 phase, yet sodium leaking from soda-lime glass destabilised side phases in reported checks. Niobium spread unevenly, causing stepwise switching on that glass, while borosilicate gave larger grains and steadier doping. The authors define a practical switching temperature to compare glazing performance fairly. The work sets a fair way to rank films for real world window use.
pmc-13307166:
Rodrigo Valle programmed printed lattice materials to collapse safely instead of shattering in a 2026 study. Auxetic and honeycomb cells printed in ABS or glass-filled polyamide were tested plain and filled with elastic polyurea.

Compression, bending and impact trials showed cell shape ruled stiffness and energy uptake, with the plain auxetic build strongest in reported results. Polyurea barely changed stiffness yet steadied post-yield behaviour, giving 96.6% elastic recovery in one glass-filled auxetic build. Base polymer governed bending stiffness, with ABS builds 68% stiffer than polyamide rivals. The programmed switch from shatter to crush could guard goods and gear in hard knocks.
pmc-13307566:
Carlos Espinal Tejada and a regional expert panel set out a 2026 blueprint for stronger dengue control across Latin America. Specialists met in Bogotá in March 2025 under the Americas Health Foundation to map gaps in vaccination, diagnosis, treatment, mosquito control, and policy. Dengue is now the region's fastest-spreading mosquito-borne disease.

Barriers named by the panel include underreporting, insecticide resistance, weak health systems, fragmented surveillance, and funding limits. Social and economic drivers also sustain transmission in crowded urban settings. Recommendations target better regional surveillance, stronger prevention and diagnosis, and tighter coordination among stakeholders. The review mixes epidemiological context with practical guidance. Its central claim is that no single sector can control dengue alone, so multisector work must replace separate efforts.
pmc-13307666:
Thi Chau Giang Tran and co-authors report in 2026 three African swine fever virus isolates from northern Vietnam that break the usual pattern of the epidemic strain. Pigs carrying them showed prolonged illness, and blood samples yielded genotype II viruses that no longer adsorb onto red cells. Whole-genome sequencing explained the change.

Each isolate carried a stop mutation in the gene for the CD2v surface protein, at one of two positions. Extra deletions and frame shifts hit gene families tied to virulence and immune evasion. One isolate also bore a partial deletion of a vaccine target gene plus an inserted marker gene, suggesting a modified live vaccine strain evolving in the field. The authors stress genomic flexibility in circulating virus. Surveillance, they imply, must watch vaccine-derived lineages as closely as wild strains.
pmc-13307866:
Hyun Cho and colleagues use contrast ultrasound in 2026 to reveal a hidden channel between a dog's ruptured gallbladder and its liver. The patient, a ten-year-old neutered Pomeranian, had eaten poorly and vomited for five days. Ordinary ultrasound left the picture unclear, which is common when inflammation glues organs together.

Microbubble contrast lit up the abnormal connection in real time and showed the liver lesion behaving like inflamed tissue rather than tumour. Surgery confirmed the rupture and the adhesion to the liver surface. The authors believe such an internal connection after rupture has not been reported in veterinary medicine before. Contrast imaging, they argue, sharpens treatment decisions when standard scans blur the boundary between bile, debris, and living tissue. The case gives clinicians a new pattern to look for.
pmc-13309266:
A 2026 conference programme gathers symposium sessions on tremor syndromes and medium vessel stroke, opening with talks dated Saturday, June 27. Four tremor talks run from disease mechanisms through diagnosis, drug and non-surgical treatment, and surgical options. No single author heads the document; it is a meeting schedule with named sessions and speakers from several European centres.

The lead tremor talk argues that rhythmic activity in the cerebello-thalamo-cortical circuit underlies almost every tremor syndrome. Differences arise from mechanisms inside that circuit, such as cerebellar shrinkage, and from outside triggers like the basal ganglia or newly found anti-tremor networks. Imaging and physiology studies, with and without interventions, supply the material reviewed. Understanding mechanism, the session claims, explains why patients respond differently and points toward mechanism-guided therapies. Later symposium blocks turn to stroke questions, including blood markers for early risk sorting.
pmc-13309366:
Gianmarco Valenti and co-authors chart in 2026 which genes switch on as the Mediterranean seagrass Posidonia oceanica grows, across roots, leaves, and seeds at four early life stages. The grass builds vast sea meadows that shelter young fish, lock sand in place, store carbon, and shield coasts, yet its beds have shrunk fast.

Leaves ran gene sets for light capture, while roots ran sets for sugar burn and wall build, a fit for grip and growth in sand. Seeds stayed live and primed, with sugar split enzymes that hint at a quick start when sprouting begins. Web maps of co timed genes named hub switches for each part. The chart may guide meadow repair work.
pmc-13309466: Priscila dos Santos Ribas is first named on a short 2026 correction notice in Veterinary Research Communications, tied to a study of reflux during dog surgery. Corrected here is only the way her given and family names were structured; the notice states the name appeared correctly in all versions at publication. Readers get no new data, methods, or findings, since the item exists solely to fix that name display.
pmc-13309666:
Shanshan Li and co-authors present two cases of gas in the liver vein system after brain surgery in a 2026 report. The finding, hepatic portal venous gas, is uncommon and rare in brain critical care. Both patients became gravely ill with belly swelling, silent bowels, and septic shock after their operations.

Scans confirmed gas in the portal vein system in both cases, alongside the belly signs. One case involved a woman near 40 treated for a tumor at the base of the skull. Care teams had to weigh gut catastrophe against other causes in patients who could not report symptoms. The authors offer the cases as a reference for belly checks in brain intensive care.
pmc-13310366:
Betelhem Tefera and co-authors measure heavy metals in Swiss chard grown along river banks in Addis Ababa in a 2026 study. Leafy greens can pick up metals from soil and irrigation water in fast-growing cities. Chard from three areas near the city was tested for food safety.

A flame-based instrument measured metals after acid digestion of dried samples, with method checks showing strong accuracy and recovery near 95.89 to 100 percent across spiked tests in the study. Mean nickel reached 0.017 mg/kg and zinc 0.088 mg/kg in the reported means. Zinc ran highest in Kotebe chard and nickel highest in Akaki chard, and the two metals tracked together closely. The authors urge cleaner irrigation as a first safety step.
pmc-13311166:
Ethan J Rowin and a large team study pouch size and risk in thick heart muscle disease in a 2026 cohort paper. Apical aneurysms in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy link to sudden death and clot spread, yet how size grades that risk was unclear. Patients from ten centers were grouped by pouch width and followed for grave events.

Patients totaled 510 in number, followed a median of 4.1 years in total. Sudden death event rates rose step by step with pouch size, from tiny rates in small pouches to the highest in very large ones. Clot or spread events also rose with size. Size alone held as a risk factor after full adjustment.
pmc-13311266:
Anna V Naumova and colleagues test in 2026 a therapy and a measuring tool in minipigs recovering from heart attacks. The therapy is human stem-cell heart muscle cells; the tool is a way to read regional heart strain from tagged magnetic resonance images. The analysis uses frequency patterns in the tag grid rather than commercial tracking software. Infarcted front-wall segments were followed before injury, before treatment, and eight weeks after cell or vehicle delivery.

Strain in cell-treated hearts recovered from about minus one percent after infarction to minus four percent by eight weeks, where more negative means stronger shortening. Vehicle hearts instead worsened, drifting to slightly positive values. Overall pumping fraction did not improve, underlining that gains were local. The new calculation agreed closely with tag tracking and feature tracking reference methods. Regional recovery without global change is what remuscularisation trials need to detect, the authors argue.
pmc-13311366:
Juan F Poyatos presents a 2026 study using a transformer language model, named Zebraformer, to probe how zebrafish embryos develop. The model learned from single-cell gene data across early growth.

The work tests the hourglass idea that mid-development is the most tightly held stage. The model's gene and cell maps traced time and body region well, with gene activity spreading apart as growth went on. Attention-based gene networks, though, tightened into neat modules at the middle stage, with fewer links between modules. The author argues that constraint at that stage lives in network layout, not in single-gene behavior.
pmc-13311466:
Joanna M Fiszdon and co-authors in 2026 report a trial of a social skills program called Understanding Social Situations for people with psychosis. Poor social function in psychosis links to weak social and general thinking skills.

The trial randomized 103 veterans with psychotic disorders to two months of the new program or to problem-solving training matched for contact time. Social function, social skills role play, and phone-based momentary surveys were tracked. The new program group improved on a clinician-aided self-report of social function, though not more than the control group. Comfort during social contact rose within the program group.
pmc-13311566:
Areesha Rashid and colleagues, in 2026, describe a cohort of patients with cleft lip and palate treated at a specialist center in Pakistan. Data on the range of cleft types in Pakistan remain scarce.

The cross-sectional study enrolled 503 patients at a tertiary hospital in Faisalabad from September 2023 to March 2024. Cleft lip alone made up 26 percent, cleft palate 36 percent, and both together 38 percent of cases in this group. Parents were related by blood in 77 percent of cases, and only 27 percent of patients had had surgery. Few mothers reported folic acid use, pointing to gaps in prevention and care.
pmc-13311966:
Luke AR Farmkiss and colleagues, in 2026, analyze a decade of British quality assessment data for mismatch repair protein staining in tumors. The stain guides Lynch syndrome detection, variant reading, and immunotherapy choices.

Between 2011 and 2022 the scheme ran 38 assessment rounds, averaging about 45 submissions per antigen per round. Participation grew steeply over the decade. Average scores edged up slightly, with tighter agreement in the second half. The report names the best-scoring antibody clones for each of the four proteins, MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, and PMS2. Labs can use the rankings to pick reagents that stain most reliably.
pmc-13312266:
Chandrashekhar T. Sreeramareddy and co-authors survey, in a 2026 study, cigarette, e-cigarette, and heated tobacco use among 1,000 Malaysian adults in a nationally representative online sample from December 2024. Current smoking stood at 28.6 percent of respondents, and awareness of e-cigarettes was nearly universal at 92.4 percent, with daily and non-daily vaping both common.

Regression analysis found that current smokers were far more likely than others to use e-cigarettes and heated tobacco products, as were men, younger adults, and people exposed to advertising. A smoke-free home, by contrast, clearly protected against both newer products. Fewer respondents knew heated tobacco products, though daily and non-daily use were both reported. The authors urge continued surveillance and rules for the newer products under Malaysia's new public health law, aimed especially at younger people.
pmc-13312466:
Jose Maria Hipola and colleagues report a 2026 prospective study of a direct route for treating pelvic venous disease in women. Instead of entering through neck or groin veins, the team punctured the abnormal veins around the uterus and cervix through the vagina, guided by ultrasound. Placement was confirmed with X-ray imaging, and a low-nitrogen polidocanol foam was injected. The cohort covered consecutive women treated between January 2023 and October 2025. Most still had symptoms after earlier vein embolization.

All 23 procedures succeeded technically, averaging 36 minutes with about a minute of X-ray time. Every patient went home the same day. Follow-up ultrasound showed the treated veins closed in all patients, with no reopening. Clinical severity scores improved from 12.91 at baseline to 7.87 at one month. They held at one year, with questionnaire scores improving in parallel. Minor vaginal bleeding the next day was common, affecting 82 percent, but no menstrual problems appeared.
pmc-13313266:
Jing Bai and co-workers search blood for signs that predict who gains from immune therapy for cervical cancer, in a study from 2026. They focused on advanced or returned disease, where first-line care now pairs immune drugs with chemotherapy or radiation.

The study ran from June 2022 to July 2024 at the Qingdao Central Hospital network and enrolled 50 patients with stage III to IVa or returned cancer. The team compared 36 responders with 14 non-responders and tracked 26 patients whose disease grew or who died. Response tied to the starting share of CD4 T cells and to post-treatment levels of CA125, SCCA, CD8 T cells, and PD-1 on T cells, all at set statistical strength. The blood panel could help doctors pick patients for this care and spot poor outlook early.
pmc-13313966:
Aly M Aly, Eman M Ismail, and Islam M Tork trace, in a 2026 study, heavy metals moving through Egyptian buffalo farms into milk. Buffalo anchor Egypt's dairy sector, yet industrial and farm pollution threaten its safety. The team sampled milk twice weekly for two months from three farms in two provinces, 48 samples. They measured seven metals with mass spectrometry and tested water, feed, and bedding to map contamination routes and calculated hazard estimates for consumers.

Mercury, nickel, and cobalt never appeared. Lead, cadmium, chromium, and arsenic all exceeded permissible limits somewhere in the system. Arsenic in one farm's milk ran thirty times its limit, and lead peaked in another farm. Both metals tracked lower milk yields. Water, feed, and bedding all showed metal enrichment, marking the water-to-feed-to-animal chain as the pathway. Formal hazard quotients stayed below one. The authors insist monitoring and source control are overdue.
pmc-13314766:
Sarfaraz K. Niazi explains a bacterial defense system that builds DNA in an odd way, in a 2026 review. In the DRT3 system, a protein pocket, not a matching strand, picks which DNA letters get added, a mode not seen before.

The system makes one fixed product: a two-strand repeat of GT and AC letters, its pattern set by the shape of the Drt3b protein pocket. Studies of the rebuilt Escherichia coli system show a complex of two reverse-transcriptase-like proteins and a non-coding RNA frame, in a neat six-part symmetry read at fine scale, as reported. One protein copies an RNA motif to make the GT strand, while the other builds the AC strand with no template at all. That hard-wired output limits how the system can be reprogrammed, a key point for would-be engineers.
pmc-13315666:
Nikita Chanana and colleagues looked in 2026 for hidden heart relaxation problems in adults with extra weight but normal pumping strength. Extra fat strains the heart through blood flow, metabolic, and inflammatory routes, and South Asian adults face risk at lower body weight levels, yet data in otherwise healthy adults were thin.

In a hospital study of 72 adults with body mass index at or above 23 and no known heart disease, ultrasound checks found grade I relaxation problems in 29 people, or 40.3 percent, with no worse grades. Affected adults were older and had slightly higher blood sugar and LDL cholesterol measures than unaffected peers.
pmc-13315766:
Zhi-Fang Liu and colleagues turned peony seed meal, a farm leftover, into healing carbon dots in 2026 through a simple heated water process. The tiny nitrogen and oxygen doped particles mimic a protective enzyme, with surface carbonyl groups driving that activity.

In a model of hemolytic anemia, the dots worked two ways at once. They cleared harmful reactive oxygen and calmed the NF-kappaB and NLRP3 inflammatory axis, while a ROS and HIF-1 signal path encouraged new red cell making. Safety looked strong. The work offers a waste-to-therapeutics route that links greener farming with nanomedicine.
pmc-13315866:
Helena Sophia Schmitt and colleagues examine, in a 2026 study, whether cue-triggered lapses in self-control track crime reoffending risk in addiction patients. Cue reactivity and impaired control feed relapse, which raises reoffending risk, yet their link to recidivism indicators was unexplored. Fifty-one sober men under German Section 64 court-ordered addiction treatment, 24 with alcohol use disorder and 27 with other substance use disorders, completed Go/NoGo tasks under alcohol-related and neutral stimuli.

Control performance was used to predict Factor 2 scores on the Psychopathy Checklist: Screening Version, a proxy of reoffending risk. Among alcohol patients, weaker alcohol-cued control strongly predicted higher Factor 2 scores, beta negative 0.79, p equals 0.004. No link appeared for neutral stimuli or for other substance disorders. The authors suggest cue-related control impairment may connect substance use to crime re-engagement, and, if replicated over time, could inform risk evaluation and care in forensic addiction treatment.
pmc-13315966:
Arnav Joshi, Ross C. Larue, and Rajgopal Govindarajan show in 2026 that a lysosomal transporter helps cells clear HIV particles from inside. The transporter, SLC29A3 or ENT3, moves nucleosides within endolysosomes, and losing it made host cells more open to HIV-1 infection and genome integration.

Working transporter was needed for efficient removal of viral proteins such as the capsid protein p24. Without it, HIV particles piled up and persisted inside endolysosomes. Clearance ran through switching on the cell's autophagy machinery, which digests trapped material. The finding names a host defense route that future drugs might support.
pmc-13316366:
Robin Herbrechter and colleagues present a 2026 method for tracking where medical graduates end up working, tested on alumni of the University of Witten/Herdecke in Germany. With doctor shortages biting hardest in rural areas, schools need ways to judge whether their teaching keeps graduates nearby.

The team traced 333 graduates through online research and mapped their jobs with geographic software. Nearly half worked in outpatient care, helped by self-employment rates well above the national norm. Alumni density near the university ran 207 times the background level within 6 km of campus, and the pull still showed at about 30 km out in the reported figures. The authors offer the method as a blueprint other new faculties can use.
pmc-13316566:
Thierry Roland Njille Ehawa and colleagues ran a 2026 national screening study of inner capacity in older adults living at home in Cameroon. Inner capacity bundles domains such as movement, nutrition, senses, mood, and thinking, and the team used the World Health Organization ICOPE first step to check it.

From January to June 2024, 597 adults aged 60 or more joined across all ten regions. Almost everyone, 96.8 percent of those screened, showed weakness in at least one domain, and counts spread up to all six domains in a small share. Checks against standard nutrition and disability scores supported the tool's cutoffs for eating and movement. The findings press for routine screening in primary care.
pmc-13316666:
Chao Ai and a large team fashioned, in a 2026 study, a tiny carrier for tea polyphenols, health compounds that break down fast in light, heat, and the gut. Their carrier joins a treated chitosan with extract from pomelo peel, turning fruit waste into a useful shell.

The peel extract proved to be a protein and pectin mix, and at mildly acid levels it locked with the chitosan into stable particles that held 39.6 percent of the loaded compound in the reported tests. After stomach-like and gut-like digestion steps, far more of the compound survived inside carriers than free, and light exposure also spared it. The design offers food makers a greener way to deliver fragile plant compounds.
pmc-13317066:
Jianwen Guo and colleagues surveyed, in a 2026 study, nearly four thousand school teachers across China on how support from their schools shapes the feeling of being valued as professionals. Many teachers feel overlooked, and surface-level support does little, so the team mapped the inner routes.

Questionnaire data from 3,983 primary and secondary teachers showed support raised recognition directly, and also through two side paths: stronger self-driven learning and stronger teaching skill. Support that helps teachers study on their own and design better lessons feeds pride in the profession, while empty gestures do not. The model joins organization-level and person-level thinking, giving school leaders concrete levers: fund learning time, coaching, and growth that teachers can feel.
pmc-13317766:
Liangcheng Xu and co-authors review, in 2026, photocatalysis boosted by adding a second form of energy. Light-driven chemistry can split water, clean pollutants and build useful compounds from sunlight. Single-mode systems, tuned by doping or defect engineering, appear to have reached their performance ceiling.

Extra energy can come as heat, electricity, magnetism, mechanical force or microwaves. Each field widens light absorption or helps separate the charges that drive reactions, through distinct mechanisms the authors explain. Progress sections cover water splitting, pollutant removal and chemical synthesis under combined fields. The review ends with open problems, including device design and scaling, and argues that multi-energy systems are a promising route past current limits in solar fuel and cleanup technology.
pmc-13318066:
Kamil Paduszyński and Marta Królikowska investigate, in 2026, how a small change to an ionic liquid's positive ion alters the way solutes dissolve. Ionic liquids are salts that stay liquid near room temperature and are prized as tunable solvents. The team compared two liquids that share the same negative ion but differ by one oxygen atom in the cation ring.

Using gas-liquid chromatography, they measured behaviour for 34 solutes across a range of temperatures. Adding the oxygen raised activity coefficients, meaning solutes were held less favourably, with the strongest effect for nonpolar compounds. Analysis showed the change raised the overall cost of making a cavity for the solute rather than reordering interaction types. Several modelling approaches supported that reading.
pmc-13318166:
Matthew Daniel and colleagues report, in 2026, an appendix found inside a groin hernia during emergency surgery on an eight-year-old boy. Inguinal hernias are common, but an Amyand hernia, where the appendix sits inside the hernia sac, is rare. It often looks exactly like ordinary appendicitis, and scans may miss it.

The boy was taken for an emergency appendectomy, where the unusual anatomy was discovered. Children are affected more often than adults, partly because a channel near the testicle stays open. Appendicitis inside such a hernia is rarer still. The authors review proposed mechanisms, including trapping of the appendix with inflammation and bacterial overgrowth, and note that surgeons still lack consensus on the best operative approach for each presentation.
pmc-13318666:
Pengfei Wang and a large team present a 2026 multilevel meta-analysis of exercise and self-control. Their population is children and teenagers living with overweight or obesity. Such young people often show weaker inhibitory control. The authors also hunt for the best exercise dose.

Searches across five databases found 11 studies from four countries. Together they covered 787 young people aged about 9 to 14 years. Exercise improved inhibitory control in the pooled results. The three-level model gave an effect size of 0.41 for that gain. Dose analysis suggested an optimum near 49 sessions of about 48 minutes each. Heavier body mass slightly weakened the benefit. The authors stress the evidence certainty is very low, so the dose is tentative.
pmc-13318766:
Roberta Scairati and colleagues present a 2026 cross-sectional study of sexual function in pregnancy. Most earlier work reports a simple overall decline. These authors instead look for distinct patterns across function domains. They also test whether gestational diabetes explains poorer function.

Eighty-three women completed a standard function index during diabetes screening at weeks 24 to 28. Dysfunction appeared in 51 women, or 61.4 percent of the sample. Clustering found three patterns: preserved function, global impairment, and a desire-satisfaction split. Older age and lower pre-pregnancy weight linked independently to global impairment. Diabetes itself showed no link to scores, dysfunction rates, or pattern membership. The authors back pattern-based profiling over simple yes-or-no labels.
pmc-13318966:
Linghao Li and colleagues present a 2026 modelling study judging instability in unruptured brain aneurysms from vessel wall MRI. Patients were screened between January 2022 and January 2024 at their centre. After exclusions, 293 patients with 312 aneurysms remained. Of these, 197 aneurysms were stable and 115 were unstable.

Each aneurysm was split into three habitat subregions by clustering. A Transformer model then fused habitat image features, deep learning features, and clinical data. It reached a validation AUC of 0.844 for instability in their testing. That beat the best habitat-only model at 0.721 and the best deep model at 0.816 in the same comparison. Reclassification also improved clearly. The authors present the tool as exploratory decision support.
pmc-13319066:
Longhua Zhang and co-authors present a 2026 retrospective study of bundled care for high-risk pregnancies with blood pressure disorders. The cohort held 103 women treated between January 2024 and February 2025. Fifty-five received cluster management: early aspirin, shifting pressure thresholds, and careful fluid control. Forty-eight received routine care.

The bundled group started heavier, yet fared better. Protein in urine appeared later, at about 34.7 weeks versus 31.5 weeks on average. Fluid build-up in chest or abdomen fell to 25.5 percent, against 52.1 percent under routine care. Delivery came near 37.5 weeks rather than 34.6 weeks on average. Newborn intensive care admissions dropped to 52.7 percent from 85.1 percent in the comparison. Hospital costs were lower too, supporting bundle-style care.
pmc-13319366:
Emily Sattora and co-authors assess teaching on climate and health across a large public university system in a 2026 study. The State University of New York runs 64 campuses, the most of any such system in the country. Health staff are now expected to deal with heat, storms, and other climate linked harms, yet class options remain scarce.

Listings for all campuses were checked and sorted by type and place. Of 225 climate linked programs and classes found, only 30 dealt with health at all, and most sat at just three sites. Rural sites and two year colleges offered the least. More staff training and shared online units are urged to close the gap.
pmc-13319866:
Jocielle Santos de Miranda leads a team study from 2026 on a scan based symmetry score after repair of a rare hernia from injury. A tear in the lower back wall is hard to fix, and bulge or uneven shape can linger even when the repair itself holds. A side to side scan ratio was tested as a plain way to grade shape after surgery.

Records covered 25 people who had open repair with a double mesh layer plus 25 peers with no wall disease, treated or seen at one center. Scans gave the score before and after repair for the hernia group and once for peers. No hernia came back in follow up. A plain score like this could help grade repair shape beyond a yes or no on return.
pmc-13320266:
Akua Adeneke McLeod and co-authors compare four learning models for sorting power faults in home meter data in a 2026 study with a policy lens. Power firms increasingly lean on such models to plan grid spending, yet a model can score well and still steer cash toward the wrong towns. Four model types were trained on the same home meter records and set side by side.

One tree based model beat a plain math model and edged the other two across most scores. Still, counts of fault length and rate built from each model pointed spending toward unlike towns. Up to 36 towns, holding more than 100000 homes, flipped priority with model choice in the counts reported. Fair and clear models matter as much as raw scores.
pmc-13320366:
Klinger Soares Faico-Filho and Nancy Bellei wrote a letter to the editor in 2026 on a missed deadly lung illness in Brazil. A rodent borne virus causes a lung and heart syndrome that kills about a third of its cases, and Brazil carries the largest load of it in the Americas through rodent contact. A world alert in May 2026 over a ship linked cluster drew eyes to a rare person to person route, not to this steady home toll.

Post COVID triage in Brazil now tests at once for flu, a child lung virus, and COVID, yet the rodent virus rarely enters the first round of thought. Its early clues, low platelet counts with thickened blood, need an active ask about rural or rodent contact. Late calls, not exotic spread, cost the most lives, the letter argues.
pmc-13320666:
Ian M. Power and co-authors argue in a 2026 perspective that spreading crushed rock on farms helps farming more than it helps the climate. Enhanced rock weathering speeds a natural process that draws carbon dioxide from the air, and it can stand in for the lime farmers already spread to cut soil acidity. Capital needs are low next to many removal plans.

Scaling the method still faces steep hurdles, since billions of tons of rock powder would be needed from new mines or waste piles, along with wide farmer uptake. Global removal by 2050 is put at 0.5 to 2 gigatons a year in cited work. The authors judge soil and crop gains the firmer promise.
pmc-13321766:
Emmanuelle Simo Yimgoua and co-authors study combined liver harm from a parasite and alcohol in Cameroon in a 2026 field study. Schistosoma mansoni infection and heavy drinking both strike the liver, yet their joint effects were poorly mapped. The cross-sectional study enrolled 310 adults in Makenéné and grouped them by infection and drinking level.

Infection was checked by stool and antigen tests and drinking by a standard audit scale. People with both exposures showed lower red cell and platelet counts and higher liver enzyme activity than those with drinking alone. Against infection alone, several liver enzymes also ran higher in the combined group. The pairing appears to deepen liver strain.
pmc-13323166:
Manuela Lopera Higuita and colleagues test, in 2026, a simpler way to preserve hearts donated after circulatory death. Such hearts could expand the donor pool substantially, but they suffer warm injury before retrieval and need careful checking. Current checking routes raise ethical concerns or demand costly machines and scarce expertise.

In pigs, donor hearts endured nineteen minutes of warm ischemia, then sat in controlled cold storage for up to seven hours before warm machine perfusion revived them. A novel loading method measured how the revived hearts actually performed. Hearts stored cold showed no meaningful functional, biochemical or protein-level differences from hearts reperfused immediately. The authors argue cold storage could cut cost and ethical friction in donor heart practice, while noting the work is preclinical.
pmc-13323566:
Jiashuo Yang and co-authors chart stroke burden tied to high fasting blood sugar in young adults, in a 2026 Global Burden of Disease analysis covering 1990 to 2023 with projections to 2050. Adults aged 20 to 44 years form the focus, split by sex, age band and development level.

Total deaths and disability years rose across the period even as age-standardised rates fell, and ischaemic stroke grew much faster than bleeding stroke. Richer regions cut their rates clearly, while middle and lower development regions held steady or rose and took the largest death increases. Projections show total disability years climbing steeply by 2050, led by ischaemic stroke. The authors press for earlier glucose control in younger adults.
pmc-13325166:
Diana E. Rodríguez-Sánchez and co-authors simulate tube layouts inside a solar reactor that splits water for hydrogen in a 2026 study. Concentrated sunlight drives the chemistry in a 1.5 MW thermal tower plant, and heat layout decides success.

Six arrangements of 80 tubes were modeled inside a single cavity receiver. Several layouts pushed tubes past the 1300 °C mark needed for the reduction step of the cycle. A tight single-layer layout gave the most even temperatures across the chamber. Even heating matters because patchy heat leaves parts of the reactor underused. The study shows internal geometry alone can tame the thermal field and offers workable layouts for solar hydrogen.
pmc-13327866:
Gayatri Mishra and co-authors test biochar and compost mixes on specialty crops in a 2026 study. Both soil additions can help crops, but results swing widely with crop type and recipe, and few trials compare several pairings at once. The team ran greenhouse and field trials with raw biochar, biochar composted together with compost, and simple blends.

Adding compost, co-composted biochar, or blends raised output in sweet basil and strawberries, though the best mix depended on compost type, biochar, and crop. Co-composted biochar lifted basil growth in both settings, one basil type gaining more than the other, which hints at a genetic side to the response. Basil chemistry stayed largely unchanged, so quality held while yield rose.
pmc-13328266:
Ashraf F Hefny and co-authors compare blunt chest trauma in older and younger adults in the United Arab Emirates in a 2026 study. Most older-adult evidence comes from Western settings, so regional patterns were missing. Records covered patients admitted to one community hospital from 2014 to 2020.

Of 861 patients assessed, 73, or 8.5 percent, were aged 60 or more, and road crashes caused 69.9 percent of their injuries, ahead of low falls at 13.7 percent in that group. Multiple rib fractures were the commonest chest injury, at 34.2 percent, while lung bruising ran less common in older patients than younger ones. Low falls, though gentle, struck older patients far more often, marking a prevention target.
pmc-13328366:
Kirstine Kløve-Mogensen and co-authors track natural swings in blood extracellular vesicles in a 2026 study. These tiny parcels are hot biomarker candidates, yet healthy day-to-day variation was barely mapped. Four healthy women gave blood over five straight days and across six weeks, and three measurement platforms profiled their vesicles.

Vesicle counts and surface markers varied notably within and between donors, and longer gaps varied more than short ones. CD9-marked vesicles stayed the most abundant across both antibody methods, while CD63 and CD81 signals ran lower and jumpier. Without shared reference ranges, the authors warn, vesicle biomarker claims risk reading noise as disease.
pmc-13328466:
Xiangming Meng and Mingjing Cai link weather to fungal ear infections in a 2026 time-series study from Wuxi, China. Fungal otitis externa is thought to love warmth and damp, but day-by-day proof was thin. Outpatient records from one hospital ran from 2014 through 2025 and were matched to daily weather data.

In total 6,260 visits fell across 4,383 days, averaging 1.43 a day and bunching from July to October. Relative humidity and rainfall showed the steadiest cumulative links: at the 90th percentile of humidity, cumulative risk reached 1.236 against the median day in their model. Clinics in humid spells may brace for more itchy, discharging ears, the authors suggest.
pmc-13329666:
Sylvia C L Durian and co-authors ask how the eye keeps useful signals when many inputs squeeze into fewer outputs in a 2026 study. Retinal ganglion cells pass visual data onward through a narrow link. The team compared squeezing methods that aim to keep future-predicting data with common methods that ignore prediction as a goal.

Across natural scenes, prediction-tuned squeezing let later cells predict what comes next almost as well as possible, the authors report. Generic methods kept fair amounts of future data but missed patterns that work across all scenes. The result hints that wiring in the eye may be shaped to keep predictive data first. The frame could guide work in other senses too.
pmc-13330666:
Hee-Ji Eom and team showed that oxidative stress drives liver failure during long-term in vivo partial reprogramming. Their 2026 study used a doxycycline-triggered OSKM mouse model, making the Yamanaka factors OCT4, SOX2, KLF4, and c-MYC. In vivo reprogramming enables tissue regrowth but raises safety concerns when factor expression lasts. Long systemic induction caused early death linked with hepatocyte dedifferentiation and oxidative stress, without tumors.

Single-nucleus RNA sequencing found reactive oxygen species, oxidative stress, and NRF2 signaling active in hepatocytes, while intestinal progenitor-like groups showed limited build-up of these signals. Increased reactive oxygen output in liver cells, with higher female resistance and sex-based gaps in antioxidant action, points to this stress as a primary driver of death during long OSKM use. N-acetylcysteine eased this stress and improved survival, backing this stress as a causal mechanism and raising safety questions for such treatments.
pmc-13330766:
Natasha J. Williams and a large team study what drove county pandemic policy choices in the United States in a 2026 article. Local rules varied widely during COVID-19, yet drivers of that spread were little known. Data from a county policy database covered 309 counties across 50 states over 2020 and 2021.

Policy breadth was scored overall and in three areas: closures, economic support, and public health steps. City-like character tied to more public health policies in the reported models. Higher Democratic voter share tied to more policies of every kind. Warmer average temperature tied to fewer policies overall. Knowing such drivers can aid fair crisis planning, the authors argue.
pmc-13331166:
Keisuke Onoda and colleagues assess internal neurolysis for facial nerve pain without vessel compression in older patients in a 2026 study. Records covered 22 patients split evenly at age 70 into older and younger groups of 11 each. Pain type, recurrence, and nerve signals during surgery were compared, with good outcome set as top grades on a standard pain scale.

Good pain control came to 19 of 22 patients overall, a rate of 86.4 percent in the reported counts. Older patients matched younger ones closely. Typical pain in older patients fared better than atypical pain in that small subgroup. Brief facial numbness arose in three patients and cleared. Nerve signal shifts during surgery tracked with good outcomes.
pmc-13331766:
Juhan Lee and co-authors analyze United States survey data from 2026 on how many substances adults used in the past month, split by HIV status. Earlier work showed people with HIV use single substances more often, but whether they combine several at once was less clear.

Pooling the National Survey of Drug Use and Health for 2021 to 2024 gave 186,823 adults. After adjusting for other factors, people with HIV reported about 1.60 times as many substances as adults without HIV, and the gap held among users and among those using two or more substances. Among people with HIV, the most common mixes were alcohol alone, alcohol with tobacco, and alcohol with tobacco and cannabis. The authors argue substance screening and treatment referrals belong inside routine HIV care.
pmc-13333366:
Sophie C Hagenaars and colleagues tested whether a simple slide measure, the share of supporting stroma inside a breast tumor, sharpens a widely used survival calculator, in a 2026 study. The tumor-stroma ratio already predicts outcomes on its own, but whether it adds anything to the established PREDICT model was untested.

Drawing on 1,770 patients from the Nottingham Breast Cancer Series, the team added the ratio to PREDICT and checked accuracy for survival at 5, 10, and 15 years. Accuracy rose everywhere, but the clear gain landed in triple-negative disease. There, the 5-year AUC climbed from 63.9 points to 70.9 points, with a hazard ratio of 2.58 for the ratio, and 15-year accuracy rose from 64.6 points to 71.6 points with a hazard ratio of 2.02 at that horizon. The authors conclude the cheap tissue measure earns its place in prediction, above all for the hardest subtype.
pmc-13333466:
Ke Wang and co-authors trained machine learning models in 2026 to flag infertile men whose sperm carries heavily fragmented DNA. They used routine semen measures and lifestyle answers instead of a dedicated DNA test. The fragmentation index informs fertility judgment and assisted reproduction choices, but the specialist assay is not run on everyone.

Data came from two Shanghai centers between March 2023 and March 2024: 1,037 men built the models and 290 others served as an outside test set. Of six algorithms, random forest performed best, reaching an AUC of 0.979 in cross-validation and 0.945 on the external set. Screening distilled prediction to eight features, sperm movement, count and viability plus daily exercise, smoking, drinking, stress, and insomnia, and the team published an online calculator. The authors are candid about a catch: outside predictions skewed too high, with a calibration slope of 2.196, so they urge caution until more testing is done.
pmc-13333766:
Xuezhi Zhao and co-authors examined parental age, the age gap between parents, and newborn health in eastern China in a 2026 retrospective cohort study. The question matters for counseling couples who delay childbearing.

The study analyzed 15,762 mother-infant pairs from Zhejiang University's Women's Hospital, covering deliveries between January 2016 and December 2022. Pairs where the father was older and pairs where the mother was older both showed higher odds of newborn disease than equal-age pairs. After adjusting for each parent's own age, the father-older link faded, while rising maternal and paternal ages each remained independent risk factors on their own. Flexible curve analysis probed nonlinear patterns. The results support age-aware risk checks before and during pregnancy.
pmc-13336666:
Seonki Hong proposed a new design idea for polymers in a 2026 conceptual paper. Many working polymers, including natural melanins and synthetic polydopamine, perform reliably even though their exact molecular makeup stays messy and ill defined. Traditional design, which prescribes one structure and one reaction path, fits such materials poorly.

Hong argues for state convergent polymerisation, where success means reaching a stable working state rather than one precise molecule. Pools of reactive groups evolve inside chemical settings bounded by factors such as acidity and redox state, which experiments can tune. The idea offers a fresh guide for making functional polymers from complex, variable chemistry.
pmc-13336866:
Luyuan Ning, Lu Lu, Sophie Leanza, and Ruike Renee Zhao teach a neural network the physics of ring origami in a 2026 study. Closed loops of elastic rods can snap between flat and three-dimensional shapes, suiting deployable structures and soft robots. Predicting those shapes, and designing loops for a wanted shape, is mathematically hard.

Their framework blends Kirchhoff rod theory with a learning model that respects physics. It finds stable states for square and hexagonal segmented rings with set or varying natural curve. A shape-matching term also works backward, finding the curve profile a ring needs to fit a target space or surface. The method extends to three-dimensional rod systems, aiding programmable shape-shifting design.
pmc-13337066:
Chrysanthi-Maria Moysidou leads a 2026 team training lab-grown neuromuscular tissue with electric pulses. Organoids from human stem cells model development well, yet their cells stay immature, weakening studies of adult disease. Gentle low-frequency pulse training began early in growth and continued for several weeks.

Trained organoids contracted more strongly and more often, and the gains persisted after stimulation stopped. Imaging and gene data showed better muscle and nerve structure, matched maturation markers, and tissue that was stiffer with faster relaxation. Those traits signal stronger force production and coupling. Non-invasive electrical training could mature many organoid systems, making late-onset disease easier to study in the dish.
pmc-13337366:
Heran Cao and co-authors chart chemical tags on sperm proteins in men with varicocele-linked weak sperm movement in a 2026 study. Varicocele is a leading cause of male infertility, but how it slows sperm was unclear. Paired sperm samples taken before and after treatment underwent deep mass spectrometry of lactylation, a tag derived from lactate.

Lactate handling was off balance, with less lactate inside sperm and more in seminal fluid, and tagging fell overall, especially in the sperm midpiece and tail. Profiling found 2,699 tag sites on 1,216 proteins, with 133 proteins changing after treatment in the analysis. Changed proteins cluster in energy and tail-structure pathways, and several key tail proteins lost tags. The lactate-tag axis may explain lost motility.
pmc-13337666:
Li He and Yang Ye present a 2026 narrative review on how metabolic problems affect lung infection in children with asthma. Asthma is the most common long-term airway disease of childhood, marked by inflamed airways and sharp reactions to triggers. Infections both follow from asthma and can set off acute attacks.

Metabolic syndrome in children is already tied to diabetes and heart disease risk. The review gathers evidence that faulty metabolism brings steady inflammation and changes gut microbes. Those changes can weaken lung function, make infection more likely, and worsen asthma control. The synthesis helps explain why weight and metabolic care may matter in pediatric asthma plans.
pmc-13337866:
Liping Li and a large team present TIC-XNet, a system for spotting tic events in children, in a 2026 study. The tool reads video together with heart rate and skin signals. Unlike a black box, it turns each decision into structured, time-aligned evidence clinicians can inspect.

Recordings came from 417 children during clinic tasks and home observation. Against a plain prediction model and a post-hoc explainer, TIC-XNet scored best on the shared test set with an AUC of 0.915 in the reported results. It missed fewer events and answered faster after buffering. Its evidence matched expert timing more closely and tracked tic severity.
pmc-13339066:
Estelle Alderson and colleagues studied mental health service use in 2026 among young women with ADHD in New Zealand. Sex gaps in ADHD diagnosis timing are well known, and delayed or missed diagnosis in girls carries wide consequences, yet service use patterns were poorly mapped. The team built a national cohort of females aged 18 to 24 between July 2021 and June 2022.

ADHD status, intellectual disability status, and age at index were derived by established algorithms, and six service use measures were tracked through June 2024. Adjusted models test how diagnosis timing relates to later service contact. The findings can help services reach young women whose ADHD was recognised late or not at all.
pmc-13339766:
Caroline Desgranges and Jerome Delhommelle speed up simulation of gas mixtures in porous materials in a 2026 study. Screening adsorbents for storage and separation needs phase behavior under confinement, yet standard simulations stall near phase changes. Their adiabatic Monte Carlo method varies temperature broadly instead.

Argon-krypton mixtures in bulk and inside MCM-41 pores tested accuracy against standard runs. Adiabatic runs matched results while converging up to a hundred times faster in the reported comparisons, as large temperature swings crossed barriers quickly. Faster sampling could let screening cover far more porous candidates for gas capture and storage.
pmc-13340066:
Sem E. H. Vellema and colleagues validate a test for living gonorrhea bacteria in a 2026 study. Standard DNA tests cannot tell live from dead bacteria, and culture is finicky for this fragile organism. A dye that blocks dead-cell DNA enabled viability PCR.

Mixtures of live and heat-killed bacteria tested the method, followed by throat, rectal, and genital patient samples versus culture. The method erased 99.998 percent of dead-cell DNA as reported, with tight tracking across dilutions. Culture-positive samples carried far higher living loads than negative ones in the reported medians. Viability testing could judge cure and resistance risk better.
pmc-13341466:
Saliva proteins that betray early colorectal cancer are sought by Sama Rezasoltani and research partners in a 2026 proteomics study from Tehran. The case-control project collected 104 saliva samples from screening patients, including stage I cancer cases and non-cancer controls.

Mass spectrometry identified 2,456 salivary proteins, of which 181 differed significantly between groups. Members of the small proline-rich protein family stood out as consistent markers, joined by immune and metabolism proteins. Clustering partly separated cancer from control samples, though age, sex, and smoking also shaped profiles. A spit test for early cancer would be far easier than current screening routes.
pmc-13343166:
Anhui Liu and co-authors review heart and vessel damage in Long COVID in 2026, arguing that immune disorder and lasting inflammation drive much of the harm. Lasting symptoms after SARS-CoV-2 infection reach well past fatigue and breathlessness, touching the heart in forms from myocarditis and heart failure to clots and rhythm trouble.

Sustained firing of innate and adaptive immune pathways, the authors contend, injures vessel linings, fuels clot-linked inflammation, and remodels heart muscle for the worse. The review gathers clinical and lab evidence for those pathways and weighs treatments aimed at calming inflammation and immune misfiring. Targeting immune drivers, rather than symptoms alone, may guide future Long COVID heart care.
pmc-13343966:
Ashish Lal Shrestha and colleagues reported swallowed twin magnets in 2026 in a 5 year old Nepalese boy, a case titled swallowed but not forgotten. Swallowed foreign bodies in children are a common emergency, and most pass through the gut without harm. Multiple magnets, or a magnet plus another metal object, pose serious bowel risks including obstruction, pressure necrosis, perforation, and fistula.

The boy reportedly swallowed twin ball magnets a month before presentation and stayed largely asymptomatic until imaging revealed them. Endoscopic retrieval succeeded and avoided invasive surgery, with close prolonged follow up showing no complications. The case urges high suspicion for magnet ingestion, since silent magnets can injure bowel if missed.
pmc-13347366:
Armanda A. Júlio and co-authors review turning plant biomass into both platform chemicals and useful carbon materials, in a review from 2026. Furfural and a second sugar-derived building block called HMF anchor the chemical side. With catalyst types compared for yield and reuse, including catalysts made from biomass itself that passed 90 percent yield in highlighted cases.

Heat routes such as pyrolysis and wet carbon treatment form the materials side, with added sulfonic, amino, and phosphate groups tailoring carbons for catalysis, energy devices, and pollutant capture. Using biomass as both feed and catalyst source closes the loop, though catalyst wear and scale-up still block wide factory use.
pmc-13348166:
Sharon D. Janssen and colleagues unite scattered harm measures into one global framework for land plant loss, in a methods study from 2026. Life cycle tools score each pressure alone at mixed scales. So the new frame scales local loss up to global extinction risk using area curves and endemism, covering land use, nitrogen fall, and greenhouse gases together.

Factors for 250 gases were set at two time spans, land factors swung across seven orders of size by region. Nitrogen factors swung across two orders in the reported set. Region drove nearly all land variation, while place and compound split nitrogen variation, giving product scorers a fairer global yardstick.
pmc-13348366:
Erna Karic, Amanda L. Haeberle, and Julia L. E. Willett report draft genomes for three soil isolates of an understudied gut-related bacterium, in an announcement published in 2026. Soil gathered in October 2023 near the University of Minnesota after rain, from under a large mushroom, grew dark colonies on selective plates. Yellow colour plus stillness marked the picks as Enterococcus mundtii.

Close kin gut species cause infections and resist drugs, yet this species is rarely studied despite colour and movement quirks that set it apart in the group portrait. Public drafts for three near-identical soil strains give researchers fresh material for tracing how harmless soil kinds relate to clinic troublemakers.
pmc-13349766:
Lawrence Merle Nelson proposes Clinical Coherence as a frame for holding patient knowledge together, in a conceptual paper issued in 2026. Modern systems store vast biology data yet scatter meaning across visits, specialties, firms, and software, causing late diagnoses and care that misses life context. So coherence is defined as keeping one steady picture of a patient over time.

Three strands must merge, covering biology, lived experience data such as symptoms, function, family, and spiritual concerns, and clinician judgement in the frame set out. Coherence is cast as a system trait, guarded by a duty-of-care structure that senses, assigns, escalates, and feeds back, drawing on quality and narrative traditions.
pmc-13351466:
Arjun Mohan and co-authors analysed in 2026 whether starting biologic drugs sooner after severe asthma begins improves their effect. Long uncontrolled inflammation scars and remodels airways, causing damage that later treatment cannot undo.

The analysis drew on a United States observational study of adults under specialist care for severe asthma. Among 244 patients starting a biologic with full data, flare rates in the year before treatment were compared with the year after, and factors tied to remaining flares were modelled. Earlier initiation was linked with greater benefit, supporting quicker escalation when standard inhalers fail rather than years of waiting.
pmc-13352366:
Eriki Yanagi and co-authors weighed in 2026 X-ray side shift and down shift in reverse shoulder surgery. The designs were onlay and inlay types in Japanese shoulders. Implant weigh-ups using standardised angles remain scarce, most of all in smaller Asian groups. Side shift and down shift angles help gauge implant placing and function after reverse shoulder replacement.

One hundred thirty-nine shoulders in 139 Japanese patients at a single centre were read. The Aequalis Ascend Flex onlay design was weighed against the Tornier Perform inlay design. Both yielded a 145-degree total neck-shaft angle through distinct stem and insert joins. Post-surgery side shift and down shift angles were measured and weighed. The weigh-up helps surgeons pick designs suited to Japanese anatomy and functional aims.
pmc-13353766:
Misha K Rowell and Tasmin L Rymer test whether mother care or mother cognition shapes offspring thinking in a wild-derived rat in 2026. The fawn-footed mosaic-tailed rat, Melomys cervinipes, is little studied outside lab strains. Mothers' care amounts were recorded, then mothers and adult offspring each took three tests: associative memory, novel object recognition, and a food extraction lever task.

Offspring receiving more indirect care were likelier to learn the lever task, perhaps because it demanded heavier brain processing than the other tests. No other care measure mattered clearly, and earlier work found no maternal effect on problem solving. Parent-offspring comparisons probed whether thinking skills carry a heritable part in this species.
pmc-13354566:
Xi Wang and co-authors tested how well labs can count brand new gene changes in a 2026 study of flat-headed loaches. They used parent and young fish trios, long and short DNA reads, and seven ways of sorting the data. Each set of results was checked against lab tests that confirmed real changes.

Even the best method missed some real changes and flagged some false ones, with error rates that varied by method. Long reads gave lower counts than short reads, and deeper reads missed fewer real changes. The authors warn that many past counts in wild species may be off, and that extra lab checks matter before results are trusted.
pmc-13354666:
Avia Merenlender Wagner and co-authors report a 2026 early-stage trial of TV-46000, a long-acting shot form of risperidone given under the skin. The drug is used for schizophrenia and bipolar I disorder and can be given once a month or every two months. The trial tested single and repeated doses in people with schizophrenia or a related illness.

Ninety-nine people took part, and most side effects were mild shot-site reactions, weight gain, or lab changes. Blood levels reached a useful range within a day and stayed there for four to eight weeks, based on dose. The authors found no new safety concerns and support the shot for longer trials.
pmc-13355166:
Brandon Itson-Zoske and co-authors report 2026 early work on a gene therapy for long-term nerve pain. The therapy uses a harmless virus to deliver a peptide that blocks several sodium channels in pain-sensing nerves at once. The team removed a marker gene and doubled the peptide copy to strengthen its grip.

In rats with nerve injury, a shot into the sciatic nerve eased pain for three to four months, in both males and females. The virus stayed in the peripheral nerves, and the peptide also calmed human nerve cells in the lab. The authors see a path to pain relief that avoids the brain and heart side effects of many drugs.
pmc-13357066:
Dejin Li and co-authors used a large United States cancer registry in 2026. They asked whether tumor traits shape the risk of dying from heart and vessel disease in lung cancer patients treated with chemo or radiation. Earlier work focused on classic risk factors and drug harm to the heart. The study covered 59,726 patients treated between 2002 and 2017.

Non-small cell lung cancer carried higher heart-disease death risk than small cell types. Patients with local or regional stage disease also faced much higher risk than those with distant spread, likely because they live longer. A prediction chart sorted patients moderately well. The authors urge tailored heart monitoring for these groups.
pmc-13358666:
Bezares and co-authors trace the travels of a rare plant in a 2026 study. Diplotaxis ibicensis grows only on the Balearic Islands and a small patch of the Spanish mainland, with sea gaps between its homes. The plant has no clear way to cross water, yet it clearly did. The team used gene data to work out how and when.

They sampled all 16 known populations and built family trees from two kinds of gene data. The trees suggest the plant crossed the sea more than once, and quite fast in plant terms, long after the Mediterranean refilled. The case shows that rare long jumps, not slow spread, can shape where island plants live.

pmc-13364166:
