pmc-13400166:
Ting Fang Tan and colleagues propose S.C.O.R.E., a five-part expert framework for judging whether a medical chatbot's free-text answers are actually good, in a 2026 study. S.C.O.R.E. instead has experts rate Safety, Consensus and Context, Objectivity, Reproducibility, and Explainability. The team validated it against the automated metrics using GPT-4o, Claude 4 Sonnet, and DeepSeek answering questions in three fields.

The scores frequently branded good answers as inaccurate. S.C.O.R.E. held together statistically, with internal consistency of 0.745 in the tuned domain, and it detected large differences between optimized and non-optimized model setups. Rankings flipped by specialty. The authors take that reversal as proof that domain tuning matters and that expert structured review can detect it. They pitch it as practical infrastructure for clinical validation and model improvement.
pmc-13400266:
Crista E Horton leads a team describing, in 2026, a 75-year-old man who had repeated strokes from severe narrowing in two places in his carotid artery. One blockage sat in the neck and the other inside the skull. His aortic arch also made the usual route through the leg risky.

Surgeons instead entered through the neck artery itself, using flow reversal for protection. Through that single entry they opened both narrowed spots and placed stents. Later scans showed good flow and less than half the neck narrowing left. The man had no new stroke signs, showing one-session treatment can suit selected high-risk patients.
pmc-13400366:
Kai Pei, Lihong Zhao, Jiao Hu and Youdong Mao review, in 2026, how the 26S proteasome is built and controlled, and how drugs can tune it. The proteasome is the cell machine that chews up tagged or damaged proteins. It is a proven cancer drug target and may help in diseases where proteins clump.

Recent structural work shows the machine changing shape as it grabs, unfolds and cuts its targets. The review covers helper enzymes that adjust its action, plus drugs that block or boost parts of it. It also covers methods that hijack the proteasome to destroy chosen disease proteins. The authors argue that knowing its moving states can guide safer, more precise new drugs.
pmc-13400666:
Priyanka Biswas, Vishwas Mishra, Julia Sanchez-Garrido and Gad Frankel ask, in 2026, whether a first bout of gut inflammation protects against, or worsens, a later one. Both infection-driven and chemical colitis damage the gut barrier and release inflammatory signals. The order of events, it turns out, matters.

Mice that recovered from a bacterial gut infection were shielded against later chemical colitis, with less weight loss and better preserved gut lining. That protection depended on the bacterium having injured the lining during the first illness and on sustained signaling by interleukin-17A. Mice recovered from chemical colitis fared oppositely: their barriers stayed leaky, immune cells lingered, and later infection hit them harder, even from weakened bacteria.
pmc-13400966:
Nahid Kord and colleagues ask, in 2026, whether blood uric acid levels predict who develops type 2 diabetes, using the long-running Tehran Lipid and Glucose Study. Uric acid, best known for gout, has been tied to metabolic risk, but its added predictive value beyond standard models was uncertain.

The analysis covered 5,719 adults free of diabetes at baseline, followed for a median of just over eight years, during which 778 developed the disease. Each step up in uric acid raised diabetes risk in men and women alike, and risk climbed across quarters of the population to nearly double at the top. The link survived adjustment for insulin resistance and diet. Yet adding uric acid to established risk models did not improve prediction.
pmc-13401166:
Selin Kalkan and co-authors describe a 2026 preliminary study of edible chitosan films carrying microencapsulated probiotics, made to protect set-type yogurt during storage. The films held Bifidobacterium animalis B94, Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus GG, or both strains together.

Adding the probiotics made films thicker, from 0.105 to 0.157 millimetres, raised moisture and swelling, increased water vapor passage, and lowered transparency and tensile strength. Between about 86 and 91 percent of the probiotics survived film drying, and the films acted against Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus. Applied to yogurt over 21 days of refrigeration, the coated samples kept pH values between 4.02 and 5.34 while quality measures were tracked.
pmc-13401266:
Rebeccah Ayoti Abutika and co-authors report a 2026 prospective study of carbohydrate antigen 125, a blood marker of body-wide congestion, in patients admitted with acute decompensated heart failure in western Kenya. Many patients leave hospital still congested, so objective markers to guide fluid removal are in demand.

At Moi Teaching and Referral Hospital, the team measured CA125 on admission and at discharge over seven months. Measures taken jointly included a clinical congestion score, NT-proBNP, body weight, and the width of the inferior vena cava. They then related marker changes to the discharge congestion score and followed patients for 30-day results, including death from any cause and readmission for heart failure. The work tests whether CA125 can flag who still carries excess fluid.
pmc-13401566:
Eunice Twumwaa Tagoe, Justice Nonvignon, Robert Van Der Meer, and Itamar Megiddo built a 2026 agent-based model of type 2 diabetes self-care in Ghana. Universal cover policies still leave daily disease control difficult there. Their simulation blends health behaviour theory with the constraints of a resource-limited health system.

Inside the model, virtual patients make daily choices about drugs and lifestyle advice. They also choose when to seek care, while system factors such as drug supply and insurance cover shift around them. The team tested three policy options: growing insurance cover, raising medicine supply, and taxing sugar-sweetened drinks. Pattern-oriented modelling and several checking levels anchored the simulation in clinical data and provider know-how. Research on how patients behave fed in as well. A sustained yearly rise in insurance cover produced large gains in blood glucose control among the options tested.
pmc-13401766:
Franciela Golden and co-authors present a 2026 case of heart valve infection caused by Streptococcus gordonii, a mouth and gut bacterium that rarely attacks a native aortic valve. Their patient was a 79-year-old man admitted with acute kidney injury, diarrhoea, and dehydration.

Blood cultures grew the bacterium, and imaging found a vegetation, an infected clump, measuring just under two centimetres on his own aortic valve. After a sudden change in his mental state, brain MRI revealed multiple septic emboli, infected fragments scattered to the brain. He was treated successfully with intravenous ceftriaxone and later needed aortic valve replacement. The likely entry point was a trigger point injection into his lower back, matching an MRI finding of a spinal abscess, though a dental procedure, gallbladder inflammation with stones. A colonoscopy with polyp removal were also possible sources in the same window.
pmc-13401966:
Shawlin Jahan, Haseen Ishraque Paabon, and Kabyar Cho report a 2026 case of diabetes triggered by the immunotherapy drug pembrolizumab in a patient being treated for triple-negative breast cancer. Checkpoint inhibitors have transformed cancer care, but they can turn the immune system against hormone-producing organs.

After several cycles of immunotherapy, the patient arrived with severe high blood sugar and ketosis, the dangerous acid build-up of insulin lack. Tests for the usual autoimmune diabetes antibodies came back negative, while C-peptide levels showed a relative insulin deficiency, a pattern typical of checkpoint-related diabetes rather than classic type 1 disease. Control stayed difficult after discharge, swinging between high and low blood sugar despite insulin treatment. The authors highlight how variably this uncommon but potentially life-threatening side effect presents, and how demanding its ongoing management can be.
pmc-13402266:
Kun Liang and colleagues identified a gene-control axis that drives brain inflammation after ischemic stroke in mice. Their 2026 study focuses on microglia, brain immune cells that can both worsen damage and aid repair after a blocked brain vessel. The molecular switches that set microglia toward harm or healing had remained inadequately defined.

Gene profiling of microglia after transient focal ischemia highlighted CEBPB, JunB, Fos, and TNF as hub genes. CEBPB switched on the AP-1 complex by binding the Fos promoter, raising inflammatory mediators including interleukin-1 beta and TNF-alpha. Blocking AP-1 with T-5224 shifted microglia toward repair, reduced neuron death, and improved long-term movement and thinking in mice. The axis is a promising drug target, pending human translation.
pmc-13402666:
Yokphonchanachai and colleagues develop, in 2026, KANLOM, a mobile application helping caregivers prevent falls among older adults in rural Thailand, where preventive care is scarce. The app was built through a five-step research and development process running from April 2022 to December 2023. It was co-designed with caregivers, tested in small groups, then piloted with thirty caregivers in a one-group pretest-posttest study.

The need was plain in the pilot group: among 30 older adults assessed with the Morse Fall Scale, 50.00 percent were at fall risk and 46.67 percent at high risk, leaving only 3.33 percent risk-free in the sample. After using the app, caregivers improved significantly in knowledge, with a mean gain of 1.07 points, and in attitudes and prevention behaviors on the study scales. Satisfaction averaged 2.80 out of 3.00, highest for content usefulness and practicality. The offline, localized design targets other low-resource aging communities.
pmc-13402866:
Jo Ciantar and co-authors test whether keeping IVF embryos in culture longer changes the newborn's DNA methylation, the chemical marks that regulate genes. Extended culture to the blastocyst stage is standard, but it coincides with heavy epigenetic remodelling and has been linked to more preterm births and larger babies. Their 2026 study compares babies from three conception routes.

Genome-wide methylation was measured in cord blood and umbilical cord artery samples from twenty-five cleavage-stage transfers, twenty-five blastocyst-stage transfers, and thirty spontaneous conceptions. Genome-wide scans, global methylation, and epigenetic age comparisons found no statistically significant differences between the two IVF groups. A few sites differed by more than ten percentage points and merit larger studies. One site differed between spontaneous and blastocyst groups in the artery samples. The authors call the absence of major effects reassuring for assisted reproduction.
pmc-13403366:
Katja I. Seitz led a 2026 study that compared three ways of asking adults about harm done to them as children. The group held 462 people, some with mental disorders and some without. Two questionnaires and one short interview each recorded types of abuse and neglect.

A smaller group of 244 people also rated how hard they find it to manage strong feelings. Scores from the three tools lined up well with each other. Emotional abuse and neglect scores linked most clearly to poor feeling control. Harm at ages 12 to 17 stood out, which gives the interview tool extra value for timing questions.
pmc-13404566:
Charles Vidal and a large team recount 15 years, from 2011 to 2026, of flying very sick heart patients from Reunion Island to mainland France. The island lies more than 10,000 kilometres away and lacked heart transplant and durable pump services for most of that time. Patients on VA-ECMO, a machine that takes over heart and lung work, had to travel to reach those treatments.

Records cover all adults moved under VA-ECMO and considered for transplant or a lasting ventricular assist device. Of 324 patients placed on the machine locally, 43 were flown out and 39 entered the analysis. The report weighs the heavy logistics, cost and family separation against scarce published experience with such long transfers.
pmc-13404866:
Małgorzata Fopka-Kowalczyk and Małgorzata Krajnik evaluated Poland's first obligatory spirituality in medicine program for medical students. Their 2026 pre-post study covers the Nicolaus Copernicus University module in Bydgoszcz, run from the second to fifth year between 2018 and 2022, with 121 participants assessed on the Spiritual Supporter Scale. Spiritual care competence matters for patient care, yet its teaching effects had been little measured in Poland.

The program brought modest changes in select subdomains, with significant shifts in spirituality related to one's own and others' suffering and in recognizing spiritual suffering, though effect sizes were small. Other domains showed insignificant changes or declines, and prayer-as-support results were mixed. The single-group design without controls limits causal claims, but the paper gives Polish medical educators a first measured baseline for spiritual care training.
pmc-13405566:
Alyssa Mariana Alvarez and colleagues test a curcumin derivative in rats with chronic kidney disease, in 2026 work. Tetrahydrocurcumin, a breakdown product of curcumin, may counter the oxidative stress and scarring that drive kidney decline. The model removes five sixths of kidney mass to mimic advanced disease.

Female rats received a fat-wrapped form of the compound by mouth twice daily for four weeks, at three dose levels. Blood creatinine and urine protein rose in untreated sick animals, confirming damage. Gene activity profiling then compared treated and untreated kidneys across immune, injury and inflammation gene groups. The design lets the authors trace which pathways the compound shifts toward normal.
pmc-13407666:
Peter Widdess-Walsh presents, in 2026, a many-country study mapping syndromes where epilepsy and movement disorders arrive together. These epilepsy-dyskinesia conditions are genetic, now more recognised, yet their range of genes, symptoms, and treatment responses had never been charted in full across many populations.

The underlying study gathered 609 patients with childhood-onset movement problems tied to variants in 105 predefined genes, drawing uniform data from more than thirty centres in 25 countries. Records covered motion patterns, seizure types, development, motor function, and treatment outcomes, and the genes were grouped by biological role using clustering methods. Widdess-Walsh's commentary frames why such a spectrum matters: matching gene to presentation can sharpen diagnosis and guide therapy for families facing two intertwined brain problems.
pmc-13407866:
Tiange Zhao and co-authors grow, in 2026, a whole family of bismuth-based crystals on specially prepared mica. These materials behave in varied ways. Some act as topological insulators, others as fast semiconductors or ferroelectrics. Each previously demanded its own recipe and a costly matched substrate. The team engineered a potassium-free mica surface instead. Elemental starting materials were paired with it.

Nine millimetre-sized single crystals grew by the one strategy, spanning all three behaviour classes. Crystal quality supported high-performance transistors and broadband light detectors with strong responses. The crystals were also built into large, uniform arrays that imaged across visible to infrared light. The authors claim a material-agnostic, scalable growth framework for exploring and deploying this many-talented family.
pmc-13410766:
Xue Deng and colleagues show in 2026 that a sugar-handling pathway makes drug-resistant E. coli bacteria more dangerous. The bacteria carry a gene that defeats colistin, a last-resort antibiotic. Resistance alone did not explain their success in patients, so the team looked at metabolism.

Bacteria fed by sorbose metabolism kept their outer coat material well supplied and held tight to host cells. Knocking out a key sorbose gene weakened the bacteria in dishes and in animals, without changing drug resistance. Gene and chemical profiling traced the loss to thinner surface coating and weaker grip signals. Restoring the pathway partly restored harm, which marks metabolism as a possible drug target beside resistance itself.
pmc-13411366:
Mazin Al-Alawi and colleagues built fuel-cell membranes in 2026 that carry protons without water at temperatures up to 240 degrees Celsius. Standard membranes dry out and fail at such heat, so the team trapped ionic liquids inside narrow channels formed by stacked boron nitride and graphene sheets coated with a charged polymer.

The ordered channels held anions near the walls and protons near the center. That gave steady proton flow and a peak fuel-cell output of 82 milliwatts per square centimeter in dry hydrogen-oxygen tests. The paper offers a tunable membrane design for hotter, simpler fuel cells that skip bulky humidifiers.
pmc-13411766:
Victor Daniel Miron and colleagues offer a 2026 travel-health guide for people living with HIV who travel abroad. Travel can be safe with planning, yet missed doses, entry rules, vaccine gaps, and malaria risk can turn a trip risky without a careful pre-travel visit.

The guide walks through keeping virus suppression steady across time zones, carrying backup medicine, checking drug clashes with malaria pills and antibiotics, and planning vaccines by immune status. Clinicians and travelers get a structured checklist that covers law, health checks, sex health, and plans for surprises on the road.
pmc-13415866:
Luisa Eilinghoff and co-authors compare professional quality of life between Vietnamese migrant and non-migrant mental health staff in Germany, in a 2026 survey. Three hundred twelve staff filled the ProQOL scale, which scores burnout, stress picked up from patients' pain, and the good felt from helping. Pay and past mind ills also entered the models.

Staff with roots abroad felt less joy in helping and more stress from patients' pain than German born staff. Burnout showed no gap by roots. Women felt more joy in helping than men, with no sex gap on the other two scales. Roots and sex did not combine in effect. A warm office culture and peer networks are put forth as supports.
pmc-13416666:
Xian Zhang and colleagues ask whether bacteria living in the mouth could help cause several inflamed skin conditions, in a 2026 genetic study. They use Mendelian randomization, a method that relies on inherited variants to limit bias from lifestyle factors. Forty three oral microbe types were tested against five diseases.

Genetic data for the microbes came from public genome studies, while disease data came from the FinnGen group. Links appeared for lupus, vitiligo, pemphigus, localised scleroderma, and dermatitis herpetiformis, each tied to different oral taxa. Checks found no clear sign of pleiotropy, where one variant acts through many paths. The authors stress that mouth care treatments were not tested.
pmc-13416766:
Mandana Yekta and colleagues make a biodegradable food film from wheat leaf fibre and protein, in a 2026 study. Silver oxide particles are added, plain or encapsulated, to fight microbes and signal spoilage. The target use is wrapping minced chicken meat, where a colour change can warn that food has gone off.

Three films were compared with structural, heat, and microbe tests. The encapsulated version performed best overall, with stronger antibacterial action and better heat stability. It slowed growth of Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli and blocked Salmonella in tests. It also slowed fat breakdown and kept meat colour during storage. Such films could extend shelf life.
pmc-13417066:
Shuaishuai Wu and co-authors review the NLRP3 inflammasome, a protein assembly that drives inflammation, as a core actor in mastitis, in a 2026 article. Mastitis is the costliest disease in dairy farming, cutting milk yield and raising antibiotic use. Many triggers seem to converge on this one inflammatory hub inside udder cells.

Bacteria, poor diet balance, heat, pollutants, and disturbed gut microbes can all switch the hub on, the review finds. Nutrition, notably selenium, plus plant compounds and gut or rumen balance may calm it. The authors sketch a path to prevention that leans less on antibiotics and more on feed and microbe care.
pmc-13417266:
Bosco A Paes and colleagues review prevention of respiratory syncytial virus in infants in a 2026 article. The virus causes about 33 million lower airway infections yearly in children under five. For 28 years one antibody, given monthly, guarded only high risk babies. New long acting antibodies and a maternal vaccine have changed the field.

Two new antibodies, nirsevimab and clesrovimab, protect for a season after one dose and can cover all infants. Trials suggest protection against severe disease is broadly similar across products, with good safety. Real world proof is strong for nirsevimab and still lacking for the newest option. Cost and local supply should guide choices.
pmc-13417966:
Victoria Chavez Uceda and a large team test patient portal messages for recruiting Latino adults into a smoking and activity trial, in a 2026 secondary analysis. Records at a Rochester medical centre identified 2,000 Latino adults who smoked. Only those with an active portal account could be messaged, which cut the pool to 1,122 people who received up to two invitations.

About 12 percent viewed a message, and 53 expressed interest. Thirteen enrolled, giving a rate just above the one percent feasibility bar. Portal access gaps among Latino patients limited reach, yet the low effort channel still proved workable. Phone follow up of interested patients did much of the converting.
pmc-13418266:
Shaohua Zhang and colleagues build a model that predicts wheat protein content whether the sample is whole grain or flour, in a 2026 study. Protein grading usually needs separate models because grain and flour scatter light differently. Their system learns shared features from light spectra using wavelet processing and adversarial transfer learning, which forces the model to ignore sample form.

Wavelet features tracked protein better than raw spectra. Top accuracy was very high for both forms, and transferring between grain and flour kept accuracy near the same level. A form blind model could speed quality checks along the whole wheat processing chain.
pmc-13420266:
Kazem Ghaemi and colleagues report a large parasitic cyst inside the skull of an 11-year-old boy from a village in South Khorasan, Iran. Brain hydatid cysts are rare yet can kill, growing slowly from the larval stage of a tapeworm until they press on the brain. The boy had a brief loss of consciousness, a sign of rising pressure inside the skull.

Imaging showed a cyst of 6.5 centimeters across in the left temporal lobe in the reported measure, pushing neighboring tissue aside. Such cysts typically show no rim swelling or dye uptake on scans, a pattern that helps separate them from tumors and abscesses. Surgery must remove the sac whole, since spilling its contents can seed new cysts. The case adds a clear imaging record for a diagnosis most brain surgeons rarely meet.
pmc-13421266:
Hernandez and colleagues report a 2026 study of shinbone fractures where the break reaches the tibial tubercle, the bump where the thigh tendon anchors below the knee. The team reviewed 132 operated fractures from 2014 to 2025 and compared breaks with and without tubercle involvement.

Tubercle involvement appeared in 38 fractures and tracked with more severe injury patterns and more open wounds. Those patients were braced more often after surgery. Their outcomes were worse on the points the study targeted: more bones failing to heal, more repeat operations, and less knee bend recovered.  Naming the tubercle as a risk marker helps surgeons warn patients early and plan fixation and therapy with the harder road in mind.
pmc-13421666:
Xiaoyun Yuan, Jianing Zhang, Youhai Liu, Yichen Wang and Lu Fang present SkinSight in a 2026 paper, an imaging skin that sticks to the body and keeps seeing clearly while it bends. Camera arrays map environments superbly, yet their rigidity keeps them off skin and soft robots, while fully flexible sensors sacrifice resolution.

Their hybrid design sets miniature rigid imagers in a soft, stretchable web. Because the surface keeps deforming, they hand geometry to a large pre-trained vision transformer, which infers three-dimensional structure without calibration or fixed assumptions about shape. Mounted on a human palm, the system perceived objects outside the direct line of sight. The authors aim at wearables and embodied robots that need sight on curved, moving surfaces.
pmc-13421766:
Bryan A. Martinez and six colleagues untangle, in a 2026 study, how a shortened decoy version of the worm insulin receptor tunes the signal of the full receptor. In the nematode C. elegans, the truncated DAF-2B floats free and soaks up insulin-like peptides, and a genetic screen for what controls its abundance landed on a gene for neuropeptide release.

Worms with that mutation piled up DAF-2B in the nervous system, leaving fewer activating peptides free. Fluorescence lifetime imaging then revealed something new: much of the decoy sits locked together with a full-length receptor, forming a hybrid class of receptor. Moving genetic levers on the decoy in the mutant background tested how its paired and doubled forms reinforce the signal shutdown.
pmc-13423066:
Takao Suzuki and colleagues study why farmers in Oriental Mindoro, Philippines, join or skip yearly mass drug treatment for schistosomiasis. The disease is a parasitic infection tied to water contact in rice farming. Their community study enrolled 342 farmers in Victoria, the municipality with the highest reported prevalence, pairing a questionnaire with abdominal ultrasound scans.

Overall, 65.2% of participants joined the annual treatment round. Ultrasound signs possibly linked to the disease appeared in 37.7% of farmers, more often among those who took treatment than those who skipped it. Family history of infection ran higher among non-adherent farmers, while personal history ran the other way. The authors use these patterns to suggest how outreach could lift participation.
pmc-13424266:
Fernando Marmolejo-Ramos leads a twelve-author, four-country study of how the mind maps musical pitch onto space and feeling. In the first experiment, sixty-three listeners rated tones; extreme highs and lows felt less pleasant than moderate pitches, giving a curved rather than straight pattern. The spatial link proved cleaner in the second experiment.

Seventy participants consistently placed rising pitches higher in space, supporting the everyday metaphor of high and low notes. A third experiment, with ninety people, tried to separate the spatial link in an indirect task and came out inconclusive. Data gathered across four countries let the team compare universal tendencies with local variation, informing how sensory metaphors are built.
pmc-13424466:
Elcin Cagatay and colleagues report a 2026 lab effort to build a copy of the cancer drug ramucirumab, which blocks a growth-signal receiver called VEGFR-2. They grew maker cells from Chinese hamster ovaries in small shaken flasks, feeding them in batches and watching acidity, sugar, growth, and output.

Seventy-five cell lines made by gene transfer were screened for yield and health, and eight strong makers went on to flask-scale runs. The lead line reached 2.79 grams per litre, and the team checked size, charge, water behaviour, and sugar patterns of the product. The paper gives makers a first map of which lines and settings merit larger trials.
pmc-13424566:
Manzuk and Philippe show an uncounted uranium stream in this 2026 study of the Democratic Republic of Congo's cobalt trade. The Copperbelt that supplies most of the world's cobalt also hosts uranium in the same oxidized ores. The authors show the radioactive metal rides along through processing. It ends up in crude cobalt hydroxide. That is the export form for over 95 percent of Congolese production.

Combining a carryover model with geological maps, geochemistry, and mine-level trade records from 2000 to 2024, they estimate 2,000 to 5,000 tonnes of natural uranium left the country embedded in cobalt shipments. Less than 10 percent of that material has been declared in public and put under international safeguards in their accounting. Another 1,000 to 4,000 tonnes likely went to tailings in easily mobilized forms, an environmental and health hazard near mines. The gap implicates nuclear accountancy and critical-mineral oversight alike.
pmc-13425266:
Sakada and colleagues reported in 2026 a case of oesophageal cancer returning after surgery, then controlled long term by layered treatment. The patient was a 68-year-old woman with stage IVB squamous cancer of the gullet that had spread to lymph nodes near the aorta. Three cycles of an immune drug plus chemotherapy shrank the tumor markedly, and robot-assisted surgery then removed the gullet with a clear margin.

Sakada describes how she started a further immune drug after surgery, yet local relapse came five months later. Radiation with chemotherapy followed, and then dual immune blockade with two checkpoint drugs at once. The returning lesions shrank remarkably, and she stayed disease-controlled for 22 months after surgery with no further treatment. The authors argue dual blockade after earlier immune exposure is a real option for selected returning cases, inside tailored team care.
pmc-13425766:
Pelayo Nieto-Gómez and colleagues study what sways Spain's public choice to pay for cancer drugs for solid tumours between 2010 and 2023. They gathered 220 drug uses approved in that span, scoring added clinical gain with a European oncology scale and value for money from drug prices and quality-adjusted life years.

Other factors weighed were novelty, rival treatments, trial quality, and whether survival and life-quality data were at hand. Health Technology Assessment reports and list prices fed the cost side. Policy readers get a test of which reasons truly move funding, so future cancer funding can be argued on evidence rather than pressure.
pmc-13425866:
Satenik Harutyunova and coauthors report the RIVER II study in 2026, a prospective phase IV trial of riociguat in pulmonary arterial hypertension. The drug improves exercise capacity and blood flow measures, yet prospective evidence on shrinking the strained right heart was limited. Patients were treatment-naive or previously treated, and those on phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors could switch when clinically indicated.

The main outcome was change in right atrial and right ventricular area at 24 weeks, with ultrasound, exercise, blood flow, and safety measures as secondary outcomes. Right heart size matters because chamber enlargement predicts outcomes in this disease. Right heart size can shift fast with good care, so a scan at six months gives a fair test of what the drug can do.
pmc-13426366:
Rajesh Patel and coauthors pooled safety data for tozorakimab, an antibody against interleukin-33, across the FRONTIER phase 2 program in a 2026 analysis. Interleukin-33 orchestrates inflammation, tissue balance, and repair, and its disruption appears in several diseases. Four randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials tested the drug in diabetic kidney disease, atopic dermatitis, asthma, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with chronic bronchitis.

Combining safety, drug level, and immune reaction data across four different diseases gives a broader harm profile than any single trial could. Developers and regulators gain an early read on tolerability before larger phase 3 studies commit thousands of patients.
pmc-13426966:
Phan and colleagues surveyed in 2026 how patients with long-term diseases in Vietnam use herbal medicine alongside prescribed drugs, and whether standard databases catch the risks of mixing them. Herbal use is widespread in Southeast Asia, yet patients rarely mention it, and the main interaction checkers document regional plants poorly.

Across two large hospitals, 658 patients were interviewed. Nearly half used herbal products, and almost none had told their providers. About a third of users carried at least one possible herb-drug or herb-herb clash flagged by the databases. The four databases agreed with each other barely at all: under one percent of flagged clashes appeared in all four. Several local plants were missing from every database. The authors call for routine herbal histories and checkers that include regional plants.
pmc-13427066:
Wong and colleagues evaluated in 2026 a tabletop game designed to improve conversation between generations, called Healthy Aging in Dialogue. The game was cocreated with potential users, then tested in a pre-post study with sixty-eight players: twenty-three young adults, fourteen middle-aged adults, and thirty-one older adults. Surveys before and after measured communication satisfaction and skill, health literacy, and how enabled patients felt to manage their health, alongside interviews.

Scores rose across the board after play. Communication satisfaction showed the largest gain, with moderate gains in communication competence and health literacy, and benefits ran strongest in the older group. Older adults also scored much higher on patient enablement than young adults did. The authors say a well-designed game gives each generation a reason to talk, contribute, and learn, making it a practical tool against the social isolation that harms healthy aging.
pmc-13427666:
Giuseppe Albi and colleagues show, in a 2026 study, that adding background knowledge helps computers predict whether a chemical is toxic. Classic models read only a molecule's structure and physical traits. The team instead fed graph neural networks extra facts from knowledge graphs, which link chemicals, genes, and known effects in plain relations. Tests used public toxicity datasets, including the Tox21 assay collection.

Models with the added knowledge separated toxic from harmless compounds better than structure-only models. Their confidence estimates stayed just as well calibrated. Explanation tools showed the models focused more on molecular parts already known to drive toxic effects. Safety assessors who screen chemicals before lab testing gain a model that is both sharper and easier to interrogate.
pmc-13427966:
Van den Dorpel and colleagues systematically reviewed in 2026 what autopsy studies show about brain damage in classic infantile Pompe disease. It is a severe inherited condition where cells cannot break down a stored sugar. They screened over 3,700 records and kept thirty-nine articles covering forty-nine patients, seven of whom had received enzyme replacement therapy.

Damage appeared throughout the nervous system. The white matter of the cerebrum and cerebellum, named deep brain nuclei, brainstem motor nuclei, and spinal motor cells were hit most often. Stored sugar piled up heavily in support cells and in neurons of the globus pallidus, while deep structures suffered more than the cortex. Autopsies showed heavy damage in infancy, years before scans, blood markers, or thinking problems usually reveal it. That gap suggests brain disease starts silently and much earlier than clinics detect.
pmc-13429466:
Esser and colleagues look to hibernating animals for ways to protect transplanted organs. Their 2026 review starts from a persistent problem. Donor organs are damaged by cold storage and by the rush of blood returning after transplant. That injury combination drives complications, especially in the bile ducts after liver transplant. Adapted animals survive far harsher cold and metabolic shutdown without such damage.

The review surveys mechanisms behind hibernation, supercooling, and enhanced regeneration in unconventional species. The authors examine how these animals resist cold injury and regrow tissue, and ask which tricks could transfer to organ preservation or repair. They frame animal adaptations as an inspiration pipeline for new therapies, aiming to widen the usable donor pool and cut post-transplant complications. The paper maps candidate mechanisms rather than reporting a single experiment.
pmc-13429566:
Fatemeh Ashrafi and colleagues load echinacea into a metal-organic framework, UIO-66, to fight Pseudomonas aeruginosa from hospital patients. The plant-loaded particles were built with amino groups, then sized and checked for loading, release, and stability.

Antibacterial tests covered lowest blocking and killing doses, kill-over-time curves, and biofilm blocking, while two resistance-linked genes, arr-2 and arr-4, were measured after treatment. The particles measured 235.0 nanometres across, with a spread index of 0.140. The study gives wound and device teams a plant-based nanoparticle candidate against a stubborn germ.
pmc-13430166:
Yichuan Liu and colleagues mine, in a 2026 study, whole-genome data to find old drugs that might treat brain and nerve conditions. Developing new drugs for the 92 central nervous system conditions covered here is slow and failure-prone. The team gathered genome sequences from 4,392 people across those diagnoses and ranked which biological pathways each condition stresses. They also cataloged 213 approved or late-stage drugs by the pathways each one touches.

Matching drugs to diseases by shared pathways produced over 12,000 candidate pairs. Filtering for genetic support, cohort size, and pathway depth left about 1,430 high-confidence pairs. Known treatment strategies resurfaced in the results, which validates the approach, alongside fresh pairings no trial has tested. Frequently implicated pathways involved growth signaling, blood vessels, immunity, and nerve support. Biomarker-guided trials are the proposed proving ground.
pmc-13430566:
Elizabeth A Matthews, Derek Southwell, and their co-authors issued a correction in 2026 to their study of a tool that tracks and steers chosen cell types in the human cortex. The tool, called CellREADR, works through RNA-based targeting. The notice fixes the name of a calcium signal dye used in the work.

The paper had named the dye as one form of the GCaMP family when the team had in fact used a sister form with a close name. The text now gives the right name, and one figure was updated to match. The authors state that the slip does not change any claim of the study. They also say sorry for any mix-up the error may have caused readers.
pmc-13430766:
Godfrey Malangwa and colleagues profile eye-surface squamous cell cancer in Tanzania, the most common eye malignancy, which hits Sub-Saharan Africa hard where strong sun and HIV overlap. Local social and clinical detail was scarce.

Ninety-nine adults with tissue-confirmed disease treated at two major Tanzanian hospitals from 2016 to 2019 were reviewed from records. Median age was 43 years, 61.6 percent were women, and 80.8 percent were subsistence farmers. HIV prevalence reached 70.7 percent, with 67.1 percent of HIV-positive patients on antiretroviral therapy at diagnosis. Cancer planners get a portrait that ties eye cancer to farming, sun, and HIV care.
pmc-13430866:
Sherene T McNeil and colleagues survey chain restaurants in Jamaica for salty foods, cooking methods, and high-sodium seasonings, as restaurant food drives much sodium intake. Chains were defined as having at least three local stores, surveyed under the Jamaica Salt Consumption Study.

Only 24 percent of identified chains took part. Across 107 menu items, chicken led at 21.5 percent, followed by fish at 15.9 percent and soup at 9.4 percent. For meat, frying led at 20.6 percent, then boiling at 18.7 percent and baking at 17.8 percent. Food-policy readers get a menu-level picture of where salt hides and where lower-salt options could land.
pmc-13432566:
Martin Griesshammer and a panel of blood cancer experts laid out the 2025 German guide in 2026 for myelofibrosis, a rare long-run disease in which the bone marrow scars over. The guide sits in a national series for cancer care and draws on experts from three lands. Panel rounds of draft review and debate shaped the final text for rigor and clinic fit.

The update refines how to spot the disease, grade its risk, and pick among drug and transplant routes in light of fresh drugs and tests. Gene reads now help sort risk with finer tools than older scores. Symptom burden earns its own formal scale. The authors frame the guide as a proof-based frame that clinics can trust for daily calls, while the full text lives on the series website for free use.
pmc-13432666:
Ao Ma and co-authors hunted gene faults in 2026 behind the gravest form of male infertility, where the testes make no mature seed cells. Gene causes explain near a third of cases, yet most stay unsolved. A protein trio that helps swap gene parts during seed cell splits drew the team's eye.

Full gene reads on 108 Chinese patients found five rare, harm-predicted changes across two genes of the trio, one in each of five men. Gene voice levels for both genes ran far lower in four of the men. Tissue snips showed tubes stripped of late-stage cells, with splits stalled at an early phase. The authors count the five changes as proven causes, which widens the map for clinic screening of men with this fault.
pmc-13432966:
Limmen and colleagues published a 2026 study building a standard outcome set for children's physical therapy. Therapists lacked one shared list of what to ask children about their progress. The team drew on talks with teens, parents, and therapists, plus a literature sweep. An expert panel then ranked which outcomes matter most for daily care.

Nine outcomes made the final set across three broad domains. Functioning covers body use, taking part, and social life at school and home. Symptoms cover pain and tiredness, and an overarching group covers life quality. Matching questionnaires were found for all outcomes except taking part in activities. The authors now urge building a workable measure for that gap. Therapists ranked the candidate outcomes through a survey round as well.
pmc-13433166:
Emmanuel O Oyewole and co-authors traced in 2026 how one alarm port on lung guard cells steers output of a repair signal when farm dust stirs swelling. The signal guards the lung's skin wall and helps heal harm, yet its control in guard cells stayed dim. The port reads germ scraps thick in farm dust.

Cell tests with set port triggers and blockers showed this port drives the repair signal more than kin ports do. One pairing of the port lit the signal, while its sister pairing did not. Mice that lack the port, dosed with dust for two weeks, made far less of the signal in lung tissue than sound mice. Stains pinned the signal to guard cells. The port thus ties dust sense to repair calls.
pmc-13433266:
Vincent Pascoli and co-authors watched a reward chemical pulse in a mouse brain hub in 2026 as mice chose between a fat treat and drug-like rewards, hunting what sets each mouse's lean. Addicts pick drugs over plain joys, a bias blamed on warped reward signals, yet hard proof stayed thin. A gene-built sensor lit the pulses live.

Pulses rose at cues that foretold either reward. At treat arrival the pulse died, while at drug arrival it held. In free choice rounds, each mouse's lean, from all-treat to all-drug, matched the size of its cue pulse. Fresh price tags on rewards shifted leans and pulses in step for most mice. Mice locked in forced drug hunts failed to update, which marks a break in worth learning.
pmc-13433666:
Haijun Chen and colleagues pinpoint a subset of fibroblasts, marked by LOXL2, that drive harmful scar-like remodelling in liver cancer. Liver tumours grow in a stiff, collagen-rich setting where matrix remodelling shapes how malignant the cancer becomes.

Bulk gene reads showed LOX, LOXL2, and LOXL4 raised in tumours, tracking advanced stage and poor outlook. Single-cell reads then split the roles: LOX and LOXL4 sat mainly in cancer cells, while LOXL2 sat mainly in fibroblasts and vessel-lining cells. A distinct LOXL2-positive fibroblast group emerged, giving drug teams a stromal target beyond the cancer cell itself.
pmc-13434266:
Haiting Fan and colleagues link poor sleep and lasting pain to one brain cell group in male mice in 2026. Nerve harm raised activity in quieting cells of the lateral septum, a small midbrain area. Both pain response to touch and broken sleep rose with that activity.

A sedative drug calmed those cells through a known receptor and eased both pain and sleep loss. The septum cells send branches to a sleep area, with two paths split by job. One path shaped touch pain and the other shaped sleep. The shared circuit gives drug makers a single target for two linked problems.
pmc-13435966:
Ah-Yeon Lee and coauthors validate a short Korean quality of life scale in cervical cancer patients in 2026. The eight item HINT-8 was checked against the standard five dimension EQ scale. Cervical cancer care often needs finer reads on daily well being than the standard gives.

Worse scores on stairs, pain, and energy items tracked lower standard index values. The two index scores linked strongly, at 0.771 by the rank count. The short scale showed a much lower ceiling effect, catching small gaps the standard misses. Memory, sleep, and happiness items add fresh ground. Clinics gain a quick add on tool for visit checks.
pmc-13436366:
Hsiao-Chun Chen, Carter J Newton, and Li Yang profile a bacterial regulator during plant infection in 2026. The regulator CvsR steers Pseudomonas syringae, a leaf pathogen, as plant immunity wakes. Gene reads taken inside leaves give a rare in place view.

In leaves the regulator directly runs only a small core set, centered on a carbonic enzyme and its carrier. Most gene shifts in mutant germs trace to the host immune climate, not to the regulator. Sulfur hunger marks part of that indirect wave. Host pressure, not bacterial command, writes most of the infection script. Plant defenses thus reshape germ behavior broadly.
pmc-13439066:
Md Rakibul Hasan's team surveyed pesticide use in 2026 among six hundred farmers along the Jamuna River in Tangail and Sirajganj, Bangladesh. Pesticide use is rising in developing farm systems, raising worker and food safety worries, yet district-level patterns were thin. Structured questionnaires in the 2025 season covered products, knowledge, safety habits, and self-reported health effects.

Tangail leaned on insecticides, Sirajganj on fungicides, moderately hazardous products dominated both, over-application was common, withholding periods were often ignored, banned products still appeared, and only nineteen percent always wore protective gear. Skin irritation hit half of Sirajganj farmers. Extension services get a district-specific safety gap map, with a knowledge-practice divide to close.
pmc-13439866:
Hyung Doo Kim's team piloted a local PM2.5 teaching program in 2026 for older adults in Incheon, South Korea, where fine particle contact threatens lungs and hearts. Fifty-nine adults aged sixty-five and older in a home visit program were placed by cluster to nurse-led teaching or usual care. The teaching group got hands-on training and text alerts, and know-how, habits, indoor air, and lung function were read at start and six weeks.

The teaching group improved lung capacity measures clearly and ended with lower indoor PM2.5 and fewer high-pollution spells than controls, while habit gains mostly favored teaching without reaching significance. Public health teams get a feasible, nurse-delivered model for protecting vulnerable elders. Larger random trials should confirm lung and exposure benefits.
pmc-13441266:
Eve Zipporah Stern and colleagues chart growth and growth hormone response in childhood medulloblastoma survivors, reporting records from 1987 to 2023 in 2026. Stunted growth and short final height are well-known late effects of this brain tumour and its treatment, yet predictors of hormone benefit were scarce. The centre review covered sixty-seven patients followed at least a year after diagnosis.

Nearly every survivor showed growth retardation, and well over half had proven growth hormone deficiency. Twenty-six received hormone treatment. Among fifteen treated patients who reached final height, scores averaged below the population mean, and only about half landed in the normal range. Untreated survivors finished slightly shorter, without a significant gap. Height standing when treatment began was the strongest predictor of final outcome. The authors press for early deficiency screening and honest family discussion of long-term treatment safety.
pmc-13443866:
Jiahao Zhai and colleagues track soil carbon shifts as tidal flats turn to land in a 2026 study. Coastal reclamation dries salt flats into farms, woods, and ponds, which rewires soil traits from salt to grain size. Their team sampled soils across reclamation ages and land uses to split carbon into living and mineral forms.

Living carbon rose with reclamation age, piled at the surface under woods and crops, with mineral-bound forms in the lead. That pool also grew steadier over time in their checks. Mineral carbon held flat in young soils, then fell in surface layers of old land soils, while fish ponds kept it high. Living carbon tracked food levels and clay share, while mineral carbon tracked sourness and salt.
pmc-13444066:
Chaofeng Zhu and colleagues trap rhodium clusters inside a zeolite to beat a wetting snag in solvent-free chemistry in a 2026 paper. Solid metal catalysts should replace pricey liquid ones, yet they often fade or slow in real runs. Their design locks sub-nano rhodium bits in a self-pillared zeolite frame.

The frame holds the bits steady while open paths speed goods in and out. In solvent-free olefin hydroformylation, the best build passed 1,100,000 total turnovers across a wide goods range. Cluster charge traits and frame shape share credit for the score. The trick extends to other metals in the same frame in their report. The authors pitch the frame as a general fix for wetting woes in dry reactions.
pmc-13445666:
Sayed Mujtaba Sadaat and colleagues read the genomes of Iranian wheat to trace how modern breeding drained stress-hardy gene variants, in a 2026 study. Iran sits in a birthplace of wheat diversity, so its old farm strains hold a deep pool of variants. New high-yield strains may have traded that pool away for uniform gains.

Gene scans of 298 strains, at more than forty-five thousand markers, showed modern strains squeezed into a narrow genetic space beside the old landraces. Loss sped up after 1990, marking recent breeding, not early farming, as the main driver. Sweeps on four chromosomes fixed dwarfing genes yet cost stress tolerance, with lost carrier and defense genes named. The authors propose surgical crossing to bring the hardy blocks back without losing yield.
pmc-13446466:
Nishimura and colleagues spoke with Kenyan fishermen in Siaya County about HIV self-testing given out through social networks. In these areas HIV rates reach up to 31 percent and clinic use is low. Their interview-based study drew on 64 interviews and four focus groups. They included 30 promoters who handed out test kits and transport vouchers to peers.

Ease, privacy, and dodging stigma drove self-testing uptake most strongly among the men interviewed. Men who saw themselves at high risk were keen to test. Some still chose clinics, for advice and faith in results. Training lifted promoters' own drive to test, and their peers' drive too. Follow-up clinic visits were eased by feeling at risk, wanting preventive drugs, spousal backing, and the travel vouchers. Distance, work demands, moving for work, and the belief a negative result needs no clinic check stayed the main barriers.
pmc-13447066:
Pushpita Nag and colleagues open a journal collection on digital tools for diabetes care, its third volume, in a 2026 editorial. Thirteen articles span the disease arc, from prediabetes and child obesity to complications and long-term care. The tools reach past meters and records to learning models, live monitoring, remote visits, and aids for the mental load of the disease.

The largest strand forecasts risk and prevention, with models that spot who may return to normal sugar or which children with obesity face type 2 diabetes. Other pieces sort complications and survival. The editors press a hard test for every tool: can it act in plain sight, fairly, and to use inside real clinics, since most proof so far is backward-looking or home-checked only.
pmc-13447566:
Eun Sun Choi and colleagues report a hidden hormone tumour found only during major surgery in a 2026 case study. A sixty-nine-year-old man arrived with upper belly pain, and scans showed a large pancreatic head mass that looked inflammatory rather than solid cancer. Needle sampling hinted at a neuroendocrine tumour, yet a specialised scan lit up only a nearby lymph node, not the mass itself.

Major surgery removed the pancreatic head and duodenum. Tissue study showed the mass was overlapping inflammation of two rare types, which can mimic cancer closely. Hidden inside the duodenum sat a tiny gastrin-making tumour, well under a centimetre, which had already spread to nodes. Scanning hot nodes beside a cold pancreatic mass should trigger a careful duodenal search, the authors advise.
pmc-13448266:
Grossman and colleagues reported on a 2026 workshop, held with the Adult Brain Tumor Consortium and the Food and Drug Administration, about judging whether drugs truly reach brain tumors. Current tests mostly measure drug levels where tumors light up on scans. Yet much tumor sits in non-enhancing brain, meaning tissue that looks normal on scans, where drug levels often stay too low to work.

Grossman and the workshop group weighed lab models of the blood-brain barrier, spinal fluid sampling, and animal brain studies as ways to judge penetration into non-enhancing tissue. Their main product is a three-level index that sorts candidate drugs as sufficiently permeable, insufficiently permeable, or impermeable for that hidden tissue. Using the index before human efficacy trials could steer funding toward drugs that reach the whole tumor and spare patients toxic treatments with little chance of brain benefit.
pmc-13448466:
Soudeh Shaabanzadeh Soufiabadi and colleagues test higher vitamin E and D doses for heat-stressed broiler chickens in a 2026 feeding study. Heat stress cuts feed efficiency, disturbs blood chemistry and loosens gut barrier control in fast-growing meat birds. A gut gene tied to leakiness, CLDN2, rises under heat, making it a useful readout alongside growth measures.

Four hundred birds were split into five groups, covering unstressed controls, stressed controls and stressed groups with extra vitamin D, extra vitamin E or both. Combined high doses lowered several blood stress markers, raised feed intake and improved feed conversion under heat. Warming alone raised gut CLDN2 expression, while vitamin groups pushed it back down. Combined supplementation is proposed as a practical resilience strategy for hot-climate poultry production.
pmc-13448666:
Zhao Yiyuan and co-authors classify green versus non-green buildings with a transformer model that shows its logic in a 2026 study. Certifying green building design by manual audit is slow and costly, limiting how many projects can be assessed as green. Machine sorting from project attributes could scale that screening, provided its logic stays open enough for professional trust.

Their network fuses grouped inputs covering energy, eco-technology, design and context through attention mechanisms built for tabular data. A trimming step cut repeated inputs before sorting across the feature groups. Attention heatmaps and two popular explainer tools expose which inputs drive each call. Its score beat four rival tabular transformer baselines in their tests. Scalable, data-driven green assessment with visible decision logic is the stated aim.
pmc-13448866:
Asma Ahmed and colleagues present in 2026 the Pakistan findings of the ACTION-APAC survey on how obesity is perceived and managed. By Asia-specific cutoffs, an estimated 150.6 million people in Pakistan live with obesity, about six in ten adults, yet the condition stays underdiagnosed and undertreated. The survey asked people with obesity and the doctors who treat them about attitudes, behaviors, and barriers to care.

The online study ran in April and May 2022 as part of a nine-country program. In Pakistan, 931 people with obesity took part, averaging 33 years of age, alongside physicians experienced in managing such patients. Responses used five-point agreement scales and were weighted to match the population. The authors offer this country baseline so education programs and treatment policy can be measured against it as care improves.
pmc-13449066:
Vaden and colleagues used Finnish national registers to follow 7,249 adults with type 2 diabetes who started oral semaglutide. Semaglutide is the pill form of the GLP-1 drug class. The follow-up ran from 2021 to 2023, and none had been on any such drug before. They tracked blood sugar, weight, lipids, and liver enzymes for up to a year in routine practice.

About 65.8 percent remained on treatment at 180 days and 55.2 percent at one year in the nationwide cohort. Modeled HbA1c fell from 7.9 percent to 6.8 percent by six months. It held near 6.9 percent at a year among those measured. Mean weight dropped from 106 kilograms to 100 at six months and 98 at twelve months in the weighed subgroup. Liver enzyme ALT declined from 50 to 37 units per liter over the year. Lipid measures improved early, supporting real-world effectiveness.
pmc-13449366:
R. S. Allodji and a European team quantify in 2026 which childhood cancer treatments raise the risk of a cancer, a soft-tissue sarcoma. Earlier studies were too small to trace dose-response curves. The team worked within a pan-European cohort of 69,460 five-year survivors. They matched 275 survivors who developed a sarcoma with 275 who did not. Then they compared radiation dose at the tumor's site and cumulative doses of chemotherapy drugs.

Soft tissue that had received thirty gray or more of radiation carried twenty-two times the odds of sarcoma, and five to nine gray tripled the odds. The excess per gray ran higher in neuroblastoma and bone sarcoma survivors and in females. Procarbazine at six grams per square meter or more carried an odds ratio of 4.7 after accounting for radiation, while other drugs showed no link. The authors say planning and follow-up guidelines should register the signals.
pmc-13449466:
Liangqin Liu and colleagues examined why some blueberry flowers drop their petals while others hold them, publishing in 2026. Corolla abscission matters because it affects fruit quality and disease risk, yet its molecular basis was poorly understood. The team compared two cultivars with opposite behavior: Magica, which sheds its corolla, and Eureka-Sunrise, which keeps it.

Microscopy showed the shedding zone's cells separating after full bloom in Magica, while the same zone stayed intact in Eureka-Sunrise. Gene-activity data across three developmental stages pointed to hormone signaling, cell-wall organization, and oxidative stress responses. Network analysis then highlighted key gene groups behind the difference. Breeders gain targets for controlling petal drop and its knock-on effects on fruit.
pmc-13449666:
Fernando Carrasquer and co-authors sample in 2026 backyard poultry flocks across eastern Spain to measure how much drug-resistant bacteria these informal farms harbor. Unlike commercial farms, backyard flocks often run with thin hygiene, and their role in spreading resistance is poorly charted. The team visited 33 farms in 24 localities, surveying farm practices and gathering hen swabs plus surface wipes, then cultured Escherichia coli as a sentinel organism.

Of 216 isolates, 95.8 percent from birds resisted at least one drug and 73.8 percent resisted many; isolates from surfaces ran slightly higher still. Resistance peaked against tetracycline, near ninety percent, and ampicillin, above eighty percent. Most farms scored low or moderate on hygiene, and contact with wildlife was common. The authors argue backyard poultry belongs inside national resistance surveillance under a One Health approach, not outside it.
pmc-13449966:
Richard Mprah and colleagues examined blood levels of CD38, an enzyme that depletes the energy molecule NAD, as a heart-failure warning sign in 2026. CD38 rises with aging and metabolic stress and may promote heart dysfunction, but whether its blood level predicts new heart failure, and whether that differs by sex or kidney function, was unknown.

Plasma CD38 was measured in 42,584 UK Biobank participants, among whom 1,659 developed heart failure. Higher CD38 went with higher risk after adjusting for standard factors, but the link vanished once kidney function was accounted for. Despite higher levels in men, the link was stronger in women, and after kidney adjustment it stayed positive in women while turning inverse in men. Mouse work tested CD38 blockade alongside related inhibitors. The sex and kidney patterns matter for any future use of CD38 as a marker.
pmc-13450466:
Xintong Li and colleagues reviewed high blood fats as a driver of clogged arteries in 2026, arguing the risk stays even when bad cholesterol is well controlled. Whether high triglycerides directly cause plaque has been debated, but fresh work on how they act has mapped several harmful routes. The review pulls that work into one frame.

High triglycerides help cholesterol stick under vessel walls, spark vessel swelling and lining harm, speed vessel aging, and spur clotting. Joined up, these routes help plaques start and grow. The authors call high triglycerides a leftover risk that can be changed, backing finer risk sorting and add-on drugs beyond standard fat-lowering pills. Doctors gain a case for treating high triglycerides as more than a side note.
pmc-13450566:
Panpan Zhang and others mapped the GRAS gene clan in oil camellia in 2026, a shrub prized for oil in south China. GRAS genes steer tissue growth, fruit ripening, and stress replies in plants, yet the clan had not been mapped in full in Camellia oleifera. The team sought a full list plus stress conduct.

Seventy-five GRAS genes were found and named by spot on the chromosomes, with gene forms, shared motifs, switch spots, gene-copy events, and gene activity all charted. Switch-spot work tied the clan to hormone cues, growth, and stress replies. Dish tests showed sharp replies to dry, salt, and cold stress, with CoGRAS70 rising most in treatment. Breeders gain a gene list for tough oil camellia.
pmc-13451866:
Anahita Bahrami, Batool Ghorbani Yekta, and Anita Baghdasarians test in 2026 a coffee-linked plant acid in rats given a drug that mimics parts of schizophrenia. The drug, ketamine, was dosed for seven days to male and female rats, and the acid was given once a day later. The team checked movement, grooming, memory for new objects, and a brain growth factor in the front brain.

Ketamine sped movement and dulled memory in both sexes, while the acid partly eased select harms, with gains split by sex. It trimmed excess movement in males, grooming in females, and partly saved memory and the brain factor in both. The authors flag a missing pure control group as a caveat.
pmc-13452366:
Wang and colleagues tested in 2026 whether tiny vesicles shed by young red blood cells can speed bone healing. Vesicles are small parcels that cells release to pass signals to neighbors. The team noticed in health survey data that red cell measures tracked with bone density and survival after fractures, which hinted the parcels might help repair.

In lab dishes, vesicles from young red cells entered bone-forming cells and boosted their bone-building activity. They also nudged macrophages, immune cells at the injury site, toward a healing state, partly rescuing stalled bone growth. In mice with leg fractures, the vesicles gathered at the break and improved regrowth without visible harm. Protein sorting fingered a cargo called VCAN, which docks onto macrophages and switches on a growth pathway.
pmc-13452566:
Olav Vestrheim and seven co-authors anchor a man made antioxidant to fat molecules so it lands inside liver cells and stays put. The catalyst, a manganese complex called EUK, breaks down harmful oxygen species but tends to clump and sink when used alone. Their 2026 study ties it by a chemical bond to a phospholipid, one of the fats that form cell walls.

The tied catalyst folded neatly into liposomes, tiny fat bubbles, and kept its activity with steady loading over time. Inside the bubbles it broke down harmful oxygen species at a rate that rose with the amount loaded. In liver cells stressed by a common pain drug and loaded with fat, the bubbles entered the cells and cut the excess oxygen species without killing them. The approach offers a precise way to place such catalysts where damage occurs.
pmc-13452866:
Jun Kawashima, Yuki Homma, Itaru Endo, and Timothy M Pawlik reflect on when clearing lymph nodes helps in a bile duct cancer inside the liver. Their 2026 piece draws on records for 1,558 patients who had surgery meant to cure this cancer, called intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma. Only 322 of them had what counts as adequate node clearing, set at six or more nodes removed.

The value of full node clearing split sharply by tumor load, a score built from tumor size and count. For patients with low tumor load, full clearing made no clear difference to survival. For patients with high tumor load, it linked to longer life and more time free of return. In real practice only 10 to 25 percent of patients get the full clearing, so the piece urges wider use where tumor load is high.
pmc-13453466:
Matsubara argues that peer reviewers must never upload manuscripts, or even their own review sheets, to AI tools. Zero confidentiality risk cannot be guaranteed. Journal guidelines usually ban uploads where secrecy is not assured. He extends the same caution to reviewers' own words.

His first reason is verification. Even when a tool promises erasure on request, no reviewer can independently confirm the data are truly gone from its systems. His own small experiment suggested a major chatbot may retain uploaded material for training despite deletion requests. That makes complete erasure impossible in his assessment. Second, review sheets can contain highly confidential keywords and candid editorial messages. Their exposure could identify or compromise the process. Authors may accept the risk for their own drafts. Reviewers hold other people's unpublished work in trust and owe far greater caution.
pmc-13453666:
Igor E. Konstantinov and others described septal reconstruction with right atrial wall for multiple ventricular septal defects in 2026, tackling Swiss-cheese defects. Children with many muscular defects often have a thin, poorly developed septum with noncompaction features, making complete closure technically hard. Precise borders between dysplastic septum and noncompaction are not always clear.

The technique uses the patient's own right atrial wall to reconstruct the septum, offering a material that can close multiple defects where patches or devices struggle. The central message is feasibility in noncompacted septum, a setting where occluder devices face limits. Congenital heart surgeons gain a reconstructive option for one of the hardest septal anatomies.
pmc-13453766:
Yao Wang, Lifei Feng, Xiaoqiu Zhu, and Miaomiao Zhang review why patients with ankylosing spondylitis drift away from their treatment plans. The disease stiffens the spine over years, and steady treatment is the only brake. Their 2026 review gathers studies from 2010 to 2024 across five databases, looking past the drugs to the person, their circle, and the care system.

Poor knowledge of the disease, weak faith in the drugs, and skipped exercise all chip away at follow through. Support from family and peers pushes the other way, while cost and clinic access shape what is possible. The authors separate proof drawn from this disease from proof borrowed from wider chronic illness, an honesty step they stress. They close with multi part plans and a call for research built on this patient group alone.
pmc-13454066:
Rui Pu and five co-authors compare vitamin A and D levels in mothers late in pregnancy with those in their newborns' cord blood. Their 2026 study follows 118 mother and baby pairs, measuring both vitamins with precision lab methods. The aim is twofold: test how tightly the levels track, and find habits a mother can change to lift her baby's start.

Cord blood vitamin A ran lower than the mother's level, while cord vitamin D ran higher. Both vitamins still tracked positively across the pair, weakly for A at 0.256 and strongly for D at 0.697. Better sleep, more vitamin A intake, and frequent vegetables came with higher cord vitamin A. Daily activity over an hour and vitamin D supplements came with better cord vitamin D. The authors shape the findings into prenatal nutrition advice.
pmc-13454466:
Siyang Wang, Jie Gao, and Xiangmei Chen offer, in a 2026 perspective, a two-sided view of high uric acid among people living at high altitude. Raised uric acid, called hyperuricemia, occurs far more often in mountain regions than at low altitude. The authors gather worldwide survey data and clinical reports to explain why.

Thin air, cold, diet, and inherited traits all push uric acid upward in these settings. In some ways the rise may help the body adapt to low oxygen. Yet the same rise feeds gout and other altitude-linked disorders, from kidney strain to heart risk. The authors map how the body makes and clears uric acid in these patients. They close by arguing for treatments tuned to altitude life rather than copied from sea-level practice.
pmc-13455266:
Motahare Shabestari and coauthors used 2026 hospital records to trace how patients change day by day after open heart surgery. Kidney injury after such surgery is common. It can lengthen stays and harm long-term health, yet fixed risk scores often miss how fast a patient shifts. The team grouped each post-surgery day by lab results and stable traits, searching for repeat patterns in the data.

Among 3,526 patients, 567 developed kidney injury, and five day-to-day states emerged from the grouping. One state looked stable. Another showed a long clotting time, and a third showed small pale red cells. A warning state came just before injury, and a fifth state matched injury taking hold. Patients heading toward injury drifted into the warning state, then the injury state, while others settled toward the stable states. The pattern may help staff watch risk as it moves, rather than from one fixed score.
pmc-13456466:
Xin Lai and co-authors tested a way to make glioblastoma, the most aggressive common brain tumor, more vulnerable to radiation. Radiation kills cancer cells partly through reactive oxygen species. These unstable molecules damage cell parts, but tumors clear them and resist treatment. In their 2026 study, the team used ionomycin, a compound that ferries calcium into cells, to overload tumor cells with calcium. The overload kept the damaging molecules building up beyond what cells could handle.

In lab-grown tumor cells, the drug-plus-radiation combination produced the highest death rates. It nearly wiped out the cells' ability to form new colonies over time. pmc-13478866:
Zhu and colleagues introduce a generative model that designs drug molecules while avoiding unwanted targets in this 2026 paper. Most molecule-generating systems chase activity at the intended target and ignore off-target binding, which causes side effects and safety failures. Their system, ActivityDiff, is a diffusion model guided by two separately trained classifiers, one scoring desired activity and one scoring activity to steer away from.

The dual guidance let the model handle several design jobs. It generated molecules for one or two targets at once. It designed around a fixed molecular fragment. And it sharpened selectivity for a chosen target. It also reduced off-target effects in the reported experiments compared with positive-only approaches. The authors argue that building avoidance into generation itself is a practical route to safer, more selective candidate drugs.
pmc-13479566:
Gutenberg Navarro-Zambrano and coauthors report a 2026 case of fatal early graft failure after heart transplantation, traced to hidden coronary disease in a young donor. Graft failure is the leading cause of death soon after transplant, and donor screening usually rests on history and ultrasound, which can miss silent artery narrowing. The recipient was a 52-year-old with advanced dilated cardiomyopathy.

The donor was a healthy 27-year-old man assessed at a secondary hospital with an electrocardiogram and heart ultrasound, both normal. Trouble began after the transplant operation, and investigation pointed to multivessel coronary disease that screening had not caught. The authors use the case to argue that donor evaluation needs stronger tools for detecting subclinical disease, since young age alone proved a false reassurance here.
pmc-13480066:
Devki Patel and colleagues report a 2026 study of health care costs tied to diabetes, heart disease, and chronic kidney disease in United States adults. The team pooled national survey data from 2021 through 2023. Groups held adults with diabetes alone, heart disease alone, kidney disease alone, or at least two of the three, and models weighed age, sex, and other social factors.

Adults with two or more of the conditions carried the highest yearly costs, with total spending near double that of diabetes alone. Their out-of-pocket drug costs also topped the list, while the kidney-only group showed the lowest drug outlay, though that group held just 44 people and its figures carry wide doubt. Total spending was lowest for diabetes alone. The pattern argues for focused financial and clinical help for people juggling several long-term conditions at once.
pmc-13480266:
Vincent and Vakamudi wrote this 2026 editorial about diagnostic anchoring, the habit of sticking with a first explanation and missing other causes. They comment on a case of purulent pericarditis, a rare bacterial infection of the sac around the heart, in a patient who also had cancer. Doctors first assumed fluid around the heart was malignant, meaning caused by the cancer itself.

Full testing of the drained fluid instead pointed to spread of infection from the gut, which changed treatment and outlook. The authors urge routine cell counts, stains, cultures, and cytology on such fluid in every case. They also stress imaging after drainage. That catches tightening of the heart sac, which followed this infection far more often than viral causes. Early teamwork matters when deciding on surgery.
pmc-13481266:
Rigel Salinas Gamboa and co-authors describe a 2026 gene hunt for what keeps chromosome swaps away from centromeres in a model plant. Swaps near the chromosome centre are shut off in nearly all species, which blocks breeders from moving prized genes parked there. Working in Arabidopsis, the team found three guards: a protein that trims a small tag, a protector of the glue that holds chromosome copies, and a loader of that glue.

Knocking out any guard let swaps appear where none formed before and boosted swaps where they were rare. Stacking the faults, or adding a fault in a DNA marking enzyme, pushed counts higher still, which shows several brakes act in parallel. Glue turnover near the centre seems central to the shut-off. Breeders may one day lift the brake briefly to unlock genes near centromeres.
pmc-13481566:
Simon Abelard and co-authors offer a 2026 assessment of hybrid key exchange schemes that marry quantum key distribution with post-quantum algorithms. Quantum computers threaten today's public-key maths, so pairing the two defences promises a safety net if either one cracks. The review weighs published schemes by proof strength, speed, and readiness for real deployment.

Settings ranged from military satellite links to banking backbones. Trade-offs turned on trust in relay nodes, link distance, and how mature each design stands today. Some cases, such as untrusted satellite relays or very long ground links, may need extra measures beyond the standard hybrids. The authors map which design fits which mission, giving planners a grounded menu rather than hype. Dual-use stakes make the proof quality, not just speed, the deciding factor.
pmc-13482366:
Afsar and colleagues followed 520 patients whose traumatic brain injuries were moderate to severe at a Tabriz, Iran hospital in 2026, testing whether simple nutrition measures predict who recovers. The prospective study tracked body mass index and blood albumin, a protein often read as a nutrition marker, at discharge and one month later, alongside mood and stress scales. Patients averaged about 32 years old, and 71.7 percent were men.

Falls caused nearly 75 percent of the injuries, and the cohort was gravely ill, with 51.2 percent dying in hospital and 48.8 percent surviving to discharge in this six-month enrollment. Coma scale scores at discharge and follow-up tracked survival strongly, confirming that injury severity, not nutrition markers, carried the prognosis in these patients. Neither body mass index nor albumin correlated with survival, anxiety, depression, or stress symptoms, and all three measures discriminated outcomes poorly, pushing the authors toward broader assessment tools.
pmc-13483566:
Godfred Darko and colleagues document daily stress among adults living with type 2 diabetes in Ghana's Ashanti Region during 2026. Focus groups and interviews gathered views from 92 patients in farming and mining communities plus 12 health workers. Discussion covered what triggers distress, how people cope, cultural taboos, and effects on quality of life.

Five themes recurred across groups, covering inability to afford medicine, travel barriers to clinics, clashes between work and care, fear of complications, and stigma inside families. Older adults stressed feared complications most, while younger adults stressed family stigma. Cultural rules also limited shrine visits, church life, and shared feasts during high blood sugar episodes. The authors urge combined attention to drug costs, local clinics, and peer support that respects local customs.
pmc-13484466:
Tzani and colleagues published a 2026 trial on teaching ostomy patients to care for themselves in Greece. Living with an ostomy, an opening that diverts body waste, reshapes daily life deeply. The team randomized 100 adults in Athens with new intestinal or urinary ostomies. Half received home teaching plus steady nursing follow-up over three months.

The taught group reported less anxiety than controls at 45 days. Their depression scores also fell further at both check points measured. Skin trouble around the stoma, the opening, eased more in the taught group. Teaching packs came in three versions matched to each ostomy type. Quality of life rose alongside the mood gains, the authors report. Printed guides matched each ostomy type, from colostomy to urostomy care.
pmc-13487166:
