Benedetti and team zapped soil with pulsed electric fields to kill weeds, parasitic worms, and plant pathogens without chemicals. Short high-voltage pulses rupture cell membranes, a process called electroporation. Their 2026 study compared two applicator shapes, vertical pins and parallel plates, across field strengths, pulse rates, and total energy doses. Model runs guided the work, showing how evenly each shape spreads the field.

Parallel plates produced the more uniform field and the stronger pest suppression, matching the simulations. A stubborn weed, yellow nutsedge, shrank steadily as energy dose rose and fell significantly at the higher doses tested. One root-knot nematode species was wiped out completely at modest dose when pulse frequency passed 60 cycles per second. Two nematode species fell by more than 98 percent at the strongest field setting. Benedetti sees plate applicators as the practical design.
pmc-13487566:
Maria Zofia Lisiecka and Joanna Luczak review the medical side of latex allergy, from glove proteins to prevention in hospitals. Published in 2026, the synthesis gathers systematic reviews, clinical and epidemiological studies, and case reports from 2013 to 2025. Most reactions trace to immune responses against natural rubber proteins or against chemicals added during manufacturing.

Two allergens carry the highest potency for healthcare workers, while children needing repeated operations sensitize mainly to two different allergens. Exposure arrives through skin, inhaled glove powder, or direct entry during procedures, and reactions span hives and hay fever up to anaphylaxis. Skin prick testing, blood antibody checks, and molecular component testing structure diagnosis. Sensitization reaches as high as 22 percent among heavily exposed staff, making glove policy an occupational safety lever.
pmc-13488066:
Jordan Stanford, Holly Supple, Clare E. Collins, and Erin D. Clarke explore links among diet, blood chemistry, gut microbes, and blood pressure in Australian adults in a 2026 exploratory study. Data came from thirty-four adults with full baseline measures in a crossover trial. Diet was recorded with a food frequency questionnaire, while blood and urine chemistry were profiled broadly and stool microbes were sequenced.

Nut eating was the only food factor tied to blood pressure, with higher intake linked to slightly lower systolic pressure. Twenty-nine blood fat molecules also tracked with systolic pressure, and nine of them partly explained the nut link in mediation models. No urine markers or gut microbes showed clear ties. The authors treat all findings as early clues needing larger studies.
pmc-13488266:
Zul-kifl Affolabi and a large team survey trypanosome parasites in blood-feeding flies in southern Benin in a 2026 field study. The parasites cause African animal trypanosomosis, a livestock disease that cuts farm productivity. More than six thousand flies were trapped in six communes across dry and rainy seasons, and 384 were tested with species-specific DNA methods, while engorged flies had their last blood meals identified.

About fourteen percent of tested flies carried trypanosomes, chiefly two species that infect cattle. Infection ran highest in two communes and somewhat higher in the dry season, without a firm statistical gap. Cattle blood dominated the meals found, with human blood second. The authors argue that flies beyond tsetse deserve a place in surveillance.
pmc-13488566:
Caitlin M. Meyer and colleagues ask Illinois caregivers about finding their way through health care for children with special health needs in a 2026 study based on group talks. The work formed part of a needs check covering the whole state. Three group talks brought together twenty-two caregivers of children and youth with disabilities or complex health needs. They were reached through partner groups, and they spoke of daily care burdens and the resources that help.

Caregivers described emotional and practical strain, plus money strain, driven by split-up services and insurance systems. Poor contact between providers, clashing computer records, scarce specialists, and patchy home nursing all added work. Gaps in cover, prior go-ahead hurdles, and supply shortfalls deepened the load. Families praised team-based care and help finding their way, asking for broader joined-up care and mental health support.
pmc-13490266:
Theofanis Liatis, Alison Robertson, and Alberta De Stefani describe muscle jerking after resuscitation in a cat and a dog in a 2026 veterinary case series. In people, acute post-hypoxic myoclonus means rhythmic jerking that follows brain oxygen loss after cardiac arrest, usually starting within two days while the patient remains comatose. Whether the same sign occurs in pets after successful resuscitation had not been documented in this form.

Both animals arrested, received CPR, and regained circulation, then developed presumed post-hypoxic jerking within twenty-four hours. Seizure medicines and sedatives failed to stop the movements in either case. Both animals were euthanized. The authors establish that the syndrome can occur in cats and dogs, and they note that human prognosis reading now weighs brain wave patterns alongside the jerking itself.
pmc-13490366:
Kim and team tested an extract from a salt-loving Korean coastal plant against MRSA, the antibiotic-resistant staph bacterium that plagues hospitals. Rather than trying to kill the bacterium outright, which breeds more resistance, they attacked its biofilm, the slime city bacteria build to shield themselves. Their 2026 study used the butanol fraction of Artemisia fukudo, checking biofilm growth, gene activity, cell infection, and survival of infected roundworms.

The fraction blocked biofilm formation without slowing bacterial growth or dissolving existing film, pointing to a pure anti-attachment effect. Genes for the surface adhesion machinery were dialed down in treated bacteria. Fewer bacteria attached to and invaded human lung cells in culture after treatment. Infected worms lived longer when exposed to the fraction, with no toxicity signs. Kim proposes adhesion blockers as a gentler class of anti-infective worth developing.
pmc-13491066:
Etchegaray commented on new multiomics evidence explaining why the intestines of premature babies with necrotizing enterocolitis fail to heal. The disease destroys the gut lining of preterm infants and kills many, and its repair failure was mechanistically murky. The 2026 commentary walks through a study by Xiong and colleagues that profiled single cell nuclei, chromatin access, and spatial gene activity in diseased tissue, centering on the silencing protein EZH2.

Damage disrupted EZH2's placement on genes controlling the Wnt pathway, the gut's main renewal signal, in the work under discussion. Key stem-cell genes, including Lgr5, lost their proper regulation, compromising the stem cells that rebuild the lining. Inflammatory genes such as IL6 switched on in parallel, feeding the destruction. Etchegaray notes a single mouse model and small samples limit certainty, and urges human tissue validation next.
pmc-13491266:
Jenny Schuster and Robert VanBuren synthesize how plants survive near-total drying in a 2026 review of desiccation tolerance. A small set of plants can lose almost all cellular water and revive on rewetting. That trick likely helped early land plants and still serves in harsh, dry habitats. A decade of genome-scale, comparative, and functional work is weighed for shared mechanisms across the green lineage and beyond. The review gives special weight to the strain drying puts on sunlit, photosynthetic tissue.

Tolerance appears to be rebuilt from ancient stress toolkits rather than invented fresh. Unrelated lineages converge on similar protection for cells and light-harvesting gear during drying and recovery in the synthesis offered. The authors treat tolerance as a whole-system trait and weigh uses in crops, medicine, and biotechnology.
pmc-13491766:
Haifeng Liu and four colleagues compare in 2026 two endoscopic operations for lumbar disc herniation where the slipped disc fragment has migrated far downward. One method uses two portals, the other a single interlaminar route, and both aim to relieve nerve pressure through small openings. Records covered sixty-one patients followed for twelve months after surgery.

The two-portal group finished operations faster and showed a wider cleared spinal canal with less leftover disc material afterward. That group also lost more blood, stayed in hospital longer, and reported worse back pain three days after surgery, with more shrinkage of back muscles on scans. Pain, disability, complication rates, and standard success ratings ended up similar overall. The authors advise choosing by surgeon experience and each patient's anatomy.
pmc-13492266: DeWitt and nine co-authors published a correction in 2026 to their review of PFAS toxicity, the health harms of a large class of long lasting industrial chemicals. The fix repairs errors in the in-text citations and the reference list. Three corrected paragraphs are printed in full, covering how these chemicals bind body proteins, strain cells, and build risk over time. One passage deals with a large health study near Parkersburg, West Virginia, where a factory fouled drinking water for decades.
pmc-13492866:
Hernández Díaz and colleagues asked nursing students in 2026 how useful they find research training during their degree. Learning to do research is meant to sharpen critical thinking and ground nursing care in evidence. The team wanted the students' own view of what that training gives them and where it falls short.

Twelve fourth-year students took part in two focus groups held in late 2024, and their answers were sorted into themes. Students named three gains: handy research tools, growth in skills such as critical thinking and scientific writing, and ideas for making training stronger. They valued how research links theory to ward practice. They also faulted uneven methods teaching by staff and weak support for publishing student work. The authors call for policies that make research a thread through the whole nursing program.
pmc-13493766:
Sanati and colleagues propose a 2026 method for judging artificial intelligence models that classify Alzheimer's disease from brain scans. Their model mixes two network types, one that reads image patterns and one that tracks sequences, and sorted 827 people from the ADNI database into healthy, mildly impaired, or Alzheimer's groups. Synthetic extra scans, generated only for training, helped offset the limited data. The novelty lies in how they graded the finished model, using information theory rather than accuracy alone.

The classifier reached high accuracy, correctly labelling most test subjects across the three groups under a strict subject-level protocol. The added measures showed how much useful information the model kept and how closely its outputs matched the real spread of cases. The authors argue such checks make medical AI easier to trust, but they insist on testing with scans from other hospitals before any clinical use.
pmc-13493866:
Abdul Hafez and Odeh present HOGNet, a small neural network that helps robots and vehicles recognise places they have seen before from camera images. Instead of learning everything from huge labelled collections, their 2026 model is supervised by a classic handcrafted descriptor called HOG, which summarises edge directions in an image. The network learns to predict those summaries, gaining interpretability and needing far less training data and computing power than giant image models.

On two demanding test sets, the compact variant recalled the correct place within its top twenty guesses more often than the much larger VGG16 network managed. It also ran about thirty-six times faster per image, reaching roughly 290 frames per second, fast enough for real-time use on modest hardware. Removing the HOG supervision cost several points of accuracy in a control experiment, confirming the handcrafted targets do real work.
pmc-13493966:
Xing Lv leads a seventeen-author team reporting in 2026 that the body's own stress signal can protect lungs in acute respiratory distress syndrome, a flooding inflammation that suffocates patients. The messenger norepinephrine was tested on lung macrophages poisoned with bacterial toxin in dishes, and its receptor's activator drug, salbutamol, was given to septic mice. The question was whether nerve signals could stop a rust-like cell death called ferroptosis.

Treated macrophages kept their mitochondria intact, limited fat oxidation damage, and survived better, powered by two antioxidant defenders switched on downstream. Blocking the receptor or the enzyme HDC erased the protection, pinning the mechanism down. In mice, salbutamol raised the same defenders in lung macrophages and eased tissue injury, nominating the pathway as a drug target.
pmc-13494266:
Kok-Siong Poon, Karen Mei-Ling Tan, and Nor Azian Abdul Murad write a 2026 letter to the editor raising doubts about a published testing pipeline for primary mitochondrial diseases. The study they discuss compared older methods with nanopore sequencing as a way to find faults in mitochondrial DNA. Their letter works through the validation and finds gaps.

One figure, they note, shows a different DNA change than the one the text names, which needs clearing up. The study also gave no read depth for the nanopore runs, yet depth decides whether rare mixed variants can be spotted, and no detection limit was set for that platform. All 22 patients tested by nanopore came back negative, which the letter writers find worrying without tests on known positive cases. They also note the study read short fragments, wasting the method's long-read strength, and ask for fuller validation.
pmc-13499666:
Alma Ramić and co-authors report in 2026 a combined lab and computer study of new molecules designed to block two enzymes that break down a key brain messenger. Both enzymes feature in Alzheimer's disease and related conditions, and selective blocking is a long-standing treatment strategy. Eleven peptide-like molecules were built through a four-component chemical reaction that assembles varied structures quickly, then tested against the human forms of both enzymes.

Every compound reversibly slowed both enzymes at micromolar levels, a modest strength range. Two stood out for strong preference for the second enzyme, favouring it by well over a hundredfold in the reported comparisons. Statistical grouping sorted compounds by which enzyme they preferred, and quantum-level docking simulations showed stacking interactions inside the favoured enzyme that explain the selectivity. The scaffold gives designers a tested starting point for stronger, more selective blockers.
pmc-13499866:
Aquila and Sacco study how a deceased person's body size changes the autopsy itself. Their 2026 prospective study timed fifty consecutive medico-legal autopsies for natural deaths, half on obese bodies and half on non-obese controls matched for age and sex, all following one strict protocol. The operators also took a vigilance test, the Mackworth Clock Test of sustained attention, before and after each case to see how demanding dissections wear down concentration.

Obese cases took markedly longer, averaging roughly thirty-five minutes more from first incision to organ removal on the study's timing, and were rated far more technically difficult. Attention suffered accordingly: missed signals on the vigilance test roughly doubled after obese cases compared with controls. The authors argue rising obesity means forensic units should plan staffing, scheduling, and double-checking around the heavier cognitive load these cases impose.
pmc-13499966:
Richard Lehnert and co-authors report in 2026 an endocrine disorder first spotted because a grown man's shinbone X-ray showed growth plates that had never closed. The condition, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, means the brain's hormone signal for puberty runs too low, leaving sex hormones minimal and sexual development stalled, and it usually surfaces in adolescence. Their patient, a 26-year-old Vietnamese man, came to emergency care in December 2022 with a spiral shin fracture from a work accident.

Examination found absent secondary sexual features, and blood tests showed testosterone and its two upstream pituitary hormones far below reference ranges, confirming the diagnosis while other pituitary tests stayed normal. A childhood mumps history raised the possibility of gland inflammation as background. The fracture was fixed with a rod inside the bone, hormone replacement injections every three months began after endocrine consultation, and the authors flag open growth plates as a diagnostic clue.
pmc-13500466:
Lihua Zhou and co-authors mine in 2026 gene data for prognostic signals in lung adenocarcinoma tied to phosphoinositide metabolism, a fat-molecule signalling system that helps govern cell growth. Public databases supplied tumour data, and differential expression screening, survival regression, and machine learning narrowed the field to candidate genes. A risk model split patients into high and low risk groups, and a combined chart added tumour stage to estimate individual outlook.

Four genes survived the screening as prognostic markers, and the model plus chart predicted survival well in the reported evaluations. Pathway analysis tied aggressive disease to protein synthesis, aberrant nerve-signal receptor activity, and anti-tumour immune responses. The two risk groups also differed in immune cell mix, mutation patterns, and sensitivity to many drugs. Single-cell data flagged epithelial cells as the key arena, with marker genes shifting as those cells matured.
pmc-13501766:
Ferenc Dőri leads a four-author team with a 2026 randomized trial comparing two repair materials for gum defects where bone has been lost between teeth. Thirty patients with periodontitis were assigned to surgery using platelet-rich fibrin, a concentrate made from the patient's blood, or enamel matrix derivative, an established biologic. The outcome was clinical attachment gain, with pocket depth, gum recession, and bone sounding as secondary measures, checked at six months and three years.

Twenty-six patients finished three years, and both treatments improved matters a lot, with gains that held steady. At three years, attachment gain averaged 3.77 millimetres with the fibrin approach and 2.54 millimetres with the derivative, a difference that did not reach significance. Pocket reductions were similar. Gum recession increased far less in the fibrin group at three years, the one between-group difference. The authors call the blood-based option a reliable homegrown alternative.
pmc-13503066:
Je-Hyun Kim and others test whether metabolic syndrome predicts Parkinson disease in Korean adults. In 2026, the National Health Insurance sample cohort follows 363,602 adults aged forty or older without prior Parkinson disease from examinations in 2010 to 2014 through 2019, with mean follow-up of 8.2 years. During follow-up, 2,834 new Parkinson cases appeared.

Energy syndrome raised Parkinson risk by about twenty-two percent after full adjustment, driven by belly obesity and raised fasting glucose, each raising risk by about twenty percent. Risk climbed as the number of syndrome components increased. The authors suggest that managing metabolic syndrome, mainly waist size and blood sugar, could reduce future Parkinson burden.
pmc-13503666:
Hongchang Zhang leads a large team studying how prostate cancer feeds its growth, in a 2026 paper. They focus on the breakdown of tryptophan, an amino acid, inside tumor cells. One cell group in the tumors makes a lot of an enzyme called HAAO and builds up a product named quinolinic acid.

The acid binds to and steadies a second enzyme, FDPS, which helps the cell make cholesterol. That boost feeds the androgen receptor, the switch that drives prostate tumor growth. A risk score built on this path beat standard clinical facts on its own. Tumors high in HAAO also responded more to a paired block of the two paths, which points to a new drug target.
pmc-13503766:
Augustine Amalraj leads a computer study of a plant-based blend sold to support testosterone and muscle, in a 2026 paper. The blend, called Testolift, mixes four plant compounds. Falling testosterone harms muscle, stamina, and metabolic health, while long-term hormone therapy has limits that push interest in gentler options.

The team screened the four compounds against three protein targets tied to hormone balance, muscle growth brakes, and oxygen use. Computer docking put each compound into the target pockets, and motion runs of 150 nanoseconds showed the pairs held steady. Two flavone compounds had the best drug-like traits and gut uptake on paper. Safety screens also looked fair. The authors say lab tests must come next to check the claims.
pmc-13504966:
Buşra Parlak Insel and others evaluate a bioactive fissure sealant containing microcapsules on man-made enamel lesions. In 2026, the study compares the bioactive sealant with a standard resin sealant, with and without a universal adhesive, on extracted human molars. It tests dye-penetration microleakage after thermocycling and mineral changes after thirty days of pH cycling. Early caries can be arrested by minimally invasive prevention.

Microleakage did not differ clearly between sealants, and adhesive pretreatment changed neither microleakage nor remineralization. The bioactive sealant produced greater mineral gains across depths, with increased calcium, phosphorus, and fluoride, while the standard sealant remineralized only shallow layers. Bioactive sealants may better restore initial lesions, pending medical confirmation.
pmc-13505066:
Hasti Naderlou leads a team linking dietary omega fats and body weight to depressive symptoms in young Iranian adults, in a 2026 study. Omega-3 fats support brain and heart health, while a high omega-6 to omega-3 balance may feed inflammation. Young adults face both tight food budgets and high rates of low mood.

The study covered 440 university students aged eighteen to thirty, with diet from a food survey and mood from a standard inventory. Higher body mass went with higher odds of depressive symptoms. Students in the top fifth for omega-3 intake had about a third the odds of the bottom fifth. A high omega ratio told the opposite story, near tenfold odds at the top. The authors call for trials to test cause.
pmc-13505166:
Salih Düzgün and others test rinse stirring methods for taking out root canal filling matter in redo work. In 2026, the lab study uses 117 same-form 3D-printed replica upper-jaw front teeth filled with GuttaFlow, sorted across canal bends of fifteen, thirty, and forty-five degrees and three rinse plans. It tests remnant volume by cone beam machine scans. Redo failure often stems from lasting illness behind left filling.

Bend clearly shaped remnant volume, with apical-third residue rising from 0.51 cubic mm at fifteen degrees to 1.80 cubic mm at forty-five degrees. Rinse methods did not differ clearly. Doctors should treat bend as the key redo factor, fitting plans mainly for highly curved canals.
pmc-13505266:
Sara Moufarrij and co-authors, writing with a FIGO committee, review four recent prospective trials on doing less radical surgery for low-risk early cervical cancer. Standard radical hysterectomy cures many women but can damage bladder and bowel function, end fertility, and harm sexual health. The trials tested cone biopsy or simple hysterectomy, each with lymph node checks, against that standard.

Recurrence stayed low across the gentler options, with cone biopsy groups showing only a few percent of cancers returning within three years. Simple hysterectomy matched radical surgery for pelvic recurrence and survival in the largest trial, and complication rates looked similar where reported. From this evidence the authors propose strict selection rules covering tumour size, scan findings, tissue type, and depth of spread. Women who meet those rules could keep their fertility and quality of life without giving up cancer control.
pmc-13507166:
Jeonghyun Kim, Diana Bajare, and Donwoo Lee ask, in 2026 work, how machine learning models for concrete strength should handle cement additives made from industrial by-products. Such additives, called supplementary cementitious materials, each react differently, so modelers must choose between listing each one apart or lumping them into a single total. Thirteen databases grounded the comparison.

Separate inputs usually predicted strength more accurately than lumped inputs. When additives pushed strength in opposing directions, lumping let their signals cancel and hid true causes. Explanation tools confirmed cleaner physical logic with separate inputs. Lumping still helped in simple mixes where one factor, such as age, dominated. The choice should follow mix complexity, not habit.
pmc-13507266:
Yaobin Wang leads a 2026 team that engineers a perovskite catalyst able to make hydroxyl radicals from oxygen in one direct three-electron step. Hydroxyl radicals shred stubborn pollutants in electrochemical water treatment, but usual routes detour through hydrogen peroxide, losing intermediates between sites. Their crystal hosts a single zinc active center with a molybdenum neighbor.

Zinc gently holds the peroxide intermediates while molybdenum polarizes their oxygen atoms, easing bond cleavage on the spot. Radical output reached 821 micromoles per hour, and oxygen use hit 37.7 percent in bench tests. A membrane-free flow cell using plain oxygen gas pushed overall efficiency to 64.7 percent. Wastewater cleanup could skip chemical dosing.
pmc-13508266:
Feroz Kabir leads an eleven-author trial comparing ways to deliver exercise therapy for long COVID fatigue in Bangladesh, in 2026 work. Long COVID can leave lasting fatigue, pain, and disability. Rehab exercise helps, yet patients can receive it in hospital, by remote sessions, or as a home plan. The trial enrolled 145 adults whose fatigue syndrome followed long COVID, drawn from across eight regions of the country. Participants were assigned to one of the three delivery routes.

Hospital and remote groups both got therapist-led sessions of 45 minutes, twice a week for eight weeks. The home group exercised alone after structured teaching. Fatigue was the main outcome, scored on a standard scale. Quality of life, years of healthy life lost, and heart and lung measures were also tracked. The design lets planners weigh whether remote rehab can match hospital care for patients far from major centers.
pmc-13508466:
Luo, in a 2026 conceptual essay, proposes that spectroscopy and artificial intelligence meet in one idea: the token. Modern AI works by chopping the world into discrete units called tokens and learning the statistical grammar between them. Luo argues that spectra, the fingerprints matter leaves when it interacts with light, form a natural token system of the physical world. It is written not by convention but by quantum mechanics and electrodynamics themselves.

The essay defines physical tokens at four levels. Raw quantum transitions are fixed by energy levels and selection rules. Visible features include peaks and line shapes. Machine-ready chunks include spectral patches, and hidden representations sit inside trained models. Framed this way, spectroscopy stops being just a measurement tool and becomes an information substrate, a language of matter that AI can learn to read, connect, interpret, and even generate.
pmc-13509166:
Han Zhang and five co-authors test a Chinese herbal pill on brain immune cells in the dish, in 2026 work. Brain inflammation sits at the core of many degenerative brain diseases. The pill, Kongsheng Zhenzhong, is famed for calming and sharpening effects, yet its cell-level action was unclear. The team set up inflammation in a mouse microglia cell line using a bacterial toxin. Doses were then tested for effects on activation, inflammation, oxidative stress, and cell death, with computer docking and protein reading to trace the route.

Profiling found sixty-seven compounds, led by flavonoids and plant chemicals. Treatment calmed the cells in a dose-linked way and cut their release of inflammatory factors. It also eased oxidative stress, protected cell power units, and reduced toxin-driven death. Docking suggested ingredients fit two proteins in a danger-sensing pathway, and protein tests confirmed that pathway quieted with dose.
pmc-13509766:
Meiser and co-authors built bispecific antibodies in 2026 that recruit neutrophils and macrophages, two white blood cell types, to attack tumors. The antibodies grab CD89, the receptor for immunoglobulin A antibodies, on the immune cells with one arm and EGFR, a common tumor surface protein, with the other. IgA-based drugs are potent but hard to make and short-lived, so the team built that function into a standard antibody frame instead.

Using yeast display, they made the bispecific candidates and tested their traits, neutrophil killing, and macrophage eating of tumor cells in the lab. The constructs drove strong neutrophil cytotoxicity and macrophage phagocytosis, and a symmetric two-plus-two design with a silenced Fc region, the antibody tail, did best across both cell types. Silencing the Fc region strengthened neutrophil killing and caused no friendly-fire damage to immune cells. The authors support further preclinical testing.
pmc-13510166:
Alexandr Shevtsov and nine co-authors describe a cell line adapted to grow floating in liquid, built to make virus-based delivery particles for CAR-T therapy at larger scale, in 2026 work. Making these particles in flat, attached cell layers is hard to scale up. The team adapted a common human cell line to a serum-free medium and checked growth, stability over 35 passages, and the best settings for adding DNA.

The adapted cells stayed healthy and grew at a steady rate across all passages checked. Tuning the mix of DNA and carrier, plus adding DNA at very high cell density, lifted working particle output in the liquid. One-liter batches yielded large particle counts, and the particles entered human T cells well in a closed clinical device. The authors offer the platform as a cheaper, scalable route for academic therapy centers.
pmc-13511266:
Rachana R. Borkar, Sai Dhanush Reddy Jeggari, Kamal Kandel, Kaviya Partheepan, Nishant Sharma, and Sandeep Samethadka Nayak review low-field and portable magnetic resonance scanners for stroke from a blocked vessel, in 2026 work. Standard scanners give key images yet demand heavy infrastructure, patient transport, and wide access that many settings lack. The team searched four databases through May 2026 for studies of portable systems at or below a set field strength in adults with suspected stroke.

Portable scanners allowed safe imaging at the bedside in emergency and intensive care rooms, and they caught most strokes that matter for care choices. Very small blocked spots, under about five to six millimeters, were missed more often than with standard machines. Performance turned on spot size and field strength. The authors say portable units can widen timely access where standard imaging is missing or delayed, pending stronger shared proof.
pmc-13511966:
Jianhui Guo and eight co-authors review biodegradable hydrogels built from biomass for removing lead ions from water, in 2026 work. Lead is highly toxic, builds up in living tissue, and resists breakdown, while standard removal methods can pollute anew, cost much, or eat energy. Adsorption onto hydrogels offers a simpler, renewable route that works well even at low lead levels.

The review covers gels made from cellulose, lignin, seaweed alginate, chitosan, and starch, plus composites that add inorganic, carbon, or framework materials. For each family it lays out structure, cross-linking routes, and ways to add grabbing groups. Lead capture works through several grips at once, including chemical binding, ion swapping, and electric attraction. The authors weigh capacity, reuse, and full breakdown, then mark gaps that must close before these gels can treat real wastewater at scale.
pmc-13513066:
Maria Lucia Cocato and five co-authors feed juvenile Nile tilapia diets containing meal from yellow mealworms or black soldier fly larvae for 82 days, in 2026 work. Fish farming leans on pricey protein feeds with a heavy environmental cost, and insects offer a leaner source. Growth, nutrient use, and blood health were tracked, then fish faced a bacterial challenge common in tilapia farming.

Insect diets did not cut growth or body condition. Fat digestion stayed high, while protein digestion varied by insect source. Some blood cell shares shifted, hinting that the diets touched the immune system. After infection, fish on insect diets died at lower rates than controls, though the gap fell short of statistical proof. The authors back both meals as promising sustainable feed ingredients.
pmc-13517366:
Oscar Sánchez-Carranza and three colleagues profile botulinum toxin machinery in human Schwann cells in a 2026 laboratory study. Schwann cells wrap peripheral nerves and lead repair after injury, switching between myelinating and fix-it states. Botulinum toxin type A eases nerve pain and may help these cells, yet nobody had mapped its docking parts. The team grew primary human Schwann cells and read the genes for the toxin's receptors and its protein target.

The cells carried moderate levels of both receptor parts and of the target, SNAP25, . A chemotherapy drug, paclitaxel, then shifted the profile: receptor genes fell up to twofold, the target and a wrapping marker rose, and a repair marker dropped. Sánchez-Carranza's team reads this as a drift toward a more mature state. The toxin's hardware exists in these non-nerve cells, which supports studying it for nerve repair.
pmc-13518866:
Jin Ming Koh and four colleagues run a 2026 experiment on a superconducting quantum processor to watch energy leak in unusual ways. In so-called non-Hermitian systems, loss can pile up briefly at the edges instead of fading evenly, a behavior called an edge burst. Interacting many-particle versions had never been observed because they are hard to build.

The team built a digital simulation method that stays efficient in circuit size, then ran an interacting ladder model across up to 64 unit cells. Edge bursts appeared, stretched, and formed patterns under interactions, while surprise cluster bursts flared inside the bulk. Koh and co-authors present quantum processors as a flexible testbed for loss-driven physics.
pmc-13520166:
Muhammed Ikbal Sasmaz leads a seven-author forward-looking study in 2026 pitting emergency doctors' gut judgment against two scoring rules for suspected pulmonary embolism, a dangerous lung artery blockage. Short breath and chest pain hint at the blockage without proving it, so sizing up the odds guides testing. Two large referral hospitals took in 248 patients with suspected embolism.

The blockage was confirmed in 38 patients, or 15.3 percent. A doctor's free-form clinical judgment did slightly better than either rule, with an area under the curve of 0.834 versus 0.766 for the Wells score and 0.757 for the Revised Geneva score. Sasmaz's team concludes seasoned clinical assessment remains a valuable part of the diagnostic pathway.
pmc-13520266:
Shuhua Deng and colleagues reviewed thigh-bone breaks after hip bone surgery in children born with shallow hip sockets. Published in 2026, the study looked back at 153 children treated with open reduction and proximal femoral osteotomy at one hospital from 2014 through 2020. Plates used to hold the bone can leave weak spots when fitted or removed, so the team tracked when and where breaks occurred.

Six children, about four percent, suffered a later thigh-bone fracture, at ages two to eight. Four breaks followed plate removal, mostly after falls, and all sat at the surgery site, while retained plates broke near screw holes. Half the fractures were treated with casting under anesthesia and half with flexible nails. The authors advise removing plates only after solid healing and holding back high-intensity activity until remodeling shows. Readers get a cautious timetable for a rare but costly complication.
pmc-13520466:
Yangsi Huang leads a 2026 randomised trial comparing two numbing drugs for chest-wall blocks in heart surgery through the breastbone, where pain control shapes recovery. One group received a long-acting liposomal form of bupivacaine, while the other received standard ropivacaine, each for combined parasternal and rectus sheath blocks.

Ninety patients were enrolled, with 88 completing the study. Pain scores, total painkiller use in morphine equivalents, recovery quality scores and side effects were recorded across time points. Early results at twenty-four and forty-eight hours begin the comparison in the opening summary. Findings should help anaesthesia teams choose between a pricier long-acting option and a standard drug.
pmc-13522066:
Marie Bjerg Larsen, Ida Kaad Faurschou and Susanne Haas ask in 2026 if skin stitch style shapes healing after cleft lift surgery. The surgery treats complex pilonidal disease near the tailbone. Records held 540 patients treated from 2016 to 2022 at one Danish hospital.

A mid-period switch in stitch style made two natural groups. Surface stitches faced buried stitches. Primary healing hit 76 percent in both groups. Healing time showed no gap at all. Five-year return rates sat near nine and six percent, with no firm gap. Slow healers returned at twice the rate of fast healers. Wound care focus should shift to preventing early wound splits.
pmc-13522466:
Angyang Guo and colleagues showed that fairness fixes for clinical language models can fail when models move to a new hospital. Published in 2026, the study tuned a clinical BERT model on one intensive care database and tested it on another, predicting ICU mortality. Fairness work aims for equal performance across patient groups, yet most tests stay inside one hospital.

Fairness-only training looked best at home but worst away, with its fairness gap growing nearly fivefold across sites. The team traced the failure to hospital-specific writing habits leaking into the model, which interacted with patient-group signals in new settings. A leakage-aware training recipe cut the outside gap sharply while lifting accuracy. The authors urge domain-aware fairness audits before any cross-hospital rollout.
pmc-13522966:
Mandeep Singh and colleagues report a case of heart valve infection whose infected clots scattered through the body of a woman with weakened immunity. She was 50, with neck-of-womb cancer, and on two immune-suppressing cancer drugs.

She arrived with fever, blistering skin sores, a rash, and new weakness down her right side. Scans showed lung cavities, liver spots, and ring-shaped brain lesions that looked like spread cancer or abscesses. Cultures from her hand and foot sores grew Streptococcus pyogenes, pointing to infection rather than tumour spread. Strong antibiotics brought clear improvement without brain surgery, and Singh urges early team review when infection mimics cancer.
pmc-13523266:
Nurmuhammet Taş and colleagues build a scoring framework for checking source lists generated by chatbots in a 2026 cross-platform study. Three chatbots were prompted under thirty medical headings in two output formats, producing more than three thousand entries. Each entry was scored for whether it could be found and verified, for record accuracy, for identifier validity, and for topical relevance.

Total scores differed clearly between models, yet the overall effect size was very small, meaning the practical gap was modest. Longer outputs in review format showed somewhat weaker record stability, with differences shrinking after correction. The authors position their score less as a league table and more as a reusable, instrument-neutral framework for large-scale trust studies of generated source lists.
pmc-13523366:
Maurits A W Unkel, Jeff A Beeler, Steven A Kushner, and Femke M S de Vrij present a software tool for gene set enrichment analysis in a 2026 paper. Enrichment analysis asks whether a defined set of genes changes together between conditions. Many existing tools require programming skill, stop at listing top terms, or cannot compare several contrasts at once. Their application runs in a common statistical environment with a point-and-click interface.

The tool extends an ordinal association method with interactive plots, multi-contrast comparison, and gene and network context for exploring pathways from the bottom up. A demonstration on paired protein and RNA data from one dataset found hundreds of shared genes for focused analysis. A strict interaction threshold highlighted high-confidence protein links, supporting hypothesis generation for users with or without coding experience.
pmc-13523466:
Jinsung Park and colleagues trace, in a 2026 animal study, the order in which blood vessels, nerves, and tendon matrix change as patellar tendinopathy develops. The painful kneecap tendon condition is common in jumping athletes, yet the sequence behind its progression was unclear. The team hypothesized that early new vessel growth starts a chain leading to nerve changes and tendon breakdown.

Forty male rats received collagenase injections to model the condition, with groups examined at two, four, eight, and twelve weeks alongside a control group. Vessel markers rose first, by week four, followed by smooth muscle and pain-related nerve markers at week eight. Matrix gene signals peaked early for some collagens and later for others. The sequence suggests vessel growth may set later neural and structural change in motion.
pmc-13524466:
Xiyao Cui and colleagues report a 2026 vaccine study against avian reovirus, a poultry virus causing arthritis, gut disease, and immune suppression with heavy economic losses. Older vaccines based on the S1133 strain protect poorly against current variants. The team built a vaccine using a human adenovirus vector carrying the viral sigma C protein, the main target of neutralizing antibodies.

The construct expressed the protein stably across thirteen passages in the laboratory. One-day-old specific-pathogen-free chickens receiving the vaccine produced strong antibody responses within a week, plus higher levels of two immune signaling molecules, showing both antibody and cellular activation. After challenge with a prevalent field strain, protection reached 86 percent, with reduced shedding, lower tissue virus loads, and milder organ damage than in unvaccinated controls.
pmc-13524966:
Edson Fiorenza-Neto leads a large team in a 2026 rat study testing whether damaging the olfactory bulb with a neurotoxin can model early cortical dysfunction seen before motor Parkinson's disease. The smell bulb is among the first regions affected in neurodegeneration and connects widely to cortex and limbic areas. The toxin 6-OHDA was injected into the left bulb.

Twelve days after surgery, lesioned animals showed altered exploration in an open field, spending more time in the center. Cortical tissue showed higher IL-6, lower interferon gamma, and unchanged levels of several other immune signals. Oxidative damage markers rose, while antioxidant enzyme activity and three neuronal signaling genes stayed unchanged. The authors argue a local bulb lesion alone can trigger behavioral, inflammatory, and oxidative change in connected cortex.
pmc-13525366:
Sánchez-Paredes and colleagues in Mexico took in 2026 the first broad blood count of silent spread of a dry land fungus in Sonora. The fungus, Coccidioides, lives in desert soil and can sicken lungs when its dust is breathed. Sonora logs the most ward cases in the land, yet how many folk meet it with no ills was not known. The team tested 534 blood samples from labs in towns across the state for the scar mark of past meet.

About seven in a hundred samples bore the mark, and a big share more sat in a gray zone. Nine towns showed clear spread. Young adults bore the mark most, and most with it had not been to the known United States zones. Of the weather marks checked, just one split the towns: how much heat swings by season.
pmc-13525466:
Ganashree and co-authors test whether intensive training sticks, in this 2026 pre-post study. The topic is airway management, the emergency skill of keeping a patient's airway open. The trainees were 100 medical interns at an Indian teaching hospital. The interns took a five-day Emergency Care and Life Support course of lectures, skill stations, and simulations, then were tested before, right after, and following each later clinical rotation.

Knowledge jumped at once: mean scenario scores rose from 12.56 before the course to 17.74 just after it, a highly significant gain. Practical skills then held steady through emergency medicine and improved further after general medicine, ear-nose-throat, and anesthesiology rotations, peaking at 19.64 after anesthesiology in the checklist scores. The outlier was obstetrics and gynecology, where skills slipped significantly to 17.47, reflecting little airway practice. Confidence rose throughout internship. The authors recommend scheduled refresher boosters so rotations without airway exposure cannot erode the competence.
pmc-13526866:
Hiroaki Masuoka and others profile, in a 2026 study, gut bacteria and stool chemicals tied to fatigue in healthy Japanese adults. Fatigue from built-up stress may come before psychiatric illness, and an upset gut appears in many such disorders, yet the marks in healthy tired people were unknown.

Tired people carried fewer helpful bacteria and more Escherichia coli than rested peers. Profiling showed more oxidative-stress pathways and fewer energy-making ones, and stool citrate, a key energy chemical, was lower. Some gut shifts matched patterns noted in psychiatric disorders and in chronic fatigue syndrome data sets. The authors frame the findings as links tying fatigue with oxidative stress and poor energy use, as groundwork for follow-up work on causes.
pmc-13527266:
Urman and colleagues present a 2026 imaging method that rebuilds sharp three-dimensional scans from a fast magnetic resonance technique called fingerprinting. It measures tissue traits in one quick pass, but turning signals into sharp 3D images takes heavy computing, and common fixes blur at high speed-up. Their method, SPUR-iG, learns part of the rebuild and grids raw signals with learned kernels instead of slow transforms.

Full 3D training is slow, so the team trained it in stages, each lifting quality while keeping run times in reach. At one-millimeter detail, SPUR-iG beat both a standard rebuild and a recent hybrid method that mixes 2D and 3D steps. It also held up on scans from a different maker's machines, a hard test for learned systems. Faster, sharper fingerprinting could bring precise tissue measures into routine care.
pmc-13527966:
Ebenezer Kwesi Armah-Ansah and five colleagues analyze home childbirth among rural women across 28 African countries in a 2026 study. They pooled Demographic and Health Surveys from 2011 to 2024. The weighted sample held 103,011 women of reproductive age. Home birth matters because skilled help is often absent when problems arise.

Overall, about 34 percent of rural women delivered at home. Rates ranged from under 6 percent in Rwanda to over 85 percent in Chad. Women with four or more births had roughly double the odds of home delivery. Living in Central Africa also raised the odds. Mistimed or unwanted pregnancies were linked with lower odds. The authors recommend programs aimed at high-parity women and heavier investment in Central Africa.
pmc-13528066:
Akhere E. Oshodin and three colleagues report a 2026 case of mpox that first looked like two common infections in Nigeria. A 21-year-old woman developed a painful vulvar ulcer three days after intercourse. Doctors first treated her for genital herpes. She worsened, with swelling, severe pain, swollen groin glands, and high fever. A new guess of chancroid brought antibiotics.

Days later a blistering rash spread over her trunk, limbs, palms, and soles. Lab testing then confirmed mpox. Supportive care plus the antibiotics already given cleared her symptoms within two weeks. The authors reviewed similar reports from recent outbreaks. Genital mpox often starts alone, without the classic rash, they note. They urge keeping mpox in mind when genital ulcers evolve oddly.
pmc-13528366:
Liang and colleagues present a 2026 paper proposing a protection framework for China's karst landscapes, the limestone cave systems covering about a third of the country. These caves store groundwater and record past climates, yet they face waste dumping, sewage, mining, farm runoff, illegal carving theft, and careless tourism. The authors review recent damage cases in three provinces.

Protection today is reactive and patchy: harm is punished after it happens, rules differ by place, and enforcement is weak. Climate extremes add pressure by shifting groundwater. The authors argue for a framework that guards whole karst ecosystems, linking caves, water, and surface land, with prevention ahead of punishment. Karst damage is hard to reverse because cave formations grow over thousands of years. A national framework would replace scandal-driven cleanups with steady guarding of a world-class natural archive.
pmc-13530666:
Modest and colleagues present in 2026, as conference poster 240, a multi-surgeon prospective study of what predicts a poor result after arthroscopic posterior labral repair. That operation is the keyhole surgery for posterior shoulder instability. The endpoint was failing to reach the patient acceptable symptom state, the point where patients call their shoulder good enough.

The cohort enrolled 177 patients across nine sites between 2015 and 2023, mostly teenage and young adult males, and 133 completed one-year surveys. About eighty-one percent reached the acceptable state. Damaged joint cartilage was the strong predictor of falling short. Patients with normal cartilage reached the state at ninety-four percent, against seventy-six percent for those with abnormal cartilage in this prospective cohort. Lower mental health scores also tracked with failure, and those reaching the acceptable state scored far higher on shoulder outcome scales.
pmc-13531066:
Teresa Bretones del Pino leads a 2026 case report on freezing out airway clots after a valve-in-valve procedure. An 84-year-old woman received a new tricuspid valve inside her old one, then suddenly coughed severe blood with falling oxygen and hard ventilation. A camera scope entered the airways.

A cryoprobe froze and pulled out large blocking clots from the bronchi. Bleeding returned, so a second session followed 72 hours later. Breathing then improved fast, the tube came out, and she left hospital stable after seven days. The technique offers rescue when standard bleeding control fails.
pmc-13531866:
Emine Mustafaoğlu and co-authors test in 2026 whether cold plasma treatment helps resin cement stick to glass ceramic dental material. Two ceramic brands and two cements were crossed with six surface preparations, including acid etching, primer, and plasma steps, for hundreds of specimens. Shear testing measured bond strength after storage.

Acid etching lifted strength across the board. Plasma helped only in one ceramic and cement pairing, pushing a weak group into the acceptable range, while other pairings gained nothing. The authors advise selective plasma use fitted to the exact ceramic, cement, and preparation recipe.
pmc-13532466:
Seungyeon Lee and colleagues report in 2026 on a light-activated surfactant that helps soft hydrogel electrodes stick to water-repelling bases. Hydrogels carry ions well and feel soft like tissue, so they suit wearable and implanted sensors. Their water-rich nature makes them peel from dry, repelling layers when wet.

The new additive lowers surface tension and, after ultraviolet light, forms strong chemical bonds with the base. Gels stayed stable when wet, could be patterned with light, and gained strength and signal quality. Tests in living tissue recorded muscle signals well, pointing to more durable soft bioelectronics.
pmc-13538566:
Jiang Chang and colleagues model buried high-voltage cable capacity with shifting soil heat traits in a 2026 simulation study. Standard ratings treat soil heat resistance as fixed, hiding true margins. A coupled electric-heat model for insulated cables built in how soil water content changes heat flow in native soil and backfill sand across wetting and drying cycles.

Native soil conductivity jumped sharply once water passed a threshold share, while backfill sand reached steadier conduction at far lower water content. In waterlogged native soil, trapped air trimmed capacity modestly. During drying, broken water networks sent capacity plunging far below the wet peak. The authors offer the model for judging true transmission headroom of buried cable systems across seasons.
pmc-13538666:
Yan Chen and colleagues dissect a regulator protein's role in staph skin infections in a 2026 animal and cell study. Drug-resistant staph causes severe skin and soft tissue infections where cell power units falter and reactive oxygen builds up. Infected mice showed lesions and cell death signals, while skin cells with the regulator lowered or raised revealed opposing effects on power unit damage and inflammatory alarm assembly.

Silencing the regulator worsened power unit stress and cell death yet muted inflammatory alarm output and fluid leakage. Raising it, paired with a power unit antioxidant, eased damage while boosting alarm signaling and a key inflammation switch. The authors cast the regulator as a balancing node between cell survival and inflammatory defense during staph infection.
pmc-13540966:
Siqiao Wang leads a 2026 systematic review of mental illness after traumatic spinal cord injury, using a purpose-built knowledge graph to search the literature more cleverly than keyword lists allow. Rehabilitation too often treats the body while mood and thinking go unchecked.

From nearly seventeen thousand screened records, pooled rates came out near a quarter for anxiety, depression, and post-traumatic stress, with cognitive impairment and drug abuse also common and sleep problems widespread. Western cohorts reported more anxiety than Asian ones, and self-report tools inflated depression against clinical interviews. Violence-caused injuries sharply raised trauma risk. Psychosocial treatments clustered on narrow subgroups such as patients in pain.
pmc-13541566:
John M Miller, Nektarios Vasilottos, and Varun Vanka write a 2026 commentary warning heart rhythm specialists not to dismiss an irregular wide-complex tachycardia too quickly. The usual reflex blames a fast atrial rhythm conducted with a bundle branch block, because ventricular tachycardia is normally regular.

A study they discuss found a small minority of ventricular tachycardias in inflammatory heart muscle disease that were frankly irregular, about four percent of such cases. Those patients shared a curious profile: normal resting electrocardiograms and normal heart pumping function despite scar capable of sustaining the rhythm. Missing the diagnosis matters because treatment diverges sharply, and the authors urge keeping ventricular tachycardia on the list.
pmc-13542066:
Kai Wang and six colleagues present, in a 2026 modelling study, a deep learning system for spotting acute kidney injury in intensive care patients twelve hours before it declares itself. Early warning is hard partly because injury cases are heavily outnumbered by stable patients, which dulls ordinary models.

Their dual-channel design learns by contrasting similar and dissimilar patients, sharpening the features that separate future cases. Tested on an imbalanced cohort, it beat conventional baselines including recurrent networks and resampling tricks on most measures, and offered net clinical benefit across a wider risk range. Explanation analysis elevated five routine measures, led by C-reactive protein and ionised calcium. Honest limits are noted where one comparison showed no clear gain.
pmc-13542166:
Lu Li, Lingyan Shi, Meirong Liu, and Qi Fang trace, in a 2026 mouse study, a signalling chain that might relieve the profound muscle weakness sepsis leaves in intensive care survivors. The chain runs through two energy-sensing proteins, AMPK and SIRT1, into a regulator of cell powerhouses called PGC-1alpha.

Sepsis was induced surgically in normal mice and in mice lacking PGC-1alpha, then tissues were examined for muscle damage, mitochondrial shape, and nerve insulation injury. Switching on the AMPK and SIRT1 pathway protected septic mice, and the protection ran through PGC-1alpha and its partner PPARgamma, which govern mitochondrial renewal. Removing the regulator broke the benefit. The authors propose this axis as a drug target for sepsis-acquired weakness.
pmc-13542266:
Burak Pacaci and Ibrahim Vedat Bayoglu published a 2026 population study on how age shapes survival after a colorectal cancer diagnosis, and whether that effect depends on stage. They drew on the United States SEER cancer registry for adults diagnosed between 2004 and 2022, keeping only microscopically confirmed cases. The main group held more than 454,000 patients, large enough to compare younger and older patients within each stage of spread.

Each added year of age worsened both cancer-specific and overall survival. Yet the penalty for being 50 or older was far from uniform. It was strongest when the cancer was still localised, with risk roughly doubling, and it shrank steadily for regional and distant disease. Stage therefore changes what age means for prognosis, a point the authors say should inform how risk is discussed with newly diagnosed patients.
pmc-13543066:
Ameije Anthony and colleagues published a 2026 case report of a Becker nevus, a pigmented skin patch with increased hair growth, appearing in the beard area of a 25-year-old man. The darkened plaque with thicker terminal hair covered the left side of his face and neck, yet he had no muscle or skeletal abnormalities. A biopsy was taken to confirm what the lesion was, and the report is framed as a teaching case.

Microscopy showed thickened skin with broadened ridges, extra pigment in the basal layer, bundles of smooth muscle, and enlarged hair follicles. The feature best supporting the accepted explanation is the combination of extra hair and onset at puberty, when rising androgens can activate the overactive androgen receptors thought to drive this condition. The case reminds clinicians that a beard-distribution patch in a young man may be a Becker nevus rather than a shaving-related problem.
pmc-13543366:
Tosha Gujarathi and Sharmila Rajendrababu published a 2026 case report of angle-closure glaucoma in a 33-year-old man whose eyes were both abnormally small, a condition called nanophthalmos. Such eyes are short, strongly long-sighted, and thick-coated, which makes them prone to fluid collecting behind the retina. This patient arrived with gradual visual loss in both eyes. Examination showed the right eye's front chamber had shallowed while the left stayed stable, with fluid lifting the choroid all around the right eye.

Ultrasound microscopy confirmed fluid above the choroid as the cause of the one-sided angle closure. Steroid treatment by mouth and drops failed to clear it. Surgeons therefore performed a posterior sclerostomy, an opening in the eye wall in one quadrant, which drained the fluid and restored anatomy and vision. The authors stress that mismatched angle closure between two small eyes should prompt imaging for hidden fluid.
pmc-13544866:
Aaron and colleagues survey 137 Indian doctors, 125 general neurologists and 12 headache experts, on how migraine is diagnosed and treated in daily practice. Migraine disables millions, especially women of working age, yet Indian care is inconsistent. Their 2026 questionnaire probed diagnostic habits, drug preferences, guideline use, and appetite for newer treatments, comparing the two clinician groups.

Headache experts carried far heavier headache loads and used the formal criteria at more than double the rate of general neurologists, with similar gaps in using the standard disability survey. Painkillers and triptans dominated prescribing in both groups, while the newest drug class, ditans, barely registered anywhere. Non-drug measures were nearly universal, adopted by about nine in ten clinicians. Reported barriers centred on limited diagnostic support and patient factors. The authors argue migraine education aimed at general neurologists, who see most patients, is where criteria use and therapy uptake will be won.
pmc-13544966:
Putthanbut and colleagues reviewed stem cell treatments for epilepsy in a 2026 survey of animal and early human research. About one third of epilepsy patients keep having seizures despite medication, and current drugs suppress seizures without changing the disease itself. Surgery can help but is rarely used because it needs extensive testing and specialist centers. Stem cells offer a possible way to repair the underlying problem.

Putthanbut describes three main ways transplanted cells may help: settling into damaged tissue, restoring the birth of new nerve cells, and calming harmful immune activity through signals they release. Newer work adds gene-edited cells, tiny message packets released by cells called extracellular vesicles, and brain organoids grown from a patient's own cells for personal testing. The authors stress that safety and real benefit in patients remain unproven and need extensive further trials.
pmc-13545066:
Damien Fisher and colleagues published a 2026 study of scleral contact lenses. They asked whether tiny holes, fenestrations, near the edge reduce the debris that clouds the fluid layer beneath the lens. Scleral lenses vault over the cornea and rest on the white of the eye, trapping a fluid reservoir that often fills with debris and forces removal. Twenty healthy adults wore plain and fenestrated versions of the same lens, on separate days, for three hours while imaging measured it.

Debris built up under both designs, yet the fenestrated lens accumulated far less. By three hours its total debris increase was a fraction of the plain lens's, between about two and nearly five times lower depending on the measure. Whether an air bubble sat in the lens made no difference, and debris levels were unrelated to corneal swelling. Longer studies in patients with eye disease are the stated next step.
pmc-13545366:
Yang and colleagues used a gentle spray-based imaging method in 2026 to map C-peptides, small proteins released alongside insulin, directly in mouse pancreas tissue. The technique scans the tissue surface and builds pictures showing where each molecule sits, while also capturing fats and other small molecules in the same pass. Follow-up fragmentation tests identified each peptide from its break pattern.

The team detected thirty-six acidic peptides and identified intact C-peptide forms plus multiple shortened variants, several never reported before. Computer networking of the fragmentation data assigned some unknown signals to the C-peptide family by shared patterns. Images showed the shortened forms in distinct zones, with gradients running from insulin-producing beta cells into the surrounding digestive tissue. That pattern hints the fragments help the hormone-producing and digestive parts of the pancreas talk to each other.
pmc-13545566:
Sue Cao and co-authors asked in 2026 whether an MRI measurement of iron in the liver and tumor could predict aggressive features in a certain type of liver cancer. They reviewed 80 patients with a single tumor that spared iron, all treated with surgery at one center between 2018 and 2025. Two markers of tumor behavior, the Ki-67 growth index and CK19 expression, were checked against imaging values and a blood marker.

High Ki-67 was more likely when the blood marker AFP was very high, while higher liver iron values pointed the other way. Combining both measures predicted a high growth index moderately well. For CK19, only the blood marker carried predictive weight, which limits what the scan adds.
pmc-13547566:
Doris Kafita and colleagues sorted 510 lung adenocarcinoma tumors in 2026 by how their metabolism genes behave, finding two subtypes with sharply different outlooks. Metabolic rewiring is a hallmark of cancer, yet its link to this cancer's uneven course was unclear. Unsupervised clustering of the tumors' metabolic profiles produced the split.

Patients in the first subtype lived significantly longer. Their tumors favored breaking down choline, a membrane nutrient. The aggressive second subtype instead ran its central carbon machinery hot, including the citric acid cycle and the respiratory chain. One enzyme from that cycle stood out as the strongest single predictor of higher risk, while a sugar-processing enzyme predicted lower risk. The authors offer the subtypes as a prognosis framework and a map of metabolic weak points.
pmc-13549966:
Bogale, Tefera, Mitiku, Solomon, and Misganaw audit malaria slide reading against DNA testing in Ethiopia. Their 2026 paper examines case finding at Dilla Zuria Health Facility. Malaria treatment depends on reading blood smears under microscopes. Wrong reads mean wrong drugs and continued spread. The team checked 474 cases against qPCR.

qPCR detects parasite DNA and served as the reference standard. Among microscopy-positive cases, about a quarter disagreed with qPCR. Nearly one in five microscopy-negative cases was actually positive. Misses clustered in low-density and mixed-species infections. Falciparum calls disagreed in about twenty-one percent of cases. Vivax disagreements ran higher, near twenty-eight percent. Mixed infections fared worst at roughly thirty-five percent. Some misses reflect infections too faint to see. Poorly prepared or misread smears explain others. The authors call for structured, repeated staff training. Quality assurance systems need strengthening alongside. Accuracy shapes control efforts directly.
pmc-13550266:
Berna Hukkamlı, Burak Dagdelen, and Feyza Sönmez Aydın assemble a seven-gene signature that separates papillary thyroid cancer from healthy thyroid tissue, in a 2026 bioinformatics study. Needle biopsies of thyroid nodules often return indeterminate answers, and single-mutation tests miss many cancers. Mining a large cancer atlas with more than five hundred tumors, the team used penalized regression to distill gene activity into a compact panel, then checked it in two independent public datasets.

Four genes ran high in tumors and three ran low. The panel scored near-perfect discrimination in the discovery set and remained highly accurate in both outside cohorts. It also split patients by time without disease returning, though that link faded once other factors entered the model. Signs of chemical gene silencing and differing immune surroundings between risk groups invite follow-up laboratory work.
pmc-13550566:
Yan Ye designs and field-tests an automated seeder that plants corn breeding plots with almost no hand work, in a 2026 agricultural engineering paper. Plot seeders must drop the right variety in the right small plot at scale, and Chinese machines lag imports in automation. The team analyzed the mechanics of seed delivery and tuned four settings, including opener angles and pushrod speed, by response surface experiments.

The best combination qualified over ninety-nine percent of seed drops. A three-stage sensing chain reads QR codes on seed cartridges, confirms cartridge position, and verifies each seed drop, tying variety to plot automatically. Field trials cut manual intervention by seventy-six percent with an error tolerance of a tenth of a percent. Ye presents the machine as a scalable upgrade path for breeding programs still sowing plots by hand.
pmc-13551266:
Ylva A. Weeda, with a large panel of co-authors, published a 2026 Dutch study of p53 staining in Barrett's oesophagus. The stain helps flag abnormal cells in the food pipe. Most proof came from hand-picked case sets. Here an expert panel re-read 1,146 referred cases. They compared hospital calls and tested accord among panel members.

Accord between hospitals and the panel was fair to strong. Yet about a quarter of stain calls changed on re-reading. Panel members also agreed well with each other. Abnormal stains moved some normal cases toward doubt or early change. They also settled many doubtful cases. The team calls the stain reliable and able to change real diagnoses.
pmc-13551866:
Chun Zhang and Jingqi Zhang published a 2026 multi-omics study of genetic drivers behind inflammation-linked aging. Chronic low-grade inflammation, called inflammaging, marks biological aging, yet its causal mediators were poorly mapped. Their four-tier framework screened 91 circulating inflammatory proteins against six aging phenotypes using Mendelian randomization, a genetic method that mimics a natural experiment, then layered gene activity data from four molecular resources.

Three proteins, IL-12B, IFNG, and IL-2, emerged as the most robust pro-aging mediators in the reported analysis. Seven high-confidence effector genes were named across different epigenetic aging clocks, with one chromosome region dominating. Mapping onto a mouse embryo atlas showed enrichment in smooth muscle and lung, and drug database mining flagged two targets as repurposable plus one as a novel candidate.
pmc-13552866:
Leonardo Mancini heads a team testing collagen pads used to thicken gum tissue in dental work. Seven shop-bought pads were soaked in pig blood and measured in three dimensions. Sound-wave scans checked their density and stretch in the lab. Pads were then tucked under flaps in pig jaws and scanned again after wetting.

Pads built to hold their shape drank in far more blood and swelled much more. One thick pad showed the largest fluid uptake and growth in volume. Another grew most in height, while weaker pads shrank or partly collapsed. Links between density and swelling were weak and not firm. The authors warn that swelling can strain a closed wound, so trimming and loose closure matter.
pmc-13554266:
Sarani Dey, Abhijit Das, and Sharba Bandyopadhyay watch the fruit fly brain fire on its own during the pupal stage in a 2026 study. Even without outside signals, young neurons fire together, and that joint firing helps wire circuits. Using light-based calcium imaging, the team followed three cell classes across development. These classes handle dopamine signals, general excitation, and inhibition.

All three classes shared one rhythm: bursts of joint firing split by quiet spells. The pattern differed from what earlier work saw in the fly's visual lobe. Classes still differed in burst timing, precision, and strength. The authors offer the maps as a base for studying how circuit building goes wrong in developmental disorders of the brain.
pmc-13554366:
Tian-Yu Li and Zhi-Ming Yu report a longitudinal analysis, published in 2026. It tests whether a combined metabolic score tracks cognitive decline in older adults. Their score added together several measures. They were uric acid, triglycerides, and fasting glucose. Reversed HDL cholesterol was also included. The group covered 7,300 Chinese adults followed from 2011 to 2018. A United States survey served as a cross-check.

The combined score showed essentially no link to the speed of decline. Formal testing showed this was not a power problem. Pulling the score apart explained why. Higher uric acid sped decline. Higher triglycerides slowed it. The two effects nearly cancelled. This argues against equal-weight composite scores in ageing research.
pmc-13555566:
Yuuki Fukai leads a six-author team building a compact gene switch that targets only the brain's calming neurons in a 2026 study. Epilepsy stems from a tilt toward excitation, and many patients resist current drugs. Their switch, just 410 letters long, drives strong gene activity in inhibitory neurons while leaving room in the delivery virus. System delivery favoured a key class of fast calming cells.

Loading the switch with a gene that boosts the calming chemical GABA brought wide gains. Seizure-like activity and abnormal slow waves fell in mouse models. Anxiety-like behaviour normalised and survival improved. Brain levels of the calming chemical rose in the cortex and memory hub. The authors offer the switch as a platform for imbalance disorders.
pmc-13555966:
Li Pan and Qihuan Chen survey why Chinese English learners intend to use AI chat tools for speaking practice in a 2026 study. Their respondents were 568 undergraduate English majors, mostly light, early users of such tools. Two motivation frameworks structured the questions: one on technology acceptance, one on inner drive. Beliefs about usefulness, enjoyment, and ease carried the most weight.

Expecting the tools to boost performance mattered most, with fun and low effort close behind. Social pressure and support conditions played weaker roles. Feelings of autonomy and competence fed intention through inner motivation, while feeling connected to others did not. The authors advise teachers to design purposeful speaking tasks with visible progress, and builders to keep tools useful and pleasant.
pmc-13556066:
Geng Lu and three colleagues set out in 2026 to rank artificial intelligence methods built for reading liver cancer CT scans. Hundreds of competing techniques exist, and clinics need a fair way to pick among them. The team searched five databases, sorted the methods by task, then used expert rounds to agree on selection criteria before applying fuzzy decision methods that weigh each option against an ideal.

They catalogued 260 techniques and settled on seven criteria, including validity, accuracy, speed, and cost. A deep learning reconstruction model topped the detection and diagnosis group, and a combined deep learning, radiomics, and clinical model topped the treatment group. Segmentation and prediction tasks each had their own winner. The rankings give radiology teams a structured shortlist instead of a marketing contest.
pmc-13559666:
Jing Long, Youzhi Wang, Mengqi Zou, Gangyong Jiang, Zhongwei Jiang and Wanxiao Peng published this 2026 cell study on how support cells help mouth cancer invade along nerves. In oral squamous cell carcinoma, cancer tracking along nerves, called perineural invasion, worsens outcomes. Schwann cells, the nerve's support cells, actively assist. The team exposed Schwann cells to fluid conditioned by cancer cells and tracked lipid peroxidation, an oxidation damage, and the cells' repair markers.

The cancer-conditioned fluid drove lipid peroxidation in the Schwann cells, with damage markers up and protective glutathione down, alongside rises in the repair markers c-Jun and NGFR. Fluid collected from those Schwann cells made cancer cells migrate and invade more, without changing their survival. Adding ferrostatin-1, a lipid peroxidation blocker, reversed the Schwann cell changes and blunted the pro-invasion effect. The authors propose redox control as a lever on this cancer-nerve partnership.
pmc-13560266:
Penelope C Rose and colleagues report that HIV prevention drugs given at birth sped up a rare mitochondrial liver-brain disease in South African infants, publishing the study in 2026. MPV17 neurohepatopathy is a lethal inherited disorder of infant liver failure and neurological decline, yet why some babies collapse within days while others survive months was unclear. The team compared 25 infants diagnosed between 2013 and 2024, eight of whom were HIV-exposed and received preventive antiretrovirals.

Exposed infants showed symptoms at a median of three days versus sixty days for unexposed infants, and liver failure was more likely. The authors point to zidovudine, a known mitochondrial toxin given to seven exposed babies, as the likely accelerant. They suggest less toxic preventive regimens for HIV-exposed newborns where this MPV17 variant is common.
pmc-13560366:
Jingtong Zeng and colleagues build an ultrasound habitat model that predicts EGFR mutation status in peripheral lung cancer without tissue sampling. Their 2026 retrospective study covers 187 patients with confirmed non-small cell lung cancer scanned by contrast-enhanced ultrasound before biopsy between April 2021 and February 2025. Habitat imaging divides each tumor into distinct regions whose features feed the model.

The habitat model reached an area under the curve of 0.898 in training and 0.784 in testing, beating a conventional radiomics model on both sets in the reported comparison. Adding clinical and radiological indicators nudged performance slightly higher. Calibration and decision-curve checks favored the combined model, suggesting real clinical net benefit. Explanation analysis kept the model interpretable for its users. The authors offer the approach as a noninvasive reference for steering patients toward or away from EGFR-targeted therapy.
pmc-13562366:
David Brower and colleagues tracked how inflation-adjusted Medicare pay for lung and critical-care doctors changed from 2003 to 2024, publishing the retrospective analysis in 2026. Medicare's fee schedule sets pay through relative value units and a yearly conversion factor, and private insurers follow its lead, so its trajectory shapes the whole payment system. The team analysed facility and nonfacility rates for each procedure code, adjusted with the Consumer Price Index.

Pay fell steeply across the board: about 45 percent in facility settings and 39 percent outside them. Repeated cuts to the conversion factor drove most of the decline, swamping even rising value units for bronchoscopy, which still fell 31 percent outside facilities. The authors conclude lung and critical-care pay fell in line with other specialties, largely because of that shared conversion-factor squeeze.
pmc-13562566:
Muren Bao designs a decision-support system that helps basketball coaches read offence and defence as a game unfolds. Traditional analysis leans on watching film and gut feeling. Bao's 2026 system gathers data through connected sensors and tracking feeds, encodes where players are and how plays develop over time, and feeds everything into a multi-task attention model. The model handles two jobs at once: labelling the current offensive or defensive state, and predicting shooting success.

Testing drew on NBA player-tracking data from the 2018 to 2023 seasons. The system classified game states with 0.897 accuracy on held-out data, and its shooting predictions beat standard baseline models on error. Because the pipeline runs in real time, coaches could receive tactical prompts during play rather than after it. Bao presents the setup as a technical frame for sharper strategy calls and training plans tailored to each player.
pmc-13563866:
Rincy M. Thomas and three colleagues ask whether motor-driven files for children's root canals shave away more tooth wall than careful hand filing. What dentin remains after cleaning decides how strong the treated baby molar stays. Their 2026 laboratory study took 51 extracted human primary molars and scanned them with cone-beam CT before and after treatment.
