The front-root canals were split into three groups of seventeen: hand K-files, or one of two rotary systems built for children, Kedo SG Blue and Kedo S Square. Wall thickness was compared at three set levels.

After cleaning, the leftover dentin thickness did not differ significantly between the three systems at any level. Both rotary systems matched the hand files for conserving tooth structure while shaping the canal. The authors conclude the rotary files are a safe, comparable substitute in these canals, offering speed without extra thinning, in extracted teeth.
pmc-13569366:
Vijaya Bhaskar Alwarnaidu Vijayarajan and colleagues study, in a 2026 paper, herbicide resistance in annual bluegrass populations from Ireland. They focus on changes at position 197 of the enzyme that many weed killers target. Twelve resistant groups were tested with two products sold together for tolerant beet crops, plus modeling of how each drug fits the enzyme.

All position-197 variants resisted one partner drug strongly yet stayed sensitive to the other drug in the pair. The combined product worked less well than that second drug alone. Modeling showed the second drug gripping the enzyme more tightly. A different change at position 574 resisted everything. The results help advisers choose products that still control these weeds.
pmc-13569566:
Leah Roberts and colleagues listened to nine Australian adults prescribed medicinal cannabis for anxiety, tracking how their quality of life changed over the first year. Past studies mostly used short follow-ups or one-off surveys, leaving the lived experience over time unclear. Through diary entries at three and six months and interviews within twelve months, this 2026 qualitative study explored daily life, not just symptom scores.

Participants described better sleep, steadier emotions, stronger relationships, more motivation, and a regained sense of agency over anxiety, alongside greater use of coping strategies. Stigma around disclosure and worries about driving laws and roadside drug testing weighed against those gains. The authors conclude that patients saw cannabis as a way to manage anxiety, not to cure it, and they urge clinicians to weigh quality of life alongside symptoms.
pmc-13570866:
Tianyan Hu leads a 2026 study of 724 symptomatic adults in the United States who tested positive for influenza at pharmacy clinics during the severe 2024-2025 season. The study tracks how flu damaged quality of life and work over a month. Participants rated health repeatedly during the first two weeks and at week four.

Self-rated health plunged on day one and stayed below baseline at day ten, while work absence jumped by well over half on the first day. Working while sick, overall productivity loss, and limits on daily activity followed the same arc, easing by week two to four. The day-by-day curve gives employers and vaccine advocates concrete numbers for what a flu case costs beyond medical bills.
pmc-13571366:
Jesmar Alejandro Ramonis Quintero and Daesub Chung Kwon present, in a 2026 case, a 73-year-old man whose electrocardiogram pattern pointed away from the usual heart attack reading. He arrived with five days of worsening breathlessness and intermittent pressing chest pain, plus blood markers showing heart strain and injury.

The tracing showed flipped T waves across front and lower leads, strongest in the right-sided chest leads and lead three. That distribution, the authors argue, signals an overloaded right ventricle, classically from a lung blood clot, rather than a blocked coronary artery. They propose a short mnemonic for the pattern so clinicians can spot pulmonary embolism earlier and avoid a costly misdiagnosis.
pmc-13572366:
Xin Zheng, with three colleagues, reports a 2026 gene study of links shared by major mental illness and Alzheimer's disease. The two kinds of illness often overlap in clinic, and both run in families. The team asked whether the same gene sites help drive both.

They drew on large gene scans covering Hispanic, African American, European, and East Asian groups. From public sources they gathered 2,871 traits and found 134 traits tied by genes to both kinds of illness. Two gene sites stood out as shared by both, near markers named rs2532240 and rs6504163. Checks in gene and cell databases then pointed to likely genes at those sites and to how they might act in the brain.
pmc-13572466:
Deepak Kumar Rakesh, with four colleagues, presents a 2026 framework for picking the most useful features in a data set before training a model. Feature selection cuts noise and run time, but hybrid methods often pair their parts with no clear reason. The framework aims to make the pairing rule open and testable.

The method joins a filter step, which ranks features by relevance and low overlap, with a classifier step in a paired search. Twelve hybrid pairings were run against classic and recent rivals, and a master-worker layout let the tests run in parallel for speed. The hybrids won on several scores, and a variance test backed the gaps as real. The authors pitch the pairing rule as a guide that does not lock users to one filter or one classifier.
pmc-13572566:
Barnabas Atwiine, with eight colleagues, reports a 2026 study of a phone app that helps front-line health workers spot childhood cancer in Uganda. Early diagnosis needs workers to suspect cancer fast and refer the child on, yet many cases are missed or found late. The app, PEDCan, guides checks and opens remote talks with specialists.

In May 2021, the team surveyed 44 health workers in the southwest of the country, then trained them on the app with mock cases. Nurses and midwives made up over half the group, and all had heard of childhood cancer before. Most owned a smartphone with internet access, though only a third had steady access. A large share, 86.3 percent, found the app easy or very easy to use, and all said they would use it. A pilot with real patients comes next.
pmc-13572966:
Kathryn A. McNaughton, with two colleagues, reports a study of head motion matching between young people as they chat. Moving in sync with a partner can build liking in lab setups, yet real talks may differ. Autistic youth face extra hurdles with peers, so the team asked whether natural sync shapes how much each partner enjoys the talk.

Pairs of autistic and non-autistic youth, in three pair types, held short getting-to-know-you talks on video. Software tracked head position frame by frame, and a wave method scored how closely the two heads moved together. Real pairs showed more sync than shuffled fake pairs, and sync levels did not differ by pair type. Across all pairs, more sync went with less reported enjoyment and more discomfort. The authors say natural sync may not carry the warm effects that staged sync shows.
pmc-13573366:
Yemane Tadesse Desta, with two colleagues, reports a 2026 survey of traditional herbal healers in Tigray, Ethiopia. Herbal care remains a backbone of primary health care in the region. The team asked how healers practise, which plants they use, and how open they are to working with modern services.

The study covered 58 healers across five zones from March to May 2024, with interviews, field checks, and plant records. Most healers were men over 50 with more than 20 years of practice, working part time. They named 22 plant species for infections and for physical and spiritual ills, with leaves the top part used. Agreement ran highest for gut and lung complaints. Schooling, family roots in the craft, and prior training each went with more openness to integration. Habitat loss and fading knowledge topped the threats named.
pmc-13573466:
Ruurd Jorritsma, with three colleagues, reports a 2026 clinical study of two treatments for bluetongue in Dutch sheep. A new virus type, BTV-3, hit the Netherlands in September 2023 and made sheep gravely ill. Vets had few labelled drugs to choose from, so the team logged signs, survival, and whether an antihistamine add-on helped.

Of 83 sheep with clear acute signs, 41 got a pain and fever protocol alone, while 42 got the same care plus antihistamine shots over three days. Death took 57 percent of the flock overall. Heavy salivation marked sheep that died sooner. The antihistamine group lived a mean of 0.8 days against 2.5 days without it, so the add-on gave no gain. The authors advise against antihistamines here and urge early calls on when to stop treatment.
pmc-13574166:
Zhigui Li, with six colleagues, reports a 2026 study of small gene switches that throttle output of the chief polycystic kidney disease gene. This inherited disease fills kidneys with cysts and causes a large share of kidney failure. Most cases trace to low output of the PKD1 gene's protein, polycystin-1, and severity tracks how far output falls.

Short reading frames that sit before the main gene, called upstream open reading frames, can cut how much protein the main frame makes. The team tested whether those frames tune polycystin-1 levels in this disease. Raising protein output is a live therapy idea, since even a small lift may cross the line that keeps cysts at bay. Knowing which frames do the throttling points to precise targets, such as blockers of one frame. The work joins gene control to disease severity in a direct line.
pmc-13574766:
Camilla Koch Ryrsø, with seven colleagues, details a 2026 study of quality of life as a warning sign in pneumonia caught outside hospital. This lung infection fills wards and often leaves patients frail. The team asked whether how patients rate their own health on arrival foretells return trips, intensive care, or death.

The study followed 552 admitted patients who filled in a standard five-part health form on arrival, with 262 reassessed 180 days after discharge. The lowest third on the health score faced near double the risk of readmission at 30, 90, and 180 days, and of death by 90 and 180 days. Poor mobility and self-care scores carried the sharpest warnings. Survivors who answered again gained modestly over six months. The authors back the short form as a risk tool.
pmc-13575166:
Nikola Vargová leads a 2026 chemistry study on how added pores change the catalytic power of a metal-organic framework called HKUST-1. Such frameworks are crystal-like sponges with huge internal surface areas. The team made two versions with extra larger pores layered over the natural tiny ones.

Both new versions kept the base structure and high surface area. They were tested on the Knoevenagel condensation, a standard reaction joining two carbon compounds. Under the best settings, the two versions converted 93 and 98 percent of the starting material within an hour. Bulky starting materials reacted poorly, showing that crowding still limits access. After five reuse cycles, activity slipped only modestly, and the framework stayed intact on later checks.
pmc-13576366:
Knut Stavem leads a 2026 cohort study following chest scans of people hospitalised with COVID-19 for up to four and a half years. Lung after-effects of severe infection were unclear beyond two years. Patients admitted in 2020 had scans at three months, with repeat imaging at one year and at four and a half years when changes persisted.

Of 187 patients scanned at three months, 99 reached the one-year scan and 54 the last scan. Breathlessness affected 33 percent and fatigue 61 percent at the final check, yet both symptoms tied only weakly to scan scores. Cloud-like opacities and patchy air trapping faded over time, while band-like scarring grew and linked to how severe the first illness was. Older age and early severity predicted lasting marks. Change largely stalled after the first year.
pmc-13576866:
Ali Jahanian and four colleagues turn spray-dried bacteria into a reusable factory for making codeine, in a 2026 study. Codeine is a medicinal opioid normally refined from plant material. Their engineered Escherichia coli carry three poppy enzymes that convert thebaine into codeine in steps, yet fresh cells for each batch are costly.

Spray drying preserved over 85 percent of enzyme activity in the dried cells. A native bacterial enzyme inside the cells regenerated two helper chemicals the poppy enzymes need, so no outside supply was required. Over ten reuse cycles the dried cells held up well overall, though one enzyme lost 40 percent of its activity, matching its heat sensitivity. The process converted all the thebaine and averaged a 68 percent molar yield of codeine. The authors present spray-dried cells as a scalable, cheaper route.
pmc-13577966:
Cassandra K. Dittman and colleagues surveyed 1,183 Australian parents to find what drives teen gambling. Gambling under 18 is illegal in most places, yet teen gambling and problem gambling are common, and parents likely shape both. Their 2026 study asked parents of 12- to 17-year-olds about their own gambling, their attitudes, how they enable gambling, their supervision, and their bond with their teen.

Parents letting teens gamble emerged as the strongest predictor of both teen gambling and teen gambling problems. Simulated gambling by teens, weak parental monitoring, and less warm parent-teen bonds also predicted problems. The authors argue that harm-reduction campaigns should target parents directly, not only teens, since parental facilitation opens the door.
pmc-13578366:
Yunsi Liu and Yueyuan Huang model the shaking a new subway tunnel feels when trains pass on a live line above it, in a 2026 study. Dense city networks force new tunnels to cross under tracks already in use, and years of passing loads can weaken the fresh tunnel roof. Heavy computer models can trace the risk, yet they run too slowly for early design work.

Their paper model treats the train as a sprung mass, the soil as springs and dampers, and the tunnel roof as a simple beam. Settings were tuned against site readings and a full computer model. Shaking spiked at two train speeds, at two beam lengths, and at one soil depth in their case. Stiffer beams calmed the response, and grout work shifted it as well.
pmc-13579866:
Fengni Liang, Zerong Pei, Xuemei Wang, and Ke Zhang map forty years of gut organoid research to see where the field is heading, in a 2026 analysis. Organoids are mini gut tissues grown from stem cells that copy the real organ's folds and cell mix. Publication records from 1986 to 2025 were mined with mapping tools that trace who cites whom and which topics flare up.

The United States leads on paper count, while the Netherlands, home of the founding team, leads on citation weight. Early work chased stem cell growing recipes, then swung to modeling colon cancer and bowel inflammation. The newest flare ups point to gut on a chip devices, force sensing in tissues, and single cell readouts. The authors frame the map as a compass toward engineered, patient matched gut models.
pmc-13582766:
Filis Cramer Necip and colleagues reviewed what tech know-how means for biomedical laboratory science, a field where AI, robots, and data tools are reshaping daily work. Their scoping review, drawing on a socio-technical model and Europe's DigComp digital skills model, looked at 19 sources on how the field views tech skills.

Two outlooks emerged. One looks backward, stressing routine use of current tools. The other looks forward, stressing AI, code thinking, data skills, and smart use of tech. The authors argue that lab-science teaching must cover both basics and careful judgement. New grads should judge new tools rather than merely run them, and keep pace as lab tech keeps changing.
pmc-13585466:
Katerina Eleonora K Rassia, Lydia Liapi, and John S Pezaris review what it takes to adapt to sight given back by a device in this 2026 paper. Visual prostheses feed camera signals to the eye or brain, yet results vary wildly: some users weave the new sense into daily life, while others set the device aside. The authors set out a five-stage path from switching the device on through social adjustment.

Early stages, such as first perception and basic calibration, are often reached. The sharp break comes later, when skills learned in training must carry into free daily behavior, and many users stall there. Timely fitting, easy-to-grasp devices, long rehab, and steady support mark the successes. The review draws on eye and ear implant trials and on stand-in sense tools to draw those lessons.
pmc-13585966:
Helene Springer, Henrik Garde, Frida Splendido, and Marianne Gullberg measure how Swedish vowels look on a speaker's lips. Seeing a face helps listeners catch speech, yet charts of lip shapes have long rested on simple yes-no features such as open versus closed or rounded versus spread. Their proof-of-concept study used computer vision to track mouth area, height, and width in running speech from one speaker.

Even with smooth drift inside each vowel, the vowels fell into groups that a watcher could tell apart. Those groups did not always match the textbook feature charts, which are built from the speaker's side, in tongue and lip terms. The authors argue that measured lip geometry gives a truer picture of what a listener can actually use, and they test the vision tools themselves as part of the work.
pmc-13586266:
Long-xiang Li and a large team chase the cause of memory loss after a brain bleed, and a possible old drug to treat it. Bleeding around the brain, called subarachnoid hemorrhage, often leaves survivors with lasting thinking problems, tied in part to loss of myelin, the insulation on nerve fibers. Their 2026 study found a protein named CNTN1 running low in patients' spinal fluid, with lower levels matching worse thinking scores.

Single-cell reads in mice showed the drop sat in neurons, the signaling cells, not the insulation makers. Turning the gene down in mouse neurons deepened thinking problems and lowered a linked enzyme, ADA, plus two myelin proteins. Turning it up protected the animals, and blocking the enzyme erased that gain. Clemastine, an allergy drug, eased the harm by limiting insulation loss, which makes it a candidate worth testing in patients.
pmc-13587466:
Siti Sabrina Kamarudin and a large team screen pregnant women in Malaysian public clinics for depression before birth. Antenatal depression is common yet underreported, above all in poorer settings. Their 2026 study gave 572 women a standard depression scale alongside questions on pregnancy history and life stress, counting a set score as probable depression.

About one woman in ten screened positive. Four factors raised the odds on their own: an unplanned pregnancy, a recent stressful event, depressive symptoms in the prior two weeks, and a self-rated high level of worry. Feeling emotionally supported by one's mother while growing up cut the odds sharply. The authors back brief routine screening at clinics, widened to catch anxiety too, with extra support aimed at women carrying those risk marks.
pmc-13591666:
Ufuk Gürer and eight colleagues report, in 2026, a strong glue made almost wholly from mistletoe berries. Most store glues come from oil, and many release harmful formaldehyde over time. Mistletoe, a plant that lives off trees, yields a sugar rich extract from its berries. Mixed with tannic and malic acid and cured with heat, and with no chemical rework, the extract becomes the glue.

The glue bonded wood, metal, and glass firmly, and even Teflon, a surface famous for shedding sticky stuff. When joints were forced apart, a fresh heat treatment woke the leftover layers so parts could be bonded again. Gürer and the team pitch the recipe as a green, repairable stand in for oil based glues.
pmc-13592666:
Jiaxuan Sun leads a team building a machine learning tool that predicts early death in sepsis patients whose blood clotting has gone wrong. Standard severity scores miss tangled, nonlinear patterns in such patients. Records came from three intensive care databases in the United States and China, totaling about twelve thousand cases. Twelve learning methods were trained on ten chosen predictors and judged against four classic scores, with explanation tools exposing what drove each call.

One boosted tree model won clearly, scoring near 0.90 on accuracy curves inside its home data and holding up in both outside sets. It beat every classic score and promised more clinical benefit. Anion gap, red cell spread, lactate, bilirubin, and age topped the driver list. Sun and the team shipped a free web tool so clinicians can run the model at the bedside.
pmc-13593366:
Jared W Freedman and two colleagues read river life from DNA traces across the lower Colorado River Basin. How stream communities connect across a dry, rugged land network was hard to test before environmental DNA sampling. Their team gathered water samples from 70 habitats, from small headwater creeks to large altered rivers in five drainage regions. Genetic barcoding named the invertebrates present, and a borrowed population genetics frame measured how similarity fades with distance.

Communities ran rich and varied between regions, shaped by place, conditions, and chance together. Distant headwater creeks often held strikingly similar life where land conditions matched, despite huge river distances between them. Freedman and the team conclude that overland links and habitat likeness bind the basin's life as much as the rivers do.
pmc-13593666:
Ferrer-Curriu and colleagues published a 2026 study on a protein that helps hearts heal after attack. After a heart attack, swelling must give way to repair at the right pace. A protein called Metrnl guides immune cells toward the repair mode. The team tracked it in mouse hearts during the first days after injury.

Immune cells entering the hurt heart made far more Metrnl by day four. Mice lacking the protein healed worse, with more hot-tempered immune cells lingering. Boosting the protein in the heart restored repair and calmer cell behavior. Metrnl works through a chain that caps how long swelling lasts. The chain offers fresh targets for guiding post-attack healing. Timing, they stress, decides whether inflammation helps or harms recovery.
pmc-13594466:
Kyara Alfred Ndisi and colleagues screened older adults at non-cardiac clinics in a Tanzanian tertiary hospital to find how much atrial fibrillation hides in this population. More than a thousand patients aged sixty and over were checked with a phone-connected single-lead heart tracing device. They were seen between June 2021 and February 2022. Positive screens were confirmed with a full tracing.

Atrial fibrillation turned up in about four of every hundred patients, and only one of those had ever been diagnosed. Most of those affected carried stroke risk scores high enough to warrant preventive treatment. Being over seventy-five, underweight, having high blood pressure, and having obstructive sleep apnea each raised the odds independently. The authors call the rhythm common, underdiagnosed, and dangerous in this group, and they argue for routine screening in clinics serving older Tanzanians.
pmc-13594766:
Biruke Temesgen and co-authors describe a 65-year-old man whose new myasthenia gravis turned out to accompany a lung cancer. Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disease that weakens muscles. The pairing was a surprise, since the condition is usually linked with thymus problems. He arrived with drooping eyelids, double vision, and tiring limbs, plus a dry cough that had lasted four months.

Blood tests found the characteristic antibodies against acetylcholine receptors, and nerve studies fit the diagnosis. Chest imaging then revealed a nodule in the right lung, and a needle sample confirmed adenocarcinoma. He improved on the standard myasthenia medicines, then had the tumor removed followed by chemotherapy. The authors discuss how cancers outside the thymus can occasionally trigger this syndrome through cross-reacting immunity, and they urge doctors facing atypical myasthenia cases to look for a hidden tumor.
pmc-13595766:
Cansu Memiç-İnan and colleagues measured functional constipation and its web of associations in 429 adults attending a public hospital clinic in Türkiye. Diagnosis followed the Rome IV criteria, and the team layered in eating behavior screens, picky eating scores, body measurements, and self-reported activity and diet in their 2026 cross-sectional study.

One in five participants met the criteria. Older age and female sex raised the odds, as did a higher eating disorder risk score. Two findings ran against common assumption: heavier participants had modestly lower odds, and physically active people had dramatically lower odds, roughly a sixth of the inactive group's. Family history, smoking, and alcohol showed no clear link. The authors frame constipation as a biopsychosocial condition and argue that middle-income settings need more such local data rather than borrowed assumptions.
pmc-13598566:
Wang and colleagues compare how four countries organise mental health services for teenagers, and draw lessons for China. Their 2026 paper builds an analysis framework linking policy elements, delivery mechanisms, and governance outcomes. The team coded Brazil, Australia, Germany, and the United States on laws, funding, service networks, workforce, digital tools, cross-department work, and early intervention, using official documents and peer-reviewed studies.

Each country followed a different path. Brazil built community-integrated care through its unified health system, though youth-specific resources were unevenly spread. Australia linked national strategy and funding to the headspace youth network and digital support. Germany paired social insurance with youth welfare but lacked a unified school-based network, while American schools acted as a main entry point despite funding and staffing shortages. The authors recommend a hybrid Chinese model anchored in schools.
pmc-13609266:
Ignacio Martin-Loeches and three colleagues argue that intensive care AI should hunt for disagreement, not death. Monitors and labs flood intensive care units with data, while clinicians' real reasoning lives in free-text notes. Studies have shown that note tone predicts mortality, yet the gain over standard severity scores is tiny. The authors say the target itself is wrong: at the bedside, nobody asks for a 28-day death probability.

Their proposed quantity is a narrative-physiology discordance score: the gap between the risk a written assessment implies and the risk measurements imply. They define it formally, fix the forecast window, and spell out controls for data leakage and copied-forward text. Alert limits become a design budget, and a staged evaluation ends with clinicians adjudicating flagged cases. Until then, a discordance flag means reassess this patient, not that deterioration was missed.
pmc-13616366:
Li Zhang and colleagues identify a trafficking protein, Rab1A, as a driver of fat build-up in the liver, working from single-cell gene data of fatty liver disease in mice and humans. Despite wide study, the roots of this metabolic liver disease stay partly hidden. A lipid-loaded liver cell type stood out in the data, with Rab1A as its hallmark. Removing the gene entirely, or silencing it only in the liver, protected adult mice from fat build-up on a western diet.

In liver cells, silencing Rab1A unleashed heavy mitophagy, the disposal of worn mitochondria, and fat drained away. The team traced the wiring through a signal chain ending in a mitophagy trigger protein. Blocking that chain reversed the benefit. A protein that parks the cell's cleanup crew turns out to be a fat keeper, and a fresh drug target.
pmc-13616766:
Wei Wang and colleagues map in 2026 how the cartilages of the external nose take shape before birth, examining slices from 22 human fetuses spanning about 9 to 40 weeks of pregnancy. Nobody had recorded when the single nasal capsule cartilage splits in two. One part becomes the lateral nasal cartilage. The other becomes the greater alar cartilage that forms the nostril rim. The timing of the alar cartilage's inner leg was also unknown.

The split happened at 10 to 12 weeks. Small sesamoid cartilages stood between the lateral cartilage and the septum below the nasal bone, while none sat between the two main cartilages themselves. After 27 weeks the inner leg of the alar cartilage appeared, growing out from the main alar part on its own rather than from the septum. Surgeons who rebuild noses gain a timetable of how the parts they move were first assembled.
pmc-13617466:
Zongyu Yang and four colleagues test whether a single bout of aerobic exercise sharpens cognitive control in college students, and whether trait anxiety, a person's habitual anxiety level, changes the answer. Students were split into high and low anxiety groups with a standard inventory. They then completed a demanding continuous performance task before and after either twenty minutes of moderate cycling-style exercise or seated rest.

Only the high-anxiety students improved after exercise, responding faster on trials that measure proactive control, the ability to hold a goal in mind ahead of time. Their error-based proactive index also rose, while accuracy and reactive control stayed put. Low-anxiety students changed under neither condition. The authors argue that exercise prescriptions for mental performance should be individualized, since the same session may help anxious students most and do little for calm ones.
pmc-13618366:
Bangshu Zhao and three colleagues map the research field linking human genetic variation to multiomics biomarker translation, the effort to turn molecular measurements into useful tests in clinics. Using bibliometric tools on papers from Scopus, Web of Science, and PubMed between 2003 and 2025, they charted who publishes, what themes dominate, and how the field's focus has moved. Strict rules kept only studies where genetic variation truly fed a biomarker endpoint.

Six hundred seventy-three papers qualified, with output accelerating steadily. The United States led the field, while China published heavily but with lower citation impact, and large medical centers and oncology consortia dominated the networks. Themes shifted from pharmacogenetics and single markers toward multiomics models, with recent heat around liquid biopsy, tumor heterogeneity, artificial intelligence, and the tumor microenvironment. The authors name the key bottleneck: connecting DNA variation to downstream molecules and clinical traits, not merely detecting variants.
pmc-13618766:
Joo Hyeong Han and six colleagues report a luminescent material whose response to moisture depends on which color of infrared light excites it. The material is a zero-dimensional halide built on cesium gadolinium chloride, with erbium partly replacing gadolinium. Such smart materials serve optical readout, security, and sensing, and this one adds a twist: the excitation wavelength itself decides whether dampness changes anything.

Under nine hundred eighty nanometer excitation the crystals kept their yellow emission when damp, while under fifteen hundred fifty nanometer excitation the same moisture drove a green-to-red shift. Spectroscopy showed the difference comes from which excited states each wavelength fills and how strongly the material absorbs there. The team used the effect for excitation-selective optical readout and built a power-free sticker dosimeter that measures moisture exposure using diffusion physics. They propose excitation selectivity as a new design rule for optical materials.
pmc-13619066:
Margarida Carvalho and colleagues compared body and sleep patterns across insomnia, sleep apnoea, and both together in Iberia. Insomnia and apnoea often appear together as COMISA, harming health, yet their joint body workings were little mapped. Their study used records on 147 patients in Portugal and 264 in Spain, leaving out heart disease, using night-time sleep studies and heart-rate shifts.

Both-together patients were older, heavier, and showed a pattern led by shallow breathing in both countries. Standard heart-rate readings barely moved, though apnoea trended toward lower calming-nerve action. A Spain-only band marked breathing burden, and pooled data showed higher heart burden in apnoea and both-together groups. Carvalho and colleagues call country gaps and methods key limits on such markers.
pmc-13619366:
Yoshiko Matsumoto and eight colleagues examined bowel problems that follow sphincter-saving surgery for rectal cancer. Standard scores sum many symptoms into one number, which can hide very different patient experiences. The team analyzed 320 patients who had low anterior resection, tracking their answers on two questionnaires over time and sorting the individual items with factor analysis.

Three separate symptom groups emerged: leakage, urgency with clustered trips to the toilet, and trouble controlling gas. Each group tied to different factors, such as age, body weight, radiation, and the exact surgical approach. Symptoms in all three groups stayed worse than before surgery even two years later. Because two patients with the same total score may suffer in different ways, the authors recommend judging and treating each domain on its own.
pmc-13619666:
Maxence Gambiez and six colleagues asked whether an early-phase nuclear scan can help diagnose frozen shoulder, in a 2026 retrospective study. Frozen shoulder brings pain and steady loss of movement from inflammation and tightening inside the joint capsule. The team reviewed eighteen affected shoulders in seventeen patients who had standard bone scans with both bloodpool and late-phase SPECT/CT imaging.

Every affected shoulder showed raised tracer uptake in one spot, the rotator cuff interval, during the bloodpool phase. Other capsule regions lit up less often, and late-phase scans showed diffuse uptake in most cases. In three shoulders that single early spot was the only abnormal sign. The authors propose the pattern may be a sensitive marker for the condition, while calling for prospective studies to prove its diagnostic worth in everyday shoulder pain.
pmc-13620166:
Mingyue Zuo and four colleagues asked how bilingual speakers learn when to switch languages, treating the choice as a lesson in reward, in a 2026 study. Chinese-English bilinguals named pictures in whichever language they liked while feedback paid out with high, medium, or low probability. Surprises in that feedback, called reward prediction errors, were expected to tune the next choice.

Computer modeling showed those surprise signals steadily updated a general switching policy rather than a narrow habit. Brain pattern analysis placed the learned value of the policy in memory-related regions, while the surprise signal itself showed up in a frontal control area. Network models traced three stages: wide exploration early, a hub-centered pattern while the policy paid off, then a tight local circuit for automatic use plus a broad network watching for odd errors. The authors frame language control as value-based learning.
pmc-13621766:
Julhash U Kazi and Ramin Massoumi wrote a 2026 editorial arguing that awareness of inherited cancer must move past simply finding a gene variant. For years the focus sat on spotting family risk and offering counselling, screening, and prevention. The authors say the harder task now is explaining what a result means for each person and each family.

They point to multi-omics, the combined study of genes, RNA, proteins, and cell chemistry, as a bridge between inherited risk and action. One variant can lead to different cancers at different ages, and DNA alone cannot explain why. Reading several layers of biology together can show which pathways are active and where prevention or treatment might work. The editorial closes by tying awareness back to families, not just molecules.
pmc-13623066:
Yuanyuan Zhao leads the author list of a 2026 phase one trial report for a new drug against extensive-stage small cell lung cancer. The cancer is aggressive, with few options once first treatment fails. The drug, izalontamab brengitecan, joins an antibody that homes to two receptors on tumour cells with a cell-killing payload. Patients had already progressed on earlier therapy.

Fifty-two patients received the drug on two days of each three-week cycle. Nearly half saw their tumours shrink, and results looked strongest in the twenty-two patients treated right after first-line therapy, where most responded and survival ran longest. Low blood cell counts were the most common side effects, matching the drug class. A marker test hinted that tumours carrying more of one target receptor responded better. A phase three trial comparing the drug with a standard is under way, the authors note.
pmc-13623966:
Peter R Mertens, Eugen Feist, and Dimitrios Mougiakakos comment on a New England Journal of Medicine study that used CAR T-cell therapy to make kidney transplants possible for two patients. Both patients' immune systems rejected nearly every donor. Such patients carry levels of anti-HLA antibodies from past exposure, and standard antibody-lowering treatments rarely last, because the cells making the antibodies survive.

The trial gave each patient their own engineered T cells aimed at two targets covering the antibody-producing cell family, in a phase one safety run-in. Antibody levels fell enough for both to receive transplants, the first proof that this approach can desensitise. The commentators place the result against the maths of waiting lists, where some patients match one donor in fifty thousand. They note open questions on targets, durability, and safety, while calling the concept an era if later trial stages hold up.
pmc-13624266:
Tang and a large team trace in 2026 an unexpected chain linking blood platelets to allergic airway inflammation, the type 2 inflammation behind eosinophilic sinus disease and asthma. Platelets gather at inflamed sites, but their active role was unclear.

Profiling human nasal polyp tissue, the team found a group of macrophages, immune cells that engulf debris, rich in the enzyme TGM2 and tied to worse disease. In mice exposed to dust mite, removing that enzyme from macrophages weakened their alternative activation state and eased airway inflammation and tissue remodeling. The enzyme works by attaching serotonin to a histone protein, opening genes for that state. The serotonin comes from activated platelets nearby. Blocking serotonin release or the enzyme improved both nose and lung disease in the mice.
pmc-13625366:
Ryo Kurokawa and three colleagues, publishing in 2026, write to the editor about a survival curve in a recent glioma study. Cheng and co-authors had gathered the largest group yet of patients with a rare H3F3B-mutant midline brain tumor and charted how long they lived. Kurokawa's team rebuilt the chart from the patient-level times printed in the study's own table, using the standard Kaplan-Meier method.

Among the eleven patients with follow-up, four deaths were listed, at seven, nine, eighteen, and forty months, while seven patients were still living at their last checks. The rebuilt curve therefore steps down only four times and touches the halfway mark at eighteen months, far later than the published figure seems to fall. The letter asks the authors to clarify the gap, since survival medians guide how doctors judge this tumor.
pmc-13625666:
Juan David Lacouture and co-authors report a hard shoulder case: a 25-year-old kitesurfer whose dislocated shoulder had stayed out of place for eight months. A first operation to fix the fracture-dislocation had failed, leaving stiff, shrunken tissues, a visible deformity, and thirty percent of the socket bone gone. The team freed the joint in stages, releasing tight muscles and capsule step by step. They partly divided one tendon and cut the coracoid bone. Then they rebuilt the socket with a Latarjet procedure, which anchors a bone block in front.

Two years on, the shoulder moved far better, stayed stable, and hurt not at all, with near-top scores on two standard rating scales. The patient even returned to kitesurfing in part. Staged release plus bone rebuilding, the case argues, suits young active patients.
pmc-13626466:
Kianti Raisa Darusman and colleagues pilot a digital eye screening platform for Indonesian schoolchildren. Untreated refractive error is a leading, fixable cause of poor sight in children, yet school screening runs unevenly across the country. Their web platform, CERMATA, pairs a validated World Health Organization phone app with referral tracking. Seventy-two children aged nine to twelve in two Jakarta schools took both screens on the same day. One was the new tool, the other the standard letter chart.

Four in five children met the referral cutoff on the standard chart. The platform caught nearly ninety-seven percent of those children, with fair accuracy on the rest and strong agreement overall. Every child finished both tests, showing the workflow runs in real schools. A cheap, tracked screen like this could carry eye care to classrooms far from specialists.
pmc-13626966:
Christopher J Mehus and co-authors separate two kinds of corporal punishment in American survey data: planned spanking and hitting a child out of anger. More than a third of United States parents report using physical discipline, and the two acts may spring from different roots. Using the long-running Monitoring the Future panel, the team modeled what predicted each behavior in parents at thirty-five, then asked whether spanking at thirty-five foretold angry hitting at forty.

The two behaviors drew on largely different predictors. Spanking at thirty-five, though, more than doubled the odds of reporting angry hitting five years later. Depression signs and disordered drinking each raised the odds of angry hitting in their own right. The findings argue for treating the two acts as distinct problems, and for watching escalation over a childhood.
pmc-13627266:
Gaizhen Kuang and co-authors stack two cancer attacks into a microneedle patch that fires them in sequence. The patch needles carry hydrogel beads holding a light-absorbing dye, plus a sleeping form of the chemotherapy drug doxorubicin. A near-infrared beam heats the dye, delivering photothermal therapy and springing the drug loose. The dye then escapes its beads. It chemically wakes the drug through a precise click reaction that only the pair can perform.

In dish tests the cascade killed tumor cells efficiently, and in mice treated after melanoma surgery it held regrowth down hard. Splitting the therapy into a light trigger and a chemical trigger keeps the drug quiet until it reaches the tumor bed. The authors present the design as a template for layered, site-specific drug delivery.
pmc-13627966:
Deepti Tiwari and five colleagues studied how place shapes the chemistry of Rubia cordifolia, a healing plant of the western Himalaya. They picked plants from open grassy, shady, and moist shady sites at different heights. Then they measured soil, plant nutrients, plant chemicals, and cell-protecting strength.

Plants from high sites carried the most phenolics and flavonoids, plus two prized compounds, alizarin and mollugin. Moist shady sites gave richer nutrition and stronger protective activity. Sour soil worked against several useful plant chemicals. The team says high plants from moist shady ground are prized stock for saving, farming, and making medicine.
pmc-13629566:
Hassan Ahmed Assiri and twelve colleagues measured the incisive canal and its opening in jaw scans. The canal carries nerve and blood vessels between the nose and the front of the upper jaw. They used one hundred cone-beam CT scans from Abha City, Saudi Arabia. Knowing this anatomy well matters for dental implants. It also matters for numbing shots near the front teeth.

The funnel was the most common canal shape. The opening was most often oval. Men's canals ran much longer than women's. Their openings also measured wider across. Most patients had a single canal with one or two openings. It angled mildly to moderately against the nasal floor. The authors present the measures as a reference. Clinicians planning surgery or numbing care in this group can use them.
pmc-13631266:
Jordan Peters and three colleagues assembled a global dataset of river nutrient pollution and streamflow, published in 2026, meant to give water researchers one place to look. Excess nitrogen and phosphorus drive algal blooms and dead zones, but the underlying measurements sit scattered across national databases with thin coverage across much of the world.

Merging seventeen sources produced records from roughly twenty thousand sites for nitrogen, forty thousand for phosphorus, and thirty-two thousand for flow. A model then estimated daily concentrations at several thousand data-rich sites, and a machine learning step extrapolated loads and concentrations into regions with little monitoring. The authors intend the dataset to support hotspot detection, local river management, and calculations of nutrient flow to the sea.
pmc-13633666:
Saikat Banerjee and five colleagues introduce a software tool that separates shared genetics from trait-specific genetics. Related diseases often share symptoms and drug responses, hinting at common biology. Genetic studies now hold association data for thousands of traits, but noise and corruption in those tables hide the pattern. Their open-source library, Clorinn, treats the data table as a blend of a simple shared structure, a sparse trait-specific layer, and outright errors.

The method uses convex optimization, a class of math that guarantees the same answer on every run. In simulations, it recovered the true disease groupings while matching rivals on reconstruction accuracy. Applied to genome study results for over two thousand traits from a British biobank, it pulled out two hundred hidden factors. It also summarized fourteen psychiatric disorders with ten factors. The authors offer the tool as a cleaner lens on genetic overlap.
pmc-13634766:
Yousefi Jordehi and colleagues publish in 2026 a hand-annotated dataset for teaching computers to extract metadata from scientific articles written in Persian, Arabic, or English. Tools for this job are far weaker for Persian and Arabic than for English.

The dataset contains 635 articles in structured files, one per paper, drawn from more than 580 journals and conferences. Persian papers form the majority, with English and Arabic splitting the rest almost evenly. Ten annotators spent over a year labeling seven header fields, from title and authors to the digital identifier. They also labeled full reference sections in 621 of the articles, totaling 17,832 individual reference strings annotated across twelve fields. Every file was checked against its source document, and each file stands alone, storing the labeled text spans so the original papers are not needed.
pmc-13639366:
Luke J Nguyen and five colleagues published a 2026 Ontario cohort study on virtual care for inflammatory bowel disease and its effect on travel emissions. When the pandemic began, nearly all specialist visits for these patients moved online almost overnight.

The study followed 98,099 people with bowel disease from 2020 to 2025. Virtual visits fell back after 2021 and settled near one third of encounters. In the first pandemic year, avoided travel saved an estimated 1,268 tonnes of carbon dioxide. The authors suggest hybrid care could keep much of that benefit while restoring in-person access where it matters.
pmc-13645966:
Giovanna Macanhã Scremin and nine colleagues pool randomized trials on a back nerve block used to ease pain after weight-loss surgery. The erector spinae plane block places numbing medicine near the spine muscles. Their search of three databases in January 2025 gathered nine trials with 553 patients in total. Outcomes covered opioid use, pain scores, nausea, and breathing problems.

Patients who got the block used clearly fewer opioids after surgery and reported lower pain scores, above all in the first twelve hours. Nausea and vomiting after surgery also fell, with consistent results across trials. Breathing complications did not differ between groups. Study results varied a good deal for pain and opioid measures, which tempers the message. Even so, the authors judge the block a useful part of combined pain care that can spare opioids after this surgery.
pmc-13646066:
Lei Jiang and eight colleagues survey dry eye disease across Gansu Province, China, hunting for regional and personal risk factors. Their cross-sectional study ran from August 2024 to August 2025 and drew 2,000 adult residents from five areas of the province. Participants answered questionnaires and took three eye tests covering tear stability, surface staining, and tear volume. Three statistical approaches, including a machine learning model, weighed the factors.

Climate type stood out as the strongest predictor, ahead of daily screen time and sleep quality. Elevation, sex, and smoking also linked with the disease. The mixed model that respected the clustered sampling gave broadly similar answers. The authors argue prevention should focus first on high-risk regions and on the habits people can change, such as screen habits and sleep. Their province-wide picture can guide where eye services and education are placed.
pmc-13647266:
Moyan Wang and nine colleagues review why dizziness sometimes stops being a short episode and becomes a chronic condition. After an inner-ear injury, the brain normally restores balance by reweighting senses and rewiring connections. That repair, though, leans harder on vision, which can leave the system oversensitive. The review pairs this neural sensitization with a psychological twin: fear-driven avoidance and catastrophic thinking that amplify every wobble.

Patients with chronic dizziness show lowered thresholds for visual and body-position signals, the signature of raised sensory gain. Worry and avoidance then feed the neural problem by distorting how the brain handles body signals and by stirring emotion centers. Each process keeps the other alive, the authors argue. They propose combined treatment aimed at sensory reweighting, fear-avoidance habits, and psychiatric comorbidity together, to break the loop before it hardens.
pmc-13648266:
Yuxin He and fifteen colleagues coated fat bubbles that carry messenger RNA with a sugar coat called heparosan. Most such bubbles wear a coat of a plastic called PEG. The coat shapes how bubbles move inside cells, and much of their load is lost in cell traps called endosomes.

The new coat raised RNA output up to tenfold in two immune cell types. Films of live cells showed less of the load stuck in late traps and in waste sacs, a sign of better escape. In mice, repeat skin doses kept output strong. A vaccine form, aimed at a virus spike, drew a stronger antibody reply than the PEG form. No tissue harm was seen. The team backs the sugar coat as a PEG-free path.
pmc-13648366:
Anna X. Luo and ten colleagues model in mice a rare variant of the gene AKAP11 that cuts its protein short and has been linked to bipolar disorder and schizophrenia. AKAP11 anchors an enzyme called PKA near its targets, and the team used gene editing to copy the exact human variant into mice.

Mutant mice made less of the protein and showed anxiety- and depression-related behaviour, at least among males. Brain profiling revealed changes in synapse organisation and signalling, with one class of PKA regulatory subunits raised and overall PKA responses to stimulation weakened. Young cortical neurons also grew new branches poorly. The authors present the mouse as a precise platform for testing future treatments.
pmc-13649466:
Mohammed Almansori and colleagues compared blood patterns of circular RNAs in two types of heart attack at two hospitals in eastern Saudi Arabia. Circular RNAs are stable ring-shaped molecules that float in blood plasma. The study held 59 patients with the more severe type, 78 with the milder type, and 109 controls from the same hospitals.

Nearly 300 of these rings differed in level between the two attack types. A model built on just three rings told the two types apart with fair accuracy in cross-checks. The ring changes often did not match changes in their parent genes, which hints at their own control system. The authors pitch the rings as fresh clues for sharper heart attack tests.
pmc-13649966:
Ruiqing Dong and seven colleagues tested a teacher-led workflow in which a chat tool drafts personal fitness plans for university students. Tailored plans are hard to give in big routine classes. Their work ran in two phases: experts first shaped a strict input frame, then two whole classes spent six weeks on either chat-drafted or standard plans, with thirty students each.

Near all students finished the trial, and class time, effort, and turnout matched between groups. The chat group spent a bit more time in the target heart zone and felt the plans were far more personal. No severe harms occurred, and most body measures did not split. The authors judge the workflow workable and safe.
pmc-13650466:
Juan Liu and six colleagues examine how the tail-adding step that finishes most messenger RNAs responds when a cell turns transcription up or down. The signals that trigger tail addition come in strong canonical forms and weaker variants, and the team asked whether all of them behave the same as gene activity changes.

Using engineered reporters with adjustable promoters, the researchers found that weaker transcription came with less efficient tail processing overall. Strong and middling signals kept working steadily at high transcription, while non-standard signals faltered as transcription rose, revealing a tiered system. The team then watched placental cells fuse under a chemical trigger, a step in building the placenta's outer layer. Fusion genes carrying strong signals were preferentially switched on, enriching the mature cell's messages. The work ties a basic RNA-processing rule to orderly placental development.
pmc-13650666:
Kensie Treacy and three colleagues review whether inherited collagen disorders raise the risk of spontaneous preterm birth, when labor begins early without a planned reason. Conditions such as Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and Marfan syndrome weaken connective tissue, which could plausibly loosen the structures that hold a pregnancy to term.

Fourteen observational studies met the review's rules after searches running to April 2025. For Marfan syndrome, four comparable studies could be pooled, and women with the condition had close to triple the odds of early spontaneous birth compared with controls. Ehlers-Danlos studies varied too much in design and subtype to pool fairly, though their narrative pattern consistently showed more early births and obstetric complications. One study covered the vascular subtype alone, and two mixed several disorders. The authors advise disorder-specific pregnancy assessment and prospective studies with standard subtype labels.
pmc-13651466:
Jing Yuan and three colleagues introduce a second collected volume on value-based medicine in China and the Asia-Pacific region, where systems are being asked to prove outcomes rather than count activity. Aging populations, chronic disease, pricey technology, and coverage promises converge faster than almost anywhere else.

The editorial threads the volume's studies through payment reform. Paying for curative effect in traditional Chinese medicine cut costs and stays for some diseases while reviving traditional services. A bundled payment scheme for diabetes lowered hospital costs yet shifted out-of-pocket burden onto certain insured groups and hospital types. High-margin cases under bundled payment tended to be low-value stays, suggesting waste can move rather than vanish. Single-disease payment for hysterectomy cut costs and complications together. The editors argue value emerges from many instruments at once, and that reforms watched only in aggregate can hide new inequities.
pmc-13671866:
Ji Heon Lee led a 2026 randomized cross-over study comparing preservative-free latanoprost with preserved latanoprost in primary open-angle glaucoma. Eye drops for glaucoma usually carry preservatives to prevent contamination, yet the preservative can damage the eye surface, driving discomfort and dropout that worsen pressure control. The team enrolled twenty-nine patients, giving each drop for two months before switching to the other, and tracking pressure, tear film, staining, and symptoms.

Both drops lowered pressure by similar amounts. Preserved drops, however, shortened tear break-up time and worsened eye-surface staining, while preservative-free drops held tear stability steady and improved staining. Burning, stinging, and itching were markedly lower without it, and patients switching from preserved to plain drops improved in burning and light sensitivity.
pmc-2815666:
Kabsch explains the working principles behind key steps in processing X-ray rotation data, as carried out by his program XDS. Rotation data come from turning a crystal in an X-ray beam and recording diffraction images as it moves. Each image must be merged into one consistent dataset.

The paper walks through integration, scaling, space-group assignment, and post-refinement: turning spots on images into measured intensities, correcting differences between images, and fixing the crystal's symmetry. Clear accounts of these steps help crystallographers judge data quality before building atomic models.  Post-refinement then polishes the merged data before structure solution begins in earnest.
pmc-3552766:
Tong, Flemming, McInnes, and co-authors develop ENTREQ, guidance for reporting syntheses of qualitative research. Combining findings across qualitative studies can reveal patterns across contexts, build new models, and expose research gaps. Such syntheses also inform the development and evaluation of health interventions.

Without transparent reporting, readers cannot judge how a synthesis was done. ENTREQ lists what authors should disclose about searching, appraising, and combining studies. The statement raised standards in a growing field, helping decision makers use patients' experiences with the same rigour as trial data.  Review teams in nursing and psychology adapted the checklist for their fields.
pmc-4174766:
Kawasaki and Kawai reviewed Toll-like receptor signaling in 2014. Toll-like receptors, or TLRs, are key sensors of the innate immune system, the body's first line of defense. They detect patterns that are typical of microbes and not found in human cells.

Once a receptor spots such a pattern, it recruits adaptor molecules inside the cell. That chain switches on transcription factors, including one known as NF-kappaB, which turn on defense genes. The review maps these pathways step by step for each receptor type. Knowing the routes helps explain infections and inflammation, and guides drugs that tune the immune response.
pmc-4283466:
Sheldrick presented SHELXT in 2015, a computer program for solving crystal structures. Crystallographers measure reflections from a single crystal and must solve the phase problem to recover the structure. SHELXT uses a new dual-space algorithm to do this, working from data expanded into a simple space group.

The program takes missing data into account and extends resolution when needed. It also works out the true space group as part of the same run. That integration saves steps that once took separate programs and expert judgment. SHELXT became a first tool many labs run when a new crystal yields fresh diffraction data.
pmc-7190266:
Mhairi Campbell, Joanne McKenzie, Amanda Sowden, and coauthors wrote the SWiM reporting guideline in 2020. Some systematic reviews cannot pool results in a meta-analysis. Authors then synthesize findings in words or tables, often with little method detail.

SWiM, short for synthesis without meta-analysis, sets nine items such reviews should report. They cover how studies were grouped, how effects were compared, and how certainty was judged. Clearer reporting lets readers check whether the summary is fair. Journals began asking authors to follow the guideline soon after it appeared. A checklist version of the guideline is provided for authors and journal editors.
pmc-8476166:
Mosè Manni and co-authors updated BUSCO in 2021, a widely used method for scoring how complete a genome assembly is. BUSCO judges data by looking for genes expected to appear exactly once in nearly every species of a group. Finding most of them suggests a complete assembly, while duplicates hint at errors or contamination.

The update adds streamlined workflows and extends coverage across eukaryotes, prokaryotes, and viruses, so more kinds of data can be scored the same way. The authors describe the new gene sets and how the scoring runs. Because nearly every genome project reports a BUSCO score, changes to this tool ripple through the whole field's quality standards.
stowe-chimney-corner-1866:
Fireside talk shapes The Chimney-Corner, Stowe's book of essays and sketches from 1866. She gathers readers near the hearth to mull over children, neighbors, and housekeeping. Grief and faith enter the talk as well, in a plain and friendly voice.

Many pieces were written during and just after the Civil War. They carry a mother's seasoned wisdom and a tired nation's mood. Small moral dramas of daily life matter more here than grand events. For readers who loved the warmth of her novels, the book feels like Stowe thinking aloud, close and unhurried, with no need to preach.
swinburne-poems-ballads-1866:
Algernon Charles Swinburne published Poems and Ballads in 1866, a year after Atalanta in Calydon made his name. The new book scandalized Victorian England. Reviewers attacked its passion and paganism so fiercely that the first publisher withdrew it, and another quickly took it up.

Dolores, a hymn to a cruel goddess of pain, leads the notorious pieces. The Garden of Proserpine imagines death as peaceful sleep beyond love and weariness. Other poems praise Sappho, freedom, and the sea in rushing, musical lines. Swinburne's technique dazzled even his enemies. The volume, complete in its first series here, made him the wild star of late Victorian poetry.
the-book-of-quinte-essence-or-the-fifth-: Frederick J. Furnivall edited The Book of Quinte Essence for the Early English Text Society, put out in London by N. Trübner and Company in 1866. The work is a short tract in English drawn out of a Latin book of quintessence. The tract is said to come from Hermes, called a prophet and king of Egypt after the flood of Noah, by word sent from an angel of God. Furnivall took the text from the Sloane Manuscript 73, dated 1460 to 1470. Type in spots is hard to read.
the-cloister-and-the-hearth-pg1366: Charles Reade's 1861 historical novel about the parents of Erasmus: a young Dutchman torn between love and the church in the 15th century. Richly researched and passionately told, it brings medieval Europe to life. A great Victorian historical novel, too little read today.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing:
Depart Switzerland, the opening part of Adventures in the South in Jacques Casanova's memoirs, follows the 1894 London edition in Arthur Machen's translation, with chapters discovered by Arthur Symons. Chapter One finds Casanova amused by the plight of the Marquis de Prie, whose company had coveted his cash-box. He changes horses at Chamberi and settles at Grenoble for a week. A letter from Madame d'Urfe introduces him to an officer named Valenglard.

Valenglard offers rooms in a beautiful house outside the town walls. Its door-keeper, an excellent cook, will lodge Casanova for nothing and make his profit through his dishes. Casanova takes three rooms and orders a supper for two, warning that he is dainty and heedless of cost. The chapter's heading promises the door-keeper's daughters, horoscopes, and a Mademoiselle Roman. Readers watch Casanova rebuild comfort and intrigue within days of crossing a border.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
Saturday, April 9, 1831, brings the Mirror's No. 484, which illustrates Corfe Castle in the Isle of Purbeck. The castle existed before the year 980, though the town gained no importance until after the Conquest and goes unnoticed in Domesday Book. Manor and castle descended together through centuries of grants and forfeitures.

Princes of the blood and royal favourites held Corfe, and the Crown as often recovered it by attainder. Richard II's reign saw Thomas Holland, Earl of Kent, hold it with his wife Alicia. Henry IV granted it to the Beauforts, earls of Somerset, and Edward IV took it back for Richard, Duke of York, then George, Duke of Clarence. On Clarence's attainder it reverted to the Crown again. Henry VII granted it to his mother for life. Readers watch a castle passed like a countersign among England's ruling houses.

John Locke's birthplace leads No. 487 of The Mirror, dated April 30, 1831, in volume 17. An engraving shows the cottage at Wrington in Somersetshire, beside the churchyard, where the philosopher was born. The house had since been split into tenements, with one room used as a school for young children.

Locke was born on August 29, 1632, the account explains. His father, who served as a captain for Parliament in the civil wars, lost much of his estate in those troubled years. Drawing on Lord King's recent Life of Locke, the piece describes a father who moved from strictness to close friendship with his son. Locke's own writings on education and the human understanding give the modest cottage its lasting interest.

Volume 19, No. 533, dated February 11, 1832, shows the cascade at Virginia Water in its opening engraving. The fall is praised as a striking imitation of nature's great works, with less visible artifice than smaller pieces of its kind. Virginia Water itself was the kingdom's largest artificial body of water, Blenheim excepted.

Near the high Southampton road, the water drops into a glen shaded by birch, willow, and acacia. Beside the fall stands a moss-covered stone cave built from huge fragments dug up at Bagshot Heath. Those stones were thought to be remains of a Saxon cromlech, an ancient stone monument. From the cascade's base, the stream winds through Surrey to the Thames at Chertsey.
the-path-of-the-king-pg1966:
John Buchan dedicated The Path of the King to his wife, who first read the chapters by a Cotswold fire. This record carries the same dedication and contents as a second record of the book. Here, though, the prologue itself also appears. Three men in a winter camp in the Selkirks talk the slow, aimless talk of wearied men.

The Soldier rides his hobby, the American Civil War. He discourses on Lee's tactics in the Wilderness. The narrator answers with the romance of it: Jeb Stuart flitting like a wraith, and Sheridan's attack at Chattanooga under a harvest moon. He names Leonidas Polk, last of the warrior bishops, baptizing fellow generals by candlelight. Talk of kingship grows from campfire history.
the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-complete-: John Lothrop Motley published his history in 1855. An editor's note sketches his life for readers. Motley was born in Dorchester, Massachusetts, in 1814. He died in 1877 after wide public service. He served as minister to Austria for six years. He later served as minister to England. Mark Twain respected him, the note reports. Holmes praised his sympathy with popular liberty in 1863. That note opens the complete record for 1555 to 1566. Only the heading is present on these pages. The opening of the note appears with it. Motley's narrative itself does not appear.
the-seven-great-monarchies-of-the-ancien:
George Rawlinson's Seven Great Monarchies turns to Parthia in this record, labeled volume three. The section is titled A History of Parthia. Maps of Parthia Proper and of Parthia precede the text. Chapter one treats the geography of Parthia Proper. Its character, climate, and surrounding countries are also promised.

East of the Caspian Sea, Rawlinson writes, a broad desert tract stretches toward the Indian Ocean. It runs above 1,500 miles from the Mougbojar hills. About midway, a strip of territory interrupts that desert. The strip possesses features of much beauty and attraction, he says. Narrow beside the deserts flanking it, the region is still considerable by itself. Rawlinson's history of the ancient eastern monarchies uses such geography as its foundation.
the-weavers-a-tale-of-england-and-egypt-:
Book six of Gilbert Parker's Weavers closes the set of volume records, with chapters forty to forty-two: Hylda Seeks Nahoum, In the Land of Shinar, and The Loom of Destiny. Chapter forty returns Hylda to Cairo, and the city strikes her as unchanged after six years, brilliant and garish with crowded life.

Craftsmen pack the dark bazaars, merchants haggle, hawkers cry their wares, and a camel train forces calmly through the crowds. Sherbet-sellers clank their brass saucers as they did when she last watched. Yet everything has changed for her. Passing the house where she, David, Nahoum, and Mizraim once met, she nearly weeps at the gatekeeper still sitting there. Her mind stays fixed on the one errand that brought her back.
thoreau-yankee-in-canada-1866:
Henry David Thoreau's A Yankee in Canada saw print in 1866, after his death, a posthumous collection. The volume joins the Canada travel tale with his Anti-Slavery and Reform Papers in one last book. Slavery in Massachusetts, Life Without Principle, and Wendell Phillips stand among its fierce reform pieces in print.

Thoreau toured Quebec in 1850 and found old French Canada quaint, priest-ridden, and unfree in its own way. The travelogue mixes soldier lore, cathedral visits, and St. Lawrence scenery with his Yankee skeptic's dry wit throughout. Slavery in Massachusetts, his angriest speech, damns his state for returning fugitives under federal law in 1854. Life Without Principle scorns the money chase and calls work a form of prayer when freely chosen. The set shows Thoreau the reformer beside Thoreau the walker, one pen, two fires.
tob-0166:
Bahá'u'lláh, founder of the Bahá'í Faith, wrote The Seven Valleys in Baghdad around 1860, in answer to a Sufi correspondent's questions. In luminous Persian prose, it maps the soul's journey to God through seven valleys: search, love, knowledge, unity, contentment, wonderment, and finally true poverty and absolute nothingness. A companion piece, The Four Valleys, accompanies it.

Each valley has its perils and its signposts, described through parable, poetry, and quotation from earlier mystics. The Seven Valleys is the Bahá'í faith's most beloved spiritual text, read devotionally far beyond its original Sufi setting. English readers meet Persian mysticism at its most concentrated, in a short book meant for a lifetime.
tob-10066:
Christian D. Ginsburg, a Christian scholar of Hebrew, wrote an early English study of the Kabbalah, the Jewish mystical tradition connected with the Zohar. His subject had few reliable guides in English when he wrote. He set out to explain its doctrines, trace its development, and survey its literature.

Readers learn what Kabbalah teaches about God and creation, how its ideas grew through the Middle Ages, and which books and teachers matter most. V1 evidence notes the study served for decades as the main English guide to a difficult subject. It remains useful as both an introduction and a record of nineteenth-century scholarship.
tob-10266:
Eliphas Levi, whose real name was Alphonse Louis Constant, published Dogme et Rituel de la Haute Magie in French in 1854. He wrote the work in two parts, doctrine first and ritual second. Most later occult writers drew on it, knowingly or not.

Levi ties magic to the tarot, the Kabbalah, and a force he calls the astral light, which trained will can direct. He gives rules, symbols, and rites for high magic while warning against fraud and black magic. Read in the original French, the book shows the style that made Levi the father of modern occultism.
tob-10466:
Volume two of Calvin's Institutes carries his system forward from Christ the Redeemer through the work of the Holy Spirit to the church and its sacraments. Where the first volume founded the doctrine of God and Scripture, this one asks how salvation reaches actual people. Prayer, providence, and the Christian life receive extended treatment.

Calvin explains the church's ministry, baptism, and the Lord's Supper, and closes with civil government and the hope of resurrection. His famous teachings stand in argued form, not slogans. Together the two volumes form Protestantism's most influential theological work, still read by students tracing how Reformed belief was built.
tob-12966:
James Legge, the Scottish missionary and scholar, spent decades translating China's classic books. His Chinese Classics series gives the Chinese text, an English translation, long notes, and full introductions for each work. The volume described by its evidence covers the Great Learning and the Doctrine of the Mean, two short Confucian treatises.

The Great Learning traces a path from ordering one's own thoughts to governing a state in peace. The Doctrine of the Mean praises balance, sincerity, and holding to the middle way. Legge's notes explain hard passages line by line. His series set the standard for all later English work on Confucian texts.
tob-4066:
Max Muller devoted much of his life to the Rig-Veda, the oldest religious text of India. His Rig-Veda-Sanhita presents the collection of 1,028 Sanskrit hymns with the learning of the age's leading orientalist. Verified from the 1919 public-domain edition, the work anchored Western study of the Veda.

Fire god Agni, storm god Indra, and Ushas the dawn receive hymn after hymn of praise, prayer, and myth. Sacrifices, battles, weddings, and riddles all enter the songs. Muller's edition, with its vast labor of editing and translation, made the hymns a subject scholars everywhere could share. The book remains a monument of Victorian Oriental scholarship.
tob-4166:
Andrew Lang, the Scottish folklorist and man of letters, published Myth, Ritual, and Religion in 1887 as his manifesto in the science of religion. Lang opposed Max Muller's school, which read all myth as a disease of language about the sun. He argued from custom instead.

Lang holds that the savage rites and beliefs of living peoples explain the strange, irrational parts of Greek and other myths: the myths are fossils of ritual ages. He ranges over totemism, sacrifice, and the making of gods. The book is the anthropological school's classic statement, complete, and a model of learned argument written with a storyteller's ease.
ufo-hearings-house-1966:
Congress called the Air Force to account on UFOs in the spring of 1966. The House Committee on Armed Services held its hearing on April 5, with the public and press at full attention. A wave of sightings over Michigan that March had forced the issue.

The astronomer Allen Hynek, the Air Force's own adviser, told the panel the subject deserved true science at last. Generals laid out the Blue Book files and held that most cases had plain causes. The hearing pushed the Air Force to seek an outside study. From that push came the Condon study and the end of Blue Book.
un-ga-res-a-69-66:
Half the world has already banned nuclear arms from its soil, and Resolution A/69/66, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session, marks that fact. Any group of states may make a pact to keep such arms out of its lands in full. That right stands in the 1968 pact against the spread of nuclear arms. Five zone pacts are named with praise, from Latin America to Africa and the Pacific.

With the Antarctic Treaty, those pacts have freed the whole southern half of the world, and the seas beside it, from nuclear arms. Mongolia's own lone-state free status is recalled as well. Till such arms end for good, the text holds, zones of this kind are a firm step toward that end.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: The General Assembly adopted Resolution 69/66 at its sixty-ninth session in 2014. It decides to convene the Third Conference of States Parties and Signatories to Treaties that Establish Nuclear-Weapon-Free Zones and Mongolia. The one-day conference is set for New York in 2015. Its purpose is to examine ways of strengthening cooperation among the zones and with Mongolia. The treaties' parties recognize Mongolia's single-state nuclear-weapon-free status alongside their own arrangements.
un-sc-res-1366:
Action on preventing armed conflict came with Resolution 1366, adopted on 30 August 2001. The Secretary-General had sent the Council a full report on prevention. Its lessons drew on failed efforts before the Rwanda genocide and the Srebrenica massacre. Small arms flows kept making wars worse and longer.

The Council vows to treat prevention as a core part of its work. It will watch danger spots closely and act early, with missions to tense regions where states agree. The Secretary-General should flag threats, rights abuses, and disputes that could turn violent. Peacekeeping mandates may add disarmament work and police for the peace that follows. Regional bodies, above all in Africa, need more capacity and funds.
un-sc-res-1466:
UNMEE was extended as demarcation approached on 14 March 2003. Prisoners of war had been freed and sent home by both sides. Crossings of the Temporary Security Zone's southern edge caused concern. The Boundary Commission's ruling of 13 April 2002 awaited marking on the ground. The peace process was about to enter its decisive phase, the Council noted.

The Council extended UNMEE to 15 September 2003, at the troop and observer levels set by resolution 1320 (2000). Both parties were urged to meet their Algiers duties and to work with the Red Cross on the questions left open. They had to work fully and swiftly with UNMEE and give it complete freedom of movement. Every limit on the mission had to go at once. The Council backed UNMEE's power to check the parties' conduct inside the zone. Mine action work by the mission was also praised.
un-sc-res-1566:
Terrorism's definition and reach were pressed forward on 8 October 2004. Beslan and other attacks had swollen the count of victims, children among them. The Council restated resolutions 1267 (1999), 1373 (2001), and 1540 (2004). It reminded states that every counter-terrorism step had to honor human rights, refugee, and humanitarian law. Its three counter-terrorism bodies were told to work more closely together.

The Council condemned all acts of terrorism in the strongest terms, whatever their motive, wherever and by whomsoever committed. It recalled that crimes meant to kill or maim civilians, or to take hostages in order to terrorize a public, can never be justified. States were called to join every anti-terrorism convention as a matter of urgency. They had to speed agreement on the draft comprehensive convention on terrorism. A working group was set up to weigh practical measures against groups and persons outside the Al-Qaida sanctions list.
un-sc-res-166:
Security Council Resolution 166, adopted on October 25, 1961, recommended Mongolia for membership in the United Nations. Mongolia had sought a seat since 1946, but Cold War bargaining kept its bid blocked for fifteen years. A package deal that year, which also cleared Mauritania, at last let the landlocked Asian state through the council.
